short_description: Exploration of penetrating wound (separate procedure); neck
lay_term: The provider explores a penetrating wound in the neck, such as from a sharp object or gunshot, to assess and repair internal damage and remove any foreign material retained in the wound. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider assesses the extent of damage to internal organs or tissues from the penetrating wound. He cleanses the wound and debrides, or removes, damaged tissues. He looks for and removes any foreign material, such as fragments of glass, metal, or cloth. He ties off or repairs small blood vessels. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the wound. Terminology Penetrating wound: A wound accompanied by disruption of the body surface that extends into the underlying tissue or into a body cavity. Tips Code 20100 is limited to the exploration of a penetrating wound in the neck. Repair of major vessels of anatomical sites, such as the neck, abdomen, chest, extremities, etc., are reported separately. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline 20100-20103 relate to wound(s) resulting from penetrating trauma. These codes describe surgical exploration and enlargement of the wound, extension of dissection (to determine penetration), debridement, removal of foreign body(s), ligation or coagulation of minor subcutaneous and/or muscular blood vessel(s), of the subcutaneous tissue, muscle fascia, and/or muscle, not requiring thoracotomy or laparotomy. If a repair is done to major structure(s) or major blood vessel(s) requiring thoracotomy or laparotomy, then those specific code(s) would supersede the use of codes 20100-20103. To report simple, intermediate, or complex repair of wound(s) that do not require enlargement of the wound, extension of dissection, etc, as stated above, use specific Repair code(s) in the Integumentary System section. Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Exploration of penetrating wound (separate procedure); abdomen/flank/back
lay_term: The provider carefully examines the inside of a penetrating wound of the abdomen, flank, or back to assess the extent of damage to underlying tissues and structures as well as to identify and remove any foreign bodies that may have entered the wound, such as bullet fragments or a knife tip. In the case of a gunshot wound, a bullet may enter the body at one point and exit at another, causing perforation and damage to internal organs and tissues along its path. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider assesses the extent of damage to internal organs or tissues of the abdomen, flank, or back by exploring the penetrating wound. Treatment may follow to include cleansing, debridement, removal and repair of damaged tissue, removal of foreign bodies, if any, ligation and repair of small blood vessels in subcutaneous tissues and fascia, and finally, closure of the wound. Terminology Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body, such as shards of metal or a bone fragment. Laparotomy: Surgical incision of the abdomen. Penetrating wound: Wound accompanied by disruption of the body surface that extends into the underlying tissue or into a body cavity. Thoracotomy: Surgical incision of the chest. Tips Exploration of a penetrating wound can range from a simple laceration repair to a major exploratory surgery, such as a laparotomy or thoracotomy. The provider should document the exploration, as indicated by his assessment of the damage, including damage to vessels and nonmajor structures. Removing a foreign body from a penetrating wound falls under this code, as would cleaning up interior wound edges and inspecting for foreign body fragments in a wound that has both an entry and exit point, also called a through and through wound. Do not code debridement, removal of small foreign bodies caused by the penetrating object, separately, as those services are included in this code. Read Less

short_description: Excision of epiphyseal bar, with or without autogenous soft tissue graft obtained through same fascial incision
lay_term: The epiphyseal bar, or physis bar, refers to a deformity of the long bones that a fracture, injury, or infection cause. It leads to fusion of the epiphysis to metaphysis and results in premature arrest, or stoppage, of bone growth. By excising the epiphyseal bar and replacing it with autogenous fat tissue, the provider can restore the process of bone growth. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized and placed in the supine position, the provider places a tourniquet on the patient's leg, and the provider makes a drill hole through the metaphysis into the epiphyseal bar. He removes a wedge–shaped piece of metaphysis and uses a high–speed bur drill to resect the epiphyseal bar completely. He uses an image intensifier to identify the exact location and depth of the bar. After resecting the epiphyseal bar, he uses a curette to remove the cancellous bone from physis until he reaches normal cartilage. He fills the defect with a fat graft harvested from the nearby tissues. He returns the wedge–shaped metaphyseal piece and screws it into position. He then closes the wound with sutures and applies a cast to immobilize the extremity for faster healing. Terminology Aspiration: Withdrawal of material, often with a needle; can also refer to breathing in fluid or food material. Autogenous tissue graft: Tissue harvested from the patient’s own body used to replace diseased, damaged, or missing tissue. Burr drill: Surgical drill; also called a high–speed burr. Cancellous bone: Spongy material occurring at the end of long bones that can be used for grafting material. Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping; also spelled curet. Diaphysis: Middle portion of a long bone. Epiphyseal bar: Abnormal bony growth on the epiphyseal plate, interfering with normal development of a long bone. Epiphyseal plate: Cartilaginous layer at the end of a long bone responsible for bone growth; also called the growth plate or physis. Epiphysis: End portion of a long bone. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Fusion: Permanent joining. Image intensifier: Component that converts X–ray images to visible images the provider views on a screen, often used in orthopedic surgery. Metaphysis: Part of a long bone between epiphysis and diaphysis; part of the growth plate. Physis: Another term for epiphyseal plate. Supine: Lying in the face up position. Additional Info This procedure is successful in restoring the growth only when the growth plate has not yet completely stopped producing healthy osseous cells, the epiphyseal bar is covering less than 50% of the growth plate, and there are at least 2 years of skeletal growth still expected. Radiological imaging is standard for diagnosis as well as surgical repair. Read Less

short_description: Removal of foreign body in muscle or tendon sheath; simple
lay_term: The provider removes a foreign body, such as a thorn, wood particle, bullet, or gravel, lodged in the muscle or tendon sheath through a surgical incision at the site to relieve swelling, pain, and difficulty in movement of the body part. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the targeted area and separates the tissues. When she reaches the muscle or tendon sheath, she inspects the area and removes the foreign body. She closes the surgical opening with sutures after thoroughly cleaning the site. The provider may rely on X–ray images taken prior to the procedure to locate the foreign body in the soft tissue and a postprocedure image to ensure the complete removal of all foreign bodies. For deeper or more complex removal, see 20525, Removal of foreign body in muscle or tendon sheath; deep or complicated. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline (For injection procedure for arthrography, see anatomical area) (For injection of autologous adipose-derived regenerative cells, use 0490T) Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. short_description: Arthrocentesis, aspiration and/or injection, small joint or bursa (eg, fingers, toes); without ultrasound guidance

short_description: Application of cranial tongs, caliper, or stereotactic frame, including removal (separate procedure)
lay_term: Cranial tongs, calipers, or stereotactic frames are devices that apply traction force to the cervical spine for treatment of cervical spine fractures, dislocations, or spinal cord injuries. These devices also help in maintaining proper alignment of the spine during diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, such as spinal surgery or a magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI procedure. This service includes applying the traction force and removing it. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, in the supine position with the head resting at the extreme end of the surgical table, the provider inserts threaded pins on both sides of the head simultaneously. He adds weights at regular intervals, gradually increasing the traction force, for example, adding 5– to 10– pound increments at 10– to 20– minute intervals. short_description: Application of halo, including removal; cranial
lay_term: A cranial halo is a ring shaped device on the head that applies a traction force to the skull to stabilize the cervical spine in patients with cervical injuries or fractures. A plastic vest the patient wears attaches to the cranial halo and provides further immobilization. This service also includes removal of the halo. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, in a supine position with the head placed at the extreme end of the bed, the provider selects a halo ring of the correct circumference and positions it around the skull. He aligns the ring around the upper frontal area of the skull and positions four halo pins diagonally to each other, with two of the pins usually just above the eyebrows in the front. He uses a torque screwdriver to tighten diagonally opposite pins until they reach the desired depth in the skull bone. He then tightens the remaining pins to affix the halo device. Once he attains satisfactory fixation of the halo device, he confirms the alignment of the cervical spine with radiological imaging. Terminology Bilateral: On both sides; opposite of unilateral. short_description: Application of halo, including removal; femoral
lay_term: Halo femoral traction is an effective procedure for treating spinal deformities, particularly scoliosis, an abnormal curvature of the spine. The provider affixes halo rings to the femoral bones through threaded pins inserted near the bone ends. This service also includes removal of the halo. short_description: Removal of tongs or halo applied by another individual
lay_term: The provider removes tongs or a halo that another provider applied. Halos and tongs apply traction, or pulling force, to correct a spinal deformity, such as scoliosis, an abnormal rightward or leftward curvature of the spine. A halo is a ring shaped device made of steel, and a tong is a U shaped device. The provider applies weighted traction to the halo or tong over time until proper alignment of the bones is achieved. The provider then removes the halo or tongs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, in a supine position with the head placed at the extreme end of the bed, the provider loosens and removes the screws and removes the halo or tongs device. The provider may apply bone wax or dressing to the wounds to heal them. Terminology Supine: Lying in the face up position. Tips In general, do not report subsequent removal of a traction device separately as it is included in the basic procedure. However, when a different provider removes a halo or tongs, report the removal separately with 20665. Payer regulations treat members of the same group practice, that is, all providers with the same provider identification number, as the same provider for billing purposes. Therefore, even if another provider in the same practice placed the halo, you cannot code and bill separately for the removal. Read Less

short_description: Application of a uniplane (pins or wires in 1 plane), unilateral, external fixation system
lay_term: The provider applies a uniplane external fixation on one side of the body. Skeletal deformities or injuries such as fractures often require the use of skeletal fixation devices to join skeletal parts and maintain their normal alignment as healing takes place. An external fixation system, also called an external fixator or ex fix, is a fixation device that is placed inside of bones, and the device itself remains outside of the body. It enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for additional invasive procedures. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider examines and plans the uniplanar fixation site. She localizes the fracture site and makes several small skin incisions in the longitudinal direction, axial and uniplanar. She introduces skeletal fixation pins through the skin incisions and drills them to the bone in a uniplanar axial pattern. She assesses fixation of the pins and then aligns an external fixation rod to the exposed pins in the uniplanar mode. She affixes the external rod to the exposed part of the uniplanar pins. The provider confirms satisfactory fixation of uniplanar fixation device with radiological studies. Terminology Axial: Situated around an axis or central point. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Distal: Location or direction away from the midline of the body or from the point of insertion. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Fixation: Stabilizing process. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. Localize: To identify a specific area of interest. Longitudinal: Lengthwise direction. Multiplane: Multiple surfaces. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Tensioning: Tightening; placing under tension. Unilateral: Single side. Uniplane: Single surface. Tips Uniplanar pin systems are used almost exclusively for shaft fractures, especially midshaft tibia, or shinbone, fractures. These fractures include the tibial plateau, or top portion of the tibia, the tibial plafond, or distal end of the tibia, and pilon fractures, at the lower end of the tibia. The pin the surgeon uses may help you distinguish between 20690 and 20692, Application of a multiplane, pins or wires in more than 1 plane, unilateral, external fixation system, e.g., Ilizarov, Monticelli type. Uniplane fixators use thicker, more solid pins for fixation than multiplane fixators. Ring fixator pins are much narrower, and the surgeon places them under tension. If you see the term thin wire, or thin pin, or see a description of tensioning the pins, this is almost certainly a ring, or multiplane, fixator. Coding examples include: The provider reduces an open tibia fracture, applies an external fixator, and performs irrigation and debridement. short_description: Application of a multiplane (pins or wires in more than 1 plane), unilateral, external fixation system (eg, Ilizarov, Monticelli type)
lay_term: The provider applies a multiplane external fixation system to one side of the patient's body. Skeletal deformities or injuries such as fractures often require the use of skeletal fixation devices to join skeletal parts and maintain their normal alignment as healing takes place. An external fixation system, also called an external fixator or ex fix, is a fixation device that is placed inside of bones, and the device itself remains outside of the body. It enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for additional invasive procedures. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider examines and plans the multiplanar fixation site. She localizes the fracture site and makes several small skin incisions in a peripheral multiplanar manner. She introduces skeletal fixation pins through the skin incisions and drills them to the bone in a unilateral axial pattern. She inserts pins or wires into the hole and attaches an external rod that holds them in position and makes the fracture joint immobile. The provider confirms satisfactory fixation of the multiplanar fixation device with radiological studies. Terminology Axial: Situated around an axis or central point. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Distal: Location or direction away from the midline of the body or from the point of insertion. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Fixation: Stabilizing process. Ilizarov fixation system: Device for stabilization of fractures and bone lengthening procedures using an external circular frame and a series of wires, nuts, bolts, and rods. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. Localize: To identify a specific area of interest. Longitudinal: Lengthwise direction. Monticelli fixation system: Type of external skeletal fixation system. Multiplane ring device: Skeletal fixation device consisting of multiple wires affixed to bone at different planes and attached to external ring shaped fixators connected to each other, resembling a stack of several bicycle wheels with spokes. Multiplane: Multiple surfaces. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Tensioning: Tightening; placing under tension. Unilateral: Single side. Uniplane: Single surface. Tips Multiplane fixation and ring fixation are basically synonymous. If you see ring fixation mentioned, you should code for multiplane fixation. Code 20692 refers directly to the Ilizarov and Monticelli types as examples of multiplane external fixation systems, so if you see either of these terms, you should home in on 20692. Uniplanar pin systems are used almost exclusively for shaft fractures, especially midshaft tibia, or shinbone, fractures. These fractures include the tibial plateau, or top portion of the tibia, the tibial plafond, or distal end of the tibia, and pilon fractures, at the lower end of the tibia. The pin the surgeon uses may help you distinguish between 20690, Application of a uniplane, pins or wires in 1 plane, unilateral, external fixation system, and 20692. Uniplane fixators use thicker, more solid pins for fixation than multiplane fixators. Ring fixator pins are much narrower, and the surgeon places them under tension. If you see the term thin wire, or thin pin, or see a description of tensioning the pins, this is almost certainly a ring, or multiplane, fixator. If you see the term olive wire, you are definitely coding a ring fixator. If a provider does not indicate whether an ex fix is uniplanar or multiplanar, it is possible to discern which type was used from the description of the procedure or the components used. You can rest assured that the provider used a multiplanar fixator if she documents that she used rings or skinny wires. Report 20692. Providers usually use Schanz pins with uniplanar fixators but occasionally with multiplanar fixators, as well. If the provider documents the use of bars or a hinged fixator, you should ask whether she used a uniplanar or multiplanar fixator because bars and hinges are used with both types of fixators. If you determine that the provider applied a uniplanar fixator, you should report 20690, Application of a uniplane, pins or wires in 1 plane, unilateral, external fixation system. short_description: Removal, under anesthesia, of external fixation system

Superficial: At the surface, especially on the surface of the skin or immediately below; the opposite of deep. Surgical forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping. Uniplanar rod: Part of an external fixation system, a metal rod that passes through a single plane. short_description: Application of multiplane (pins or wires in more than 1 plane), unilateral, external fixation with stereotactic computer-assisted adjustment (eg, spatial frame), including imaging; initial and subsequent alignment(s), assessment(s), and computation(s) of adjustment schedule(s) Notes: (Do not report 20696 in conjunction with 20692, 20697)
lay_term: Skeletal deformities or injuries such as fractures may need skeletal fixation devices for repair. Skeletal fixation devices, like pins, rods, or wires, are used to join two skeletal parts and maintain their normal alignment while helping in faster healing. Computer assisted stereotactic guidance is the methodology used to exactly locate and plan the external fixation approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses a stereotactic frame attached to a computer to plan and examine the fixation site and the spatial approach of external fixation. He works intraoperatively, if necessary, to exactly locate the fixation point for insertion of the fixation pins and rods. After proper stereotactic localization of the fracture site, he makes several small skin incisions in a peripheral multiplanar manner. He introduces skeletal fixation pins via the external skin incisions and further drills to the bone in a unilateral axial pattern. He inserts pins or wires into the hole and attaches an external rod that holds them in position and makes the fracture joint immobile. The provider may confirm the satisfactory fixation of the fixation devices with an X–ray. Terminology Axial: Situated around an axis or central point. External fixation, or ex fix: Type of skeletal traction, also called an external fixator or ex fix, that enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for invasive procedures. Localization: Process of identifying a specific area of interest. Multiplanar: Multiple surfaces. Peripheral: Along the outside boundary or edges. Skeletal traction: Application of a pulling force on bones to treat skeletal disorders and fractures, keeping the bones aligned and immobilized, while relieving pressure on the muscles and nerves, allowing normal healing of a defect or fracture. Spatial approach: Three dimensional view of an activity. Stereotactic frame: Structure or imaging markers applied to the head as a surgical guide; from Greek and Latin roots meaning to touch in space. Unilateral: One side. Tips Remember to report only one of 20692, Application of a multiplane, pins or wires in more than 1 plane, unilateral, external fixation system, e.g., Ilizarov, Monticelli type, 20696, Application of multiplane, pins or wires in more than 1 plane, unilateral, external fixation with stereotactic computer assisted adjustment, e.g., spatial frame, including imaging, initial and subsequent alignments, assessments, and computations of adjustment schedules, or 20697, Application of multiplane, pins or wires in more than 1 plane, unilateral, external fixation with stereotactic computer assisted adjustment, e.g., spatial frame, including imaging, exchange, i.e., removal and replacement, of strut, each. lay_term: Skeletal deformities or injuries such as fractures may need skeletal fixation devices for repair. Skeletal fixation devices, like pins, rods, or wires, are used to join two skeletal parts and maintain their normal alignment while helping in faster healing. Computer assisted stereotactic guidance is the methodology used to exactly locate and plan the external fixation approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider determines which strut needs to be exchanged based on the computer schedule for correction. After positioning of the patient, the provider places a temporary strut on the stereotactic frame to maintain stability. He removes the appropriate strut, places a new strut and secures it, and then removes the temporary strut. The provider may confirm the satisfactory alignment of the fixation device, or strut, with an X–ray. Terminology External fixation, or ex fix: Type of skeletal traction, also called an external fixator or ex fix, that enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for invasive procedures. Multiplanar: Multiple surfaces. Skeletal traction: Application of a pulling force on bones to treat skeletal disorders and fractures, keeping the bones aligned and immobilized, while relieving pressure on the muscles and nerves, allowing normal healing of a defect or fracture. Stereotactic frame: Structure or imaging markers applied to the head as a surgical guide; from Greek and Latin roots meaning to touch in space. Strut: Rod or bar that is part of a framework. lay_term: The provider manually prepares a drug delivery device and inserts the device into a joint as part of a separately reported primary procedure. Report this code in addition to the code for the primary procedure. Explanation Prior to the procedure, the provider takes the necessary steps to manually prepare the drug delivery device. With the patient appropriately prepped and under anesthesia for a primary procedure, the provider inserts a biocompatible and biodegradable microsphere (small ovoid structure), nanoparticle (ultrasmall, submicroscopic particle), or liposome drug delivery system encapsulating a drug into the joint of a patient to provide stable, sustained, localized delivery of a drug(s), such as corticosteroids, DMARDs, and other anti–inflammatory drugs to treat osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis flare–ups, synovitis, and joint pain. After placement of the drug delivery system, he continues with the primary procedure. Terminology Anti–inflammatory: Substance that reduces pain, swelling, and inflammation. Biocompatible: Able to be placed in a body without causing a physiological reaction, injury, or immune response. Biodegradable: Refers to substances or devices, such as sutures, mesh, implants, or drug reservoirs, that disintegrate or break down in the body over time. Corticosteroid: A substance that reduces inflammation; sometimes shortened to steroid; also known as a glucocorticoid. Disease–modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs): Medications that treat specific types of inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (an inflammatory joint disease); also known as antirheumatic drugs. Intra–articular: Within a joint, the point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Liposomes: Double–layered, liquid–filled bubbles made from phospholipids (a fatty compound containing phosphorus) that can be filled with nutrients or pharmaceutical agents and delivered into specific sites or cells within the body. Osteoarthritis: A degenerative condition of a joint due to wear and tear that causes the cartilage or cushion in the joints between bones to break down and results in pain, stiffness, and swelling. Rheumatoid arthritis: A chronic (long lasting) disease that causes disabling inflammation and deformity in the joints; in this autoimmune connective tissue disease, the body attacks itself. Synovitis: Inflammation of the membrane that lines the cavities of joints that flex, extend, and move through a full range of motion; fluid lubricates the synovium and reduces friction within the joint. Tips For removal of an intra–articular drug delivery device, report +20705 in addition to the code for the primary procedure. For insertion and removal of subfascial drug delivery device, see +20700 and +20701, respectively. These codes must be reported in addition to a code for the primary procedure. For insertion and removal of an intramedullary (within a bone marrow canal) device, see +20702 and +20703, respectively. These codes must be reported in addition to a code for the primary procedure. short_description: Replantation, foot, complete amputation
lay_term: Replantation is the reattachment of a body part, such as the foot, that has been amputated, or severed, from a person's body. She frees, identifies, and tags with sutures the arteries and veins, or vascular supply, of the amputated foot. She places an arterial clamp on the patient's leg to control blood flow during surgery. First, she fixes the innermost structure, the tarsal and metatarsal bones. She shortens bones, as necessary, to fix the bones properly. She applies 4–hole bone plates and or Kirschner (K) wires to fix the detached bones. Once the fixation of tarsal and metatarsal bones of the foot is complete, she pulls out the deep flexor and extensor tendons from both the patient's body and from the amputated foot and fixes them with tight sutures. Once the fixation of deep bones and tendons is complete, she turns her attention to fixing the vascular supply, beginning with the arteries. She pulls previously tagged arteries from the amputated foot along with similar arteries from the patient's body. She performs microvascular anastomosis, or reconnection, of the corresponding arteries. The provider repairs as many arteries as possible to regain the proper vascular flow. If required, she harvests vein grafts from other sites to aid in the repair of the amputated foot. After arterial repair, she pulls out corresponding nerves and repairs them from one to another. She ensures arterial and nerve preservation and then targets the venous supply. In the same manner, she pulls tagged veins out from the detached body part as well as the patient's body and repairs the corresponding veins. If necessary, she utilizes vein grafts for the microvascular anastomosis. She performs forceful extension or flexion of the foot, as necessary, to check for proper alignment. She then turns her attention to repairing the skin and open wound. In the case of major loss of skin, she harvests skin grafts or flaps from other body areas to repair the skin loss and open wound. She packs the open wound of the reattachment site and performs an extensive repair of the upper skin surface from end to end, longitudinally and circumferentially. short_description: Bone graft, any donor area; minor or small (eg, dowel or button)
lay_term: A bone graft restores structural integrity and natural osseous, or bony, tissue to the site of a bony defect, which increases its strength so it will last over a period of time. She closes the wound at the donor site by suturing in a layered fashion. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Fibula: Smaller of the two bones of the lower leg; the fibula is the outermost bone, the tibia the innermost. Iliac crest: Upper edge of the ilium, the upper part of the pelvic bone; also called the crest of the ilium. Retractor: Surgical instrument used to retract, or hold back, wound edges or deeper tissues to give better visualization and access to the provider performing surgery. short_description: Cartilage graft; costochondral
lay_term: Cartilage grafting is a procedure to obtain a cartilage graft from a donor area to fill a larger defect of other cartilage or bones like the temporomandibular joint. A provider uses a costochondral, or rib, cartilage graft in the reconstruction of facial defects, including those of the nose and temporomandibular joint, and in repair of the trachea. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the rib area donor site. She extends the incision down to fascia and underlying muscles. She uses a surgical retractor to pull back soft tissue, fascia, and muscles to expose part of the bone. She then incises, shaves, and extracts a large oval shape of cartilage using a rongeur or bone shaver. She uses the cartilage graft to fill major bone and cartilage defects. She closes the wound at the donor site by suturing in a layered fashion. Terminology Bone shaver: Surgical instrument used to remove a very thin slice of bone. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Donor site: Location from where tissue is harvested for use in a grafting procedure, such as a bone graft or skin graft. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Retractor: Surgical instrument used to retract, or hold back, wound edges or deeper tissues to give better visualization and access to the provider performing surgery. Rongeur: Surgical instrument similar to forceps that can cut through bone. Temporomandibular joint, or TMJ: Union of the temporal bone, at the base of the cranium, and the mandible, the lower jaw bone. Trachea: Respiratory structure composed primarily of muscle and cartilage that connects the pharynx and larynx, or throat and voice box, to the lungs; also called the windpipe. short_description: Fascia lata graft; by stripper
lay_term: The fascia lata, the deep fascia of the thigh, is a good source of fascial graft for repairing ruptured tendons, e.g., Achilles tendon, chest wall defects, eyelid and orbital defects, and for treatment of fecal incontinence through unilateral gluteoplasty. The provider uses a stripper device to obtain the graft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a horizontal incision over the lateral part of the lower thigh to the fascial level, over the iliotibial band. She tags the proximal end of the fascia with a silk suture. She pulls the silk suture upward and then brings a fascia lata stripper into the operative field. She pressed the stripper close to the leg and pushed upward. She grasps the previously placed silk suture and pulls the fascia through the stripper, obtaining a fascial strip. She removes the stripper and closes the horizontal incision with sutures. Terminology Achilles tendon: Large tendon at the back the heel that connects the muscles of the calf to the calcaneal bone, or heel; also called tendo calcaneus. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Fecal incontinence: Loss of control of bowel movements. Gluteoplasty: Plastic surgery to repair or reshape the gluteus muscle in the area of the buttocks; sometimes called a butt lift. Orbit: Bones around the eye socket. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Stripper: Surgical instrument used to cut, strip, and extract material, such as fascia or tendon grafts or varicose veins. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Unilateral: On a single side; opposite of bilateral, on two sides. Tips If you are coding 54111, Excision of penile plaque, Peyronie disease, and if the procurement, or harvest, of the graft is separately performed, this procedure may be reported in addition to 20920. This code is reported for procuring a fascia graft. Read Less

short_description: Fascia lata graft; by incision and area exposure, complex or sheet
lay_term: The fascia lata, the deep fascia of the thigh, is a good source of fascial graft for repairing ruptured tendons, e.g., Achilles tendon, chest wall defects, or eyelid and orbital defects, and for treatment of fecal incontinence through unilateral gluteoplasty. The provider harvests complex or larger sheet grafts through an open excision procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision over the thigh in the upper lateral part. She extends the incision to the level of the fascia lata. She takes extra care to avoid incising the muscle. She dissects the fascia free from the upper fat pad and the muscle beneath. She extends the dissection to the distal lower level medially and laterally and obtains the desired width of fascial sheet. She detaches the fascia through transverse cuts made distally and proximally at the desired length. After the harvesting of the fascia lata sheet, she sutures the incision in a layered fashion. Gluteoplasty: Plastic surgery to repair or reshape the gluteus muscle in the area of the buttocks; sometimes called a butt lift. Longitudinal: In a lengthwise direction. Orbit: Bones around the eye socket. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. short_description: Tendon graft, from a distance (eg, palmaris, toe extensor, plantaris) Notes: (To report autologous soft tissue grafts harvested by direct excision, use 15769) (To report autologous fat grafting harvested by liposuction technique, see 15771, 15772, 15773, 15774)
lay_term: A provider repairs damage to tendons and ligaments by harvesting graft material from tendons elsewhere in the patient’s body, such as the palmaris tendon in the palm of the hand, the toe extensor tendon in the toes of the feet, or the plantaris tendon in the ankle. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin in the area over the donor site of the graft in the patient's body, such as the palmaris longus, extensor tendon of the fifth toe, or the plantaris tendon. She extends the incision in a longitudinal fashion and performs blunt dissection to free the tendon for grafting. After detaching the tendon at its insertion, or attachment to bone, the provider dissects its points of origin and then harvests the tendon for placement at the repair site. She may utilize a tendon stripper or make small incisions in the tendon to aid in harvesting the tendon graft. After harvesting the tendon graft, she sutures the incision in a layered fashion. Terminology Blunt dissection: Separation of tissue layers using the fingers; sharp dissection separates tissue layers using a blade. Donor site: Location from where tissue is harvested for use in a grafting procedure, such as a bone graft or skin graft. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Longitudinal: In a lengthwise direction. Stripper: Surgical instrument used to cut, strip, and extract material, such as fascia or tendon grafts or varicose veins. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips Practices that perform patellofemoral ligament reconstruction with graft may be able to report 20924, Tendon graft, from a distance, e.g., palmaris, toe extensor, plantaris, if the provider documents that she harvested the graft from a distance. The procedure report should document that the provider obtained the graft through either a separate skin incision or fascial exposure. If a provider operates on a knee for any lesion or defect and harvests the graft from the patient's opposite knee, report the main surgical code and 20924, Tendon graft, from a distance, e.g., palmaris, toe extensor, plantaris, together. Additional Info The palmaris longus, toe extensor, and the plantaris tendons are preferred choices for harvesting a graft for repair of damaged extensor tendons of the hand. The palmaris tendon graft is the most widely used graft for tendon and ligament repairs in the hand, such as the ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction, extensor tendon repair in the wrist, etc. Extensor tendons of the hand are more prone to injury due to their location and superficial position. lay_term: A provider uses an autograft, a type of donor bone, to fill in bony defects as she performs a spinal surgery procedure. She extracts the autograft from the patient’s own bone, taken from the same surgical incision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized for a spinal surgery procedure, the provider fills in bony defects during the surgical procedure with an autograft obtained from the same incision. She extends the incision longitudinally, or lengthwise, upward or downward, as applicable. For a fusion procedure in the cervical spine, or neck, she takes graft material from a rib by extending the incision upward. For a fusion procedure in the lumbar spine, which is the lower back, or in the sacrum, the area at the base of the spine, she takes graft material from an adjacent vertebra, generally the lower vertebra. She localizes the donor site and uses an osteotome or bone shaver to shave and pull the graft. After completing the grafting portion of the procedure, she turns her attention to the remainder of the major operative procedure. Localize: To identify a specific area of interest. Morselize: To break into very small pieces, or morsels. Osteopromotive: Substance that encourages new bone growth. Osteotome: Surgical instrument used to cut bone. Spinous process: Bony projection on the back of each vertebral bone. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. lay_term: The provider uses an autograft, a type of donor bone, to fill in bony defects as she performs a spinal surgery procedure. She extracts the autograft from the patient’s own body during the surgical procedure, through a separate incision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized for a spinal surgery procedure, the provider fills in bony defects during the surgical procedure with a morselized autograft obtained through a separate incision. She selects and prepares the donor area, typically the iliac crest, rib, or femoral head. She makes a longitudinal, or lengthwise, incision. She incises and retracts superficial skin, fascia, and muscles to expose the bone for grafting. She localizes the donor site and uses an osteotome or bone shaver to shave and pull the graft. She obtains sufficient bone pieces for the graft and then closes the donor site incision by suturing it in a layered fashion. She then prepares the autograft outside the patient's body. She uses a rongeur and bone shaver to morselize, or crush, the autograft into granules of various shapes and sizes. This allows the bone pieces to confirm to the bony defect and fill in the gap, or cavity, in the bone. After completing the grafting portion of the procedure, she turns her attention to the remainder of the spinal surgery procedure. Iliac crest: Upper edge of the ilium, the upper part of the pelvic bone; also called the crest of the ilium. Localize: To identify a specific area of interest. Osteotome: Surgical instrument used to cut bone. Rongeur: Surgical instrument similar to forceps, or tongs, that can cut through bone. lay_term: The provider harvests bone marrow, the spongy tissue inside the large bones; as donor material to fill in bony defects in the spine. The provider aspirates the bone marrow during the same session as spine surgery but through a separate skin or fascial incision. Explanation After appropriate preparation and anesthesia and during primary spinal surgery, the provider prepares the separate site from which to aspirate the bone marrow. The provider makes a small incision in the skin or through fascia adjacent to the primary site, through which a bone marrow aspiration needle is inserted. Once the marrow cavity is reached, bone marrow is aspirated (sucked up through the needle). The aspiration needle is removed, and the site checked for bleeding, which is controlled if there is any. The provider continues to perform the primary spinal procedure, transferring the bone marrow graft to fill the defect in the spine. short_description: Monitoring of interstitial fluid pressure (includes insertion of device, eg, wick catheter technique, needle manometer technique) in detection of muscle compartment syndrome
lay_term: The provider measures interstitial fluid pressure to check for the presence of compartment syndrome, an abnormal buildup of fluid in the tissues within a muscle compartment, a space partitioned by a layer of fascia, which can occur following injury, surgery, or repetitive muscle use. Increasing fluid pressure within a muscle compartment compresses small blood vessels and nerves, requiring immediate attention to avoid permanent tissue damage. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider inserts a needle or a wick catheter of a manometer, a pressure monitoring device, through the skin and into the muscle compartment in the affected extremity. She records the pressure reading from the monitoring device. She removes the needle and applies a sterile dressing to the insertion site. Terminology Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Wick catheter: A catheter, or tubing, with a wick positioned at one end so as to draw bodily fluid up into the catheter. Tips Experts recommend reporting 20950 per extremity, per session. You should not report this code per compartment. A provider measures compartment pressures in anterior and posterior compartments of bilateral legs. You should report 20950 RT, right side, followed by 20950 LT, left side. If a provider repeats pressure measurement later on the same day, such as to test for exercise induced compartment syndrome, you may report those studies separately. Remember to append modifier 76, Repeat procedure or service by same physician or other qualified health care professional, if the same provider repeats the procedure at a separate session on the same day. short_description: Bone graft with microvascular anastomosis; fibula
lay_term: A provider obtains bone graft material from the fibula along with its active vascular supply, arteries and veins, to fill a major bone defect at the recipient site along with the regained vascular supply. The regained vascular supply promotes faster healing and growth at the recipient site. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal, or lengthwise, incision at the donor graft site over the soleus and the long fibular muscle of the leg. She extends the incision down to the level of fascia and muscle. She incises and retracts muscle tissue to expose the grafting area on the fibula. She localizes fibular bone and then dissects a piece of bone from the fibula in a proximal and distal osteotomy. She takes extra care to preserve and dissect the vascular blood supply along with the dissected bone. She ensures satisfactory preparation of the bone graft along with intact vascular supply and then sutures the donor site in a layered fashion. She then turns her attention to the recipient site. She brings the extracted graft into the operative field of the recipient site. She performs microvascular anastomosis, ligating, or attaching, the vascular supply of the bone graft to the bone of the recipient site. She then fits the bone graft into the defect area of the recipient site. She affixes the bone graft to the site with bone plates, screws, and bone paste. She closes the recipient site using layered sutures. Terminology Bone paste: Substance that acts as a bone substitute to fill in bony defects; also called bone cement. short_description: Bone graft with microvascular anastomosis; iliac crest
lay_term: The provider harvests bone graft material, along with its attached vascular supply, from the hip bone. With the aid of an operative microscope, he reconnects the vascular supply at the recipient site to promote faster healing where bone was missing or damaged due to injury or disease. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the hip over the iliac crest. He extends the incision down to bone. He excises a piece of bone, taking care to dissect and preserve the vascular supply along with the dissected bone graft. He then makes an incision at the recipient site, dissecting down to bone, while preserving the vascular supply in the area. He places the graft in position and uses an operating microscope to view the site as he joins the small arteries and veins in the graft to the local vessels. He closes both the donor and recipient sites with layered sutures following successful placement of the graft. short_description: Bone graft with microvascular anastomosis; metatarsal
lay_term: A provider obtains bone graft material from metatarsal bone along with its active vascular supply, arteries and veins, to fill a major bone defect at the recipient site along with the regained vascular supply. The regained vascular supply promotes faster healing and growth at the recipient site. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal, or lengthwise, incision at the donor graft site over the metatarsal area of the foot. She extends the incision down to the level of fascia and muscle. She incises and retracts muscle tissue to expose the grafting area on a metatarsal bone. She localizes the metatarsal bone and then dissects a piece of bone from the metatarsal in a proximal and distal osteotomy. She takes extra care to preserve and dissect the vascular blood supply along with the dissected bone. She ensures satisfactory preparation of the bone graft along with intact vascular supply and then sutures the donor site in a layered fashion. She then turns her attention to the recipient site. She brings the extracted graft into the operative field of the recipient site. She performs microvascular anastomosis, ligating, or attaching, the vascular supply of the bone graft to the bone of the recipient site. She then fits the bone graft into the defect area of the recipient site. She affixes the bone graft to the site with bone plates, screws, and bone paste. She closes the recipient site using layered sutures. Terminology Bone paste: Substance that acts as a bone substitute to fill in bony defects; also called bone cement. Bone plate: Flat or contoured metal plating attached with screws to a bone to provide stabilization or repair a fracture. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Microvascular anastomosis: Surgical connection of small arteries and veins, usually between a tissue graft and the site of repair. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Temporomandibular joint, or TMJ: Union of the temporal bone, at the base of the cranium, and the mandible, the lower jaw bone. Tips Besides the procedure itself, all postdischarge office visits for this procedure, including removal of sutures; dressing, cast, and splint changes; evaluation of periodic imaging and laboratory reports, if needed; and antibiotic and pain medication adjustments, for 90 days after the day of the operation are considered part of the postoperative work for this code. short_description: Free osteocutaneous flap with microvascular anastomosis; other than iliac crest, metatarsal, or great toe
lay_term: The provider harvests bone graft material, along with its active vascular supply, arteries and veins, and an attached layer of cutaneous tissue, or skin, to fill a bony defect at the recipient site and to compensate for soft tissue loss due to trauma or disease. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision at the graft site. She extends the incision through the fascia and muscle layers, down to bone. She excises a piece of bone along with the layer of skin above it. She takes extra care to preserve and dissect the vascular blood supply along with the dissected bone. She ensures satisfactory preparation of the bone graft along with its intact skin and vascular supply and then turns her attention to the recipient site. She debrides and removes any necrotic, or dead, tissue at the recipient site before she brings the extracted graft into the operative field. She places the graft in position and performs microvascular anastomosis, ligating, or attaching, the vascular supply of the bone graft to the bone of the recipient site using microsurgery techniques. She closes both the donor and recipient sites with layered sutures following successful placement of the graft. Metatarsal bones: Five bones that make up the foot; they connect to the tarsal bones of the ankle and to the phalanges, or bones of digits, or toes. Microsurgical techniques: Procedures employing very small instruments while viewing the surgical field through an operative microscope. Microvascular anastomosis: Surgical connection of structures performed under a surgical microscope. Osteocutaneous flap: Tissue graft consisting of bone and its attached vascular supply, subcutaneous tissue, and skin. lay_term: The provider harvests bone graft material from the great toe, along with its active vascular supply and an attached layer of cutaneous tissue, or skin, to fill a bony defect at the recipient site and to compensate for soft tissue loss due to trauma or disease. He excises a piece of bone along with the layer of skin above it. He preserves and dissects the vascular blood supply along with the dissected bone. He ensures satisfactory preparation of the bone graft along with its intact skin and vascular supply and then turns his attention to the recipient site. He debrides and removes any necrotic, or dead, tissue at the recipient site before he brings the extracted graft into the operative field. He places the graft in position and performs microvascular anastomosis, joining of the arteries and veins of the graft with the local vessels, using microsurgery techniques. He closes both the donor and recipient sites with layered sutures following successful placement of the graft. Metastasis: Spread of cancer to other parts of the body from its original site. short_description: Computer-assisted surgical navigational procedure for musculoskeletal procedures, image-less (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Do not report 20985 in conjunction with 61781-61783) (For computer-assisted navigational procedures with image guidance based on pre-operative and intraoperatively obtained images, see 0054T, 0055T)
lay_term: A provider using a computer assisted navigation system, or CANS, performs musculoskeletal procedures, such as a joint replacement surgery, with the aid of a computer screen that provides a three–dimensional digital image of the patient’s anatomy. With the use of a CANS, the provider makes more accurate measurements, ensuring better fitting surgical components, with faster healing and less postoperative pain for patients. An imageless CANS does not require the use of preoperative imaging studies, such as computed tomography, or CT scanning. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider brings the CANS into the operative field. He activates the navigation software and enters patient specific information, such as patient identifiers, name of provider, and site of surgery. He positions pins that hold trackers, or markers, on the surgical site within the camera’s field of view, to be used as a navigational aid during the surgical procedure. He registers the trackers with the computer navigation system, a process that causes the computer navigation system to recognize and remember the trackers and their location, helping the system to render a more accurate digital image of the surgical site. The provider then proceeds with the surgical procedure, viewing the operative site through the screen of the computer navigation unit. Terminology Digital image: A picture converted to numerical data for storage and viewing on a computer. Joint replacement surgery: Surgical removal and replacement of a diseased or damaged joint, the union of two bones, such as a knee joint or hip joint, with an artificial joint made of plastic or metal. Musculoskeletal: Involving muscles and bones. Navigation software: A computer program that helps the user find his way around in unfamiliar territory. Patient identifiers: Forms of identification for the patient, such as name, date of birth, healthcare record number, etc. Tips Code 20985 is an add–on code describing intraoperative application of the computer assisted navigational system and must be reported with an allowable primary musculoskeletal procedure code. Medicare will reimburse you for 20985 when the computer assisted navigation is medically necessary and performed with another procedure. Read Less

short_description: Arthrotomy, temporomandibular joint Notes: (To report bilateral procedure, report 21010 with modifier 50)
lay_term: The provider incises, or cuts into, the temporomandibular joint on one side of the jaw, to facilitate inspection of the joint for the presence of adhesions, infection, tumors, or other conditions, including temporomandibular joint disorder. He performs minor debridement and irrigation, as required. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in front of or behind the ear, depending upon the objective of the procedure. He extends the incision through the tissues down to the temporomandibular joint. He incises the joint to gain access to the joint capsule, the fluid filled sac that encloses the joint. He performs minor bone debridement as necessary to release, or free up, the associated vascular supply, nerves, and or muscles. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery, that form between tissues and organs; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Arthrotomy: Surgical incision of a joint, the point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Temporomandibular joint, or TMJ: Union of the temporal bone, at the base of the cranium, and the mandible, the lower jaw bone. Temporomandibular disorder, or TMD: A condition of the temporomandibular joint, which connects the lower jaw to the skull, characterized primarily by pain and discomfort but may also be accompanied by swelling, difficulty chewing, and or jaw locking, clicking, or popping; the cause is not well defined but felt to be muscular in origin; commonly but erroneously referred to as TMJ, which stands only for the name of the joint and not the disorder. Vascular supply: The vessels that provide blood to an area of the body; arteries carry oxygen rich blood away from the heart to the rest of the body, and veins carry oxygen poor blood from the body to the heart. Tips Report 21010 for a unilateral arthrotomy, on one side of the jaw. For a bilateral arthrotomy, on both sides of the jaw, append modifier 50, Bilateral procedure. Read Less

short_description: Radical resection of tumor (eg, sarcoma), soft tissue of face or scalp; less than 2 cm Notes: (To report excision of skull tumor for osteomyelitis, use 61501)
lay_term: The provider excises a small tumor, or abnormal mass, from the face or scalp, in a radical, or extensive resection procedure to ensure the tumor has not spread to the surrounding area. He performs a radical resection when the tumor is known or suspected to be malignant, or cancerous. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the area of the tumor, mostly in line with the skin creases in the case of a facial tumor. He extends the incision into the deep tissues around the tumor. He raises, or incises and pulls back, flaps of soft tissue and or muscle to adequately expose the underlying anatomy. He identifies and preserves, or protects, neurovascular structures, the nerves and vessels in the area. He separates the tumor from surrounding tissue, localizing it and then uses a sharp scalpel, or surgical knife, to dissect the tumor from the surrounding tissue margin and remove it. To rule out further malignancy, he dissects and removes a wide area, or margin, of surrounding tissue. He submits the dissected tumor and tissue margin for laboratory analysis. The provider then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Localized: Confined to a single or small area. Malignancy: Cancerous tissue. Osteomyelitis: Infection in the bone. Radical resection: Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Sarcoma: A malignant, or cancerous, tumor of connective tissue origin, that occurs in the bone or soft tissues anywhere in the body. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Tips This code is for radical resection of tumors of musculoskeletal origin, such as a sarcoma. Wide margins of excision beyond the tumor dimensions are necessary to report this code. Compare with 21016, Radical resection of tumor, e.g., sarcoma, soft tissue of face or scalp, 2 cm or greater. short_description: Excision of bone (eg, for osteomyelitis or bone abscess); mandible
lay_term: In mandibular osteomyelitis, the mandible, or lower jaw bone, and its surrounding soft tissue become inflamed due to a bacterial infection, such as Staphylococcus aureus, which may have spread from an infected tooth.
