He removes dead bone tissue using an osteotome or bone drills. In the case of extensive damage to the tissue, he may use a bone graft to compensate for the bone loss. He treats the infected area with antimicrobial agents to stop the spread of the infection. He closes the surgical opening through simple or layered sutures. short_description: Removal by contouring of benign tumor of facial bone (eg, fibrous dysplasia)
lay_term: Removal of a benign, or noncancerous, tumor by contouring is a major invasive procedure used to treat severe congenital bone abnormalities, like fibrous dysplasia, a condition in which normal bone growth is disrupted by abnormal embedded fibrous tissue, resulting in abnormal shape of the bone and surrounding soft tissues. The provider removes the abnormal tissue by surgically contouring, or reshaping, it. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider plans and marks the area for removal of abnormally shaped diseased bone and or tissues using a three dimensional, or spatial, system. He makes a curvilinear incision on the face to locate the diseased facial bone. He extends the incision down to fascia, muscle, and finally to the bone to localize the diseased facial bone and tissue, such as an area of fibrous dysplasia. He removes the abnormal fibrous sheet from the bone using blunt, or finger, dissection. He dissects additional abnormal tissue from the surrounding bone and or muscular tissue. He removes the freed bone tumor or abnormal fibrous tissue using surgical forceps. He checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and then closes the incision with sutures in a layered fashion. short_description: Excision of benign tumor or cyst of maxilla or zygoma by enucleation and curettage
lay_term: A provider removes benign, or noncancerous, tumors of the upper jaw and cheekbone by enucleation and or curettage. Enucleation is the process of removal of an entire tumor as a single mass. Curettage refers to removal of diseased tissue through scraping, using a tool called a curette. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the oral mucosa, the membrane layer inside the mouth, for an intraoral approach to access the tumor on the maxilla or zygomatic arch bone. If an extraoral approach is necessary, he incises the skin of the face over the tumor area, extending the incision through the fascia and muscle down to bone. He localizes the maxillary or zygomatic tumor and then marks it to aid in dissection. He dissects the tumor from the surrounding tissue and removes it in its entirety. He uses a curette to scrape surrounding tissues to remove all traces of the tumor. He submits a tissue specimen for laboratory analysis. He checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision by suturing in a layered fashion. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Curettage, in medical procedures, is the use of a curette to remove tissue by scraping or scooping. Maxillary cyst: An abnormal fluid filled sac in the bone of the upper jaw. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, can be benign or cancerous. Zygomatic arch bone: The cheekbone; also called zygoma. Report 21030, entering the fee for the procedure on the first line of the claim form, and report 21030 with modifier 47, Anesthesia by surgeon, on the second line, entering the fee for the anesthesia, although you may have to write it off for some payers. Alternatively, you can report 21030 with modifier 47, Anesthesia by Surgeon, with no extra fee included in the main procedure. Read Less

For an extensive tumor, he performs radical dissection, surgically removing the blood supply and lymph system surrounding the tumor for laboratory analysis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the oral mucosa, the membrane lining the inside of the mouth. Alternatively, he incises the skin over the mandible, if making an extraoral approach, extending the incision through fascia and muscle down to bone. He localizes the tumor in the mandible and then marks it along with proper margins as an aid in dissection. He uses a bone drill or osteotome to cut and remove the bone tumor along with the appropriate surrounding margins. He performs extensive, or radical, dissection, removing tissues that provide the blood supply and lymph system surrounding the tumor, as well as surrounding mandibular bone. He uses a curette to scrape surrounding tissues to remove all traces of the malignant tumor. He may use bone grafts to fill in bony defects resulting from the radical dissection. He may also perform an adjacent tissue transfer, called an ATT flap, a complex tissue repair in which a flap of tissue is transferred from another location in the patient’s body. The provider submits the surgical specimen for laboratory analysis. He checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision by suturing in a layered fashion. Terminology Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping; also spelled curet. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Localize: To identify a specific area of interest. Osteotome: Surgical instrument used to cut bone. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, can be benign or cancerous. Tips If a bone graft is performed in conjunction with 21045, report also 21215, Graft, bone, mandible, includes obtaining graft. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Excision of benign tumor or cyst of mandible; requiring intra-oral osteotomy (eg, locally aggressive or destructive lesion[s])
lay_term: A cyst or other benign, or noncancerous, tumor of the mandible, or lower jaw bone, is removed in an open surgical procedure. The provider may use either an intraoral approach, through the mouth, or an extraoral approach, through the skin. For an aggressive, or fast growing, tumor, he performs intraoral osteotomy, cutting into bone to completely excise the tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the layer of mucosa covering the palate, at the roof of the mouth, in an intraoral approach to access the cyst or benign tumor of the mandibular bone. He extends the incision through fascia and muscle, down to bone. He localizes the abnormal mass and marks it along with proper margins as an aid in dissection. He uses a bone drill or osteotome to cut and remove the mass in the bone along with the appropriate surrounding margins. If the mass is fast growing, he excises surrounding bone tissue using a bone drill and curettes. He may use bone grafts or perform an intraoral flap reconstruction procedure to fill in defects resulting from the extensive dissection. The provider submits the surgical specimen for laboratory analysis. He checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision by suturing in a layered fashion. Cyst: Sac usually containing fluid; the term cyst can refer to an abnormal growth or to any saclike structure, such as the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Flap reconstruction: Performing a surgical repair using a flap, or section of tissue, from another location in the patient’s body. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, can be benign or cancerous. Read Less

short_description: Excision of benign tumor or cyst of mandible; requiring extra-oral osteotomy and partial mandibulectomy (eg, locally aggressive or destructive lesion[s])
lay_term: The provider excises a benign, or noncancerous, mass of the mandible, or lower jaw bone, such as a tumor or cyst. Due to the aggressive growth or destructive nature of the mass, the provider removes a portion of the lower jaw. He uses an extraoral approach, accessing the jaw through an incision in the skin of the face or neck. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the mass and extends the incision down to bone. He marks the tumor along with the proper surgical margin. He uses a bone drill or osteotome to excise the mass and the appropriate margin of surrounding tissue. To rule out further extension of the tumor, he drills, separates, and excises the associated part of the mandibular bone. He may perform bone grafting and or flap reconstruction to fill in any defects. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Cyst: Sac usually containing fluid; the term cyst can refer to an abnormal growth or to any saclike structure, such as the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Flap: Tissue for grafting, typically removed from one place on the body and positioned in another; however, it may remain anchored and rotated from one side of an area to another. Mandibulectomy: Excision, or removal, of the lower jaw. Osteotome: Surgical instrument used to cut bone. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Tips If a bone graft is harvested for reconstruction of the mandible, report the graft harvest separately. Read Less

short_description: Excision of benign tumor or cyst of maxilla; requiring extra-oral osteotomy and partial maxillectomy (eg, locally aggressive or destructive lesion[s])
lay_term: A benign, or noncancerous, tumor of the maxilla, the upper jaw bone, is removed in an open surgical procedure. The provider performs an extraoral osteotomy, cutting into the maxillary bone, and a partial maxillectomy to remove a fast growing or destructive tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a curvilinear incision in the skin of the neck or cheek region, depending on the location of the tumor. She localizes the mass and marks it along with the proper margins as an aid in dissection. She uses a bone drill or osteotome to remove the portion of the maxillary bone containing the mass. She prevents further extension of the complex benign tumor or deep–rooted cyst by drilling, curetting, and excising surrounding bone and tissues. She applies bone grafts to fill in bony defects. short_description: Condylectomy, temporomandibular joint (separate procedure) Notes: (For bilateral procedures, report 21050 with modifier 50)
lay_term: A provider performs a condylectomy, or surgical excision of the rounded ends of the mandible, or lower jaw bone, where they connect to the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) to treat dislocated or diseased condyles that interfere with movement of the joint or cause pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reviews any radiological studies of the condyles done prior to the surgery. She makes a curvilinear incision in front of the tragus line, an anatomical landmark in front of the ear. She dissects and retracts fascia and underlying muscles to expose the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). She identifies the TMJ joint and then uses a bone drill or osteotome to remove the diseased or restrictive part of the condyle. She removes the dissected condyle using surgical forceps. She assesses movement of the jaw. She applies a bone graft or synthetic graft material to fill the defect left by the condylectomy. She checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision by suturing in a complex layered fashion. Terminology Ankylosis: A condition that leads to stiffness or fusion (permanent joining) of a joint, following an injury, surgery, or infection. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Condyle: A rounded, knoblike projection at the end of a bone, typically where it meets or articulates with another bone at a joint. Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping; also spelled curet. Curvilinear: Curving line. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Osteotome: Surgical instrument used to cut bone. Temporomandibular joint (TMJ): A type of ball and socket joint that forms the union of the temporal bone at the base of the cranium (skull) and the mandible (lower jaw bone) and facilitates movement of the lower jaw. When the condyles become dislocated or diseased, movement of the jaw becomes difficult and very painful. TMJ ankylosis is a condition which leads to fusion of the joint following an injury, e.g. fracture of the mandible, or an infection. Read Less

short_description: Meniscectomy, partial or complete, temporomandibular joint (separate procedure) Notes: (For bilateral procedures, report 21060 with modifier 50)

She dissects and retracts fascia and underlying muscles to expose the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). She uses a rongeur or bone shaver to resect the diseased or injured part of the meniscus. She removes the dissected meniscus using surgical forceps. She assesses the jaw for satisfactory movement. She applies a bone graft or synthetic graft material to fill the defect left by the meniscectomy. short_description: Coronoidectomy (separate procedure) Notes: (For bilateral procedures, report 21070 with modifier 50)
lay_term: A provider performs a partial or complete coronoidectomy, an open surgical procedure to remove the coronoid process of the mandible, or lower jaw bone, to treat injury, ankylosis, arthritis, etc. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reviews any radiological studies of the mandible done prior to the surgery. She makes a curvilinear incision in front of the tragus line, an anatomical landmark in front of the ear. She dissects and retracts fascia and underlying muscles to expose the mandible. She identifies the coronoid process of the mandible and drills the diseased or restricted part of the coronoid process with the help of a bone drill or osteotome. She takes extra care to keep the condyle and meniscus intact. She removes the dissected coronoid using surgical forceps. She assesses the jaw for satisfactory movement. She applies a bone graft or synthetic graft material to fill the defect left by the coronoidectomy. She checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision by suturing in a complex layered fashion. Terminology Ankylosis: A condition which leads to stiffness or fusion, or permanent joining, of a joint, following an injury, surgery, or infection. Arthritis: An inflammatory condition affecting one or more of the body’s joints, resulting in pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Condyle: Rounded projection on the lower end of a bone, usually associated with a joint connecting with another bone. Coronoid process: Bony projection at the anterior end of the mandible. Curvilinear: Curving line. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. short_description: Application of halo type appliance for maxillofacial fixation, includes removal (separate procedure)
lay_term: A provider applies a halo type appliance to treat maxillofacial defects, which may be congenital in nature or acquired, resulting from trauma, bone growth disturbance, maxillary, or mandibular neoplastic or degenerative processes. The appliance allows for gradual skeletal lengthening and advancement, enabling the skin and soft tissue envelope to adapt to and accommodate the skeletal movement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider places halo pins in position in diagonally opposite pairs. He tightens them until they enter the bone. He tightens the pins opposite one another together until all the pins reach the desired depth in the maxillofacial bone. He uses a torque screwdriver to apply pressure to each of the pins. He secures the pins in position on the halo ring using nuts. Finally, he applies traction weights and checks the alignment through radiological imaging. Terminology Congenital: Present at birth. Halo: Ring shaped device used in applying skeletal traction. Mandible: The lower jaw bone. Maxilla: The upper jaw bone. Maxillofacial: Related to the maxilla, or upper jaw, and the face. Neoplasia: Presence of neoplasm, abnormal tissue mass that grows rapidly; neoplasms can be benign or cancerous. Torque screwdriver: Tool that measures the amount of force being applied to the screw or pin it is inserting. Tips You should not separately report 20694, Removal, under anesthesia, of external fixation system, when you remove a halo that your provider applied, because 21100 includes the halo removal. short_description: Injection procedure for temporomandibular joint arthrography Notes: (For radiological supervision and interpretation, use 70332. Do not report 77002 in conjunction with 70332)
lay_term: The provider injects contrast material into the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) for imaging during TMJ arthrography. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the provider inserts a needle into the temporomandibular joint cavity under fluoroscopic guidance. He removes the needle and takes the images. Temporomandibular joint (TMJ): Union of the temporal bone, at the base of the cranium, and the mandible, the lower jaw bone. Tips Report 21116 twice if the provider performs the procedures on both the right and left sides. If another provider group performs the injection, that practice should report 21116, and the other provider should report 70332. short_description: Genioplasty; augmentation (autograft, allograft, prosthetic material)
lay_term: A provider augments a receding chin with the use of a chin implant, in a genioplasty procedure. He performs the procedure to improve cosmetic appearance or for reasons of medical necessity, such as correcting problems with a patient’s bite. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision either under the lower lip inside the mouth or under the chin. He deepens the incision to form a pocket in the tissue. He selects an implant, using either autograft, allograft, or prosthetic material, such as a silicone chin implant. He places the implant in the appropriately sized pocket, using sizers, or trial implants of different sizes, to achieve the best appearance. He secures the implant and closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called allogeneic graft and homograft. Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Silicone: Synthetic material commonly used to form medical devices, like catheters and tubing, as well as implants inserted in the body, due to its durability and biocompatibility. Tips Most payers only cover genioplasty when it is performed for noncosmetic, medically necessary reasons such as abnormalities that result in significant functional impairment. Read Less

short_description: Genioplasty; sliding osteotomy, single piece
lay_term: A provider changes the appearance of a receding chin in a genioplasty procedure. He incises the jaw bone and slides it forward. He performs the procedure to improve cosmetic appearance or for reasons of medical necessity, such as correcting problems with a patient’s bite or to treat obstructive sleep apnea. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the bottom lip. He incises down to bone. He uses an electric saw to cut and slide a single piece of bone into a new position. He uses wire to secure the bones in their new position. He closes the incision with dissolvable sutures inside the mouth or uses regular sutures under the chin and applies a dressing. Terminology Obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA: Condition occurring during sleep in which breathing stops intermittently for brief periods, disrupting the sleep cycle and resulting in daytime sleepiness; it is caused by obstruction, narrowing, or incompetence of the airway. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. short_description: Genioplasty; sliding osteotomies, 2 or more osteotomies (eg, wedge excision or bone wedge reversal for asymmetrical chin)
lay_term: A provider corrects an asymmetrical chin in a genioplasty procedure. He incises the jaw in two or more places and removes or repositions wedges of bone. Genioplasty improves cosmetic appearance but may also be performed to improve conditions like obstructive sleep apnea. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the bottom lip. He incises down to bone. He closes the incision with dissolvable sutures inside the mouth or uses regular sutures under the chin and applies a dressing. short_description: Genioplasty; sliding, augmentation with interpositional bone grafts (includes obtaining autografts)
lay_term: The provider augments a patient's chin in a sliding genioplasty. He slides the chin bone forward to improve the cosmetic appearance of the face or to treat medical conditions like obstructive sleep apnea. He uses bone graft from the patient’s own body to augment, or build up, the chin bone in layers. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the site chosen for harvesting a bone graft, usually the hip bone. He removes sufficient autograft material and closes the wound. He then accesses the chin bone through an incision in the gingivobuccal space, the area between the gum line and the cheek. He dissects down to bone, taking care to avoid the mental, or chin, nerve. He uses a bone saw to perform a long osteotomy, an incision in the bone, in the chin area to free up the bone and permit it to slide forward into its new position. He injects the autograft material around the bone in an interpositional graft, or sandwich, technique. He secures the grafted area with wires or plates. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Interposition graft: Graft, or transplanted, material that is applied in between layers of the patient’s own tissue. Obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA: Condition occurring during sleep in which breathing stops intermittently for brief periods, disrupting the sleep cycle and resulting in daytime sleepiness, due to obstruction, narrowing, or incompetence of the airway. Tips Most payers only cover genioplasty when it is performed for noncosmetic, medically necessary reasons such as abnormalities that result in significant functional impairment. Read Less

short_description: Reduction forehead; contouring and application of prosthetic material or bone graft (includes obtaining autograft)
lay_term: The provider reshapes the forehead using contouring and placement of prosthetic material or bone graft from the patient’s own body to lower a patient's brow or hairline. He performs forehead reduction to correct a facial abnormality, or more commonly, to improve cosmetic appearance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the site chosen for harvesting a bone graft, usually the hip bone. He removes sufficient autograft material and closes the wound. He then makes a coronal incision in the scalp. He brings the forehead skin forward. He uses a burr drill and microsaw to contour the forehead into the appropriate shape. He applies the autograft and or applies a prosthesis, if an autograft was not harvested, and secures it in place. He returns the forehead skin to his normal position. The provider then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Burr drill: Surgical drill; also called a high speed burr. Coronal incision: An incision across the scalp on the crown, or corona, of the head from one side to the other; used synonymously with bicoronal and bitemporal incision. Prosthetic: Artificial, man made; a device that functions like the structure it replaces. Read Less

short_description: Reduction forehead; contouring and setback of anterior frontal sinus wall
lay_term: The provider reshapes the forehead to correct a facial abnormality or improve appearance. She contours the forehead and incises the underlying wall of the frontal sinus cavity Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a coronal type incision across the top of the scalp. She brings the forehead skin forward. She reduces the size of the forehead down to an adequate level using a microsaw. She contours, or shapes, the areas using high speed drills and burrs. She sets back the frontal sinus by resecting and shaping its anterior wall. She obliterates the frontal sinus with a right side flap excision using a bicoronal approach, from either side of the head. She inserts the trimmed anterior wall into the frontal sinus and secures it with sutures to the bone edges. She then moves the forehead skin back up into place. She closes the scalp incision with layered sutures. Terminology Burr drill: Surgical drill; also called a high speed burr. Coronal incision: An incision across the scalp on the crown, or corona, of the head. Frontal sinuses: One of four pairs of hollow chambers in the skull, connected to the nasal cavity and are a part of the respiratory system; the frontal sinuses are located in the center of the forehead. Microsaw: Wand shaped powered surgical instrument with a sawtooth blade for cutting bone. Tips Preauthorization is normally recommended for this procedure to alert the insurer when the procedure is performed for medically necessary reasons and not for cosmetic purposes. Read Less

Palatal obturator: Device used to block an opening in the palate, or roof of the mouth, to enable speech and swallowing; it can also be used during intraoral surgery to separate structures. short_description: Reconstruction midface, LeFort I; 2 pieces, segment movement in any direction, requiring bone grafts (includes obtaining autografts) (eg, ungrafted unilateral alveolar cleft)
lay_term: In a LeFort I midface surgery, the provider reconstructs the patient's facial bones using microsurgery and bone grafting to correct congenital deformities or acquired deformities. The provider moves the maxilla, or upper jaw bone, and associated bones forward, repositioning the teeth bearing part of the maxilla. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the site chosen for harvesting a bone graft. She removes sufficient autograft and closes the wound. She then makes an incision in the maxillary area. She separates the maxilla from the skull base and repositions it into the appropriate, predetermined location. She repositions two predetermined bone segment into place. She fills the defect with bone graft material previously harvested. When required, she molds and shapes a dental appliance to the defect intraoperatively, which she reduces as an outpatient as the defect contracts. She then packs the cavity with surgical gauze or a similar material. She positions a palatal obturator and secures it in place with a single screw through the residual hard palate. The provider checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision with layered sutures. Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Congenital: Present at birth. Dental appliance: A device anchored to the teeth, such as a dental bridge, retainer, or bite guard. Microsurgical techniques: Procedures employing very small instruments while viewing the surgical field through an operative microscope. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Palatal obturator: Device used to block an opening in the palate, or roof of the mouth, to enable speech and swallowing; it can also be used during intraoral surgery to separate structures. Unilateral: On a single side; opposite of bilateral, on two sides. Tips Preauthorization is normally recommended for this procedure to alert the insurer when the procedure is performed for medically necessary reasons and not for cosmetic purposes. She performs a LeFort II osteotomy by repositioning the nasal bones and upper jaw, with minimal impact on the orbit and zygomatic regions. A provider typically performs either a LeFort II or LeFort III osteotomy as one of a series of procedures to correct a severe congenital anomaly with significant facial deformity, also called craniofacial dysostosis. short_description: Reconstruction midface, LeFort II; any direction, requiring bone grafts (includes obtaining autografts)
lay_term: In a LeFort II midface surgery, the provider reconstructs the patient's facial bones using microsurgery and bone grafting to correct deformities, acquired or congenital, such as Treacher Collins syndrome. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the site chosen for harvesting a bone graft, usually the hip bone. She fills in any gaps after the upper jaw and nose have been moved using the previously harvested bone graft material. She places suction drains in the scalp to reduce bruising. short_description: Reconstruction midface, LeFort III (extra and intracranial) with forehead advancement (eg, mono bloc), requiring bone grafts (includes obtaining autografts); without LeFort I
lay_term: In a LeFort III midface surgery, the provider performs extensive reconstruction of the patient's facial bones, including advancing, or moving forward, the forehead, using microsurgery and bone grafting to correct deformities, acquired or congenital, such as Apert Syndrome. She frees any sensory nerves to the forehead from their bony canals. She repositions the bones in a predetermined fashion until the appropriate appearance is achieved. She advances the forehead in a mono bloc, or single piece, technique. She fills in any gaps after the upper jaw, forehead, zygomatic arch, and nose have been moved, using the previously harvested bone graft material. short_description: Reconstruction, bifrontal, superior-lateral orbital rims and lower forehead, advancement or alteration (eg, plagiocephaly, trigonocephaly, brachycephaly), with or without grafts (includes obtaining autografts) Notes: (For bifrontal craniotomy performed for craniosynostosis, use 61557)
lay_term: The provider performs extensive reconstruction of the bones of the upper face, over the eye sockets, including reshaping the forehead, and may use bone graft material obtained from another location in the patient’s body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a zigzag incision over the upper orbital area, above the eyes, and dissects down to the subgaleal plane. She gains access to the lateral wall of the orbit and uses a small burr drill to perform the initial craniotomy. She carefully separates the periosteal layers of the orbit and retracts the ocular globe, or the eye ball, with a malleable retractor. She performs orbital osteotomies as needed. She advances the forehead, bringing it forward to the correct position. She fills in any bony defects using autograft, bone graft material she obtains from another location on the patient, such as the hip. She checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes all incisions with layered sutures. short_description: Reconstruction, entire or majority of forehead and/or supraorbital rims; with grafts (allograft or prosthetic material)
lay_term: A provider reconstructs most or all of the forehead and or the supraorbital rims, the bony structure surrounding the eyes, with placement of prosthetic material or allograft, donor bone. He performs the reconstruction to repair forehead defects due to congenital malformations, cancer surgery, or trauma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the defect in the forehead and or supraorbital rim area using microdissection techniques. He uses surgical tools to reconstruct and or reshape the area. He applies the allograft and or applies a prosthesis and secures it in place. The provider then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called allogeneic graft and homograft. Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Congenital: Present at birth. Microdissection: Dissecting, or separating tissues and structures by cutting, with the use of very small instruments while viewing the surgical field through an operative microscope. Prosthetic: Artificial, man made; a device that functions like the structure it replaces. Supraorbital: Referring to the area above the orbit, the bony cavity that holds the eyes. Tips When the provider performs a cranioplasty with allografts on the frontal bone, report 21179 as it best describes this procedure. If autografts were used in the procedure, report 21180, Reconstruction, entire or majority of forehead and or supraorbital rims, with autograft, includes obtaining grafts. Avoid using 21299, Unlisted craniofacial and maxillofacial procedure, as you should always try to report a code that most closely describes the procedure performed. If no code is sufficiently close, however, and you must use an unlisted procedure code, you must append a special report to the claim providing sufficient documentation to identify the procedure. short_description: Reconstruction of orbital walls, rims, forehead, nasoethmoid complex following intra- and extracranial excision of benign tumor of cranial bone (eg, fibrous dysplasia), with multiple autografts (includes obtaining grafts); total area of bone grafting less than 40 sq cm
lay_term: The provider performs extensive reconstruction of the bones of the upper face, forehead, and nasal sinus area, using bone graft material obtained from another location in the patient’s body. She performs this procedure following the removal of a benign, or noncancerous, tumor of the skull. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the site chosen for harvesting a bone graft, usually the hip bone. She removes sufficient autograft and closes the wound. She then makes an incision over the tumor and accesses the bone using microdissection. She dissects the tumor away from surrounding tissues and uses surgical instruments to reconstruct the facial bones following the tumor excision. She fills in bony defects using the autograft material, up to 40 square cm in total. She checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes all incisions with layered sutures. Terminology Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Cranium: The skull; specifically, the portion of the skull that contains and protects the brain, consisting of the frontal, temporal, sphenoid, and ethmoid bones, plus two parietal bones and two temporal bones. Fibrous dysplasia: Condition characterized by the abnormal growth of fibrous tissue within a single or multiple bones, displacing normal bone tissue and resulting in distortion and weakness of the bone. Microdissection: Surgical technique employing a microscope to provide better visualization while dissecting, or separating, tissues and structures. Nasoethmoid complex: Bony structure consisting of the nasal bones and the ethmoid bone, one of the bones of the cranium, or skull, that form the base of the nasal cavity. Orbit: Bony cavity that holds the eyes; the orbital area is formed by seven bones, the frontal, lacrimal, ethmoid, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, and sphenoid bones. Tips Report 21182 only when the provider documents the use of autograft material of no more than 40 square cm. Read Less

lay_term: The provider performs surgical reconstruction of the midface to correct deformities of the bony structures in the face and cranium, or skull, using bone grafts harvested from the patient's own body to fill in defects. short_description: Reconstruction of mandibular rami, horizontal, vertical, C, or L osteotomy; with bone graft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: A provider performs surgical reconstruction of the perpendicular portions, or rami, of the mandible, or lower jaw, to correct facial deformities, often the result of trauma. She uses bone graft harvested from the patient's own body to fill in defects. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the site chosen for harvesting a bone graft, usually the hip bone. She removes sufficient autograft and closes the wound. She makes an incision along the jaw line, over the mandible, and or intraorally, through the mouth. She carries the incision down to the ramus of the mandible on one side of the jaw. She performs an osteotomy in an orientation that is horizontal, vertical, C shaped, or L shaped. She uses small burrs, both spherical and cylindrical in shape, to fracture the bone. She then repositions the bone and secures it in place. She applies the bone graft to fill in any defects and secures it in place. She repeats the procedure on the ramus of the opposite side of the jaw. She checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision with layered sutures. Terminology Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Burr drill: Surgical drill; also called a high speed burr. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Ramus: A structure that branches off, like a tree limb, such as a blood vessel, nerve, or a portion of a bone; plural is rami. Tips You should report 21194 when the reconstruction requires bone grafting. Code 21194 is inherently bilateral. However, for a unilateral procedure, modifier 52, Reduced services, may be reported, in addition to the surgical reconstruction code, to indicate that the service performed was partially reduced at the provider's discretion. Additionally, you may wish to check with your payers for more information concerning the reporting of unilateral procedures. If a provider applies a midface distractor in association with a procedure reported as 21194, it is a more intensive procedure from the provider's viewpoint. short_description: Reconstruction of mandibular rami and/or body, sagittal split; without internal rigid fixation
lay_term: A provider performs surgical reconstruction of the body of the mandible, or lower jaw, and or its perpendicular portions, or rami, to correct facial deformities, often the result of trauma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision along the jaw line, over the mandible, and or intraorally, through the mouth. She carries the incision down to the mandible and or to the ramus area of the mandible, on one side of the jaw. She performs a sagittal split osteotomy by dividing the jaw into anterior and posterior, or front and back, portions. She uses small burrs, both spherical and cylindrical in shape, to fracture the bone. She then repositions the bone and secures it in place. She repeats the procedure on the opposite side of the jaw. She checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision with layered sutures. Terminology Burr drill: Surgical drill; also called a high speed burr. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Ramus: A structure that branches off, similar to a tree limb, such as a blood vessel, nerve, or a portion of a bone; plural is rami. Sagittal split osteotomy: Surgical reconstruction of the mandible, or lower jaw, by dividing it on each side into front and back portions to enable realignment. Tips Code 21195 is inherently bilateral. However, for a unilateral procedure, modifier 52, Reduced services, may be reported, in addition to the surgical reconstruction code, to indicate that the service performed was partially reduced at the provider's discretion. Additionally, you may wish to check with your payers for more information concerning the reporting of unilateral procedures. Read Less

short_description: Osteotomy, maxilla, segmental (eg, Wassmund or Schuchard)
lay_term: A provider performs a maxillary osteotomy, incising the maxilla, or upper jaw, and moving portions of the bone to correct facial deformities, congenital or acquired. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision in the medial palatal area, or the roof of the mouth. She carries out an osteotomy, incising through the bone, and creates bony segments. She elevates the mucoperiosteum around the anterior, or frontward, portion of the incision and widely elevates the periosteum, the membrane covering the surface of the bone, along with its muscular insertions, in the direction of the infraorbital foramen and the root of the zygomatic process. She takes care to preserve the gingiva, or gum tissue, as she forms a spacious tunnel beneath the soft tissue of the cheek. She takes care to preserve the palatal vessels. She checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the gum incision with absorbable sutures. Terminology Congenital: Present at birth. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Infraorbital foramen: An opening, or foramen, in the orbit, the bony cavity that holds the eye. Longitudinal: In a lengthwise direction. Mucoperiosteum: Tissue formed from the periosteum, a membrane covering the surface of a bone, and the mucous membrane, a layer of endothelial cells that line the insides of body cavities and the insides of structures that open to the outside of the body, like the mouth; mucoperiosteum covers the hard palate, in the roof of the mouth. Schuchard, or Schuchardt, procedure: Surgical procedure in which portions of the back and sides of the maxilla, or upper jaw bone, are incised and repositioned; also known as a posterolateral segmental maxillary osteotomy; used to reduce a gap between the upper and lower jaw, correcting an open bite. Wassmund procedure: Surgical procedure in which a portion of the front part of the maxilla, or upper jaw bone, is incised and repositioned; also known as an anterior segmental maxillary osteotomy; used to reduce protruding gums. Zygomatic process: A projection, or protrusion, on the zygoma, or cheek bone. Tips Preauthorization is normally recommended for this procedure to alert the insurer when the procedure is performed for medically necessary reasons and not for cosmetic purposes. Read Less

short_description: Graft; rib cartilage, autogenous, to face, chin, nose or ear (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: The provider applies autogenous cartilage graft, taken from the patient’s own rib, to the face, including the chin, nose, or ear, to repair deformity due to fracture, injury, tumor resection, or congenital defect, such as saddle nose deformity. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the rib area at a site chosen for harvesting the cartilage graft. He removes sufficient autograft material and closes the wound. To repair a saddle nose deformity, he carves the rib graft into two pieces, a dorsal graft and a columellar strut, which are interdigitated, or interlocked, to recreate an intact L shaped strut, which provides the normal shape of the nose. Once the graft is in the correct position, the provider sutures the dome of the nose over the graft with a transdomal suture, or suture over the nasal tip, closing the wound. Terminology Autogenous tissue graft: Tissue harvested from the patient’s own body used to replace diseased, damaged, or missing tissue. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Columellar strut: A column shaped graft of cartilage used to support the nasal tip in a nasal reconstruction. Congenital: Present at birth. Rhinoplasty: Cosmetic surgery of the nose; nasal reconstruction. Tips In many cases, providers perform rib cartilage grafting for cosmetic purposes, and in these situations, most insurers do not reimburse this procedure. If your provider performs this service for medically necessary reasons and not for cosmetic purposes, be sure and get preauthorization to alert the insurer of the medical necessity of the procedure. Additional Info An external rhinoplasty approach allows exposure for efficient placement of grafts. A tip graft allows improved tip projection and definition. Read Less

guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline (For cranioplasty, see 21179, 21180 and 62120, 62140-62147) Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Arthroplasty, temporomandibular joint, with or without autograft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: A provider performs an arthroplasty, joint surgical reconstruction or replacement, of the temporomandibular joint, the hinge that connects the lower jaw to the temporal bone of the skull. He uses graft material he obtains from the patient’s own body to repair, reposition, or replace parts of the temporomandibular joint, or TMJ, to improve function of the jaw. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the joint area in front of the ear and exposes the fascial tissue layer to examine the TMJ capsule. He carefully examines the articular disk and the bony surfaces of the TMJ. If the disk is sufficiently healthy, he pulls the disk into a more normal position and sutures it in place. If the disk is abnormally stretched out, he excises a wedge of tissue from behind the disk and sutures the edges together. However, if the disk is damaged beyond repair, he excises the articular disk completely and fills the resulting space with autograft cartilage. He obtains autograft through a separate incision over the rib area. He removes sufficient autograft material and closes the wound. He then irrigates the joint, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Articular disk: An oval of flexible cartilage separating two bones that form a joint. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Temporomandibular joint, or TMJ: Union of the temporal bone, at the base of the cranium, and the mandible, the lower jaw bone. Read Less

short_description: Arthroplasty, temporomandibular joint, with prosthetic joint replacement
lay_term: A provider performs an arthroplasty, or joint replacement, of the temporomandibular joint, the hinge structure that connects the lower jaw to the temporal bone of the skull, to improve function of the jaw. He uses an artificial, or prosthetic, joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision along the ear and another incision along the jawline to expose the fascial tissue layer and examine the TMJ capsule. He uses microdissection to excise the condyle, or ball of the joint, on either side, as well as both fossae, or joint sockets. He replaces the joint on each side of the jaw with a prosthetic joint, normally made of titanium. He ensures proper fit and function and then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Microdissection: Dissecting, or separating tissues and structures by cutting, with the use of very small instruments while viewing the surgical field through an operative microscope. Prosthesis: An artificial, or man made, replacement for a body part. Temporomandibular joint, or TMJ: Union of the temporal bone, at the base of the cranium, and the mandible, the lower jaw bone. Titanium: Lightweight but extremely strong metal used in medical fixation devices and implants due to his durability and biocompatibility. Read Less

short_description: Reconstruction of mandibular condyle with bone and cartilage autografts (includes obtaining grafts) (eg, for hemifacial microsomia)
lay_term: A provider reconstructs the mandibular condyle, the rounded projection where the lower jaw connects to the skull, to treat facial deformity or jaw dysfunction, typically as a result of a condition present at birth, such as hemifacial microsomia. He uses graft material he obtains from the patient’s own body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the rib area at a site chosen for harvesting costochondral graft. He removes sufficient autograft material and closes the wound. He then makes an incision along the jawline and dissects through the surrounding tissue to reach the mandibular condyle. He prepares the bone graft and inserts it into the correct position on the condyle and secures it into place using screws or wires. He checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision with layered sutures. Terminology Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Costochondral: Referring to the rib bone and rib cartilage. Hemifacial microsomia: A common birth defect resulting in underdevelopment of a portion of the fact, usually involving the ear and jaw; also called craniofacial microsomia, branchial arch syndrome, and other names. Mandibular condyle: A rounded protrusion at the end of the ramus, or perpendicular extension, of the mandible, or lower jaw; functions as the ball of the temporomandibular joint, the union of the mandible with the temporal bone of the skull. short_description: Reconstruction of zygomatic arch and glenoid fossa with bone and cartilage (includes obtaining autografts)
lay_term: The provider reconstructs the zygomatic arch, which extends along the side or front of the skull beneath the eye socket, and the glenoid fossa, the cavity at the root of the zygomatic arch that holds the upper jaw in place, to treat injuries or deformities. He uses bone and cartilage graft material he obtains from the patient’s own body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the rib area at a site chosen for harvesting costochondral graft. He removes sufficient autograft material and closes the wound. He then makes an incision along the scalp from the vertex, or peak, of the skull to the helical root, where the ear joins the side of the head. He incises through the fascia to the zygoma. He incises the temporalis muscle fascia superior to, or above, the zygomatic arch and reduces, or realigns, the unstable bones. He dissects any damaged cartilage away from the injury to repair it. He then fits the autograft material into the space and secures it with wire. He irrigates the wound, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision with layered sutures. Terminology Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Costochondral: Referring to the rib bone and rib cartilage. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Glenoid fossa of mandible: Another name for the mandibular fossa, the cavity, or socket, that connects to the mandibular condyle, or ball of the temporomandibular joint, joining the mandible, or lower jaw bone, to the temporal bone of the skull; glenoid fossa also refers to the glenoid cavity of the scapula, part of the shoulder joint. Temporal muscle fascia: Fibrous connective tissue covering and protecting the temporalis muscle on the side of the head; the temporalis muscle is involved in mastication, or chewing. Zygoma: The cheekbone; also referred to as the zygomatic arch, mala, or malar area. Read Less

short_description: Periorbital osteotomies for orbital hypertelorism, with bone grafts; extracranial approach
lay_term: The providers performs periorbital osteotomies, incisions of the bones around the eye sockets, to treat orbital hypertelorism, a congenital disorder that results in an abnormal amount of space between the eyes. lay_term: The provider performs periorbital osteotomies, incisions of the bones around the eye sockets, to treat orbital hypertelorism, a congenital disorder that results in an abnormal amount of space between the eyes. He reshapes the bone structure of the forehead and uses bone grafts to fill in defects. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the site chosen for harvesting a bone graft, usually the hip bone. He removes sufficient autograft material and closes the wound. Alternatively, he uses donor bone graft. He then makes bicoronal and maxillary vestibular incisions. He creates a frontal craniotomy, incising the frontal bone of the skull, to access the orbit from inside of the patient's cranium, or skull. He uses a microsaw to cut into the orbits, the nasal bones, and the ethmoid bone. He realigns the bones into the correct anatomical position and secures them in place with wires. He shapes the bone graft material to fill in spaces that remain after repositioning the bones. He secures the grafts in place with wires or screws. He advances the frontal bone to bring it forward as he closes the craniotomy incision. He irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the remaining incisions in layers.
