If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic. Skull, facial bones, and temporomandibular joint.

short_description: Unlisted craniofacial and maxillofacial procedure
lay_term: Use 21299 to report craniofacial and maxillofacial procedures that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs a craniofacial and maxillofacial procedure that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Terminology Craniofacial: Referring to the cranium, or skull, and face. Maxillofacial: Related to the maxilla, or upper jaw, and the face. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes, and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis, and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of nasoethmoid fracture; without external fixation
lay_term: The provider reduces, or realigns, a fracture of the nasal and ethmoid bones, through a nasal incision to restore function and appearance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to gain access to the fracture site. He identifies the supraorbital and supratrochlear pedicles, the areas that contain the supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries, and releases them from their grooves. He elevates the orbital contents to allow the scalp flap to reflect, or drop, down to the nasal bridge. He dissects the medial orbital wall until he reaches all fracture segments. He identifies the medial canthal tendon and stabilizes it with a suture. He reduces, or realigns, the fracture, using small screws, wires, and or miniplates to hold it in place, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Canthal tendons: Fibrous bands that connect the orbicularis oculi muscle, which closes the eyelids, to the bony structure of the eye sockets. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Ethmoid bone: One of the bones of the cranium, or skull, located at the base of the nose; it is composed of three small bony plates. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body. Nasal septum: Thin wall that divides the inside of the nose into left and right nostrils; it is composed of cartilage and bone. Orbit: Bony cavity that holds the eyes; the orbital area is formed by seven bones, the frontal, lacrimal, ethmoid, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, and sphenoid bones. Supraorbital artery: A vessel in the head that supplies blood to structures on the face and scalp. Supratrochlear artery: A vessel in the head that supplies blood to the area of the forehead. short_description: Open treatment of complicated (eg, comminuted or involving posterior wall) frontal sinus fracture, via coronal or multiple approaches
lay_term: The provider repairs a complicated fracture of the bones of the frontal sinus, below the ridge of the brow, by accessing the fracture through one or more incisions in the corona, or crown of the head. He performs the procedure to repair damage that occurs through blunt force trauma or a crush injury. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes bicoronal incisions to expose the frontal sinus and investigates whether the patient suffered an injury to the nasofrontal duct, the opening that drains the frontal sinus into the nasal cavity, in addition to a frontal sinus fracture. The provider repairs the anterior table, or front portion of the sinus, typically grafting the segments with cancellous bone he harvests from the calvaria, the topmost portion of the skull. He reduces, or realigns, the sinus fracture and repairs any nasofrontal duct injury, if present. If he finds a dural tear, he repairs the dura, the tough membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord. In a fracture involving the posterior wall, he may cranialize the sinus, allowing the brain and dura to rest against the frontal wall of the sinus. He then checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Bicoronal incision: An incision across the scalp on the crown, or corona, of the head from one side to the other; used synonymously with coronal and bitemporal incision. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Comminuted fracture: A bone that is fractured, or broken, into 3 or more pieces. Frontal sinuses: One of four pairs of hollow chambers in the skull, connected to the nasal cavity and are part of the respiratory system; the frontal sinuses are located in the center of the forehead. short_description: Open treatment of nasomaxillary complex fracture (LeFort II type); with wiring and/or local fixation
lay_term: The provider repairs a nasomaxillary complex fracture to treat an injury of the bones in the nose and the maxilla, or upper jaw, to restore function and appearance. Sublabial: Below a labial, or lip shaped, structure. Zygomaticomaxillary buttress: The bony area formed by the maxilla, or upper jaw, and the zygomatic arch, or cheekbone, that gives shape to the face; also called the zygomaticomaxillary complex. short_description: Open treatment of orbital floor blowout fracture; transantral approach (Caldwell-Luc type operation)
lay_term: The provider repairs the floor of the orbit, the bony structure that holds the eyes, to restore function and appearance to the face after a blowout fracture, the result of blunt force trauma. He accesses the orbital floor through an incision in the mouth. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision inferior to, or behind, the buccogingival sulcus, the space between the gum and cheek. He exposes a wide mucosal band. He uses a periosteal elevator to strip the anterior maxillary wall of its periosteum and creates a Caldwell Luc antrostomy, an opening through the maxillary sinus cavity. He uses surgical tools to increase the diameter of the antrostomy and provide access to the orbital floor. The provider strips the mucosa from the maxillary antrum and repairs the orbital fracture. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Antrostomy: Creation of a surgical opening in a cavity, such as a sinus. Blowout fracture: Fracture, or breakage, of the bones of the orbit, the bony cavity that contains the eyes; in a blowout fracture, the force of the trauma literally blows out the walls of the orbit. Caldwell Luc type operation: Surgical procedure in which a maxillary sinus is accessed through an oral incision. Maxilla: The upper jaw bone. Maxillary sinuses: A pair of hollow chambers in the skull, located on either side of the nose, that function as part of the respiratory system. Mucosa: Another name for mucous membrane, the layer of endothelial cells that line the insides of body cavities and the insides of structures that open to the outside of the body, like the mouth, rectum, etc. Orbit: Bony cavity that holds the eyes; the orbital area is formed by seven bones, the frontal, lacrimal, ethmoid, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, and sphenoid bones. Periosteal elevator: Surgical tool used to lift and separate tissue flaps, in particular the periosteum, or membrane covering a bone. Periosteum: Membrane covering the surface of a bone. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of orbital floor blowout fracture; combined approach
lay_term: The provider repairs the floor of the orbit, the bony structure that holds the eyes, to restore function and appearance to the face after a blowout fracture, the result of blunt force trauma. He accesses the orbital floor through incisions in different areas. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts corneal shields to protect the eyes. He places soft tissue retractors and visualizes the anterior maxillary wall. He enters the antrum, or cavity, of the maxillary sinus and visualizes the orbit floor. He then makes a transconjunctival incision and dissects through the tissue to the floor of the orbit to allow definition of the margins of the fracture. short_description: Open treatment of palatal or maxillary fracture (LeFort I type); complicated (comminuted or involving cranial nerve foramina), multiple approaches
lay_term: A provider treats a complicated fracture of the roof of the mouth or upper jaw bone, typically caused by blunt force trauma, through incisions in different areas. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes gingivolabial, or gum and lip, incisions through the oral mucosa to the apex, or top, of the sulcus and down to alveolar bone from one molar region to the other. In addition, he makes subciliary or transconjunctival incisions to better visualize the fracture and any involved cranial nerves as they pass through the foramina, or openings in the skull. He uses a periosteal elevator to separate the periosteum and expose the fracture lines, the nasomaxillary and zygomaticomaxillary buttresses, the piriform aperture, and the premaxilla and nasal spine. He then shapes miniplates to fit the fractured area and secures them with screws. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. short_description: Open treatment of craniofacial separation (LeFort III type); with wiring and/or internal fixation
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture resulting in separation of the cranium, or skull, from the facial bones, to repair injuries to the nasal bridge or upper jaw following severe trauma to the face. He accesses the fracture through an incision and applies wire or other fixation to hold the fracture in place as it heals. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places arch bars on the upper and lower teeth. He uses wire to secure the bars to the teeth and confirms intermaxillary fixation. He makes a coronal incision to expose the fractured bones and reflects a scalp flap down to just above the zygoma, or cheekbone, to expose the zygomatic arch and visualize the fracture. He reduces any fractured bones and applies internal fixation using plates, screws, and or wires to stabilize the fractures. The provider irrigates the wounds and closes the incisions. Terminology Arch bar: Device used to provide stabilization of the jaw or teeth following oral surgery; arch bars follow the natural arch, or curve of the teeth. Coronal incision: An incision across the scalp on the crown, or corona, of the head from one side to the other; used synonymously with bicoronal and bitemporal incision. Craniofacial: Referring to the cranium, or skull, and face. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Intermaxillary fixation: Method of stabilizing facial bone fractures by wiring the maxilla and mandible, or upper and lower jaws, together to prevent movement; also called mandibulomaxillary fixation. LeFort fracture: Facial bone fracture classification system based on the plane of fracture and increasing level of complexity; type I is horizontal through the maxilla, or upper jaw; type II is pyramidal, with the maxilla separated from the nasal skeleton; type III involves separation of the maxilla, zygoma, or cheekbone, and the nasal skeleton. Maxilla: The upper jaw bone. Zygomatic arch: The cheekbone; also referred to as the zygoma, mala, or malar area. Read Less

Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. short_description: Open treatment of mandibular fracture with external fixation
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the mandible, or lower jaw bone, to repair damage caused by blunt force trauma to the face. He accesses the fracture through an incision and applies an external fixation device to secure the fracture in place while it heals. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the mandible and dissects through the fascia and down to the fracture site. He reduces, or realigns, the fractured bones back into their proper positions. He then applies wires and or screws to the fractured bones to hold them in position. He attaches an external splint to the screws or wires. The provider irrigates the wound and closes the incision. Terminology Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of complicated mandibular fracture by multiple surgical approaches including internal fixation, interdental fixation, and/or wiring of dentures or splints
lay_term: The provider treats a complicated fracture of the mandible, or lower jaw bone, to repair damage caused by blunt force trauma to the face. He accesses the fracture through multiple incisions and applies a fixation device to secure the fracture while it heals. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes incisions in front of the ear and along the jawbone. He then dissects down to the fractured bones. He reduces, or realigns, the mandibular fracture and places wires and screws along the upper and lower arches to stabilize the fracture. He attaches metal wires around the teeth and secures them to arch bars for fixation. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Arch bar: Device used to provide stabilization of the jaw or teeth following oral surgery; arch bars follow the natural arch, or curve of the teeth. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Interdental: Between the teeth. Interdental fixation device: Medical appliance that is fixed, or connected, to the teeth to hold the device in place. Tips When there are multiple fractures, it can be difficult to distinguish between 21465 and 21470, Open treatment of complicated mandibular fracture by multiple surgical approaches including internal fixation, interdental fixation, and or wiring of dentures or splints, when the provider uses multiple approaches to access a single, complicated fracture site. If he accesses multiple fracture sites, choose between 21465 and other appropriate codes such as 21461, Open treatment of mandibular fracture, without interdental fixation, or 21462, Open treatment of mandibular fracture, with interdental fixation. If the provider treats two complicated sites, however, report 21470 twice and append modifier 52, Reduced services, to the second code because he only wires the patient's jaw shut once. But if you report more than one code for less complicated fractures, such as 21462, Open treatment of mandibular fracture, with interdental fixation, in the case of an angle fracture, along with 21465 for the condyle fracture, append modifier 51, Multiple procedures, to the second code instead. short_description: Closed treatment of temporomandibular dislocation; complicated (eg, recurrent requiring intermaxillary fixation or splinting), initial or subsequent
lay_term: The provider treats dislocations of the temporomandibular joint, which causes the jaw to lock in an open position and causes significant pain and discomfort. He manipulates it back into its proper location and then applies a fixation device to prevent movement of the jaw during healing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider moves the mandibular condyle back into the correct position by pulling the lower jaw downward and moving the chin upward. This frees the condyle, and he then guides it back into its socket. He then places arch bars on the teeth and secures wires between the bars to fix the jaw in position. The provider may advise the patient regarding a modified diet to limit jaw movement and assist in healing. Terminology Arch bar: Device used to provide stabilization of the jaw or teeth following oral surgery; arch bars follow the natural arch, or curve of the teeth. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Intermaxillary fixation: Method of stabilizing facial bone fractures by wiring the maxilla and mandible, or upper and lower jaws, together to prevent movement; also called mandibulomaxillary fixation. Mandibular condyle: A rounded protrusion at the end of the ramus, or perpendicular extension, of the mandible, the lower jaw; functions as the ball of the temporomandibular joint, the union of the mandible with the temporal bone of the skull. Temporomandibular joint, or TMJ: Union of the temporal bone, at the base of the cranium, and the mandible, the lower jaw bone. Temporomandibular joint disorder, or TMD: A condition of the temporomandibular joint, which connects the lower jaw to the skull, characterized primarily by pain and discomfort but may also be accompanied by swelling, difficulty chewing, or jaw locking, clicking, or popping; the cause is not well defined but felt to be muscular in origin; commonly but erroneously referred to as TMJ, which stands only for the name of the joint and not the disorder. Tips If your provider fits and makes his own appliances to treat TMJ disorder, you may be able to bill for the devices in addition to reporting 21485. Check with your carrier regarding its reimbursement for TMJ appliances. Read Less

short_description: Radical resection of tumor (eg, sarcoma), soft tissue of neck or anterior thorax; less than 5 cm
lay_term: The provider performs an extensive excision of a tumor, or mass, in the soft tissues in the neck or anterior thorax, suspected to be malignant, or cancerous, such as a sarcoma. He excises the surrounding tissues along with the mass, with the diameter of the tumor and its margins measuring less than 5 cm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the area of the tumor, raises subplatysmal flaps, and isolates the tumor. He divides any muscles surrounding the mass and dissects the deep aspect of the tumor and any attached muscle free of the fascia, taking a margin of fibrofatty tissue as he removes the tumor from the muscle and prepares it for pathologic analysis. The provider excises a wide margin of additional tissue to ensure that no pathology, or diseased tissue, remains in the surrounding structures, irrigates the wound, places a drain, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Fibrofatty: Containing both fibrous and fatty tissue. Radical resection: Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Sarcoma: A malignant, or cancerous, tumor of connective tissue origin, that occurs in the bone or soft tissues anywhere in the body. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Subplatysmal: The area below the platysma muscle, which covers the lower face and neck down to the collarbone area. Thorax: Chest. Tips This code is for radical resection of tumors of musculoskeletal origin, such as sarcomas. Wide margins of excision beyond the tumor dimensions are necessary to report this code. Compare with 21558, Radical resection of tumor, e.g., sarcoma, soft tissue of neck or anterior thorax, 5 cm or greater. Read Less

short_description: Excision of chest wall tumor involving rib(s), with plastic reconstruction; without mediastinal lymphadenectomy
lay_term: The provider excises a tumor of the chest wall that involves the ribs, which creates defects that need reconstruction; he reconstructs the chest wall using myocutaneous flaps and bone grafts or prosthetic materials for the ribs. He does not remove lymph nodes in the upper chest area. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia, the provider accesses the tumor through an incision in the chest wall. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissues, fascia, and muscle. He excises the tumor in its entirety along with surrounding soft tissues and adjacent ribs above and below the tumor. Following the excision, the provider reconstructs the chest wall using myocutaneous flaps taken from the pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, rectus abdominis, or serratus anterior muscles. Autogenous rib grafts or prosthetic materials such as Prolene® or Marlex® mesh and acrylic fiber are used to repair the bone defect. He controls bleeding with electrocautery or ligation and closes the surgical wound with layered sutures. He may place a drain into the depths of the wound and bring it out through the skin for drainage and better healing of the wound. Terminology Autologous (or autogenous) tissue graft: Tissue that a provider harvests from the patient's own body and uses to replace diseased, damaged, or missing tissue; also referred to as an autograft. Chondroblastoma: A very rare malignancy of cartilages that occur more commonly in the epiphyses of the long bones of the extremities due to abnormal growth of the chondroblasts. Chondrosarcoma: A malignant neoplasm of the cartilages and bone, which can originate in the intramedullary canal as well as in the peripheral region of the bones, particularly in the metaphysis of femur, humerus, pelvic bone, ribs, sternum, scapula, and spine; they can be highly metastatic and commonly spread to the lymph nodes. Fibrosarcoma: A malignancy (cancer) that originates in fibroblasts (the cells that produce connective tissues), most commonly in the bones, especially in the long bones of the extremities and the pelvic bones. Lymphadenopathy: Swelling and enlargement of the lymph nodes due to disease or inflammation. Mediastinal lymph nodes: The lymph nodes located in the part of the chest that lies between the sternum or the breastbone and the spine; this is the area that contains the heart, windpipe, and large blood vessels. Myocutaneous flap: Tissue flap consisting of skin, subcutaneous tissue, fat, and muscle; frequently used for breast reconstruction and repair of irradiated wounds; also called musculocutaneous flap. Osteosarcoma: The most common form of bone cancer that mostly occurs in the metaphyseal regions of long bones such as the femur and humerus, although it can occur in other bones. Reconstructive surgery (plastic reconstruction): Surgery usually performed to improve function, ability, and appearance of structures whose appearance or functionality have been adversely affected by surgery, trauma, disease, or congenital or acquired defects. Tips For excision of a chest wall tumor involving the ribs with plastic reconstruction when mediastinal lymphadenopathy is present, see 21603. For excision of chest wall tumor including ribs, without plastic reconstruction, see 21601. Do not report 21601, 21602, or 21603 in conjunction with 32503 or 32504 for resection of an apical lung tumor; chest resection, chest reconstruction, and rib resection are included in both these codes, and chest wall reconstruction is included in 32504. Most health insurance policies cover reconstructive plastic surgery, as opposed to cosmetic plastic surgery, although coverage may vary. Check with the payer to determine their coverage and requirements for submitting codes for reimbursement for plastic reconstructive procedures. Additional Info A tumor of the chest wall may manifest itself in the form of a lump or swelling, sometimes accompanied by pain. The tumors may be found on the sternum or the ribs. Such a tumor can be primary or secondary. The primary method of diagnosis of a chest wall tumor includes radiological diagnostic procedures such as X–ray, CT, or MRI of the region. Malignancy and metastatic characteristics are established through pathological evaluation of the biopsied tissue samples. The available treatment options include surgical excision of the tumor or the combination of surgery and chemotherapy/radiation therapy. For tumors of the rib cage, partial ribs above and below the tumor must be removed. Secondary tumors are always found to be malignant. Benign tumors don't cause major health concerns unless they cause discomfort or start affecting the adjacent organs such as the lungs or heart. Malignant tumors are always a cause of concern and can be life–threatening. The most common type of malignant chest wall tumor is the chondrosarcoma that develops in the ribs or sometimes from the sternum. Osteosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, chondroblastoma, etc. are some other types of malignant tumors in the chest wall. Read Less

short_description: Costotransversectomy (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider removes a piece of rib and the transverse process of the vertebra, or back bone, to which it connects, to relieve back pain due to compression of spinal nerves. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the rib to be excised. He divides the paravertebral muscles horizontally. He clears the costotransverse joints and transverse processes of their muscle attachments. He incises the periosteum of the rib and strips it from the costotransverse joint. He cuts the rib from the joint with a bone cutting tool, severs the ligaments of the costotransverse joint, and removes the rib. He accesses the intervertebral foramen by removing the transverse process with bone cutting tools and exposes the lateral surface of the vertebral body, or main portion of the vertebra. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, and places drainage tubes. He removes any instruments and closes the incision in layers. Lateral: Furthest from the middle of the body. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Paravertebral muscles: Muscles surrounding the vertebrae, the interlocking bones that form the spine. Periosteum: Membrane covering the surface of a bone. Transverse process: One of the bony projections on either side of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones that form the spine. Read Less

lay_term: A provider incises the muscle tissue around the hyoid bone, which supports the tongue, and suspends, or attaches it, to another structure for support. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the hyoid and dissects through the tissue to visualize the bone. He removes the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscle attachments at the top and front of body of the hyoid bone. He divides the insertion of the stylohyoid ligament onto the lesser cornu, or smaller arms of the hyoid. He then fixes the hyoid bone to the lamina of the thyroid cartilage, or Adam’s apple, with sutures and passes them through the upper aspect of the thyroid cartilage and around the body of the hyoid bone. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, inserts a drainage tube, removes any instruments, and closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Hyoid bone: A small bone at the base of the lower jaw that is shaped like the letter U and serves to support the tongue to facilitate speech and swallowing; it is the only bone in the human body that does not connect to any other bone and is instead connected only through muscle tissue. Myotomy: Surgical incision of a muscle. Obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA: Condition occurring during sleep in which breathing stops intermittently for brief periods, disrupting the sleep cycle and resulting in daytime sleepiness, due to obstruction, narrowing, or incompetence of the airway. Stylohyoid ligament: A fibrous band that originates from the styloid process on the skull, a bony projection next to the ear, and attaches to the lesser cornu, or smaller arm, of the hyoid bone. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline (For superficial wound, see Integumentary System section under Repair-Simple) Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. short_description: Division of scalenus anticus; without resection of cervical rib
lay_term: A provider divides the scalenus anticus muscle, at the side of the neck, to treat scalenus anticus syndrome, a painful condition due to pressure of this muscle on the surrounding nerves. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the neck over the scalene muscle. He dissects through tissue to the tendon of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and its attachment to the clavicle, or collarbone. He divides the attachment and reflects, or pulls back, the overlying muscle, exposing the scalenus anticus muscle and the phrenic nerve. He dissects the muscle from the phrenic nerve and divides the muscular fibers. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Phrenic nerve: A nerve that passes from the neck to the chest, transmitting signals to the diaphragm, the muscular structure that contracts to permit inflation of the lungs. Scalenus anticus muscle: A deep muscle in the neck, residing behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle; it bends and tilts the neck and assists with inspiration, or taking a breath. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: A large muscle in the neck; it rotates the head, bends the neck, and assists with inspiration, or taking a breath. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. short_description: Division of sternocleidomastoid for torticollis, open operation; without cast application Notes: (For transection of spinal accessory and cervical nerves, see 63191, 64722)
lay_term: The provider divides the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the neck to treat torticollis, a condition that causes a stiff neck and muscle spasms that make the head tilt to one side. He does not apply a cast. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision superior to, or above, the medial end of the clavicle, or collar bone. He exposes the sternocleidomastoid muscle. He makes an incision into the tendon sheath and draws the tendon outside of the wound and cuts the ends. He confirms that no remaining contracted muscle exists. He confirms restoral of the patient's neck movement. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Cervical nerves: Eight pairs of nerves branching off from the spinal cord; they carry signals to specific muscles in the upper body; enumerated C1 through C8 and named for the cervical vertebra, or neck bone, that it passes over. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body. Spinal accessory nerves: The eleventh cranial nerve pair; they carries signals from the brain to the muscles in the neck, permitting tilting and rotation of the head. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: A large muscle in the neck; it rotates the head, bends the neck, and assists with inspiration, or taking a breath. Tendon sheath: Covering surrounding a tendon. Read Less

short_description: Division of sternocleidomastoid for torticollis, open operation; with cast application
lay_term: The provider divides the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the neck to treat torticollis, a condition that causes a stiff neck and muscle spasms that make the head tilt to one side. He applies a cast to hold the neck in place. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision superior to, or above, the medial end of the clavicle, or collar bone. He exposes the sternocleidomastoid muscle. He makes an incision into the tendon sheath and draws the tendon outside of the wound and cuts the ends. He confirms that no remaining contracted muscle exists. He confirms restoral of the patient's neck movement. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. He applies casting material to limit patient movement during healing. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body. Spinal accessory nerves: The eleventh cranial nerve pair; they carries signals from the brain to the muscles in the neck, permitting tilting and rotation of the head. Sternocleidomastoid muscle: A large muscle in the neck; it rotates the head, bends the neck, and assists with inspiration, or taking a breath. Tendon sheath: Covering surrounding a tendon. Read Less

lay_term: The provider performs an excision procedure for a soft tissue malignant tumor, such as a sarcoma, from the back or flank. The excision of the tumor is performed in an extensive manner, not being limited to the dimensions of the tumor itself but expanding to its surrounding area/anatomical structures suspected for involvement. The diameter of the tumor and the margins required measure less than 5cm. Explanation After administration of proper anesthesia and the usual prep and drape of the operative site is performed, a curvilinear incision is made around the tumor site, mostly in line with the skin creases. Incision is further extended deep and around the tumor. Fascial, subfascial, and/or muscle flaps may be raised to adequately expose the underlying anatomy. Neurovascular structures in that area are identified and preserved. Once the tumor is well localized, a sharp scalpel is used to dissect the tumor from the surrounding tissue margin, and the tumor is removed. To rule out further malignancy, an additional surrounding wide area of margin is also dissected and removed. After satisfactory radical removal of the fascial tumor along with the appropriate surrounding margin from the back or flank, the incision is repaired in the layered fashion. A total excision diameter of less than 5 cm is reportable with this code. Terminology Radical resection of soft tissue tumor: Surgical removal of the tumor as well as wide margins of surrounding tissue. Sarcomas: Malignant tumors that can involve bony tissues as well as soft tissues such as bone, cartilage, joint synovium, fat, muscle, tendons, nerves, etc., and originate in the soft tissues. Tips This code is for radical resection of tumors of musculoskeletal origin, such as sarcomas. Wide margins of excision beyond the tumor dimensions are necessary to report this code. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). lay_term: A provider excises portions of a thoracic vertebra, one of the interlocking bones in the upper back, to correct kyphosis, an abnormal curvature of the spine. He performs the bony excision, or osteotomy, in a three column approach, removing bone from the back and both sides, or columns, of the vertebra. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the upper back over the target vertebra. He dissects down through the tissues to expose the vertebra in question. He performs a laminectomy and then a facetectomy on the vertebra to provide better exposure and decompression, or relief of pressure from adjoining vertebrae. The provider resects, or removes, the pedicle on one side of the vertebra and applies bone wax to seal the bony surfaces. He retracts the nerve root while resecting a wedge of vertebral body. He then repeats the pedicle and wedge resection procedures on the opposite side of the vertebra. He then repositions and stabilizes the spine to correct the deformity and assesses it with intraoperative imaging. The provider irrigates the area, places a drain, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Facetectomy: Surgical excision of a facet, an area of a bone characterized by its smooth surface. Laminectomy: Surgical excision of the lamina, one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Nerve root: Portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system; origin of a nerve. Pedicle: A bony tube running through either side of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones in the back; the sides of the pedicle function as the walls of the spinal canal, protecting the spinal cord. Subtraction procedure: Excision or removal of a structure. Tips If a provider performs a spinal osteotomy on multiple thoracic vertebrae, report 22206 for the initial level. For each additional vertebra, report 22208, Osteotomy of spine, posterior or posterolateral approach, 3 columns, 1 vertebral segment, e.g., pedicle and vertebral body subtraction, each additional vertebral segment; list separately in addition to code for primary procedure. Note that because 22208 is a designated add–on code, there is no need to add modifiers. Read Less

lay_term: The provider incises a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine, in three areas and removes a wedge of bone to change the alignment of the spinal column. short_description: Osteotomy of spine, posterior or posterolateral approach, 1 vertebral segment; cervical
lay_term: The provider incises a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine, in three areas and removes a wedge of bone to change the alignment of the spinal column. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the skin overlying the affected vertebra. Pedicle: A bony tube running through either side of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones in the back; the sides of the pedicle function as the walls of the spinal canal, protecting the spinal cord. short_description: Osteotomy of spine, posterior or posterolateral approach, 1 vertebral segment; thoracic
lay_term: The provider performs an osteotomy, a bony incision, of a thoracic vertebra, one of the bones in the upper back, to realign the spine and correct spinal deformities. He makes the incision in the posterior, or back, portion of the vertebra, or posterolaterally, from the back and side. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the skin overlying the affected vertebra. He dissects down through the muscle and fascia to expose the spinous process and lamina of the central vertebra in question and removes them. He then removes facets, pedicles, and lateral bone to protect the nerve roots, and undercuts the laminae above and below to protect the dura and central neural elements, or spinal cord. He then realigns the spine. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Dura mater: The outer fibrous membrane just underneath the skull, the toughest of three membranes or meninges that protect the brain and spinal cord. Facet: An area of a bone characterized by its smooth surface. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Lamina: Thin layer on the surface of a bone; one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Nerve root: Portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system; origin of a nerve. Pedicle: A bony tube running through either side of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones in the back; the sides of the pedicle function as the walls of the spinal canal, protecting the spinal cord. Spinous process: Bony projection on the back of each vertebral bone. Tips Decompression of the spinal cord, cauda equina, and or single or multiple nerve roots is implied in osteotomies and the codes for osteotomies are inclusive of these. Osteotomy procedures entail removing a piece of the vertebra to correct spinal alignment; these codes replace laminectomy, laminotomy, and diskectomy procedures and should not be reported at the same levels. short_description: Osteotomy of spine, posterior or posterolateral approach, 1 vertebral segment; lumbar
lay_term: The provider performs an osteotomy, a bony incision, of a lumbar vertebra, one of the bones in the lower back, to realign the spine and correct spinal deformities. He makes the incision in the posterior, or back, portion of the vertebra, or posterolaterally, from the back and side. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision into the skin overlying the affected vertebra. He dissects down through the muscle and fascia to expose the spinous process and lamina of the central vertebra in question and removes them. He then removes facets, pedicles, and lateral bone to protect the nerve roots, and undercuts the laminae above and below to protect the dura and central neural elements, or spinal cord. He then realigns the spine. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Dura mater: The outer fibrous membrane just underneath the skull, the toughest of three membranes or meninges that protect the brain and spinal cord. Facet: An area of a bone characterized by its smooth surface. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Lamina: Thin layer on the surface of a bone; one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Nerve root: Portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system; origin of a nerve. Pedicle: A bony tube running through either side of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones in the back; the sides of the pedicle function as the walls of the spinal canal, protecting the spinal cord. Spinous process: Bony projection on the back of each vertebral bone. Tips Report 22214 when the provider performs an osteotomy on one vertebral segment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin overlying the affected vertebra and dissects down through the muscle and fascia to expose the lamina and intervertebral disk space. He reflects soft tissues subperiosteally from the adjacent vertebrae and uses bone cutting instruments to remove the adjacent disk material. He excises a wedge–shaped piece of bone from the vertebral body at its midportion. He then realigns the spine. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Diskectomy: Surgical excision of an intervertebral disk. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Intervertebral disk: Cushion of cartilage material separating two vertebrae. Lamina: Thin layer on the surface of a bone; one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Lumbar spine: Lower back, containing vertebrae enumerated L1 through L5. Nerve root: Portion of a nerve where it connects to the central nervous system; origin of a nerve. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Subperiosteal: Below the periosteum, the membrane covering the surface of a bone. Thoracic spine: Upper and middle back, containing vertebrae enumerated T1 through T12. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. Vertebral body: Main or largest part of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Tips Report this code when the provider performs an osteotomy on one vertebral segment. If he addresses additional segments, report add on code +22226. Decompression of the spinal cord, cauda equina, and or single or multiple nerve roots is implied in osteotomies and the codes for osteotomies are inclusive of these. Osteotomy procedures entail removing a piece of the vertebrae to correct spinal alignment. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline To report arthrodesis, see codes 22590-22632. (Report in addition to code[s] for the definitive procedure with modifier 51.) To report instrumentation procedures, see 22840-22855, 22859. (Report in addition to code[s] for the definitive procedure[s].) Do not append modifier 62 to spinal instrumentation codes 22840-22848, 22850, 22852, 22853, 22854, 22859. To report bone graft procedures, see 20930-20938. (Report in addition to code[s] for the definitive procedure[s].) Do not append modifier 62 to bone graft codes 20900-20938. For the following codes, when two surgeons work together as primary surgeons performing distinct part(s) of an anterior spine osteotomy, each surgeon should report his/her distinct operative work by appending modifier 62 to the procedure code. In this situation, modifier 62 may be appended to the procedure code(s) 22210-22214, 22220-22224 and, as appropriate, to associated additional segment add-on code(s) 22216, 22226 as long as both surgeons continue to work together as primary surgeons. Spinal osteotomy procedures are reported when a portion(s) of the vertebral segment(s) is cut and removed in preparation for re-aligning the spine as part of a spinal deformity correction. For excision of an intrinsic lesion of the vertebra without deformity correction, see 22100-22116. For decompression of the spinal cord and/or nerve roots, see 63001-63308. The three columns are defined as anterior (anterior two-thirds of the vertebral body), middle (posterior third of the vertebral body and the pedicle), and posterior (articular facets, lamina, and spinous process). Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Open treatment and/or reduction of odontoid fracture(s) and or dislocation(s) (including os odontoideum), anterior approach, including placement of internal fixation; without grafting
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture or dislocation of the odontoid, the uppermost bone in the neck, in an open procedure. He makes an incision in the neck, restores normal alignment, and inserts screws or wires to secure the fracture while healing takes place. He does not apply a bone graft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the anterior cervical spine and dissects through the tracheoesophageal tissue and the carotid sheath to visualize the fracture. He dissects the prevertebral space to expose the cervical disk space in question. He dissects the longus colli muscles laterally and places a retractor system. He makes an incision on the anulus and drills down the anterior superior, or front and top, margin of the vertebral body to expose an entry point. The provider drills a pilot hole through the vertebral body, across the fracture line, into the odontoid fragment, using fluoroscopy to confirm placement. He places a screw along the pilot hole and confirms that the fracture is stabilized. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body or a structure. Anulus: A ring; a dense ring of fibers surrounding the openings or ostia between the atria and ventricles. Carotid sheath: Fibrous and connective tissue, or fascia, that encloses the portion of the neck that contains vascular structures. Cervical spine: Neck, containing vertebrae enumerated C1 through C7. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Longus colli muscle: A muscle in the neck located in the prevertebral space. Odontoid process: The first cervical vertebra, or C1, one of the interlocking bones in the neck; it arises as a bony projection from the top of the ring shaped axis, or second cervical vertebra, and provides a pivot point for the skull; also called the dens, the peg, and the atlas. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Os odontoideum: A congenital abnormality in which the odontoid, the first cervical vertebra, is not fused to the second cervical vertebra. Prevertebral space: An area in the neck in front of the vertebrae, or neck bones. Retractor: Surgical instrument used to retract, or hold back, wound edges or deeper tissues to give better visualization and access to the provider performing surgery. Tracheoesophageal: Referring to the trachea, or windpipe, and esophagus, or digestive tube. Vertebral body: Main or largest part of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Tips Odontoid fractures are the most common cervical spine fractures and are typically the result of trauma. Read Less

lay_term: The provider repairs a fracture or dislocation of the odontoid, or first cervical vertebra, the uppermost neck bone, from its normal attachment to the second cervical vertebra. The provider accesses the odontoid through an incision in the front of the neck. He uses internal fixation and bone grafting to repair the vertebra. Odontoid fractures, the most common cervical spine fractures, typically result from trauma to the neck. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the neck, over the anterior cervical spine. He dissects through the tissues around the structures in the neck to visualize the fracture or dislocated segment. He dissects the prevertebral space, the area in front of the vertebrae, to expose the cervical disk space in question. He dissects the muscles and inserts a retractor system that spreads the tissues to provide better visualization of the fracture. He makes an incision on the annulus, the covering of the intervertebral disk, and drills down through the vertebral body, or main portion of the vertebra, to expose an entry point. He drills a pilot hole through the vertebral body, across the fracture line, and into the odontoid fragment. He uses fluoroscopy to confirm placement. He places a screw along the pilot hole and confirms that the fracture is stabilized. He then places a bone graft on the odontoid process surface and screws it into place. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. lay_term: The provider treats a fracture or dislocation of a lumbar vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the lower back, in an open procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the affected vertebra and dissects through the fascia and muscle to visualize the fractured or dislocated segment.
