short_description: Percutaneous vertebroplasty (bone biopsy included when performed), 1 vertebral body, unilateral or bilateral injection, inclusive of all imaging guidance; cervicothoracic
lay_term: The provider performs cervicothoracic vertebroplasty, or the surgical repair of a fractured vertebra in the cervicothoracic (neck and upper back) spine, usually involving the injection of bone cement. The provider commonly performs this procedure to treat osteoporotic compression fractures in patients where conservative treatment fails. He may also perform a bone biopsy for diagnostic purposes. The procedure takes place under imaging guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs percutaneous vertebroplasty that involves an injection through the skin into the cervicothoracic area of a substance such as methyl methacrylate, a type of acrylic cement that is useful to fuse fracture fragments or bone cement into a cervicothoracic vertebral body lesion. He performs this injection under imaging guidance, either fluoroscopy or computed tomography. The provider may inject one or both sides of the vertebra. He may also perform a bone biopsy by removing bone tissue for laboratory analysis while he is performing the vertebroplasty procedure. Terminology Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Computed tomography (CT): An imaging procedure in which an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors rotate around a patient and produce a tomogram, a computer–generated three–dimensional image of the inside of an object from a large series of cross–sectional two–dimensional X–ray images taken around a single axis of rotation; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. Vertebroplasty: Surgical repair of a fractured vertebra, usually involving the injection of bone cement. Tips For each additional vertebral body, report add–on code 22512. For the same procedure on the lumbosacral (lower) spine, see 22511. Read Less

The provider commonly performs this procedure to treat osteoporotic compression fractures in patients where conservative treatment fails. He may also perform a bone biopsy for diagnostic purposes. The procedure takes place under imaging guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs percutaneous vertebroplasty that involves an injection through the skin into the lumbosacral area, of a substance such as methyl methacrylate, a type of acrylic cement that is useful to fuse fracture fragments or bone cement into a lumbosacral vertebral body lesion. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Codes 22510, 22511, 22512, 22513, 22514, 22515 describe procedures for percutaneous vertebral augmentation that include vertebroplasty of the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral spine and vertebral augmentation of the thoracic and lumbar spine. For the purposes of reporting 22510, 22511, 22512, 22513, 22514, 22515, "vertebroplasty" is the process of injecting a material (cement) into the vertebral body to reinforce the structure of the body using image guidance. "Vertebral augmentation" is the process of cavity creation followed by the injection of the material (cement) under image guidance. For 0200T and 0201T, "sacral augmentation (sacroplasty)" refers to the creation of a cavity within a sacral vertebral body followed by injection of a material to fill that cavity. Supplies may be reported separately. Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Codes 22510, 22511, 22512, 22513, 22514, 22515 describe procedures for percutaneous vertebral augmentation that include vertebroplasty of the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral spine and vertebral augmentation of the thoracic and lumbar spine. For the purposes of reporting 22510, 22511, 22512, 22513, 22514, 22515, "vertebroplasty" is the process of injecting a material (cement) into the vertebral body to reinforce the structure of the body using image guidance. "Vertebral augmentation" is the process of cavity creation followed by the injection of the material (cement) under image guidance. For 0200T and 0201T, "sacral augmentation (sacroplasty)" refers to the creation of a cavity within a sacral vertebral body followed by injection of a material to fill that cavity. The procedure codes are inclusive of bone biopsy, when performed, and imaging guidance necessary to perform the procedure. Use one primary procedure code and an add-on code for additional levels. When treating the sacrum, sacral procedures are reported only once per encounter. (For thermal destruction of intraosseous basivertebral nerve, see 64628, 64629) Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. lay_term: The provider applies heat energy through a needle inserted into an invertebral disk, one of the cartilage cushions between the interlocking bones of the spine, to treat chronic back pain. He uses fluoroscopy, live X–ray, to guide the application of the treatment on one or both sides. He performs this procedure on an additional level after performing the procedure on one or more other levels. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, and after having undergone this procedure at one or more levels, the provider uses fluoroscopic guidance to identify another target area. He inserts a guidance needle over which he passes a catheter probe into the annulus fibrosus. He attaches the catheter to a generator box to heat the resistive element at the catheter's tip and coagulate or decompress the disk material. Terminology Annulus fibrosus: Fibrous outer ring of the intervertebral disk, the cartilage cushion between the interlocking bones in the spine; also known as the annular ring. Bilateral: On two sides; opposite of unilateral. Chronic: A condition that is long lasting, typically slow to develop, and with symptoms of less severity than an acute condition. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Percutaneous intradiscal electrothermal annuloplasty: Application of a heat energy through a needle inserted through the skin into an intervertebral disk to treat back pain. Unilateral: On a single side; opposite of bilateral, on two sides. Tips This code must be reported in conjunction the appropriate primary code, 22526 (Percutaneous intradiscal electrothermal annuloplasty, unilateral or bilateral including fluoroscopic guidance; single level). Be aware that Medicare does not cover thermal intradiscal procedures or services and will deny claims for this code. Providers are liable for charges if a thermal intradiscal procedure is used in surgery, unless the beneficiary was informed that she would be financially responsible prior to performance of the procedure. To avoid this liability, the provider should have the beneficiary sign an advance beneficiary notice, or ABN. Don’t confuse use of the abbreviation TIPS, which refers to both the thermal intradiscal procedure and to transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt. Read Less

lay_term: The provider places spinal instrumentation in the neck across a single interspace (C1–C2) to correct a spinal deformity during the course of a spinal surgery, such as a spinal fusion, or arthrodesis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and while undergoing a spinal surgery, the provider uses fluoroscopy to assess the alignment of C1 and C2. He makes an incision caudally, on the back of the neck. He places a trocar through which he inserts the C1–C2 transarticular screw. He removes the obturator that covers the opening in the trocar, and a small hole is drilled using fluoroscopic guidance. A cannulated screw, with a hollow shaft, is placed across the C1–C2 joint. The same procedure is performed on the opposite side of the vertebra. The provider then continues the primary procedure to completion, closing the wound. Terminology Arthrodesis: Fusion, or permanent joining, of a joint, or point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Atlantoaxial transarticular screw fixation: Spinal fixation across the atlantoaxial joint, the union of the first and second cervical vertebrae. Cervical spine: Neck, containing vertebrae enumerated C1 through C7. Facet screw fixation: Spinal fixation involving screws placed through the facets, the joints between the vertebrae. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Harrington rod: Stainless steel rod used to straighten the spine by implantation in the spinal column. Pedicle fixation: Spinal fixation through pedicles, the bony tubes running through either side of a vertebra. Posterior nonsegmental instrumentation: Spinal fixation device that attaches from either end instead of attaching segmentally to intervening vertebrae at the back of the spine. Sublaminar wiring: Stabilization of the spine by passing wires through the sublaminar surface of the vertebrae. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. Tips This is an add–on code and must be reported with an appropriate primary procedure. There are multiple codes you can choose from when you report spinal instrumentation from the section 22840 to 22870, Spinal instrumentation procedures on the spine, vertebral column. Identify the correct code beginning with the approach for the instrumentation, anterior or posterior. Next, determine if the device is segmental or nonsegmental. Count the fixation points. Irrespective of the span, if the instrumentation is done to only two vertebral segments, consider the instrumentation to be nonsegmental. If, however, the instrumentation involves three or more vertebral segments, the instrumentation is considered segmental. If there is a proximal and distal fixation point with at least one intervening fixation point, the fixation is considered to be segmental. Confirm the removal of vertebral portions. Know the difference between segments and levels; count one vertebra per segment, two vertebrae per level. You can report instrumentation removal if the provider removes the instrumentation for damage or rejection. You can also report the instrumentation removal if your provider did it to adjust the instrumentation. If, however, the provider does the removal to explore the spinal fusion, you cannot report the instrumentation removal. Confirm with your payer which modifiers are approved for spinal instrumentation services, as not all may be accepted. Some will permit modifier 59, Distinct procedural service, to demonstrate that the provider did the instrumentation at separate anatomic locations. When your provider is removing the instrumentation in the global period and an infection necessitates the return of the patient to the operating room for removal, append modifier 78, Unplanned return to the operating or procedure room by the same provider following initial procedure for a related procedure during the postoperative period. lay_term: The provider places spinal instrumentation at the back of the spine across three to six vertebral segments to correct a spinal deformity during the course of a spinal surgery, such as a spinal fusion, or arthrodesis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and while undergoing a spinal surgery, the provider identifies the target segments and detaches surrounding tissues and ligaments. He drills the posterior cortex, or bony covering, directly posterior to the pedicle. He enters the pedicle with imaging guidance. He places screws through the pedicle into the vertebral body on each side of each vertebra to be segmentally fixed. He may apply hooks and clamps near transverse processes and laminae at the chosen vertebrae. He bends the rod or plate to get the desired shape of for the spine and attaches it to the segmental fixation at each segment with nuts or screws. He checks the alignment on imaging. The provider then continues the primary procedure to completion, closing the wound. Terminology Arthrodesis: Fusion, or permanent joining, of a joint, or point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Lamina: Thin layer on the surface of a bone; one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Pedicle: A bony tube running through either side of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones in the back; the sides of the pedicle function as the walls of the spinal canal, protecting the spinal cord; also a stalk. Posterior segmental instrumentation: Spinal fixation device that attaches individually to each vertebral segment it traverses from the posterior, or back, of the spine. Sublaminar wiring: Stabilization of the spine by passing wires through the sublaminar surface of the vertebrae. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. Tips This is an add on code and must be reported with an appropriate primary procedure. Although coding guidelines define instrumentation procedures according to vertebral segments, fusion, or arthrodesis, procedures, which must accompany instrumentation claims, are defined according to vertebral interspaces. So, you must be careful to avoid confusion. Generally, the type of instrumentation will correspond to the surgical approach, anterior or posterior. The provider’s documentation should explicitly state the type of instrumentation she places. If the provider's operative report does not specify, be sure to ask. Read Less

lay_term: The provider places spinal instrumentation at the front of the spine across eight or more vertebral segments to correct a spinal deformity during the course of a spinal surgery, such as a spinal fusion, or arthrodesis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and while undergoing a spinal surgery, the provider identifies the target vertebral segments. He prepares a passageway for the fixation screw through the vertebral body. He places screws in each vertebral body to be internally fixed. He takes care to avoid pressure on the dura, the covering of the spinal cord, and the spinal nerves. He secures the plate, rod, or cable to the screws according to the protocol of that particular device. He may apply a few hooks to hold the plate at its anterior element. He may apply a cement material, like methyl methacrylate, to supplement the fixation. He contours the rods to give the desired shape to the instrumentation. The provider then continues the primary procedure to its completion, closing the wound. Terminology Anterior instrumentation: Spinal fixation device applied to the front of the spine. Arthrodesis: Fusion, or permanent joining, of a joint, or point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Pedicle: A bony tube running through either side of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones in the back; the sides of the pedicle function as the walls of the spinal canal, protecting the spinal cord; also a stalk. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. Vertebral body: Main or largest part of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Tips This is an add–on code and must be reported with an appropriate primary procedure. There are many codes you can choose from when you report spinal instrumentation from the section 22840 to 22870, Spinal instrumentation procedures on the spine, vertebral column. Identify the correct code beginning with the approach for the instrumentation, anterior or posterior. Next, determine if the device is segmental or nonsegmental. Count the fixation points. Irrespective of the span, if the instrumentation is done to only two vertebral segments, consider the instrumentation to be nonsegmental. If, however, the instrumentation involves three or more vertebral segments, the instrumentation is considered segmental. If there is a proximal and distal fixation point with at least one intervening fixation point, the fixation is considered to be segmental. Confirm the removal of vertebral portions. Know the difference between segments and levels; count one vertebra per segment, two vertebrae per level. You can report instrumentation removal if the provider removes the instrumentation for damage or rejection. You can also report the instrumentation removal if your provider did it to adjust the instrumentation. If, however, the provider does the removal to explore the spinal fusion, you cannot report the instrumentation removal. Confirm with your payer which modifiers are approved for spinal instrumentation services, as not all may be accepted. Some will permit modifier 59, Distinct procedural service, to demonstrate that the provider did the instrumentation at separate anatomic locations. When your provider is removing the instrumentation in the global period and an infection necessitates the return of the patient to the operating room for removal, append modifier 78, Unplanned return to the operating or procedure room by the same provider following initial procedure for a related procedure during the postoperative period. lay_term: The provider inserts a metallic cage or mesh device between two vertebrae and may use screws or flanges to attach it to the front part of the vertebrae; the device maintains the disc space, provides spinal stability, and yet preserves some range of motion, which helps relieve persistent pain caused by a herniated, or bulging, disk or other spinal condition. The provider performs this procedure during a spinal interbody arthrodesis procedure, which is fusion, or permanent joining, of vertebrae over the joint space. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and during a primary interbody arthrodesis procedure, the provider exposes the intervertebral disc (a round, flat, fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae) and retracts the surrounding tissues and muscles. He inserts a synthetic (man–made) device between two adjacent vertebrae (the interlocking bony segments that form the spine) to expand or maintain the disc space. He may use screws or flanges on the device to attach it to the vertebrae. Once he has inserted the planned number of devices, the provider continues the primary procedure to its completion, controls bleeding, and closes the wound. Report this code once for each interspace that the provider treats in addition to the primary code for the procedure. Terminology Biomechanical: Pertaining to biomechanics, particularly the mechanisms involved in musculoskeletal activity (e.g., bending, twisting, walking, running). Interbody: Between the vertebrae, the interlocking bony segments that form the spine. Interspace: Space between two body parts as in the space between two vertebral bodies, which contain the intervertebral disc; also known as the intervertebral space. Tips Code +22853 is an add–on code and must be reported with an appropriate primary procedure, such as 22548–22586 (Anterior or anterolateral approach technique arthrodesis procedures on the spine [vertebral column]), but there are many other codes that can be reported as a primary code. Report one unit of this code for each interspace treated, not for the number of devices inserted. For example, if the provider inserts two cages into a single interspace, you report this code only once. If the provider inserts a device at two separate interspaces, e.g., between C3–4 and C5–6, then you would report this code twice. This code is for the application of a device to expand or maintain an intervertebral disc space. For a similar procedure to cover a defect created by removal of a vertebral body, report +22854. For insertion of a similar device to treat an intervertebral disc space or vertebral body removal defect but without interbody fusion (arthrodesis), report +22859. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider places an artificial disc into a single cervical interspace to treat conditions such as degenerative disc disease, disc disruption, internal disc derangement, and symptomatic disc desiccation. He also removes the intervertebral disc and removes bone spurs, or growths, that may develop on the upper or lower edges of the vertebrae to reduce pressure on the nerve root or spinal cord. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the anterior neck and dissects down through the tissue, protecting the carotid vessels, the esophagus, or food pipe, and the trachea, or wind pipe, to expose the prevertebral space. He then uses retractors to hold back the tissues. Next, he incises the disc space and removes the disc material with a surgical instrument. He then uses an operating microscope and performs microdissection to clear the disc space. He removes the bulging disc and bone spurs decompressing the nerve root. Then he guides a drill into the disc space to create a clear space for placing the artificial disc. Next, he uses the drill to adjust the disc space and places an artificial disc into place. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the incision wound by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Terminology Anterior: Situated in front. Arthroplasty device: Device used to replace or reconstruct a joint. Bone spurs: Small bony growths that occur at the edge of a bone where it meets another bone, often the result of arthritis; also called osteophytes. Carotid vessel: Vein or artery in the neck. Cervical vertebrae: Vertebra located in the upper neck of the spinal column, the vertebral column, indicated by the symbols C1 through C7. Decompression: A procedure to relieve pressure on a structure. Degenerative disc disease: Age related changes in the spine causing spinal deterioration. Disc or intervertebral disc: This is a round, flat fibrous tissue layer between two adjacent vertebrae that consists of a hard outer layer called annulus fibrosis and a gel like central part called nucleus pulposus; the intervertebral disc acts as a flexible cushion between the two vertebrae that helps in load bearing and shock absorption. Disc derangement: A condition in which the intervertebral disc degenerates or is torn. Disc desiccation: A degenerative condition in which the interior of the intervertebral disc dries out. Disc disruption: Internal changes in the disc that effect the internal structure of the disc, such as the nucleus, while the disc externally appears normal and intact. Diskectomy: Surgical removal of the all or a part of an intervertebral disc. Herniated disc: Herniation occurs when an intervertebral disc moves out of its place, there is a tear in the annulus of the cervical disc from an accident or pathological causes, and the nucleus pulposus bulges out; a herniated disc puts pressure on the nerve roots or spinal cord and causes pain in the patient; when medication fails, herniation needs surgical intervention. Interspace: Space between two body parts as in the space between two vertebral bodies, which contain the intervertebral disc; also called the intervertebral space. Microdissection: Dissection, or surgical splitting or separation, under the microscope. Operating microscope: Binocular microscope, meaning two eyepieces for simultaneous viewing with both eyes used to view fine structures during operations. Osteophytectomy: Removal of bone spurs, or growths that may develop on the upper or lower edges of the vertebrae. Osteophytes: Bone spurs, or smooth excess bone growths, that may develop on the upper or lower edges of the vertebrae. Prevertebral: Situated, or occurring anterior to, or in front of a vertebra or the spinal column. Prosthesis: An artificial, fabricated implant that acts as a substitute for a damaged or missing body part, such as a limb, or bone joint, or a heart valve. Retractors: Surgical instruments used to separate the edges of a surgical incision or wound or to hold back tissue or organs. Vertebrae: The bony segments that form the spine; there are 33 segments designated into 5 different levels: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 4 coccygeal. lay_term: At the same session as an initial interspace cervical spine total disc arthroplasty, the provider uses an anterior approach to perform a second level interspace procedure. He removes the painful degenerated disc and replaces it with an artificial mobile disc that helps in the normal movement of the disc. He also removes the intervertebral disc and removes bone spurs, or growths, that may develop on the upper or lower edges of the vertebrae to reduce pressure on the nerve root or spinal cord. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the anterior neck and dissects down through the tissue, protecting the carotid vessels, the esophagus, or food pipe, and the trachea, or wind pipe, and exposing the prevertebral space. He then uses retractors to hold back the tissues. Next, he incises the disc space and removes part or the majority of the vertebral body in between the involved discs using an operating microscope and performing microdissection to clear the disc space. He removes the bulging disc and bone spurs decompressing the nerve root. Then he guides a drill into the disc space to create a clear space for placing the artificial disc. The provider then places an artificial disc in the area in place of the discs he removes. He may also place a plate on the front of the adjacent vertebral bodies for support. The provider commonly performs this procedure in cases where there are multilevel disc herniations, or spurs, or spinal cord compression. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the incision by suturing the soft tissues in layers. This code is applicable for a second level procedure. Terminology Anterior: Situated in front. Arthroplasty: Reconstruction or replacement of a joint, the point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Arthroplasty device: Device used to replace or reconstruct a joint. Bone spurs: Small bony growths that occur at the edge of a bone where it meets another bone, often the result of arthritis; also called osteophytes. Carotid vessel: Vein or artery in the neck. Cervical vertebrae: Vertebra located in the upper neck of the spinal column, the vertebral column, indicated by the symbols C1 through C7. Decompression: A procedure to relieve pressure on a structure. Degenerative disc disease: Age related changes in the spine causing spinal deterioration. Diskectomy: Excision of an intervertebral disk; also called discectomy. Herniated disc: Herniation occurs when an intervertebral disc moves out of its place, there is a tear in the annulus of the cervical disc from an accident or pathological causes, and the nucleus pulposus bulges out; a herniated disc puts pressure on the nerve roots or spinal cord and causes pain in the patient; when medication fails, herniation needs surgical intervention. Interspace: Space between two body parts as in the space between two vertebral bodies, which contain the intervertebral disc; also called the intervertebral space. Microdissection: Dissection, or surgical splitting or separation, under the microscope. Operating microscope: Binocular microscope, meaning two eyepieces for simultaneous viewing with both eyes used to view fine structures during operations. Osteophyte: A projection of the bone that leads to degeneration and nerve impingement. Osteophytectomy: Excision of the osteophyte; or bone spurs, or growths that may develop on the upper or lower edges of the vertebrae. Prevertebral: Situated, or occurring anterior to, or in front of a vertebra or the spinal column. Retractors: Surgical instruments used to separate the edges of a surgical incision or wound or to hold back tissue or organs. Vertebra: One of the interlocking bones of the spine. lay_term: The provider revises a prior total disk arthroplasty in the neck to treat a degenerated or diseased intervertebral disk. He replaces the device due to infection or device failure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a skin incision through the old incision at the anterior neck. He uses sharp and blunt dissection to dissect through the scar tissue between the carotid sheath laterally and the esophagus and trachea medially. He exposes the prevertebral space and identifies the target segment. He loosens the old implant from the vertebral segments and removes the pins. He places retractors to keep the disk space open. He guides a new implant into the space using fluoroscopy. He adjusts the instrument into the disk space. He removes the retractors. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Anterior approach: Surgical approach from the front, in this case from the front of the spine. Carotid artery: One of two large blood vessels that supply the head and neck, the left and right common carotids. Cervical spine: Neck, containing vertebrae enumerated C1 through C7. Esophagus: The muscular tube that carries substances from the throat down to the stomach. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Interspace: The intervertebral disk space. Intervertebral disk: Cushion of cartilage material separating two vertebrae. Prevertebral space: An area in the neck in front of the vertebrae, or neck bones. Sheath: A protective covering, natural, like a membrane, or artificial, such as an introducer sheath for a needle. Total disk arthroplasty: Surgical implantation of an artificial intervertebral disk to treat disk disease. Trachea: Respiratory structure composed primarily of muscle and cartilage that connects the pharynx and larynx, or throat and voice box, to the lungs; also called the windpipe. Read Less

lay_term: The provider removes a single artificial disk in the lower back placed in a prior total disk arthroplasty procedure to treat degenerative disk disease or other symptomatic disk condition. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reopens the incision on the left side of the abdomen and exposes the muscles of the anterior abdominal wall. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. short_description: Insertion of interlaminar/interspinous process stabilization/distraction device, without fusion, including image guidance when performed, with open decompression, lumbar; single level
lay_term: Through an open approach, the provider inserts an interlaminar stabilization or interspinous distraction, or decompression, device (IPD) and attaches it to the bony projections (spinous processes) on the back of adjacent vertebrae at one site in the lumbar spine to restrict painful motion (stabilize) or open up (distract) the neural foramina, relieving pressure on the nerve roots. The provider does not fuse (permanently join) the vertebrae. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a 2– to 5–inch incision in the skin over the middle of the lower back at the appropriate lumbar level. She dissects down through the tissues, then elevates and dissects the muscles on both sides of the spinous processes off the laminae. She preserves the supraspinous ligament, the strong fibrous cord that runs through the spine. The provider may use image guidance to confirm the level of stenosis. The provider then sizes the space to determine the correct implant size. She may need to remove bone or ligament to make room for the device. She then inserts a distraction device between the spinous processes and locks it in place. This device enlarges the openings (foramina) through which the nerves and vessels exit the spinal canal. Alternatively, she may insert an interlaminar device. The interlaminar device has "wings," which are placed around the lower and upper bony projections (spinous processes) on the back of the vertebrae. This device restricts extension (backward bending), which causes pain in patients with spinal stenosis, but does not prevent normal movement. Both devices are used to decompress (relieve pressure on) the nerve roots and relieve spinal stenosis but they do not fuse the vertebrae. The provider removes all retractors, controls bleeding, reapproximates the tissues, closes the incision with sutures, and applies a sterile dressing over the wound. Terminology Fusion: Surgical procedure involving permanent joining of vertebrae over the joint space; also called arthrodesis. Image guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound, high frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Lamina: Thin layer on the surface of a bone; one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Lumbar spine: The lower back region containing vertebrae enumerated L1 through L5. Foramina: Openings or passages, particularly in bone; typically, a passage for nerves or vessels. Tips For the same procedure performed at an additional level during the same session, report 22868 in addition to this code for the primary procedure. For the same procedure without open decompression, report 22869. Some payers consider this procedure investigational for certain indications; always check with the payer to confirm their policies for coverage. Read Less

lay_term: Through an additional minimally invasive approach, the provider inserts an interlaminar stabilization or interspinous distraction, or decompression, device (IPD) and attaches it to the bony projections (spinous processes) on the back of adjacent vertebrae at an additional level in the lumbar spine to restrict painful motion (stabilize) or open up (distract) the neural foramina, relieving pressure on the nerve roots. The provider does not fuse (permanently join) the vertebrae. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a similar 1– to 1–1/2–inch incision in the skin over the middle of the lower back at an additional lumbar level. She dissects down through the tissues, then lifts and retracts the muscles on both sides of the spinous processes. She preserves the supraspinous ligament, the strong fibrous cord that runs through the spine. The provider may use image guidance to confirm the level of stenosis. The provider then sizes the space to determine the correct implant size. She may need to remove bone or ligament to make room for the device. She then inserts a distraction device between the spinous processes and locks it in place. This device enlarges the openings (foramina) through which the nerves and vessels exit the spinal canal. Alternatively, she may insert an interlaminar device. The interlaminar device has "wings," which are placed around the lower and upper bony projections (spinous processes) on the back of the vertebrae. This device restricts extension (backward bending), which causes pain in patients with spinal stenosis, but does not prevent normal movement. Both devices are used to decompress (relieve pressure on) the nerve roots and relieve spinal stenosis but they do not fuse the vertebrae. The provider removes all retractors, controls bleeding, reapproximates the tissues, closes the incision with sutures, and applies a sterile dressing over the wound. Report this add–on code for each additional level that the surgeon treats. Terminology Fusion: Surgical procedure involving permanent joining of vertebrae over the joint space; also called arthrodesis. Image guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a television monitor; ultrasound, high frequency sound waves to view tissues; or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. Lamina: Thin layer on the surface of a bone; one of the surfaces of a vertebra, one of the interlocking bones of the spine. Lumbar spine: The lower back region containing vertebrae enumerated L1 through L5. Foramina: Openings or passages, particularly in bone; typically, a passage for nerves or vessels. Tips Code +22870 is an add–on code; it must be reported with a primary code. Report 22869 (Insertion of interlaminar/interspinous process stabilization/distraction device, without open decompression or fusion, including image guidance when performed, lumbar; single level) for the primary procedure. lay_term: Use 22899 to report procedures in the spinal column that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs a procedure on the spinal column that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Read Less

If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic. The area known as the shoulder is made up of the clavicle, scapula, humerus head and neck, sternoclavicular joint, acromioclavicular joint, and shoulder joint.

short_description: Radical resection of tumor (eg, sarcoma), soft tissue of shoulder area; less than 5 cm
lay_term: The provider performs an excision procedure for a soft tissue malignant tumor, such as a sarcoma, from the shoulder area. The excision of the tumor is performed in an extensive manner, not being limited to the dimensions of the tumor itself but expanding to its surrounding area/anatomical structures suspected for involvement. The diameter of the tumor and the margins required measure less than 5cm. Explanation After administration of proper anesthesia and the usual prep and drape of the operative site is performed, a linear incision is made around the tumor site, mostly in line with the muscle creases. Incision is further extended deep and around the tumor. Fascial, subfascial, and/or muscle flaps may be raised to adequately expose the underlying anatomy. Neurovascular structures in that area are identified and preserved. Once the tumor is well localized, a sharp scalpel is used to dissect the tumor from the surrounding tissue margin, and the tumor is removed. To rule out further malignancy, an additional surrounding wide area of margin is also dissected and removed. After satisfactory radical removal of the fascial tumor along with the appropriate surrounding margin from the shoulder area, the incision is repaired in the layered fashion. A total excision diameter of less than 5 cm is reportable with this code. Terminology Radical resection of soft tissue tumor: Surgical removal of the tumor as well as wide margins of surrounding tissue. Sarcomas: Malignant tumors that can involve bony tissues as well as soft tissues such as bone, cartilage, joint synovium, fat, muscle, tendons, nerves, etc., and originate in the soft tissues. Tips This code is for radical resection of tumors of musculoskeletal origin, such as sarcomas. Wide margins of excision beyond the tumor dimensions are necessary to report this code. Compare with 23078. Read Less

short_description: Arthrotomy; glenohumeral joint, with synovectomy, with or without biopsy
lay_term: The provider incises the shoulder joint to inspect and repair the synovium, the membrane covering the bony surfaces of the joint. He excises synovial tissue that has become inflamed, to relieve pain and limitation of motion. If needed, he takes a sample of the tissue to submit to a laboratory for analysis and diagnosis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the glenohumeral joint and extends the incision down to the joint capsule. He incises the joint capsule to view the structures within. He excises the inflamed portions of synovium, including the entire synovial membrane lining the joint, if necessary. He biopsies any suspicious tissue and submits the specimen for laboratory analysis. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Synovectomy: Excision of synovial tissue, the membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Read Less

lay_term: The provider incises the sternoclavicular joint, where the breastbone joins the collar bone at the shoulder. short_description: Acromioplasty or acromionectomy, partial, with or without coracoacromial ligament release
lay_term: The provider reshapes the acromion, the bony projection at the end of the shoulder blade, to restore motion to the shoulder and protect the rotator cuff. He may partially remove the acromion and or incise the ligament that attaches the muscle the shoulder blade. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a sharp incision from the center of the AC joint inferiorly, or downward. He dissects through skin and subcutaneous tissues down to the deltoid muscle. He incises the deltoid fibers in line with the clavicle and extends the dissection, splitting the deltoid up to the dorsal, or rear, aspect of the acromion. He detaches the deltoid from the acromion subperiosteally to split and expose the anterior, or front, part of the acromion from the lateral corner to the AC joint. He then reshapes the acromion and, if necessary, releases the coracoacromial ligament. To protect the rotator cuff, he makes a vertical cut with an osteotome or bone saw and resects the anterior, or frontward, acromion. He excises the corner of the acromion anteroinferiorly, or in front and below, with an osteotome to create a flat or slightly angled up acromion. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Acromioclavicular, or AC, joint: Union of the acromion, a bony projection on the shoulder blade, and the clavicle, or collar bone. Acromion: A bony process, or projection, on the scapula, or shoulder blade, that extends over the joint. Acromionectomy: Surgical excision of the acromion, a bony projection on scapula, or shoulder blade, that extends over the joint. Acromioplasty: Surgical revision of the acromion, a bony projection on the end of the shoulder blade, to relieve compression on the rotator cuff. Clavicle: The collarbone, a horizontal bone that connects the sternum, or breastbone, to the scapula, or shoulder blade. Coracoacromial ligament: A ligament, or fibrous band, that connects the acromion, a bony projection on one part of the shoulder blade, to the coracoid process, a hook shaped bony projection on the shoulder blade. Deltoid muscle: Triangular shaped muscle that controls movement of the shoulder. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Osteotome: A surgical instrument used to cut bone. Rotator cuff: The grouping of muscles and tendons that surround and support the shoulder joint. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Subperiosteal: Below the periosteum, the membrane covering the surface of a bone. Read Less

short_description: Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor of proximal humerus; with autograft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: The provider removes a cyst or other noncancerous mass from the humerus, a bone in the upper arm, with a cutting or scraping instrument. He fills the defect with bone graft taken from another location in the patient’s body. He submits the specimen to a laboratory for analysis to confirm its nature. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the upper arm over the area of the mass. He dissects down to the level of the bone and opens the periosteum, the membrane covering of the bone. He excises the mass down to healthy tissue with an osteotome or bone curette, bone cutting instruments. He submits the specimen to a laboratory for analysis. He harvests bone graft material through a small incision in another location, such as the iliac crest in the pelvis, and fills the defect in the humerus. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes all incisions. Terminology Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient's own body. Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called an allogeneic graft or homograft. Curettage: Use of a curette to remove tissue by scraping or scooping. Cyst: Sac usually containing fluid; the term cyst can refer to an abnormal growth or to any saclike structure, such as the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to the structure’s point of attachment. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass; can be benign or cancerous. Tips If the provider uses allograft, bone graft taken from someone other than the patient, report 23156, Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor of proximal humerus; with allograft. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an injection of a contrast agent into the shoulder joint for a shoulder arthrography procedure, a diagnostic test in which the provider obtains a series of X–ray images of the shoulder joint after injection of the contrast. He uses this test to assess the joint for any soft tissue injury. The provider may also perform computed tomography, or CT, or magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI images, after the injection of contrast, which is referred to as an enhanced CT or MRI shoulder arthrography. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a needle into the shoulder joint cavity under the guidance of fluoroscopy and injects a solution of contrast until resistance is felt indicating that the joint is full. Next, the provider removes the needle and performs a separately reportable X–ray, CT or MRI imaging of the joint to assess it for injury. Use this code only for injection of the contrast. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Computed tomography: Computed tomography, or CT, is when the provider rotates an X–ray tube and X–ray detectors around a patient, which produces a tomogram, a computer generated cross sectional image; providers use CT to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Magnetic resonance imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, uses magnetic fields and radio waves to visualize body tissues to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Read Less

short_description: Scapulopexy (eg, Sprengels deformity or for paralysis)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider attaches the patient's scapula to a rib or vertebra to correct shoulder asymmetries or deformities that create issues with the patient's motion. The provider performs this service for conditions such as sprengels deformity, a congenital deformity in which the person has one shoulder blade that sits higher on the back than the other. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a linear oblique skin incision on the inner border of the scapula and incises the trapezius muscle. He next detaches the rhomboid and the elevator scapulae muscles from the vertebral border of the scapula and releases the rotator cuff muscles and serratus anterior muscles from the vertebral border of the scapula. The provider then exposes a small portion of the scapula and places the scapula in a more medial and caudal position to choose the corresponding ribs to prepare. The provider exposes several ribs and passes a double metal wire under each rib, after which he places the scapula over the rib cage to its definitive position. He then drills several small holes opposite the prepared ribs and passes one end of each wire through the adjacent hole of the inner border of the scapula. With the scapula held in its final position, the provider tightens the metal wires to achieve bone to bone contact between the scapula and the ribs. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. Terminology Caudal: Refers to or directed towards the hind part or tail. Congenital: Present at birth. Levator scapulae: A muscle on the back and side of the neck that perform the function of elevating the shoulder blade. Linear oblique: Straight and slanted. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body. Paralysis: Inability to voluntarily move a body part. Rhomboid muscle: A muscle that connects the shoulder blade to the spinal column. Rotator cuff: A group of four muscles — the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis — that stabilizes the shoulder joint. Scapula: Shoulder blade. Scapulopexy: Surgical procedure to connect the scapula to the chest wall or the vertebrae. Serratus anterior muscle: A muscle that extends from the eighth or ninth rib to the inner border of the shoulder blade. Trapezius muscle: A flat superficial muscle that covers the upper back and back of the neck. short_description: Tenotomy, shoulder area; multiple tendons through same incision

short_description: Repair of ruptured musculotendinous cuff (eg, rotator cuff) open; acute
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open surgical repair of an acute tear of the rotator cuff in the shoulder. The rotator cuff is a group of four muscles that stabilizes the shoulder joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin on the outer side of the shoulder in line with the deltoid muscle fibers. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin, and retracts the muscles, blood vessels, and nerves. This exposes the subacromial space, a space between the acromion process of the shoulder blade and the head of the humerus bone. He now has access to the rotator cuff muscles and the rupture, or tear. A rupture or tear causes the muscles to avulse, or forcibly detach, from their normal attachments on the bone. The provider then assesses the shape of the tear and removes the frayed segments of the tendons. Next, he sutures the tear in the tendon and places bone anchors to fix the tendon to the bone. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. Use this code only when the provider performs open treatment of an acute muscle tendon tear. Terminology Acute: A disease or an ailment that has rapid onset or short course. Acromion process: Bony projection of the shoulder blade that forms the point of the shoulder. Chronic: A disease or an ailment that is persistent and has long lasting effect. Deltoid muscle: A fan shaped muscle that surrounds the shoulder joint. Humerus: A long bone in the arm. Tips When the provider performs an open surgical repair of a chronic, or persistent, tear of the rotator cuff, in the shoulder, use code 23412, Repair of ruptured musculotendinous cuff, eg, rotator cuff open; chronic. short_description: Coracoacromial ligament release, with or without acromioplasty Notes: (For arthroscopic procedure, use 29826)

short_description: Reconstruction of complete shoulder (rotator) cuff avulsion, chronic (includes acromioplasty)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider reconstructs the complete shoulder in a patient with chronic rotator cuff tear or rupture. He also performs an acromioplasty, a procedure in which the provider shaves a portion of bone from the underside of the acromion process to release abnormal pressure that it might be causing on underlying muscles or tendons. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises across the front of the shoulder from the middle of the collarbone to the middle of the arm bone. The provider continues to dissect down through subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin, to access the joint. Next, he retracts the muscles, nerves, and blood vessels. He first releases the deltoid muscle from the acromion process and preserves the bony attachment for later reattachment. Next, he exposes the rotator cuff muscle, which is torn away from the greater tuberosity, and he assesses the shape and extent of the tear. He then repairs the rotator cuff muscle by using multiple sutures and fixes it to bone by placing anchors. Next, the provider may perform acromioplasty in which the provider uses a surgical burr, or small cutting tool, and shaves off a portion of the bone from the under surface of the acromion process. This releases the friction or pressure on the underlying structures and relieves pain in the shoulder joint. Next, he repairs the deltoid muscle with sutures by drilling holes in the bone. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. He may place the patient’s arm in an abduction splint or pillow to stabilize the help with healing. short_description: Tenodesis of long tendon of biceps Notes: (For arthroscopic biceps tenodesis, use 29828)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically cleans the long tendon of the biceps from its damaged fragment and fixes the tendon to the upper end of the humerus to improve the stability of the joint. He performs this procedure to restore function to patients with severe damage of the biceps tendon due to conditions such as recurrent shoulder impingement or degenerative changes in the shoulder joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin. He then has access to the joint and the bicep tendon to anchor. He first removes the damaged portion of the long tendon of the biceps and sutures the remaining stump of the bicep tendon to the upper end of the humerus bone after drilling holes in the bone. The provider passes a stay suture through the tendon stump. He then ties a simple knot and sutures the knot to keep it in place. He then uses a drill to make a hole in the bone, passes the knotted tendon through the hole, and secures it with an absorbable suture, anchor, or screw. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Biceps: A muscle present in the front of arm that bends the elbow. Shoulder impingement: A compression of the tendons between the head of the humerus, the bone of the upper arm and the shoulder blade, the bone that connects the humerus with the clavicle, or collarbone. Stay suture: A surgical stitch a provider places during a procedure to hold or manipulate a structure. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tenodesis: A surgical procedure to suture or anchor a tendon to a bone. Read Less

short_description: Capsulorrhaphy, anterior; Putti-Platt procedure or Magnuson type operation Notes: (To report arthroscopic thermal capsulorrhaphy, use 29999)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs a tear in a patient’s shoulder joint capsule and tightens the joint capsule in case of hyperlaxity, an excessive movement in an abnormal plane of movement for the shoulder. He performs this procedure to treat conditions like severe shoulder instability. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the shoulder joint and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin, to expose the joint capsule. He visualizes the upper and lower borders of the subscapularis tendon. He transects the subscapularis tendon down to the capsule and reflects the medial part of the tendon off the capsule until no additional connections exist between the tendon and the capsule. He then explores and assesses the capsule, and then irrigates the area to remove loose bodies from the joint cavity. The provider divides the capsule vertically, midway between its attachments on the glenoid rim and the humeral head, and places stay sutures along the free edge of the medial capsular leaflet. He makes sure that the capsule is appropriately tightened to his satisfaction. Finally, he stops all bleeding, places a drain, and closes the wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Magnuson type operation: A procedure to correct shoulder instability in which the provider shifts the insertion of subscapularis muscle over the arm bone to provide a sling effect. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body. Stay sutures: Surgical sutures that the provider uses to hold the tissue around an incision. short_description: Capsulorrhaphy, anterior, any type; with coracoid process transfer Notes: (To report open thermal capsulorrhaphy, use 23929)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs a tear in the shoulder joint capsule and tightens the joint capsule in the case of hyperlaxity, an excessive movement in an abnormal plane of movement for the shoulder. He performs this procedure to treat conditions like severe shoulder instability. He performs capsulorraphy with transfer of the coracoid process of the shoulder blade. He visualizes the upper and lower borders of the subscapularis tendon. He transects the subscapularis tendon down to the capsule and reflects the medial part of the tendon off the capsule until no additional connections exist between the tendon and the capsule. He then explores and assesses the capsule, and then irrigates the area to remove the loose bodies from the joint cavity. The provider divides the capsule vertically, midway between its attachments on the glenoid rim and the humeral head, and places stay sutures along the free edge of the medial capsular leaflet. He makes sure that the capsule is appropriately tightened to his satisfaction. short_description: Capsulorrhaphy, glenohumeral joint, posterior, with or without bone block Notes: (For sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular reconstruction, see 23530, 23550)
lay_term: The provider repairs the capsule, or membrane covering, of the posterior shoulder joint to improve shoulder stability. He may perform this procedure in conjunction with other shoulder surgeries in cases where the shoulder condition is severe. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the shoulder joint. He splits the posterior deltoid muscle. He splits the infraspinatus muscle horizontally between its superior and inferior, or top and bottom, portions. The provider moves the back and bottom portions of the joint capsule superiorly, or the top. He shifts the superior, or top, portion inferiorly, to the bottom. If the provider identifies a detachment of the capsule from the labrum, he passes sutures through bone tunnels to reattach it. When necessary, the provider may perform a posterior glenoid bone graft as a bone block in addition to a posterior capsular shift. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Bone block: Placement of bone graft material to augment the glenohumeral joint, in the shoulder, to reduce shoulder instability. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Capsulorrhaphy: Repair of a torn or damaged joint capsule. Deltoid muscle: Triangular shaped muscle that controls movement of the shoulder. Infraspinatus muscle: Shoulder joint muscle. Glenohumeral joint: Union of the humerus, or forearm, and the glenoid fossa, a depression on the end of the scapula, or shoulder blade. Glenoid fossa of shoulder: A depression on the end of the scapula, or shoulder blade. Labrum of the shoulder: A rim of tissue lining the shoulder socket, or glenoid fossa, a depression on the end of the scapula, or shoulder blade. Posterior: Closer to the back of the body or a structure. Read Less

short_description: Arthroplasty, glenohumeral joint; hemiarthroplasty
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs glenohumeral joint hemiarthroplasty in which the provider replaces the damaged head of a humerus with a prosthetic implant while the other half of the shoulder, the glenoid cavity is left intact. The provider performs this procedure when arthritis damages only the humerus head of the shoulder joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises across the front of the shoulder from the middle of the collarbone to the middle of the arm bone. The provider continues to dissect down through subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin, to access the joint. Next, he retracts the muscles, nerves, and blood vessels. He then incises the joint capsule and dislocates the glenohumeral joint to dislodge the head of humerus from the glenoid socket. He then removes all the loose bodies present in the cavity. Next, he incises the damaged head of the humerus using an osteotome and places a prosthetic humeral head implant stem into the humerus shaft by drilling into the medullary canal. Next, he places the prosthetic humerus head into correct alignment and reduces it into the glenoid cavity. He sutures the muscle around the joint to provide the appropriate stabilization. He removes all the osteophytes around the joint. Finally, he stops all bleeding, places drains, and closes the wound by suturing the layers of tissue. He then places the shoulder in a brace or sling for a period of four to six weeks to help with healing. Terminology Arthritis: An inflammatory condition affecting one or more of the body’s joints, resulting in pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Arthroplasty: Surgical repair of a joint. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in the correct position. Glenoid cavity: A hollow socket in the shoulder blade, which articulates with the humeral head to form the shoulder joint. Glenohumeral joint: A synovial ball and socket joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the shoulder blade, also known as the shoulder joint. Hemiarthroplasty: A surgical procedure in which the provider replaces on joint surface with an artificial implant. Humerus: A long bone in the arm. Osteotome: Surgical instrument used to cut bone. Osteophytes: Bone spurs that form along the joint margin. Prosthesis: An artificial device that replaces a body part. Sling: A soft material support that immobilizes the arm and the shoulder. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider exposes the shoulder joint through the previous skin incision. The provider continues to dissect down through the subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin, to access the joint. Next, he retracts the muscles, nerves, and blood vessels. He first removes the accumulation of granulation tissue that may occur over the components.
