short_description: Osteotomy, clavicle, with or without internal fixation; with bone graft for nonunion or malunion (includes obtaining graft and/or necessary fixation)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises a portion of the clavicle, or collar bone to repair a patient's poor clavicular alignment or a fracture, to shorten or lengthen the bone, or to correct damage due to arthritis. He performs this procedure with a bone graft and may internally fixate the bone. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the clavicle and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin. Next, he removes a portion of the clavicle bone and may fix the bone using implants like screws, a plate, or wires. He also harvests a bone graft from another bone in the patient's body through a separate incision and uses this graft to fix the clavicle bone in correct alignment. Once he correctly aligns and secures the bone, the provider closes both wounds by suturing the soft tissue. Terminology Arthritis: An inflammatory condition affecting one or more of the body’s joints, resulting in pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Tips When the provider removes a portion of the clavicle bone and fixes the bone with or without internal fixation; without using a bone graft, use code 23480, Osteotomy, clavicle, with or without internal fixation. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of an acute shoulder dislocation, which is an abnormal separation of a joint. short_description: Closed treatment of shoulder dislocation, with fracture of greater humeral tuberosity, with manipulation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a shoulder joint dislocation, which is an abnormal separation of a joint. He also reduces a fracture of the greater humeral tuberosity and performs manipulation to passively move and stretch the shoulder joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reduces, or realigns, the shoulder joint dislocation. He first performs a separately reportable X–ray to examine the dislocated joint. He then manually adjusts the bones by pushing or pulling to bring them to their normal alignment. If his manual efforts are unsuccessful, he may suspend a weight from the patient’s arm to move the shoulder back into place. He also reduces the fracture in the greater tuberosity of the humerus. A greater humeral tuberosity fracture is a crack in the rounded projection at the upper end of the humerus bone. Finally, he places the shoulder joint in a sling or brace for a period of four weeks to help with healing. He may perform a separately reportable X–ray examination of the joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation and tubercle fracture. Terminology Anatomical neck humerus: The portion of the humerus that separates the greater and lesser tubercles from the humeral head, or the forearm muscles. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in the correct position. Greater tuberosity: Lateral projection at the upper end of the humerus, near the shoulder. Humerus: A long bone in the arm. Lesser tuberosity: Smaller more prominent projection than greater tuberosity situated at the front of the upper end of the humerus. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. Sling: A soft material support that immobilizes the arm and the shoulder. Surgical neck humerus: The slightly narrowed area, or depression just below the greater and lesser tuberosities. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips When the provider performs a closed treatment of a shoulder dislocation and a surgical or anatomical neck fracture of the humerus along with manipulation, use code 23675, Closed treatment of shoulder dislocation, with surgical or anatomical neck fracture, with manipulation. short_description: Closed treatment of shoulder dislocation, with surgical or anatomical neck fracture, with manipulation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a shoulder joint dislocation, which is an abnormal separation of a joint. He also reduces, or realigns, a surgical or anatomical neck fracture at the upper end of the humerus bone and performs manipulation to passively move and stretch the shoulder joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reduces, or realigns, a shoulder joint dislocation. He first performs a separately reportable X–ray to examine the dislocated joint. He then manually adjusts the bones by gently pushing or pulling the shoulder and arm to bring the shoulder into normal alignment. He also reduces a fracture in the surgical or anatomical neck of the humerus. The anatomical neck is the portion of the humerus that separates the greater and lesser tubercles from the humeral head, or the forearm muscles. The slightly narrowed or depressed area just below the greater and lesser tubercles is known as the surgical neck. Finally, he places the shoulder joint in a sling or brace for a period of four weeks to help with healing. He may perform a separately reportable X–ray examination of the joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation and fracture. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically refers to the manipulation of fractures or dislocations; can be open (through a surgical incision) or closed (without an incision). Sling: A soft material support that immobilizes the arm and the shoulder. short_description: Open treatment of shoulder dislocation, with surgical or anatomical neck fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed

He makes an incision to open the shoulder joint and reduces, or realigns the dislocation. He also repairs any muscle damage that occurs because of the dislocation. He then reduces a surgical or anatomical neck fracture of the upper end of the humerus and may fix it using implants. He then closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. Finally, he places the patient in a sling or brace for a period of four to six weeks to help with healing. He may perform a separately reportable X–ray examination of the shoulder to confirm the reduction of the dislocation and fracture. short_description: Manipulation under anesthesia, shoulder joint, including application of fixation apparatus (dislocation excluded)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider manipulates a patient’s shoulder joint with the patient under anesthesia. He may also apply a fixation apparatus. He performs this service to treat conditions such as a frozen shoulder. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider evaluates the patient and then passively moves or stretches the shoulder joint in the direction of the restricted range of motion. He anesthetizes the patient to help reduce pain, spasm, and reflex muscle guarding. The provider breaks the joint and soft tissue adhesions through the manipulation, resulting in improvement in the range of motion of the joint. He may also apply a fixation apparatus to maintain the joint in the anatomical position. Terminology Fixation apparatus: A device that enables a provider to make adjustments to the fixation of a bone, and eliminates the need for invasive procedures; placement of the device can be externally or internally. Frozen shoulder: A condition characterized by pain and stiffness in the shoulder joint. Manipulation: A technique that consists of passive movement and stretching of the shoulder joint with an aim to break up the fibrous and scar tissue to relieve pain and improve range of motion. short_description: Arthrodesis, glenohumeral joint
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes the glenohumeral joint with the help of fixation devices. He performs this procedure to restore function to the shoulder for conditions such as arthritis or a failed shoulder replacement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the shoulder extending from the acromion process to the shaft of the humerus. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin, and retracts the muscles, blood vessels, and nerves. This exposes the glenohumeral joint. The provider first resects the rotator cuff muscles. He then cuts the capsule to enter the joint. Next, he thoroughly debrides the glenohumeral joint cartilage using a surgical burr, or small cutting tool. He then fuses the painful glenohumeral joint using K wires, powered staples, plates, or headless screws to restrict the movement causing pain. Finally, he stops all bleeding at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider then places the shoulder joint in a sling or brace for a period of four to six weeks to help with healing. Terminology Acromion process: Bony projection of the shoulder blade that forms the point of the shoulder. Arthritis: An inflammatory condition affecting one or more of the body’s joints, resulting in pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Arthrodesis: The surgical immobilization of a joint by fusion of the bones. Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in the correct position. Glenohumeral joint: A synovial ball and socket joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the shoulder blade, also known as the shoulder joint. Humerus: A long bone in the arm. K wire, Kirschner wire: A thin, flexible wire or pin type structure a provider uses to join and stabilize bone fragments. Rotator cuff: A group of four muscles that stabilizes the shoulder joint. Sling: A soft material support that immobilizes the arm and the shoulder. short_description: Interthoracoscapular amputation (forequarter)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes the upper extremity, scapula, or shoulder blade, and clavicle, or collar bone usually due to bone cancer of the shoulder. This procedure is also known as a forequarter amputation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises along the shoulder girdle. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, or just under skin, and creates a skin flap to cover the wound when the procedure is complete. Next, he exposes the muscles around the shoulder joint and releases them. He ligates, or ties off, the blood vessels and divides the nerves. The provider then releases the muscles anchoring the scapula to the chest wall and disarticulates the clavicle, or collar bone, from the sternum, or breast bone. In this way, the provider removes the entire upper extremity along with the collar bone and the shoulder blade. Finally, he stops all bleeding at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the skin flap in layers over the wound. Terminology Amputation: Surgical removal of a complete or partial appendage of the body. Disarticulation: Separation of the bones at their joint. Flap: A patch of skin taken from one area of the body to cover another area that needs a reconstruction or repair; unlike a graft, the flap retains its original blood supply that helps in a quicker healing with a near normal cosmetic look to the site of repair; the inclusion of the blood supply also facilitates transfer of a thicker flap that may include the underlying muscle and fascial tissues. Interthoracoscapular: In between the thorax and the scapula, or the shoulder blade. Shoulder girdle: The bones which connect the upper limb to the skeleton on each side consisting of the clavicle and scapula. Read Less

short_description: Disarticulation of shoulder
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes the entire upper extremity through the shoulder joint. The provider removes the humerus, or upper arm bone, and the entire arm from the scapula, or shoulder blade and the clavicle, or collar bone without incising bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises across the front of the shoulder from the middle of the collarbone to the middle of the arm bone. He then extends this incision along the posterior border of the deltoid muscle to end at the posterior axillary fold. He retracts the deltoid muscle and divides the pectoralis major muscle at its insertion. He ligates, or ties off, and divides the blood vessels and incises the nerve supplying the hand. He incises the rotator cuff, muscles, and dissects all the ligaments. He next incises the shoulder joint capsule and disarticulates, or separates, the humerus bone from the glenoid cavity of the shoulder blade. Finally, he stops all bleeding at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the skin flap around it. Terminology Axillary fold: A fold of skin and muscle that bounds the axilla, or armpit, in front and back. Deltoid muscle: A fan shaped muscle that surrounds the shoulder joint. Disarticulation: Separation of the bones at their joint. Glenoid cavity: A hollow socket in the shoulder blade, which articulates with the humeral head to from the shoulder joint. Humerus: A long bone in the arm. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Pectoralis major muscle: A fan shaped muscle situated in front of chest. Posterior: Closer to the back part of the body. Rotator cuff: A group of four muscles — the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis — that stabilizes the shoulder joint. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline (For incision and drainage procedures, superficial, see 10040-10160) Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic. The elbow area includes the head and neck of the radius and olecranon process.

short_description: Incision, deep, with opening of bone cortex (eg, for osteomyelitis or bone abscess), humerus or elbow
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the bone cortex to relieve pain, pressure, or infection due to such conditions as osteomyelitis or a bone abscess in a localized site on the upper arm or elbow area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the affected site along the humerus or elbow. He divides the soft tissues and muscles underneath to reach the bone. He then divides the periosteum covering the part of bone with the infection or abscess and opens the medullary cavity using either a series of drill holes or creating a window in the bone cortex. He then drains the abscess. He may also scrape off the infected bone to reveal healthy bone. He irrigates the wound and rejoins the periosteum. The provider may close the incision in layers or keep it open for subsequent discharge if any and may perform a secondary closure later. Finally, he may apply a splint to help with healing. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled off sac or pocket, caused by infection. Bone cortex: The outer shell, or cortex, of a bone; also called compact bone. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Irrigate: Wash out. Localized: Confined to a single or small area. Medullary cavity: The inner chamber of a bone that contains the marrow, the substance that produces new blood cells. Osteomyelitis: Infection in the bone. Periosteum: A dense fibrous connective tissue that wraps the outer surface of the bone except the surface of the bone that goes in to forming joints with other bones. Splint: A device that supports and immobilizes an injured part of the body. Read Less

short_description: Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor of head or neck of radius or olecranon process; with autograft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises or removes a bone cyst or noncancerous tumor from part of the radius bone. He then fills the defect with grafting material, which he harvests from the patient. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the tumor or cyst in the radius, or the forearm bone. He then dissects down through the underlying muscle and tissue to expose the radius bone or the elbow joint and locate the lesion. Once he exposes the lesion, he then uses surgical tools, such as a curette or osteotome, to remove the growth from the bone, often excising a very small rim of healthy margin along with the tumor. The provider then places an autograft in the defect to fill the space, irrigates the wound, and closes the patient's incision in layers. Terminology Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping; also spelled curet. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Olecranon process: The bony prominence of the elbow, visible on the rear aspect when the elbow is flexed. Osteotome: A surgical instrument used to cut bone. Radius: One of the forearm bones, on the side of the thumb. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass; can be benign or cancerous. Read Less

short_description: Excision, radial head Notes: (For replacement with implant, use 24366)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider enters the elbow joint and excises the radial head following an elbow injury or fracture of the radial head. These are the most common elbow fractures in adults, and can result in major disability. The radial head has a specific role of fixation in the joint. So, the decision to excise the radial head fracture is influenced by the presence of injuries and their severity. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the lateral side of the elbow. He enters the elbow joint, incising the capsule, and he exposes the radial head. With the help of a small bone saw, he excises the radial head and closes the capsule. After completion of the procedure, the provider ensures control of bleeding and sutures the wound in layers. Terminology Elbow capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses the elbow joint between the humerus in the upper arm and the radius and ulna in the forearm. Lateral: In a sideward direction; to or from a side. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Radial head: The proximal aspect of the radius bone. Tips Use 24366 instead of 24130 for replacement of the radial head with implant. Read Less

short_description: Resection of elbow joint (arthrectomy)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises the distal part of the humerus and the proximal part of the radius and ulna that collectively form the elbow joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a long incision over the elbow area and brings the incision deep down to the bone. The provider exposes the joint completely by retracting the muscle layer. With the help of a cutting instrument, typically an electric saw, the provider cuts the distal humerus and heads of the radius and ulna to completely remove the joint. After taking out the excised sections of bone, the provider sutures back the muscles to enclose the remaining structure to give some support. But overall the joint remains grossly unstable until outer support is provided. At the end of the surgery, the provider irrigates the operative site and closes it in layers. The provider performs this surgery in a case where the joint is not treatable by conventional measures after fracture or progress of a degenerative disease. Read Less

short_description: Removal of prosthesis, includes debridement and synovectomy when performed; humeral and ulnar components Notes: (To report removal of foreign body, elbow, see 24200, 24201) (To report removal of hardware from the distal humerus or proximal ulna, other than humeral and ulnar prosthesis, use 20680) (Do not report 24160 in conjunction with 24370 or 24371 if a prosthesis [ie, humeral and/or ulnar component(s)] is being removed and replaced in the same elbow during the same surgical session)
lay_term: The provider removes a previously implanted prosthesis from the elbow joint. The implant being removed has a humeral component as well as an ulnar component. Explanation After anesthesia is administered to the patient and prepping and draping is done, the provider makes an incision over the prosthetic implant area, usually overlying the earlier incision or using a posterior approach. He reflects (bends back) skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, tendons, and muscular layers as encountered to reach the implant, making a point of protecting the ulnar nerve via instrumentation or technique. He debrides any necrotic area. He exposes the humeral and ulnar components of the prosthesis. Synovectomy (removal of inflamed joint tissue) may also be necessary to adequately expose the prosthesis and facilitate its removal from the joint. The prosthesis is normally taken out along with any cement in the joint, for which curettement or debridement may be required. The wound is washed with saline and antibiotic solution. The wound is closed in layers in an aseptic manner. Terminology Humeral: Related to the humerus, the upper arm bone Prosthesis: An artificial, fabricated implant that acts as a substitute for a damaged or missing body part Ulnar: Related to the ulna, the larger of the two forearm bones Tips This code is not appropriate if an implant is removed and replaced at the same session. Instead, see 24370 or 24371. Read Less

short_description: Tendon lengthening, upper arm or elbow, each tendon
lay_term: In this procedure the provider surgically increases the length of a tendon of the upper arm or elbow, to release the contracture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the anterior side of the elbow or upper arm area. He incises it down to the level of the tendon. To prevent any damage to blood vessels and nerve tissues he retracts these toward the sides. After exposing the tendon, the provider makes an elongated Z–shape incision, stretches the tendon, and sutures both the ends. The provider may also excise some part of the capsule if required to treat the joint contracture, which is inclusive to this procedure. At the end, he irrigates and sutures the operative site and places a drain if required. Terminology Joint capsule: A ligamentous sac that surrounds the articular cavity of a freely movable joint; is attached to the bones and completely encloses the joint. Joint contracture: Permanent tightening of nonbony tissues, such as muscles, tendons, ligaments. Tendon: A tendon is a fibrous connective tissue that attaches muscle to bone. Tips This code is for lengthening of a single tendon. If the provider performs the procedure on more than one tendon of the same area, use the code more than once with modifier 59 appended to the additional code. Read Less

short_description: Flexor-plasty, elbow (eg, Steindler type advancement)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider increases elbow flexion strength by transferring the group of flexor muscles from the medial condyle of the humerus to a few inches up on the humeral bone surface. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal curved incision over the protruded area known as the medial condyle toward the midline of the elbow. He incises down to the level of the muscles. To prevent any damage to blood vessels and nerve tissues, he retracts these toward the sides. The provider locates the common origin of the flexor muscles group that includes the pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum sublimis, and flexor carpi ulnaris. He separates the origin from the medial condyle and attaches it a few centimeters above on the humeral bone surface laterally. This transposition changes the function of the muscles from pronation of the forearm to flexion of the elbow. This procedure is helpful in the treatment of biceps brachii muscle injury or paralysis. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the incision in layers and places a splint while the elbow is flexed. Terminology Condyle: A round prominence at the end of a bone. Flexion: Movement that decreases the angle between the bones of the limb at the joint. Flexor muscles: A group of muscles that helps in reducing the angle between the two bones of a joint. Insertion of tendon or muscle: End of tendon or muscle that is attached to a moving bone of the joint. Medial: Toward the midline of the body. Origin of tendon or muscle: End of tendon or muscle that is attached to stationary bone of the joint. Pronation: Rotation of the hands and forearms so that the palms face downward. Read Less

guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic. The elbow area includes the head and neck of the radius and olecranon process.

short_description: Reinsertion of ruptured biceps or triceps tendon, distal, with or without tendon graft
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider reattaches the torn or separated distal end of a biceps or triceps tendon back to the bone from where it detached. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the anterior elbow near the location of biceps tendon detachment on the bicipital tuberosity of the radial head. The provider drills holes in the radial head, trims and cleans the torn end of the tendon, and sutures it tightly on the holes. In a case involving a triceps tendon, the provider makes an incision on the posterior side of the upper arm and exposes the triceps tendon. In a similar fashion to biceps tendon reinsertion, the provider drills the holes in the olecranon, pulls the trimmed end of the triceps tendon, and sutures it on the holes. The provider may use a tendon graft, usually obtained from forearm, to facilitate the reinsertion. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the operative site in layers and immobilizes the arm with a splint. Terminology Biceps tendons: The tendons that connect the ends of a biceps muscle to the shoulder joint and elbow. Bicipital tuberosity: An oval projection on the inner aspect of the neck of the radius. Olecranon: A bony prominence at the elbow, on the upper end of the ulna. Rupture: Sudden breakage or bursting of a structure. Triceps tendons: The tendons that connect the ends of a triceps muscle on the back of the upper arm and serve to extend the forearm. Tips Do not report harvesting and preparation of graft separately. Read Less

short_description: Reconstruction medial collateral ligament, elbow, with tendon graft (includes harvesting of graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses a tendon graft to reconstruct the patient’s injured medial collateral ligament to restore the function of the elbow. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the medial epicondyle, making sure to avoid the cutaneous nerve that innervates the skin. He identifies the damage in the medial collateral ligament, MCL, and splits it from the epicondyle to the sublime tubercle, anteromedial facet of coronoid. He drills a hole in the medial epicondyle creating a tunnel. Similarly, he drills two more holes in the proximal site of the humerus creating a second tunnel. He makes a transverse incision at the wrist. Then, using a tendon stripper that cuts the tendon into layers, the provider harvests the palmaris longus tendon. He secures this harvested graft through the epicondylar and humerus tunnels by suturing the free ends and also to the fascia near the intermuscular septum that separates each different muscle and the remnants of the MCL. After restoring the position of the tendon graft, the provider closes the wound in sutures and places the hand in a splint, cast. Terminology Cast: Plaster and bandage that the provider molds to protect broken or fractured limbs. Elbow: The joint or bend of the arm between the forearm and the upper arm. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structures with another material — artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis (joining) of two structures. Harvest: Obtaining cells or tissues from a donor and preserve them for transplantation. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Medial collateral ligament, MCL:A ligament present posterior to the axis of elbow flexion; it is the primary medial stabilizer of the flexed elbow joint. Medial epicondyle: A bony protrusion located on the medial side of the bone's distal end. Reconstruction: Revising a structure to approximate its normal anatomy or restoring it to its appropriate function. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Splints: Rigid material to secure and immobilize a fractured or dislocated bone, holding it in a fixed position. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips If the provider performs a repair of medial collateral ligament, elbow, with local tissue, use 24345. Read Less

short_description: Tenotomy, elbow, lateral or medial (eg, epicondylitis, tennis elbow, golfer's elbow); debridement, soft tissue and/or bone, open with tendon repair or reattachment Notes: (Do not report 24357-24359 in conjunction with 29837, 29838)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the medial or lateral site of a tenotomy for debridement of the fibrosed tissue to relieve the contracture of the tendon. He also reattaches the residual tendons. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a skin incision at the site of the tenotomy to access the tendons at the lateral or medial epicondyle of the elbow. She makes this incision for an open tenotomy procedure. She performs debridement of the soft tissue or bone along with the tenotomy. The debridement helps to remove more bony tissue and scar tissue in order to provide better movement or stretch of the tendons. This breaks up the scar tissue and relieves the contracture of the tendon. While performing this procedure, if there are any residual tendons after debridement, she reattaches them to the site of the respective epicondyles. At the end of the procedure, she achieves hemostasis and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Contracture: Abnormal premature contraction, or shortening, of a muscle. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Elbow: The joint or bend of the arm between the forearm and the upper arm. Epicondyle: A rounded protuberance at the end of a bone, serving as a place of attachment for ligaments, tendons, and muscles. Epicondylitis: Inflammation of the epicondyle caused by various factors including repetitive movements. Golfer's elbow: Inflammation of the tendon on the medial epicondyle. Hemostasis: Process that causes bleeding to cease, which involves a balance of coagulation and clot breakdown. Scar: Areas of fibrous tissue that replace normal skin after injury. Tennis elbow: Inflammation of the tendon on the lateral epicondyle. Tenotomy: To surgically cut or make a hole in a tendon. Tips If the provider performs a tenotomy, elbow, lateral or medial epicondylitis, tennis elbow, golfer's elbow; debridement, soft tissue and or bone, open, use 24358. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs membrane arthroplasty of an elbow, a procedure that is also known as interposition arthroplasty. In this procedure, the provider uses a graft like fascia lata, dermis, or Achilles tendon to resurface the articular surface of the arthritic elbow. The aim of this procedure is to relieve the pain and disability in a severely damaged elbow. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the back or side of the elbow joint. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue just under the skin and farther down, moving the tendons and ligaments out of the way. He ensures the nerves and blood vessels are not damaged. He exposes the joint and removes any spur and scar tissue. short_description: Arthroplasty, elbow; with distal humeral prosthetic replacement
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs elbow joint arthroplasty in which he replaces the arthritic end of the humerus bone with a prosthesis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the back side of the elbow joint. She then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue just under the skin and farther down, moving the tendons and ligaments out of the way. She ensures that she doesn’t damage the nerves and blood vessels. She then exposes the joint and removes any spur and scar tissue. She excises the distal arthritic end of the humerus bone near the elbow and incises the bone to prepare it for inserting the prosthesis. She next fixes the prosthesis into the distal end of the humerus and hammers or otherwise affixes it into the humerus. She aligns the prosthesis with the upper end of the radius and ulna. She then reattaches the muscle and soft tissue. She finally closes the wound and leaves a drain in place. Tips Use 24360 when the provider performs membrane elbow arthroplasty. Use 24362 when the provider performs elbow arthroplasty with implants and fascia lata ligament reconstruction. short_description: Arthroplasty, elbow; with implant and fascia lata ligament reconstruction
lay_term: In this procedure the provider fits an artificial prosthesis cap on the distal end of the humerus and reconstructs the joint capsule with the fascia lata graft taken from the thigh. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal curved incision over the protruded area, the medial condyle, toward the midline of the elbow. He incises down to the level of the joint capsule. To prevent any damage to blood vessels and nerve tissues, he retracts these toward the sides. The provider excises the capsule and exposes the bony surface of the joint. The provider separates the elbow joint to work on the surfaces of the bones. First, he rasps and smooths the surface of the humerus with the help of a burr or other sharp object and fits an artificial surface cap on the humeral end. Next, he removes any dead or diseased tissue from the surfaces of the radius and ulna and brings together the surfaces of all three bones. Then the provider reattaches the flexor tendon back to the epicondyle of the humerus. To provide a strong union the provider harvests a fascia lata graft of appropriate length from thigh area and folds the graft in half crossway. He attaches the lower end of the graft to the trochlear notch of the ulna and attaches the upper part to the capsule. He inserts the middle portion between the space left between the radius and ulna. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the incision in layers and places a splint while the elbow is flexed. Terminology Epicondyle: A rounded protuberance at the end of a bone. Fascia lata: A deep fascia of the thigh region. Prosthesis/implant: An artificial device used to replace a missing or damaged body part. Trochlear notch: A deep depression in the proximal end of the ulna by which the ulna articulates with the trochlea of the humerus at the elbow. Read Less

short_description: Arthroplasty, radial head; with implant
lay_term: In this procedure the provider fits an artificial prosthesis cap on the upper end of the radius for smooth and painless movement of the elbow. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal curved incision over the protruded area, the medial condyle, toward the midline of the elbow. He incises down to the level of the joint capsule. To prevent any damage to blood vessels and nerve tissues, he retracts these toward the sides. The provider excises the capsule and exposes the bony surface of the joint. Then the provider accesses the head of the radius by incising ligaments above it. He rasps and smooths the surface of the radius with the help of a burr or other sharp object. He fits an artificial surface cap from the top and nails it in the center of the radius head. Next, he realigns the radius into the depression of the humerus and sutures the ligaments back around the joint. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the incision in layers and places a splint while the elbow is flexed. Terminology Prosthesis/implant: An artificial device used to replace a missing or damaged body part. Read Less

short_description: Revision of total elbow arthroplasty, including allograft when performed; humeral or ulnar component
lay_term: The provider revises a prior total elbow replacement surgery due to failure of one of the components of the artificial joint, i.e., the humerus in the upper arm or the ulna in the lower arm. She replaces the component and may insert donor bone graft material. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the previous incision. She dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue just under the skin and moves the tendons and ligaments out of the way, taking care to avoid damage to nerves and blood vessels. She incises the joint capsule, exposes the joint, and removes any scar tissue. She removes the old cement, removes the failed component, and examines it for defects. She uses a rasp, a sanding instrument, to smooth the edges of the lower end of the humerus or the upper end of the ulna for good prosthetic fit. She may augment the bone with allograft. She applies fresh cement, flexes the elbow, and inserts the replacement component. She closes the tissues over the joint and inserts a drain. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called an allogeneic graft or homograft. Arthroplasty: Reconstruction or replacement of a joint, the point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connects bones and joints as well as holds organs in place. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part. Radial head: Disk shaped end of the radius nearest the elbow, where it joins the humerus, the other forearm bone. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Ulna: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the medial, or inside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the fifth finger. Tips In this procedure, only a single component is replaced, i.e., humerus or ulna, not both. For variations on this procedure, see codes in the section 24300 to 24498, Repair, revision, and or reconstruction procedures on the humerus, or upper arm, and elbow. Read Less

Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the previous incision. She dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue just under the skin and moves the tendons and ligaments out of the way, taking care to avoid damage to nerves and blood vessels. She incises the joint capsule, exposes the joint, and removes any scar tissue. She removes the old cement, removes the failed components, and examines them for defects. She uses a rasp, a sanding instrument, to smooth the edges of the lower end of the humerus and the upper end of the ulna for good prosthetic fit. She may augment the bones with allograft. She applies fresh cement, flexes the elbow, and inserts the replacement components. She closes the tissues over the joint and inserts a drain. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called an allogeneic graft or homograft. Arthroplasty: Reconstruction or replacement of a joint, the point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connects bones and joints as well as holds organs in place. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part. Radial head: Disk shaped end of the radius nearest the elbow, where it joins the humerus, the other forearm bone. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Ulna: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the medial, or inside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the fifth finger. Tips In this procedure, both components are replaced, i.e., humerus and ulna. For variations on this procedure, see codes in the section 24300 to 24498, Repair, revision, and or reconstruction procedures on the humerus, or upper arm, and elbow. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic. The elbow area includes the head and neck of the radius and olecranon process.

short_description: Multiple osteotomies with realignment on intramedullary rod, humeral shaft (Sofield type procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts an improperly developed humeral bone shaft in multiple sections to straighten it with the help of an intramedullary rod. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a long incision over the humerus shaft. He takes the incision down to the level of the bone and exposes the bone by retracting the adjacent muscles. He retracts the nerves and blood vessels to prevent any damage. The provider cuts both ends of the humerus through the necks, the provider cuts both ends from the necks to insert an intramedullary rod later in middle of the humeral shaft. Next the provider cuts the shaft in multiple sections if required to correct the alignment. After cutting the sections, the provider chips out any deformed bony areas and inserts an intramedullary rod in the center of the bone to support it. Next the provider fixes back both the epiphyses cut initially. After confirmation of proper alignment and rotation, he fixes the bone sections with the help of screws or nails over the rod. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the operative site in layers and immobilizes the arm with a splint. Terminology Epiphysis: Growing end of long bones. Intramedullary rod: A metal rod that can be inserted into the medullary cavity of a bone; also know as IM nails used to treat fractures of the shaft of long bones. Osteotomy: Surgical cutting of bone. Read Less

short_description: Osteoplasty, humerus (eg, shortening or lengthening) (excluding 64876)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider takes out a piece of the humerus bone shaft to correct the length of the bone. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the humeral shaft, bringing the incision down to the level of the bone. He retracts the nerves and blood vessels to prevent any damage. Next, the provider cuts a section of bone in a wedge shape. To shorten the bone, the provider reduces the angle of the horizontal V–shape formed after wedge osteotomy and fixes both the ends together with the help of plates and screws. In case lengthening is required, the provider retracts both ends of the osteotomy and fixes the ends at the appropriate extended distance with the help of screws and plates. At the end of the surgery, he irrigates and sutures the operative site and places a drain if required. Terminology Osteoplasty: Surgical repair or alteration of bone. Wedge resection: Surgical procedure to remove a triangle–shaped slice of tissue. Tips Report an X–ray code separately if performed before or during the procedure. See +64876 if the provider shortens the bone for a nerve shortening procedure. Read Less

short_description: Repair of nonunion or malunion, humerus; with iliac or other autograft (includes obtaining graft) Notes: (For proximal radius and/or ulna, see 25400-25420)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider treats a nonunion or malunion deformity in the upper arm by cutting the undeveloped or improperly grown bone and fixing it with the help of a bone graft taken from the patient’s own body. He excises the irregular bony area. The provider harvests a graft from the iliac bone or other long bone of the patient’s body and uses it to bridge the humerus gap created after excision of the irregular bone ends. The provider confirms the alignment of the repaired site. At the end of the surgery, he irrigates and sutures the operative site and places a splint for the immobilization of the arm. Terminology Iliac graft: A graft of tissue taken from iliac bone of the pelvic girdle. Malunion: Incomplete union or union in a faulty position of a bone after a fracture. short_description: Hemiepiphyseal arrest (eg, cubitus varus or valgus, distal humerus)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses a technique such as stapling or placing a plate in part of the epiphyseal area near the elbow to halt growth. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the distal humeral area near the elbow. He incises down to the level of the joint capsule. To prevent any damage to blood vessels and nerve tissues he retracts these toward the sides. He locates the growth plate. The provider places screws or screw–fixated plates across half of the growth plate to stop growth in that part of the bone. This allows for correction of the patient's inward or outward forearm deviation over time. The provider ensures no soft tissue is stuck under the plates/screws. He uses imaging to confirm placement. The provider achieves hemostasis at the site and may inject pain medication into the wound. He closes the wound in layers and applies a dressing. Terminology Cubitus varus: Inward deviation of the forearm. Cubitus valgus: Outward deviation of the forearm. Epiphysis: Part of a long bone, such as the end, that converts into bone separately from the shaft. Physis: Growth plate. Read Less

short_description: Decompression fasciotomy, forearm, with brachial artery exploration
lay_term: The provider incises the fascia of a membrane enclosed compartment in the forearm to relieve pressure and increase blood flow in the presence of compartment syndrome, after an injury or surgery. He examines the brachial artery for signs of damage. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the anterior aspect of the forearm. He excises the fascia and checks the compartment pressure of the compressed deep flexor muscles. The provider decompresses the compartment. He analyzes the brachial artery and checks for areas of reduced circulation. He cuts through the fascia and debrides all the damaged, nonviable muscle and or nerve tissue, thereby reducing the pressure on neurovascular structures underneath the fascia. This restores the restricted blood supply and relieves symptoms. Finally, the provider may leave the wounds open at the end of the session or close the wounds by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body or a structure. Brachial artery: Major blood vessel of the upper limb. Compartment syndrome: Critical build up of pressure due to fluid accumulation within a membrane covered compartment that contains vessels, nerves, and other structures; without prompt attention and release of pressure, permanent damage to these delicate structures ensues. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow.
