short_description: Open treatment of humeral supracondylar or transcondylar fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed; without intercondylar extension
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the humerus, the upper arm bone, through or above a condyle, a rounded projection at the end of the bone, but without extending between the condyles in a open procedure. He makes an incision in the arm and may apply hardware to stabilize the fracture during healing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the fractured bone. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He next retracts the muscles to gain adequate exposure of the fracture. He then adjusts the bone to reduce the fracture. He may stabilize the fracture with a plate and screws or other internal fixation. He ascertains the alignment on imaging. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. He applies a splint or brace. Terminology Condyle: Rounded projection on the end of a bone, usually associated with a joint connecting with another bone. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Intercondylar: Between two condyles, rounded projections on the end of a bone. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Supracondylar: Immediately above a condyle, a rounded projection on the end of a bone. Transcondylar: Through a condyle, a rounded projection on the end of a bone. Tips When reporting the global method of fracture care, an evaluation and management (E/M) service may also be reported. Documentation must support a decision for surgery, modifier 57, Decision for surgery, and or a separate identifiable service. Because modifier 57 claims involve an E/M service that results in a decision for surgery, you would expect to see the same diagnosis code for both the E/M and the surgical procedure. The provider would not make a decision for surgery based on a significant problem unrelated to the procedure. Do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. CMS has approximately 50 Q HCPCS codes that address supply issues with casting and splinting applications. Read Less

guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic. The elbow area includes the head and neck of the radius and olecranon process.

short_description: Open treatment of humeral epicondylar fracture, medial or lateral, includes internal fixation, when performed
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of an epicondyle of the humerus, a small bump on either side of the elbow, above the condyle, the rounded projection at the top of the upper arm bone, in an open procedure. She makes an incision in the arm and may apply hardware to stabilize the fracture during healing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the fractured bone. She dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. She retracts the muscles to gain adequate exposure of the medial or lateral humeral epicondylar fracture. She then adjusts the bone to reduce the fracture. She may apply a plate and screws, wires, or pins to stabilize the reduction. She checks the alignment on imaging. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. She applies a splint or brace. Terminology Condyle: Rounded projection on the end of a bone, usually associated with a joint connecting with another bone. Epicondyle: A small bump on either side of the elbow, above the condyle, a rounded bony projection on the humerus, or upper arm bone. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Lateral epicondyle: The outer of two small bumps on either side of the elbow, above the condyle. Medial epicondyle: The inner of two small bumps on either side of the elbow, above the condyle. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Tips When reporting the global method of fracture care, an evaluation and management, or E/M, service may also be reported. Documentation must support a decision for surgery, modifier 57, Decision for surgery, and or a separate identifiable service. Because modifier 57 claims involve an E/M service that results in a decision for surgery, you would expect to see the same diagnosis code for both the E/M and the surgical procedure. The provider would not make a decision for surgery based on a significant problem unrelated to the procedure. Do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. CMS has approximately 50 Q HCPCS codes that address supply issues with casting and splinting applications. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of humeral condylar fracture, medial or lateral, includes internal fixation, when performed Notes: (To report closed treatment of fractures without manipulation, see 24530, 24560, 24576, 24650, 24670) (To report closed treatment of fractures with manipulation, see 24535, 24565, 24577, 24675)
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of a condyle of the humerus, one of two rounded projections at the top of the upper arm bone, in an open procedure. He makes an incision in the arm and may apply hardware to stabilize the fracture during healing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the fractured bone. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He retracts the muscles to gain adequate exposure of the medial or lateral humeral condylar fracture. He then adjusts the bone to reduce the fracture. He may apply a plate and screws, wires, or pins to stabilize the reduction. He checks the alignment on imaging. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. He applies a splint or brace. Terminology Condyle: Rounded projection on the end of a bone, usually associated with a joint connecting with another bone. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Lateral condyle: The outer of two rounded projection on the end of a bone, usually associated with a joint connecting with another bone. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Medial condyle: The inner of two rounded projection on the end of a bone, usually associated with a joint connecting with another bone. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Tips When reporting the global method of fracture care, an evaluation and management, or E/M, service may also be reported. Documentation must support a decision for surgery, modifier 57, Decision for surgery, and or a separate identifiable service. Because modifier 57 claims involve an E/M service that results in a decision for surgery, you would expect to see the same diagnosis code for both the E/M and the surgical procedure. The provider would not make a decision for surgery based on a significant problem unrelated to the procedure. Do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. short_description: Open treatment of periarticular fracture and/or dislocation of the elbow (fracture distal humerus and proximal ulna and/or proximal radius)
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the elbow joint and or displacement of the bones in the elbow joint, the upper arm bone, or humerus, and one or both of the lower arm bones, the radius and ulna. He makes one or more incisions over the elbow to make the repair. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure's point of attachment. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure's point of attachment. Periarticular: Around a joint, unions of structures like two bones. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the thumb. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. short_description: Open treatment of periarticular fracture and/or dislocation of the elbow (fracture distal humerus and proximal ulna and/or proximal radius); with implant arthroplasty Notes: (See also 24361)
lay_term: Through an opening in the skin, the provider treats a fracture related to the elbow joint, an elbow dislocation, or both using one or more implants. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the treatment area through one or more openings in the skin, such as by making an incision over the fracture or dislocation site and dissecting through subcutaneous tissue and muscle to expose the bones. Fracture involves the humerus (upper arm bone) and the ulna and/or radius (lower arm bones), specifically the ends near the elbow. If necessary, the provider aligns the bones in proper position. As appropriate, the provider removes portions of bone to be replaced and prepares the implant site, such as by debridement or making canals to make space for the implant. The provider inserts the implant, securing it in place while protecting and preserving nerves and ligaments. The provider checks the elbow movement and closes the surgical site. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of Monteggia type of fracture dislocation at elbow (fracture proximal end of ulna with dislocation of radial head), includes internal fixation, when performed
lay_term: The provider repairs a fracture of the ulna at the elbow with displacement of the head of the radius, the bones in the forearm. He realigns the joint and may attach wires and plates to stabilize it during healing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the dislocation site and carries it down deep to the bone, dissecting the surrounding muscles. He identifies the site of the injury, with the fracture of the proximal end of the ulna and dislocation of the radial head. He reduces the fracture and the dislocation. If required, he inserts wires and plates to stabilize the reduction. He confirms the alignment with imaging. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Fracture dislocation: A dislocation, or displacement, of two bones that normally connect to form a joint, accompanied by a fracture, or break, in one of the bones. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Ligament: Fibrous band that connects bones and joints as well as holds organs in place. Monteggia type fracture dislocation: Fracture of the proximal ulna, one of the bones in the forearm, at its point nearest the elbow, with dislocation, or displacement, of the head of the radius, the other forearm bone. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure's point of attachment. Radial head: The top of the radius, one of the bones of the forearm, located adjacent to the elbow. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm. Reduce: To restore normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Ulna: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the medial, or inside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the fifth finger. Tips When reporting the global method of fracture care, an evaluation and management, or E/M, service may also be reported. Documentation must support a decision for surgery, modifier 57, Decision for surgery, and or a separate identifiable service. Because modifier 57 claims involve an E/M service that results in a decision for surgery, you would expect to see the same diagnosis code for both the E/M and the surgical procedure. The provider would not make a decision for surgery based on a significant problem unrelated to the procedure. Read Less

short_description: Amputation, arm through humerus; with implant
lay_term: In this procedure the provider completely cuts through the upper arm at any point on the humerus and inserts an implant to maintain the length of the amputated limb or to place an artificial limb in the future. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision just below the area of the resection. The provider brings the incision down to the level of the bone; at this point he ligates any blood vessels and retracts the nerves. Next, he cuts the humerus and rasps the edges with an electric burr. After reshaping of the bone, the provider inserts an implant in the center of the bone in the intramedullary space. The provider cuts the muscles and skin, keeping sufficient margin to cover the wound. At the end of the surgery, the provider covers the wound with muscle, sutures the muscle and fascia, and then he closes the skin with sutures after placing a drain. Terminology Intramedullary: The medullary cavity is the central cavity of bone shafts where red bone marrow and/or yellow bone marrow are stored. Read Less

short_description: Decompression fasciotomy, forearm and/or wrist, flexor AND extensor compartment; without debridement of nonviable muscle and/or nerve
lay_term: The provider incises the forearm and or wrist down to the level of fascial tissue to relieve a buildup of pressure in a membrane covered compartment that could damage muscles and nerves. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the inside aspect of the forearm extending into the hand. He carries out dissection carefully so that nearby neurovascular structures do not get disrupted. He releases the fascia at the volar, or palm side, surface of the forearm in both the flexor and extensor compartments. He releases the fascia around the deep compartment muscles as well. He takes care to protect the radial nerve. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Compartment syndrome: Critical buildup of pressure due to fluid accumulation within a membrane covered compartment that contains vessels, nerves, and other structures; without prompt attention and release of pressure, permanent damage to these delicate structures ensues. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Fasciotomy: Incision of fascial tissue, fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Flexor muscle: Muscle that bends at a joint. Flexor compartment: Membrane covered compartment that contains the flexor muscle and nerve tissue in the forearm; also known as anterior compartment. Extensor compartment: Membrane covered compartment that contains the extensor muscle and nerve tissue in the forearm; also known as posterior compartment. Nonviable: Dead or dying tissues or structures. Tips This procedure describes decompression fasciotomy in two compartments. When coding for compartment syndrome, you first confirm if the provider worked on the flexor or extensor compartment or both. Next, you read further in the operative note to learn if any muscle or nerve debridement was done. Lastly, you should determine if the provider explored the brachial artery to improve blood supply in the limb. Once you've completed these steps, you'll be better equipped to select the appropriate code. Read Less

short_description: Decompression fasciotomy, forearm and/or wrist, flexor AND extensor compartment; with debridement of nonviable muscle and/or nerve
lay_term: The provider incises the forearm and or wrist down to the level of fascial tissue to relieve a buildup of pressure in a membrane covered compartment. He excises damaged muscle and or nerve tissue. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the inside aspect of the forearm extending into the hand. He carries out dissection carefully so that nearby neurovascular structures do not get disrupted. He releases the fascia at the volar, or palm side, surface of the forearm in both the flexor and extensor compartments. He releases the fascia around the deep compartment muscles as well. He resects any nonviable muscle or nerve tissue. He takes care to protect the radial nerve. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Compartment syndrome: Critical buildup of pressure due to fluid accumulation within a membrane covered compartment that contains vessels, nerves, and other structures; without prompt attention and release of pressure, permanent damage to these delicate structures ensues. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Fasciotomy: Incision of fascial tissue, fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures. Flexor muscle: Muscle that bends at a joint. Flexor compartment: Membrane covered compartment that contains the flexor muscle and nerve tissue in the forearm; also known as anterior compartment. Extensor compartment: Membrane covered compartment that contains the extensor muscle and nerve tissue in the forearm; also known as posterior compartment. Nonviable: Dead or dying tissues or structures. Tips This procedure describes decompression fasciotomy in two compartments. When coding for compartment syndrome, you first confirm if the provider worked on the flexor or extensor compartment or both. Next, you read further in the operative note to learn if any muscle or nerve debridement was done. Lastly, you should determine if the provider explored the brachial artery to improve blood supply in the limb. short_description: Arthrotomy, distal radioulnar joint including repair of triangular cartilage, complex
lay_term: In this procedure the provider makes an incision to expose the wrist joint and treat the triangular cartilage using sutures or by debridement, typically in patients with cartilage damage due to injury or degenerative diseases. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision on the posterior side of the wrist joint. He incises down to the level of the joint capsule. To prevent any damage to blood vessels and nerve tissues, he retracts these toward the sides. The provider excises the capsule and exposes the joint surface. He retracts the joint between the wrist's carpal bones and the lower end of the arm's ulna bone to gain access to the triangular cartilage. If the damage to the cartilage is repairable, the provider sutures the damaged area. If the damage is in the central portion of the cartilage or not repairable, the provider performs debridement of the area to smooth the surface to reduce the friction between the bone and cartilage. After the repair, he confirms the alignment and motion of the joint. At the end of the procedure, he sutures the joint capsule back over the bones and closes the wound in layers after irrigation. Terminology Arthrotomy: Cutting into a joint to expose its interior. Triangular cartilage: Structure located on the small finger side of the wrist that cushions and supports the small carpal bones in the wrist. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure the provider makes an incision to expose the extensor tendon to excise the synovial layer from the extensor tendon sheath. short_description: Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor of radius or ulna (excluding head or neck of radius and olecranon process); with autograft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider removes any abnormal benign growth from a large area of the arm's radius or ulna bones. He repairs the defect created due to cyst or tumor excision with the help of a graft taken from any other body part of the patient. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the target forearm area. To prevent any damage, he retracts blood vessels and nerves. He exposes the area where the bone cyst or benign tumor has developed. First the provider incises and retracts the periosteum layer of the bone. Then with the help of an osteotome or sharp object, he cuts or scrapes out the cyst or tumor. After excision of the lesion in its entirety, he harvests a graft from the patient’s body and places it over the defect created by the excision of the cyst or tumor. He repairs both the graft and tumor excision site with sutures after irrigation with antibiotics. Periosteum: A dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones except at the surfaces of the joints. short_description: Radical resection of tumor, radius or ulna
lay_term: In this procedure the provider excises a tumor of the arm's radius or ulna bones, including some of the surrounding healthy tissues to make sure that no diseased bony or soft tissue is left in that area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the tumor area of the radius or ulna. He brings the incision down through the muscles to expose the bone, and then he retracts the periosteum to access the tumor. The provider excises the tumor in its entirety along with diseased soft tissue. In addition to that he also excises the nearby healthy bone and soft tissues like tendon or muscles. After confirming the complete excision of affected structures, the provider places back the periosteum on the bone surface and uses nearby muscles to provide stability to the joint. At the end, he irrigates the site, repairs the area with the help of sutures, and places a drain if required. Terminology Periosteum: A dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones except at the surfaces of the joints. Read Less

short_description: Repair, tendon or muscle, extensor, forearm and/or wrist; secondary, with free graft (includes obtaining graft), each tendon or muscle
lay_term: The provider repairs an extensor tendon or muscle in the forearm or wrist. He applies a tissue graft obtained from another location in the patient’s body. He performs the repair after the passage of time from the original traumatic injury. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the affected tendon or muscle. He deepens the incision, taking care to avoid nerve tissue. He clears any adhesions. He harvests a free graft from nearby tendon or muscle tissue and lays the graft over the injured tendon or muscle. He sutures the graft in place. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. He applies a splint. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery, that form between tissues and organs; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Flexor muscle: Muscle that bends at a joint. Flexor tendon: Tendon associated with a flexor muscle, a muscle that bends at a joint. Free graft: An excised piece of tissue, unattached to its vascular supply, suitable for grafting, or transplanting, to another location. Secondary repair: Surgical repair done remotely after an injury, after healing has already begun. Tenosynovectomy: Excision of the membrane sheath covering a tendon. Tips Report 25274 once for each tendon repair. Hence, if repairing five tendons, 25274 should be coded five times. Additional Info There are eight different zones on the extensor surface of the hand, zone I to zone VIII, based on the location of the tendons. In the case of severe injury, first it is required to stabilize the fracture or laceration of the forearm or wrist and next to suture digital nerves. Later, tendons are repaired with sutures or with grafts. Read Less

short_description: Tendon transplantation or transfer, flexor or extensor, forearm and/or wrist, single; each tendon Notes: (Do not report 25310 in conjunction with 25447, 25448, when performed for intercarpal or carpometacarpal joint arthroplasty)
lay_term: The provider transfers a tendon from one location in the forearm or wrist to another to replace a damaged or diseased tendon and restore motion of the hand. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision over the forearm or wrist and exposes the tendons. short_description: Tendon transplantation or transfer, flexor or extensor, forearm and/or wrist, single; with tendon graft(s) (includes obtaining graft), each tendon

short_description: Flexor origin slide (eg, for cerebral palsy, Volkmann contracture), forearm and/or wrist
lay_term: The provider releases the origin of the flexor tendons to allow the muscles to slide distally in a procedure to improve the appearance and function of a severely deformed hand, wrist, or fingers. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the inner aspect of the volar, or palm, side of the forearm up to its midpoint, over the ulna. He releases the ulnar nerve. He incises the tendon origin from the medial epicondyle and the muscles are released from the medial epicondyle and ulna, extending almost to the wrist. He releases the artery and nerve. He releases the origin of the flexor digitorum profundus from the radius to the index finger and the remaining origin of the flexor digitorum sublimis from the coronoid process. He extends the wrist and fingers to identify any remaining tight bands and releases them. He transplants the ulnar nerve anterior to the brachialis tendon. He divides the tendon in the presence of any remaining contracture. He divides the tendons proximal to the wrist. He then slides the muscles over the periosteum and fixes them in place. He returns the median and ulnar nerves. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Brachialis tendon: Fibrous band attaching the brachial muscle in the forearm to the bone. Cerebral palsy: Congenital disorder of movement, muscle tone, and or posture as a result of damage to the brain before birth. Contracture: Abnormal premature contraction, or shortening, of a muscle. Coronoid process: Rounded bony projection on the wrist. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure's point of attachment. Flexor digitorum profundus tendon: Connects the muscle that flexes the fingers to its associated bony attachment. Flexor digitorum sublimis tendon: Connects the muscle that controls the fifth finger to its associated bony attachment. Flexor origin slide: Surgical procedure releasing the origin of the flexor tendon to allow the muscles to slide distally in a procedure to improve the appearance and function of a severely deformed hand, wrist, or fingers. Flexor tendon: Tendon associated with a flexor muscle, a muscle that bends at a joint. Medial epicondyle: The inner of two small bumps on either side of the elbow, above the condyle. Median nerve: Responsible for muscles in the forearm and sensation in the fingers; originates from the brachial plexus and branches out to the thumb, index, and middle fingers of the hand. Periosteum: Membrane covering the surface of a bone. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the thumb. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Ulna: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the medial, or inside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the fifth finger. Ulnar nerve: Responsible for movement in the hand, one of three main nerves in the arm. Volkmann's contracture: Claw like deformity of the hand and fingers from a permanent flexion contracture; also known as Volkmann's ischemic contracture. Read Less

short_description: Capsulorrhaphy or reconstruction, wrist, open (eg, capsulodesis, ligament repair, tendon transfer or graft) (includes synovectomy, capsulotomy and open reduction) for carpal instability
lay_term: The provider reconstructs the wrist joint. He repairs the joint capsule and excises synovial membrane. He repairs ligaments and tendons as necessary, to restore the stability of the wrist, due to arthritis, an inflammatory condition of the joints, or prior trauma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the wrist to expose the carpal bones. He repairs the joint capsule, and excises synovial membrane as necessary. He reduces the involved carpal bones and inserts multiple stabilizing pins. He harvests tendon graft strips, usually from the long extensor tendons of the wrist. He passes these grafts through carpal bone tunnels to reconstruct the injured ligaments. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. He applies a cast. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connects bones and joints as well as holds organs in place. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Read Less

short_description: Arthroplasty, wrist, with or without interposition, with or without external or internal fixation Notes: (For obtaining fascia for interposition, see 20920, 20922) (For prosthetic replacement arthroplasty, see 25441- 25446)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider excises the diseased cartilage and bone sections of the distal radius and carpal bones of the wrist. He may affix a metal implant or fixation devices to provide stability to the joint, or he may reposition the radius and carpal bones and stabilize them using nearby soft tissues. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the dorsal surface of the hand from the middle of the hand to a little beyond the hand on the forearm. He brings the incision down through the muscles to expose the affected joint area. He may use different approaches to treat the painful and stiff wrist joint caused by arthritic changes. Either he may cut the distal end of the radius and carpal bones and replace them with artificial metal implants, or he may do an extensive synovectomy, realign the area between the distal radius and carpal bones, and fix the structures with screws and plates. The provider may also choose to perform interposition of the wrist by creating a space between the distal radius and carpal bones by filling the space with nearby tendons and muscles. At the end of the surgery, the provider irrigates the area with antibiotics and closes it in layers. He may also place a splint or other external fixation device to immobilize the joint for better soft tissue healing. Terminology Arthroplasty: Surgical reconstruction or replacement of a joint. Interposition arthroplasty: Surgical correction of stiffness by separation of the immobile part of a joint from the mobilized part and interposition of a substance such as fascia, cartilage, metal, or plastic between them. Prosthesis/implant: An artificial device used to replace a missing or damaged body part. Tips If performed, report 25820 intercarpal fusion separately. It is not included in the service. Read Less

short_description: Centralization of wrist on ulna (eg, radial club hand)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider centralizes the wrist over the ulna to surgically treat conditions like radial club hand, a congenital anomaly in which the radius bone in the forearm is missing or underdeveloped causing the hand to bend radially, or towards the body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the lower end of the forearm to expose the lower portion of the ulna. Next, the provider incises the wrist joint capsule and creates a slot in the carpal bone to adjust the ulna bone. He also shaves a portion of the lower end of the ulna bone. He then makes a Z–plasty incision on the radial side of the forearm to provide some extra length to the skin on this side. The provider now rebalances the unequal muscle forces by shortening the extensor carpi ulnaris muscle and by transferring the deforming radial wrist muscles to the ulnar side of the wrist. Next, the provider using a K wire to unite the lower end of the ulna with the carpal and metacarpal bone. The aim of the provider is to maintain some motion between the ulna and carpal bones. Finally, the provider stops bleeding and closes the incision by suturing the layers of tissue together. Terminology Carpal bone: Eight small bones arranged in two rows in the wrist. Extensor carpi ulnaris: One of the muscles present on the ulnar side of the back of the forearm. Joint capsule: Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. K wire: Thin steel wire that provider uses to stabilize the bone fragments. Metacarpal: Five small bones of the hand located between the bones of the wrist, or the carpal bones and the finger bones, or the phalanges. Radial side: Towards the radius bone. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm. Ulna: One of the two bones in the forearm. Z–plasty incision: A Z–shaped incision that provider makes in the area of high skin tension to allow skin lengthening and relaxation. Read Less

short_description: Osteotomy, radius; middle or proximal third
lay_term: In this procedure the provider excises bone from the middle or upper one third of the arm's radius to correct conditions such as an angular deformity of the forearm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the middle of the forearm or just below the elbow joint to reach the radius. He brings the incision down through the muscles to expose the bone, and then he retracts the periosteum to access the required area of the radius. The provider excises a part of the radius, adjusts the bone to an appropriate angle, and fixes it in place with the help of screws and plates for stability. Next the provider places back the periosteum on the bone; he irrigates the site and repairs the area in layers with the help of sutures, placing a drain if required. Terminology Periosteum: A dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones except at the surfaces of the joints. Read Less

short_description: Osteotomy; radius AND ulna
lay_term: In this procedure the provider excises pieces from both the radius and ulna bones of the arm to correct conditions such as an angular deformity of the forearm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider may make two separate incisions to access both the bones. The provider excises parts of the bones in the same region or at different areas. Next, he adjusts the bones to an appropriate angle and fixes them in place with the help of screws and plates for stability. Next the provider places back the periosteum on the bones; he irrigates the site and repairs both the incisions in layers with the help of sutures, placing a drain if required. short_description: Multiple osteotomies, with realignment on intramedullary rod (Sofield type procedure); radius OR ulna
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts an improperly developed radius or ulna bone shaft in multiple sections to straighten it with the help of an intramedullary rod. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a long incision over the radial or ulnar shaft. He takes the incision down to the level of the bone and exposes the bone by retracting the adjacent muscles. He retracts the nerves and blood vessels to prevent any damage. The provider cuts both ends of the radius or ulna through the necks to insert an intramedullary rod later in middle of the shaft. Next the provider cuts the shaft in multiple sections if required to correct the alignment. After cutting into the sections, the provider chips out any deformed bony areas and inserts an intramedullary rod in the center of the bone to support it. Next the provider fixes back both the epiphyses cut initially. After confirmation of proper alignment and rotation, he fixes the bone sections in place with the help of screws or nails over the rod. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the operative site in layers and immobilizes the arm with a splint. Terminology Epiphysis: Growing end of long bones. Intramedullary rod: A metal rod that can be inserted into the medullary cavity, or marrow cavity, of a bone; also known as IM nails, used to treat fractures of the shaft of long bones. Osteotomy: Surgical cutting of bone. Tips Report this code if either the radius or ulna is treated with multiple osteotomies. See code 25375 if the provider treats both the radius and ulna in the same session. Read Less

short_description: Osteoplasty, radius OR ulna; lengthening with autograft
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts the radius or ulna and affixes an additional piece of bone graft taken from the patient’s body to increase the length of the radius or ulna. short_description: Repair of nonunion or malunion, radius OR ulna; without graft (eg, compression technique)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider treats a nonunion or malunion deformity in a radius or ulna bone of the lower arm. He cuts through the undeveloped or improperly grown bone and fixes it by pulling together the ends. With the help of a cutting instrument like an electrical saw, he excises the irregular bony area. The provider pulls both the bone ends to attach them together. Terminology Malunion: Incomplete union or union in a faulty position of a bone after a fracture. Nonunion: Lack of union of a bone after a fracture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the radial and ulnar shafts and brings the incision down to the level of the bone. He retracts the nerves and blood vessels to prevent any damage. Next, the provider exposes the areas of nonunion or malunion. With the help of a cutting instrument like an electrical saw, he excises the irregular bony areas. The provider pulls both the bone ends to attach them together. He fixes the ends in place, such as with screws and plates. At the end of the surgery, he irrigates and sutures the operative site and places a splint for the immobilization of the arm. Terminology Malunion: Incomplete union or union in a faulty position of after a bone fracture. Nonunion: Lack of union of a bone after a fracture. Tips See 25420 for repair with autograft. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Repair of nonunion or malunion, radius AND ulna; with autograft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider treats a nonunion or malunion deformity in the radius and ulna bones of the lower arm by cutting the undeveloped or improperly grown bones and fixing them with the help of bone grafts taken from the patient’s own body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the radial and ulnar shafts and brings the incision down to the level of the bone. He retracts the nerves and blood vessels to prevent any damage. Next, the provider exposes the area of nonunion or malunion. With the help of a cutting instrument like an electrical saw, he excises the irregular bony area. The provider harvests grafts from the iliac bone or any other long bone of the patient’s body and uses them to bridge the gap created after excision of the forearm’s irregular bone ends. The provider confirms the alignment of the repaired sites. At the end of the surgery, he irrigates and sutures the operative site and places a splint for the immobilization of the arm. short_description: Repair of defect with autograft; radius OR ulna

short_description: Insertion of vascular pedicle into carpal bone (eg, Hori procedure)
lay_term: This procedure provides blood supply to dead bone tissue of a carpal bone of the wrist. The blood supply is created via implant of a vein/artery or a bone graft with live supply of blood. Explanation After adequate anesthesia and prep and drape of the wrist area, the provider usually utilizes a dorsal (back) wrist approach to make an incision into the appropriate compartment (usually the 2nd or 3rd extensor compartment). Then, she performs capsulotomy (making an opening in the joint capsule) to reach the necrotic or avascular carpal bone. The provider then curettes out the avascular/necrotic bone material and drills a small hole in the necrotic bone area for placement of a vascularized bone graft. A branch of the extensor compartment artery or anterior interosseous artery is traced and followed to its origin to raise a vascular bone graft. Alternatively, the incision may be extended to access the metacarpal artery. The provider then creates a vascular pedicle bone graft after ligation of the interosseous artery or extensor compartment artery branch. The vascular pedicle is sharply raised and inserted into the previously prepared space in the necrotic carpal bone. The provider fixates the vascular pedicle with insertion of small pieces of corticocancellous bone graft into that area. Alternatively, he may use a vascular pedicle bone graft fed by the metacarpal artery in a similar fashion. The capsule is then closed, and the wound is closed in layers in an aseptic manner and dressed. short_description: Repair of nonunion, scaphoid carpal (navicular) bone, with or without radial styloidectomy (includes obtaining graft and necessary fixation)
lay_term: The provider repairs a nonhealing fracture of a scaphoid carpal bone in the wrist. If necessary, he excises the radial styloid, a bony projection at the end of the radius bone in the forearm, and applies a bone graft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision along the radial border of the flexor carpi radialis tendon to expose the fracture site. He divides the capsule longitudinally, retracting the underlying ligaments. He creates an oval cavity in the fracture fragments. He obtains a bone graft from another location on the patient’s body, inserting it between the fragments as the provider distracts them, or pulls them apart. He fixes the graft in place. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Flexor carpi radialis tendon: Fibrous band that connects muscle tissue to the bones in the wrist. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connects bones and joints as well as holds organs in place. Navicular bone of the hand: Name sometimes used for the scaphoid carpal bone in the wrist; navicular bone more commonly refers to one of the tarsal bones in the ankle. Nonunion: Failure of a fractured bone to heal normally; in this case, the ends of a fractured bone do not unite properly. Scaphoid carpal bone: One of the eight small bones of the wrist; sometimes known as the navicular, the name of one of the tarsal bones in the ankle. He incises down to the level of the joint capsule. To prevent any damage to blood vessels and nerve tissues, he retracts these toward the sides. The provider excises the capsule and exposes the bony surface of the joint. Then the provider accesses the lower end of the radius by incising ligaments above it. He excises the head of the radius and fits an artificial substitute for the head of the radius in the appropriate position. He nails it in the center of the radius shaft. Next, he realigns the radius with the carpal bones and sutures the ligaments back around the joint. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the incision in layers and places a splint for immobilization. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Arthroplasty with prosthetic replacement; scaphoid carpal (navicular)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider fits an artificial prosthesis replacing the wrist’s scaphoid bone, typically in the case of a non–healing scaphoid fracture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a V–shape incision over the thumb and index finger on the dorsum, meaning back, of the hand. He incises down to the level of the joint capsule. To prevent any damage to blood vessels and nerve tissues, he retracts these toward the sides. The provider excises the capsule and exposes the bony surface, keeping the tendons intact. Next the provider detaches the scaphoid from the surrounding soft tissues and pulls the scaphoid out. He replaces it with an artificial implant made of metal or a synthetic material, fixing one side on the ulnar styloid and the other side with the lunate or trapezium carpal bones. He may further fix the prosthesis in place with sutures or a pin to increase stability. Next, he sutures the joint capsule and ligaments back around the joint. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the incision in layers and places a drain if required. Terminology Prosthesis/implant: An artificial device used to replace a missing or damaged body part. Scaphoid: A large carpal bone articulating with the radius and trapezium on the thumb side; also called navicular. Trapezium: A carpal bone below the base of the thumb. Ulnar styloid: A cylindrical, pointed projection from the medial and posterior aspect of the head of the ulna. Read Less

short_description: Arthroplasty with prosthetic replacement; trapezium
lay_term: In this procedure the provider fits an artificial prosthesis replacing the wrist’s trapezium bone, typically in cases of arthritis of the thumb’s base. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small transverse incision on the dorsum, meaning back, of the hand over the thumb base. The provider excises the capsule and exposes the bony surface, keeping the tendons intact. Next, the provider detaches the trapezium from the surrounding soft tissues and pulls the trapezium bone out. He replaces it with an artificial implant made of metal or synthetic material. He fixes it in place by nailing one side on the trapezoid bone and the other side on the metacarpal of the index finger. He may further affix it with sutures or a pin to increase stability. Next, he sutures the joint capsule and ligaments back around the joint. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the incision in layers and places a drain if required. short_description: Arthroplasty with prosthetic replacement; distal radius and partial or entire carpus (total wrist)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider treats the wrist joint by replacing the radial head on the lower part of the arm as well as the wrist's carpal bones with artificial prostheses. To complete this procedure, he excises the heads of the radius and ulna, and removes all or a few carpal bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal curved incision over the dorsum, meaning back, of the hand and wrist area. The provider excises the capsule and exposes the bony surface of the joint. Then the provider accesses the lower end of the radius by incising ligaments above it. Next, he excises the heads of the radius and ulna at the necks and fits an artificial substitute head for the radius in the appropriate position and nails it in the center of the radial shaft. He may leave the ulna without a prosthesis. The provider removes all or a few carpal bones as required and replaces them with a prosthesis nailed on the centers of the metacarpal shafts. Next, he realigns the radial prosthesis with the carpal implant and confirms the stability and smooth movement of the replaced joint; he sutures the ligaments and capsule back around the joint. short_description: Arthroplasty, intercarpal or carpometacarpal joints; interposition (eg, tendon) Notes: (Do not report 25447 in conjunction with 25448) (Do not report 25447 in conjunction with 25310, 26480, when performed for intercarpal or carpometacarpal joint arthroplasty) (For wrist arthroplasty, use 25332)
lay_term: The provider performs arthroplasty (joint replacement) of the intercarpal joints (between the small bones in the wrist) or carpometacarpal joints (where the carpal bones of the wrist meet the metacarpal bones that lead to the fingers). In this interposition arthroplasty, the provider inserts a cushion, such as a tendon graft, to reconstruct and restore mobility of the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins the interposition arthroplasty by making an incision over the affected intercarpal or carpometacarpal joint, commonly at the wrist or base of the thumb. Intercarpal joints are between the small bones (carpal bones) in the wrist. Carpometacarpal joints are where the carpal bones of the wrist meet the metacarpal bones, which lead to the fingers. The provider dissects down through and retracts tissue as needed. The provider incises the joint capsule and removes damaged bone and cartilage from the joint to reduce pain and improve movement. The provider places a cushion (such as tendon fashioned into a suitable shape) between the resected bone surfaces to prevent direct bone–on–bone contact. After securing the tendon, the provider closes the tissues and incision, as needed, and stabilizes the joint to promote healing and proper function. This technique alleviates pain and restores mobility in the affected joint. Read Less

short_description: Arthroplasty, intercarpal or carpometacarpal joints; suspension, including transfer or transplant of tendon, with interposition, when performed Notes: (Do not report 25448 in conjunction with 25447) (Do not report 25448 in conjunction with 25310, 26480, when performed for intercarpal or carpometacarpal joint arthroplasty)
lay_term: The provider performs arthroplasty (joint replacement) of the intercarpal joints (between the small bones in the wrist) or carpometacarpal joints (where the carpal bones of the wrist meet the metacarpal bones that lead to the fingers). In this suspension arthroplasty, the provider stabilizes the joint by suspending or holding bones in place using soft tissue or implants to maintain proper spacing. The service also may include interposition, where the provider inserts a cushion, such as tendon, to reconstruct and restore mobility of the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins the suspension arthroplasty by making an incision over the affected intercarpal or carpometacarpal joint, commonly at the wrist or base of the thumb. The provider dissects down through and retracts tissue as needed. The provider incises the joint capsule and removes damaged bone and cartilage from the joint to reduce pain and improve movement. short_description: Revision of arthroplasty, including removal of implant, wrist joint
lay_term: In this procedure the provider reopens the previously repaired wrist joint, and either removes or replaces the artificial prosthesis placed on the forearm’s radius and metacarpals of the hand. He typically performs this procedure in cases of a joint infection due to the prosthesis or loosening of the prosthesis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider re–incises the wrist joint. He exposes the repaired area that has prostheses. He retracts the joint area and removes the prosthesis placed on the radial head and removes the prostheses from one or more metacarpals. He may cleanse and debride the area and, if required, he may place new prostheses on the same sites. After achieving the desired outcome, he irrigates and sutures the operative site and places a splint for the immobilization of the arm. Terminology Metacarpals: The metacarpals are long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpals, or wrist bones, at the wrist, and connect from there to the phalanges, or finger bones. short_description: Epiphyseal arrest by epiphysiodesis or stapling; distal radius AND ulna
lay_term: The provider implants screws or specialized staples into the epiphyseal area of the radius and ulna near the wrist (distal). This causes a temporary pause in the growth of that bone. Explanation With the patient under general anesthesia and with tourniquet control applied, the provider makes an incision over the epiphyseal area of the distal radius at the wrist. The epiphysis may be identified by fluoroscopy for this purpose. The provider deepens the incision to the bone after reflecting (bending back) the appropriate layers of subcutaneous and fascial tissue and splitting the periosteum (membrane covering the bone). The procedure may be accomplished through epiphysiodesis, in which screws are implanted on to the epiphysial growth plate at approximately 90 degrees to the bone. Alternatively, the provider may insert specialized stapling devices into the growth plate in a similar fashion. The wound is closed in layers in an aseptic manner after checking for clear implantation of devices. Fluoroscopy may be used for confirmation. A similar procedure is performed on the distal ulna of the same forearm/wrist area usually through a different incision. Terminology Epiphysis: Part of a long bone that converts into bone separately from the shaft, such as the end of a long bone Tips This code describes a procedure for the radius AND ulna. For a procedure on the radius OR ulna, see 25450. Read Less
