short_description: Open treatment of radial shaft fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed, and open treatment of distal radioulnar joint dislocation (Galeazzi fracture/ dislocation), includes internal fixation, when performed, includes repair of triangular fibrocartilage complex
lay_term: The provider repairs a fracture of the shaft of the radius in combination with displacement of the two bones in the forearm at the wrist, or distal radioulnar joint in an open procedure. He makes an incision to repair the fracture and the dislocation, applying hardware for stabilization, as necessary. He repairs the triangular fibrocartilage complex cartilage, or TFCC. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the area of the fracture. He reduces the fracture. If necessary, he applies a plate and screws or wires to maintain the reduction. He repairs the triangular fibrocartilage complex through this incision. He then incises the area over the dislocation and realigns the bones at the radioulnar joint. If necessary, he inserts pins or wires to stabilize them. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. He applies a splint or cast. Terminology Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure's point of attachment. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Galeazzi fracture dislocation: Fracture of the shaft of the radius in combination with dislocation of the radioulnar joint, the union of the two bones in the forearm at the wrist. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Radioulnar joint: Union of the of the two bones in the forearm, the radius and ulna; the ulnar head sits in a notched area on the radius, separated from the carpal bones in the wrist by a fibrocartilaginous ligament cushion called an articular disk. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the thumb. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Triangular fibrocartilage complex, or TFCC: A piece of fibrous connective tissue on the outer aspect of the wrist that cushions and provides support to the carpals, or wrist bones, and stabilizes the radius and ulna, the bones of the forearm. Tips To successfully code fractures, keep in mind the following questions. Is treatment open or closed? Open treatment refers to a surgical incision and not the appearance of the wound. Did the provider use manipulation? Look for key words like move, distract, and realign. Do you need modifier 54, Surgical care only? If your provider will not see the patient for follow–up care, you are billing only for the surgical portion of the code. Can you report a separate evaluation and management, or E/M, service? For fracture patients, the answer to this question is nearly always yes. Do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. short_description: Closed treatment of distal radial fracture (eg, Colles or Smith type) or epiphyseal separation, includes closed treatment of fracture of ulnar styloid, when performed; without manipulation
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the wrist end of the radius, one of the bones in the forearm, in which the fracture fragment displaces upward or downward, in a closed procedure. The growth plate at the end of the bone may be displaced or the ulnar styloid, the bony bump on the ulna, fractured. He does not make an incision and does not manipulate the bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider determines the presence of the distal radial fracture of the wrist using radiographic imaging and he determines satisfactory alignment. For this service, the growth plate at the end of the bone may also be fractured or the ulnar styloid, the bony bump on the ulna. However, he does not need to incise or manipulate the fracture. He applies a splint or cast material to prevent movement of the bones until healing takes place. Terminology Closed treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, without making a surgical incision, with or without manipulation, and with or without the use of a traction device that applies a force. Colles fracture: Fracture of the distal radius, near the wrist, with the fragment tilted upward. Epiphyseal separation: An injury in which the growth plate, or cartilaginous layer at the end of a long bone responsible for bone growth, splits off. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the thumb. Smith fracture: Fracture of the distal radius, near the wrist, with the fragment tilted downward; sometimes called a reverse Colles fracture. Ulnar styloid: Also called the styloid process of the ulna, a bony projection, or bump, of the ulna, one of the bones in the forearm, at its distal aspect, closest to the wrist. Did the provider use manipulation? Look for key words like move, distract, and realign. Do you need modifier 54, Surgical care only? If your provider will not see the patient for follow–up care, you are billing only for the surgical portion of the code. Can you report a separate evaluation and management, or E/M, service? For fracture patients, the answer to this question is nearly always yes. Do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. CMS has approximately 50 Q HCPCS codes that address supply issues with casting and splinting applications. Read Less

short_description: Percutaneous skeletal fixation of distal radial fracture or epiphyseal separation Notes: (Do not report 25606 in conjunction with 25650) (For percutaneous treatment of ulnar styloid fracture, use 25651) (For open treatment of ulnar styloid fracture, use 25652)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs treatment of a distal radial fracture or epiphyseal separation using screws and pins through the skin. A distal radius fracture is a break in the lower end of the arm’s radius bone. Epiphyseal separation is a break in the epiphyseal plate, the growth plate of the radius bone at the lower end. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the fractured fragment by exerting pushing or pulling force on the lower end of the forearm to reduce the fracture. He next creates a small incision in the skin over the fractured site. He then inserts fixation devices such as pins and screws through this incision to hold the reduced fracture fragments in place. He next places the forearm in a cast or brace for a period of four to six weeks. He may perform a separately reported X–ray examination of the radius bone to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: The provider places fixation across the fracture site, usually under X–ray imaging such as fluoroscopy, but the fracture fragments are not visible to the naked eye. short_description: Open treatment of distal radial extra-articular fracture or epiphyseal separation, with internal fixation Notes: (Do not report 25607 in conjunction with 25650) (For percutaneous treatment of ulnar styloid fracture, use 25651) (For open treatment of ulnar styloid fracture, use 25652)
lay_term: The provider surgically repairs a fracture of the lower radius, the larger of the two lower arm bones, beyond the joint or a separation of the radius from the joint through an incision and fixes the radius in place with internal wires, screws, or pins. Explanation The provider surgically opens the fracture site so that the fracture or separation is visible. The provider manipulates the bone into the correct position. If the provider places an intramedullary nail for fixation, he approaches the area proximal or distal to the fracture site and threads a nail down into the intramedullary canal, through the bone, and across the fracture site. He may also place interlocking screws at angles to the nail or wires across the fracture site to further stabilize the fracture. Once the fracture is stabilized, the provider controls any bleeding and closes the wound. Terminology Closed treatment: The fracture site is not surgically opened (exposed to the external environment and directly visible). Closed treatments can be performed with or without manipulation and/or traction. With manipulation, the physician must move or adjust the involved bone(s) to improve their position or alignment. External fixation: This is a device that is fitted to the outside of the limb that is fixed securely using pins or wires to the bone fragments. The external fixator is used to support the bone while it is healing. External fixation usually allows joints to move normally while the bone is healing. This may shorten a patient's hospital stay shorter and help them get back to their normal life as soon as possible. Internal fixation: This uses a variety of different types of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires to stabilize the fracture. Internal fixation is a fracture reduction procedure that results in fracture stabilization. When internal fixation is performed the fracture site is opened. Intramedullary nailing or rodding: Another internal fixation method that helps stabilize the fracture. This is the most common type of IM rodding performed on the femur. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: An internal fixation method that also requires direct exposure of the fracture site. This method is performed with fluoroscopic imaging. In this procedure, the surgeon inserts hardware such as screws, Steinmann pins, or Kirschner wires into the bones across the fracture site to aid in stabilization. Tips When choosing a surgical fracture code, you need to consider external and internal fixation. The reimbursement for fracture fixation, whether internal or external, is frequently included in the CPT® code. Use codes for external fixation when external fixation is not listed as part of the basic procedure. Consider debridement a separate procedure only when gross contamination requires prolonged cleansing. Documentation must support that an appreciable amount of devitalized or contaminated tissue had to be removed or carried out separately without primary closure. Report debridement for these conditions with CPT® codes 97597–97610, Active wound care management. If the fracture is open, it may be necessary to clean and prepare the fracture site prior to any restorative treatment and/or stabilization of the bone. The wound site may be contaminated with foreign material such as glass, dirt, grass, metal, gravel, etc. Open fracture debridement is separately reported under these circumstances and reported with 11010 and 11012. Questions Determine Fracture Care Intent: Fracture care intent is the next step to determine your code choice. Are you going to code "global" or "itemized"? Physicians are given both options. Here are some key questions to ask: Will restorative treatment or procedure(s) be performed? Will the same physician assume all subsequent fracture care? Are there risks associated with the fracture? Global reporting will include the initial cast application and all professional services for a 90–day period. Your physician should not report further reassessment separately. You may report items separately such as: further castings, splinting, radiographs, and supplies. These items are not included in the global period. Itemized reporting utilizes the evaluation and management code section rather than a surgical fracture care code. In addition, the initial cast application and/or splinting is also reported with the evaluation and management code. Many times, the fracture's type and severity also determines this. For example, if a patient suffers a scaphoid fracture, they may exceed more than the allowed two follow–up visits within the 90–day global period. Therefore, E/M coding (CPT® code range 99212–99215, Office or Other Outpatient Services) would be more advantageous. But, if the patient has a simple fracture of the distal phalanx, they may return only one time — in this circumstance the surgical fracture code (26750) is better. Documentation should also reflect the type of care and treatment. Key items in the initial assessment should have neurologic and vascular status clinically assessed and documented. Documentation should also note the realignment of the broken limb segment and/or assessment of the broken segment. Ask yourself, what type of immobilizing was performed on the fracture? Splinting is critical in providing symptomatic relief for the patient. It also prevents potential neurologic, vascular injury, and further injury to the local soft tissues. When reporting the global method of fracture care, an E/M service may also be reported. Documentation must support a decision for surgery (modifier 57) and/or a separate identifiable service (modifier 25, Significant, separately identifiable E/M service by the same physician on the same day of the procedure or other service). With either method, do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. CMS has approximately 50 "Q" HCPCS codes that address supply issues with casting/splinting applications. The HCPCS level–II manual offers "A" codes. CPT® contains 99070. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of distal radial intra-articular fracture or epiphyseal separation; with internal fixation of 3 or more fragments Notes: (Do not report 25608, 25609 in conjunction with 25650) (For percutaneous treatment of ulnar styloid fracture, use 25651) (For open treatment of ulnar styloid fracture, use 25652)
lay_term: The provider surgically repairs a fracture of the lower radius, the larger of the two lower arm bones, beyond the joint or a separation of the radius from the joint through an incision and fixes three or more radial bone fragments in place with internal wires, screws, or pins. Explanation The provider surgically opens the fracture site so that the fracture or separation is visible. The provider manipulates the three or more bone fragments into the correct position. The provider places interlocking screws at angles across the fragments or wires across the fracture site to further stabilize the fracture. Once the fracture is stabilized, the provider controls any bleeding and closes the wound. Terminology External fixation: This is a device that is fitted to the outside of the limb that is fixed securely using pins or wires to the bone fragments. The external fixator is used to support the bone while it is healing. External fixation usually allows joints to move normally while the bone is healing. This may shorten a patient's hospital stay shorter and help them get back to their normal life as soon as possible. Internal fixation: This uses a variety of different types of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires to stabilize the fracture. Internal fixation is a fracture reduction procedure that results in fracture stabilization. When internal fixation is performed the fracture site is opened. Intramedullary nailing or rodding: Another internal fixation method that helps stabilize the fracture. This is the most common type of IM rodding performed on the femur. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: An internal fixation method that also requires direct exposure of the fracture site. This method is performed with fluoroscopic imaging. In this procedure, the surgeon inserts hardware such as screws, Steinmann pins, or Kirschner wires into the bones across the fracture site to aid in stabilization. Tips When choosing a surgical fracture code, you need to consider external and internal fixation. The reimbursement for fracture fixation, whether internal or external, is frequently included in the CPT® code. Use codes for external fixation when external fixation is not listed as part of the basic procedure. Consider debridement a separate procedure only when gross contamination requires prolonged cleansing. Documentation must support that an appreciable amount of devitalized or contaminated tissue had to be removed or carried out separately without primary closure. Report debridement for these conditions with CPT® codes 97597–97610, Active wound care management. If the fracture is open, it may be necessary to clean and prepare the fracture site prior to any restorative treatment and/or stabilization of the bone. The wound site may be contaminated with foreign material such as glass, dirt, grass, metal, gravel, etc. Open fracture debridement is separately reported under these circumstances and reported with 11010 and 11012. Questions Determine Fracture Care Intent: Fracture care intent is the next step to determine your code choice. Are you going to code "global" or "itemized"? Physicians are given both options. Here are some key questions to ask: Will restorative treatment or procedure(s) be performed? Will the same physician assume all subsequent fracture care? Are there risks associated with the fracture? Global reporting will include the initial cast application and all professional services for a 90–day period. Your physician should not report further reassessment separately. You may report items separately such as: further castings, splinting, radiographs, and supplies. These items are not included in the global period. Itemized reporting utilizes the evaluation and management code section rather than a surgical fracture care code. In addition, the initial cast application and/or splinting is also reported with the evaluation and management code. Many times, the fracture's type and severity also determines this. For example, if a patient suffers a scaphoid fracture, they may exceed more than the allowed two follow–up visits within the 90–day global period. Therefore, E/M coding (CPT® code range 99212–99215, Office or Other Outpatient Services) would be more advantageous. Documentation should also note the realignment of the broken limb segment and/or assessment of the broken segment. Ask yourself, what type of immobilizing was performed on the fracture? Documentation must support a decision for surgery (modifier 57) and/or a separate identifiable service (modifier 25, Significant, separately identifiable E/M service by the same physician on the same day of the procedure or other service). short_description: Open treatment of carpal scaphoid (navicular) fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the scaphoid bone, one of the carpal bones in the wrist, in an open procedure. He makes an incision in the wrist to access the fracture and may apply wires or screws to secure the bones while healing takes place. A scaphoid bone fracture commonly results from extending the hand to break a fall. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the fracture site. He reduces, or realigns, the fracture into the correct position. He inserts wires or screws to secure the bones in place. He closes the incision. He obtains a radiographic image to confirm adequate reduction of the fracture. He applies a splint or cast material to prevent movement of the fracture until healing takes place. Terminology Carpal bones: The eight small bones of the wrist, including the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Navicular: One of the bones in the foot; former name of the scaphoid bone in the wrist. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation. Radiographic: Pertaining to X–rays and, by extension, other imaging procedures. Scaphoid bone: The largest of the eight small bones of the wrist and the most likely to be fractured, or broken. Tips Fracture care can be reported as a global code or itemized. In making a choice, consider if restorative treatments or procedures will be performed, if the same provider will assume all subsequent fracture care, and if there are risks associated with the fracture. short_description: Closed treatment of ulnar styloid fracture Notes: (Do not report 25650 in conjunction with 25600, 25605, 25607-25609)
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the ulnar styloid, in the wrist, in a closed procedure. He does not make an incision. A wrist area fracture commonly results from extending the hand to break a fall. Explanation The provider determines the presence of the fracture with radiographic imaging. He assesses the type of fracture and the amount of displacement. For an avulsion fracture, where a small piece of bone separates from the main bone, but with no displacement, he prescribes only local treatment, such as ice, and medication to reduce pain and inflammation, if necessary. For avulsion with minimal displacement, he may apply a long arm splint. He prescribes limitation of activity for the wrist until the fracture heals. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the thumb. Ulna: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the medial, or inside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the fifth finger. short_description: Open treatment of ulnar styloid fracture
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the ulnar styloid, in the area of the wrist, in an open procedure. He makes an incision in the wrist to access the fracture. He may insert pins or wires to stabilize the fracture while it heals. A wrist area fracture commonly results from extending the hand to break a fall. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the fracture site. He reduces, or realigns, the fracture into the correct position. He assesses the ligaments in the area. If required, he inserts pins or wires to stabilize the fracture as it heals. He obtains a radiographic image to confirm adequate reduction of the fracture. He closes the incision. He applies a splint or cast material to prevent movement of the fracture until healing takes place. Terminology Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation. Ulnar styloid: Also called the styloid process of the ulna, a bony projection, or bump, of the ulna, one of the bones in the forearm, at its distal aspect, closest to the wrist. Tips Fracture care can be reported as a global code or itemized. In making a choice, consider if restorative treatments or procedures will be performed, if the same provider will assume all subsequent fracture care, and if there are risks associated with the fracture. Global reporting with a surgical fracture care code, like 25652, includes the initial cast application and all professional services for a 90 day period. Your provider should not report further reassessment separately. You may report items separately such as subsequent castings, splinting, radiographs, and supplies. These items are not included in the global period. Itemized reporting utilizes the evaluation and management code section rather than a surgical fracture care code. In addition, the initial cast application and or splinting is also reported with the evaluation and management code. When reporting the global method of fracture care, an E/M service may also be reported. Documentation must support modifier 57, Decision for surgery, and modifier 25, Significant, separately identifiable evaluation and management service by the same provider on the same day of the procedure or other service. With either method, do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. Consider 99070, Supplies and materials, except spectacles, provided by the provider over and above those usually included with the office visit or other services rendered, list drugs, trays, supplies, or materials provided. short_description: Open treatment of radiocarpal or intercarpal dislocation, 1 or more bones
lay_term: The provider treats a dislocation injury of one or more bones in the wrist, in an open procedure. He makes an incision in the wrist to access the dislocated bones and may apply wires or screws to secure the bones while healing takes place. Radiocarpal dislocations occur infrequently, usually the result of an impact injury of considerable force. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the dislocation. He uses his hands to manipulate the bones in the wrist to return them to their correct positions. If required, he inserts pins or wires to stabilize the bones. He obtains a radiographic image to confirm adequate realignment, of the dislocation. He closes the incision. He applies a splint or cast material to prevent movement of the bones until healing takes place. Terminology Carpal bones: The eight small bones of the wrist, including the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation. Radiocarpal joint: Union of the radius, one of the two bones in the forearm, and the carpal bones in the hand; the wrist joint; also called radial carpal joint. Radiographic: Pertaining to X–rays and, by extension, other imaging procedures. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the thumb. Tips Fracture care, including dislocations, can be reported as a global code or itemized. In making a choice, consider if restorative treatments or procedures will be performed, if the same provider will assume all subsequent fracture care, and if there are risks associated with the fracture. Global reporting with a surgical fracture care code, like 25670, includes the initial cast application and all professional services for a 90–day period. Your provider should not report further reassessment separately. You may report items separately such as subsequent castings, splinting, radiographs, and supplies. These items are not included in the global period. Itemized reporting utilizes the evaluation and management code section rather than a surgical fracture care code. In addition, the initial cast application and or splinting is also reported with the evaluation and management code. When reporting the global method of fracture care, an E/M service may also be reported. Documentation must support modifier 57, Decision for surgery, and modifier 25, Significant, separately identifiable evaluation and management service by the same provider on the same day of the procedure or other service. With either method, do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. Consider 99070, Supplies and materials, except spectacles, provided by the provider over and above those usually included with the office visit or other services rendered, list drugs, trays, supplies, or materials provided. short_description: Open treatment of distal radioulnar dislocation, acute or chronic
lay_term: The provider treats a dislocation of the radioulnar joint, the union of the two forearm bones at the wrist, in an open procedure. He makes an incision in the wrist area to access the joint and may apply wires or screws to secure the bones while healing takes place. A radioulnar dislocation commonly results from extending the hand to break a fall. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the dislocation site. He reduces, or realigns, the bones into the correct position. He may insert wires or screws to secure the bones in place. He obtains a radiographic image to confirm adequate alignment. He closes the incision. He applies a splint or cast material to prevent movement of the bones until healing takes place. Terminology Acute: A medical condition or injury of sudden onset, sometimes severe in nature, and typically last a short period of time; opposite of chronic. Chronic: A condition that is long lasting, typically to slow develop, and with symptoms of less severity than an acute condition. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation. short_description: Arthrodesis, wrist; limited, without bone graft (eg, intercarpal or radiocarpal)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically fuses a limited portion of the wrist joint. The aim is to reduce pain by surgically immobilizing the affected joint and to preserve as much motion as possible. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the back of the wrist, starting from the proximal part of the hand’s metacarpal to the distal end of the forearm. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue preserving the nerves and veins. He then dissects the wrist capsule, creating two flaps to open the wrist like a window. He then resects the rear rim of the radius and decorticates it, meaning he removes a portion of the proximal carpal bones. He then fuses the painful radiocarpal joint using K wire, powered staples, or headless screws to restrict the movement causing pain. Similarly, he may fuse the intercarpal joints as required. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider then places the joint in a long arm cast for a period of four to six weeks. Terminology Arthrodesis: The surgical immobilization of a joint by fusion of the bones. Intercarpal joint: Joint between the carpal bones of the wrist. Metacarpal: Five small bones of the hand that lie between the wrist’s carpals and fingers’ phalanges. Radiocarpal joint: A synovial joint between the distal end of the radius and the proximal row of carpal bones. Read Less

short_description: Arthrodesis, distal radioulnar joint with segmental resection of ulna, with or without bone graft (eg, Sauve-Kapandji procedure)
lay_term: The provider performs arthrodesis of the distal radioulnar joint and resecting the ulna. The provider may also perform a bone graft. Explanation While the patient is prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a curved dorsal radial incision around the ulnar head and extends it proximally along the dorsoulnar margin of the ulna. He opens the distal radioulnar joint and resects the articular cartilage. He corrects the ulnar joint by rotating the bone to 90 degrees. He predrills a hole for a transverse screw in the ulna. The provider performs proximal pseudarthrosis and performs a transverse osteotomy 1 cm proximal to the ulnar styloid. He then excises an ulnar segment. The provider performs a synovectomy and excises the distal radioulnar joint. He then drills the radius with the ulna into the desired position. He inserts a transverse screw or pin to hold them together. The provider may use additional cancellous grafts, such as from the iliac crest, to fill the pseudarthrosis. The provider repairs the dorsal capsule and closes the wound with sutures. He applies an elbow plaster splint. Terminology Arthrodesis: Surgical procedure involving fusion of vertebrae over the joint space. Distal radioulnar arthrodesis: Joint fusion generally performed by the Sauve–Kapandji approach; this approach is taken in the case of the loss of a hand due to irreversible post traumatic damage to the distal radioulnar, a healed fracture with deformity, or arthritis; the procedure consists of fusion of the distal radioulnar joint with resection of the ulna with or without graft. Pseudarthrosis: False joint, the movement of a bone at the site of a fracture due to inadequate healing of the fracture. Read Less

short_description: Amputation, forearm, through radius and ulna; open, circular (guillotine)
lay_term: The provider completely cuts through the forearm at any location on the arm's radius and ulna bones by running the cutting instrument around them in a circular motion and then cutting through the bones. The provider uses a cutting device to cut through the radius and ulna, which are the bones of the forearm. The provider leaves the wound without any skin or muscle repair and, after irrigation with antibiotics, wraps the wound, such as with cotton gauze and dressings. short_description: Krukenberg procedure
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider separates the ulna and radius bones of the forearm stump left after amputation to create a pincer or forceps–like grasp controlled by the pronator teres muscle. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes incisions both on the anterior and posterior aspect of the forearm to split the forearm stump into radial and ulnar rays. The goal of this procedure is to convert the forearm into a strong active pincer with a radial ray opposing the ulnar ray. He next divides the muscle and tendons, transferring some to the ulnar side and others to the radial side. He may also remove some of the muscles that are not necessary. He then divides the interosseous membrane at the ulnar periosteal attachment, preserving the interosseous nerve and vessels. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He ensures that contact surfaces of both the rays are covered with skin having enough sensory nerve supply to give a good tactile sensation. Terminology Interosseous membrane: A fibrous sheath present between the ulna and radius bone. Periosteal attachment: Bony attachment of any tissue. Read Less

short_description: Disarticulation through wrist
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically separates the hand from the forearm at the wrist joint. Explanation Disarticulation is the separation of bones at their joint. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to create a long palmar flap. Providers prefer to use a long palmar flap as the skin of the palm is thick and well adapted to pressure. He makes an incision just below the radial styloid process that he continues to the ulnar side up to the styloid process of the ulna. He then raises the flap, which includes the palmar fascia and part of the thenar and hypothenar muscles. The thenar muscles are short muscles present over the palm and base of thumb while hypothenar muscles are present over the ulnar side of the palm. Then, he makes an incision on the back of the hand to raise the dorsal flap. He ligates the blood vessels and retracts the muscles and nerves. Next, he proceeds further to disarticulation of the wrist joint. He typically begins from the ulnar side moving toward the radial side and cutting in a circumferential manner around the joint. He rounds off the styloid processes. He then closes the wound by suturing the flaps in layers and packs the wound with antiseptic gauze. Terminology Styloid process: A projection of the bone that serves as a point of muscle attachment. Tips See 25922 for secondary closure or scar revision following disarticulation through the wrist. See 25924 for re–amputation following disarticulation through the wrist. Read Less

short_description: Transmetacarpal amputation; re-amputation
lay_term: The provider performs amputation, or surgical removal, through the bones of the hand. The provider commonly performs amputation of metacarpal bones due to trauma, infection, or tumor resection. For this code, he performs another amputation following initial amputation, commonly to correct a problem left after the first amputation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the metacarpal bone or bones he decides to remove from a hand that has undergone previous transmetacarpal amputation. He then incises the tendons and allows them to retract. The provider then reaches the bones to be amputated and surgically removes the target sections of bone. He resects each metacarpal bone and detaches it from its soft tissues. The provider ligates and resects the nerves. While performing reamputation of the metacarpal bones, the provider takes special care that the nerves he is resecting are away from the scar. After surgical removal of the metacarpal bone segments, the provider covers the stump with a skin flap. He closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Amputation: Surgical removal of a body extremity, commonly to control pain or progression of a disease in the affected limb. Flap closure: Tissue for grafting, typically removed from one place on the body and positioned in another; however, it may remain anchored and rotated from one side of an area to another. Ligate: Close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure using a material such as sutures, wire, or surgical tape. Resect: To excise or cut out tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also called excise. Stump: The part of the limb left after the rest of it has been amputated. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Transmetacarpal: Through the metacarpals, bones of the hand that connect the wrist to the fingers. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, benign or cancerous. Tips When the provider performs initial transmetacarpal amputation, use 25927, Transmetacarpal amputation. When the provider performs transmetacarpal amputation for secondary closure or scar revision, use 25929, Transmetacarpal amputation; secondary closure or scar revision. Read Less

short_description: Drainage of tendon sheath, digit and/or palm, each
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider drains fluid from the infected tendon sheath of a finger and/or palm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin over an infected tendon in the finger and/or palm. He then has adequate exposure of the tendon, and he examines the tendon sheath for signs of infection. He then makes several incisions over the patient’s finger and distal palm. He holds the tendon sheath open with a hook or retractor and drains the fluid by inserting a catheter. Finally, he removes the catheter after proper drainage and closes the wound by suturing the skin in layers. Tips Report one unit of 26020 for drainage of each tendon sheath. Remember that the catheter insertion is integral to the procedure, and you do not report it separately. Read Less

short_description: Drainage of palmar bursa; single, bursa

short_description: Decompression fingers and/or hand, injection injury (eg, grease gun)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider decompresses the fingers and/or hand following an injection injury, an injury sustained by an individual following an injection of fluid usually while operating pressurized hydraulic equipment. The fluid or materials involved may be paint or paint solvents, grease, etc. Explanation Injection injuries commonly occur in the dominant hand and the index finger of the operator of pressurized hydraulic equipment. This injury results in the introduction of toxic material into the pulp of the finger. This toxic material may lead to a severe inflammatory response and may cause great damage. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the entry point of the injection injury. He retracts the ends of the wound and removes all the injected material. He debrides all the damaged tissue while preserving the vital structures. He may extend the incision and area of lavaging if there is a spread of the toxic material to nearby areas. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Terminology Decompression: Releasing from pressure. Lavaging: Washing. Read Less

short_description: Decompressive fasciotomy, hand (excludes 26035) Notes: (For injection injury, use 26035)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts through the fascia in the hand to relieve pressure and increase blood flow. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to treat pressure such as that caused by compartment syndrome of the hand, a painful condition that involves increased pressure in a muscle compartment leading to muscle and nerve damage with reduction of blood flow. The syndrome is characterized by symptoms like decreased sensation, numbness, weakness, and severe pain. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin overlying the affected area and gets access to the fascia lying above the muscle compartment affected by compartment syndrome. He then cuts through the fascia and debrides all the damaged nonviable tissue, thereby reducing the pressure on the neurovascular structures underneath the fascia. This restores the restricted blood supply and relieves the patient from symptoms. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Tips See 26035 for decompression of finger and/or hand following injection injury. Read Less

short_description: Fasciotomy, palmar (eg, Dupuytren's contracture); open, partial Notes: (For palmar fasciotomy by enzyme injection (eg, collagenase), see 20527, 26341) (For fasciectomy, see 26121-26125)
lay_term: The provider incises the palmar fascia in an open procedure. The palmar fascia is connective tissue under the skin in the palm of the hand. The procedure treats Dupuytren's contracture, a condition which causes the tissues of the hand to contract and the fingers to permanently bend, impairing movement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin and carries the incision down through the subcutaneous tissue to the palmar fascia, or the connective tissue in the palm of the hand. He then retracts the subcutaneous tissue to access the contracture and releases the contracted tissue by incising the thick or shortened tissues to release the tension. He then sutures the wound closed in layers. Terminology Fasciotomy: A surgical procedure in which the fascia is cut to relieve tension or pressure; a limb–saving procedure that is used to treat acute compartment syndrome or chronic compartment stress syndrome. Open incision: Surgical approach that involves making a large enough incision that the provider can directly visualize the target anatomy. Tips Code 26040, Fasciotomy, palmar, e.g., Dupuytren's contracture; percutaneous, and 26045 are often used for the treatment of Dupuytren's contracture, a disease of the palmar fascia resulting in thickening and shortening of fibrous bands on the palmar surface of the hands and fingers. short_description: Tenotomy, percutaneous, single, each digit
lay_term: The provider performs a tenotomy, the surgical division of a tendon to relieve a deformity due to a congenital or acquired shortening of the muscle. The provider commonly performs a tenotomy to treat spastic hand disorders in which a tendon contracture occurs. The provider performs tenotomy of a single digit using a minimally invasive percutaneous approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin over the affected tendon. The provider uses a sharp scalpel to sever the tendon a little above its insertion onto the bone. The provider may insert the scalpel perpendicular to the skin or alternatively at a 45–degree angle to the skin. Complete transection often results in an immediate improvement in the movement that the tendon restricted. If incomplete transection occurs, the provider adjusts the position of the scalpel as needed and completes the release of the tendon. The provider takes special care not to pull the scalpel through the tendon to prevent laceration of the overlying skin. After the completion of the procedure, the provider makes sure that the bleeding stops. The provider closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Congenital: Present at birth. Contracture: Abnormal premature contraction, or shortening, of a muscle. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Scalpel: Surgical knife. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips When the provider performs the procedure on multiple digits during the same surgery, report the code more than once according to the payer’s preference, such as using finger modifiers. Read Less

short_description: Synovectomy, carpometacarpal joint
lay_term: The provider removes the synovium, which is membrane lining the joint, from the carpometacarpal joint. This joint occurs where a carpal bone of the wrist meets a metacarpal bone of the hand. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the target carpometacarpal joint near the wrist. She extends the incision through the soft tissues and into the capsule surrounding the joint. She visualizes the membrane lining the joint, called synovium, and identifies the inflamed or abnormal area. She removes this target area of the synovium. The provider may place a drain to assist with healing. She closes the incision and then may place a splint. Providers may choose this procedure to treat patients with conditions such as severe rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, or hemarthrosis in which there’s bleeding in the joint. Terminology Carpometacarpal joint: Union of the bones of the wrist, carpals, with the bones of the hand, metacarpals; the wrist area. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Synovectomy: Removal of the membrane, or synovium, lining a joint. Read Less

short_description: Synovectomy, metacarpophalangeal joint including intrinsic release and extensor hood reconstruction, each digit
lay_term: The provider surgically removes the synovial membrane over the metacarpophalangeal, or MCP, joint between the finger and hand. He divides the intrinsic muscles and performs reconstruction of the extensor hood tissue. He may perform this procedure in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The code applies to each digit separately. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the metacarpophalangeal joint. The provider divides the soft tissues and reaches the joint. He enters the joint capsule and removes the synovial membrane covering the joint. He releases contractions of the intrinsic muscles, which are muscles fully contained within the hand. He then reconstructs the extensor hood, a triangular sheet of tissue on the top of the finger that connects to the extensor tendons that allow the finger to straighten. The provider closes the incision with sutures. The provider also applies a plaster cast to hold the metacarpophalangeal joints in an extended position. Use the code once for each digit. Terminology Metacarpophalangeal joint, or MCPJ: Union of the bones of the hand, the carpal bones, and the finger bones, or phalanges. Reconstruction: Revising a structure to approximate its normal anatomy or restoring it to its appropriate function. Synovectomy: Excision of synovial tissue, the membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips Use 26135 once for each digit the provider performs the procedure on. Read Less

If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic.

short_description: Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor of metacarpal; with autograft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the skin over the dorsal side of the hand, to remove a cyst or noncancerous tumor of the metacarpal bones. The provider also applies a healthy graft from another part of the patient’s body to fill the cavity to help with healing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the dorsal side of a patient’s hand directly over the metacarpal bones. He increases the size of the incision as large as the lesion or cyst on the metacarpal. Once he locates the growth and fully exposes the cyst or tumor, he scrapes or scoops the entire growth along with any dead tissue, and a margin of healthy tissue out of the cavity. He uses curettes, a burr, and electric cautery as necessary to remove all disease from the area. He then irrigates the space with saline to remove any debris. He then applies a healthy graft from another part of the patient’s body to fill the cavity to help with healing. Finally, he removes all instrumentation, stops any bleeding, and closes the tissue in layers. Terminology Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Benign tumor: An unwanted and abnormal growth in body part. These tumors do not invade neighbouring tissues or organs but can cause mechanical pressures which may damage normal functioning of neighbouring organs, nerves or vessels. Burr: Surgical drill; also called a high speed burr. Curettage: Process of removing dead tissues or abnormal growth from body cavity by scrapping. Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping; also spelled curet . Cyst: Sac usually containing fluid; the term cyst can refer to an abnormal growth or to any saclike structure, such as the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Dorsal: The back of a structure such as the knuckle side of the hand, the back, buttocks, or calf area of a patient. Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. Macroscopic: Things that is visible with naked eye. Metacarpal bone: Metacarpal are the long bones of hand. Their proximal end joins wrist and distal end joins fingers. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass, benign or cancerous. Tips When provider performs an excision or curettage of a bone cyst or benign tumor of the metacarpal bone without the need for use of an autograft, use 26200, Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor of metacarpal. short_description: Partial excision (craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy) bone (eg, osteomyelitis); metacarpal
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider partially excises a portion of the metacarpal bone in the hand using a variety of techniques like craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the metacarpal bone. The goal of this procedure is to remove a portion of metacarpal bone that might be infected. He dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue to get adequate exposure of the affected area of the metacarpal bone. He incises the periosteum, the outer layer of bone, and reflects it. He then removes the infected area of bone using methods like craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy. In craterization, he excises a portion of bone tissue to create a crater–like depression. In saucerization, he excavates the infected bone tissue to form a shallow saucer–like depression to facilitate the drainage of infection. In diaphysectomy, he removes diaphysis, the shaft of the long bone. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Metacarpal: Five small bones of the hand that lie between the carpal and phalanges. Tips See 26235 for partial excision of the proximal or middle phalanx of a finger. See 26236 for partial excision of the distal phalanx of a finger. Read Less

guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision.
