short_description: Partial excision (craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy) bone (eg, osteomyelitis); distal phalanx of finger
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider partially excises a portion of the distal phalanx at the end of the finger using a variety of techniques like craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the phalanx bone. The goal of this procedure is to remove a portion of the distal phalanx of the finger that might be infected. He dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue to get adequate exposure of the affected area of the phalanx bone. He incises the periosteum, the outer layer of bone, and reflects it. He then removes the infected area of bone using methods like craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy. In craterization, he excises a portion of bone tissue to create a crater–like depression. In saucerization, he excavates the infected bone tissue to form a shallow saucer–like depression to facilitate the drainage of infection. In diaphysectomy, he removes the diaphysis, the shaft of the long bone. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Phalanx or phalanges: Bones present in the fingers of the hand; there are fourteen in each hand, with three in each finger and two in the thumb. Tips See 26230 for partial excision of the metacarpal bone. See 26235 for partial excision of the proximal or middle phalanx of the finger. Read Less

short_description: Repair or advancement, flexor tendon, in zone 2 digital flexor tendon sheath (eg, no man's land); secondary, with free graft (includes obtaining graft), each tendon
lay_term: The provider repairs an injury, such as a laceration, to the flexor tendon of one of the fingers. He incorporates a free graft to complete the repair of the injured tendon. He performs the procedure to restore function and relieve pain. He takes care to prevent damage to the pulleys, the structures that hold the tendons close to the bone, and also to preserve the tendon sheath as much as possible. He excises, or removes, any ragged edges on the tendon. He determines that a graft is needed to completely repair the tendon. He harvests the graft, typically from another tendon in the hand, such as the palmaris longus tendon. He places the graft into position and sutures the superficial flexor tendon with horizontal mattress stitches or the deep flexor tendon with simple running stitches. The provider then controls any bleeding, removes all instruments, and closes the surgical wound in layers. Terminology Digit: A finger or toe. Flexor tendon: Tendon associated with a flexor muscle. Free graft: A graft completely removed from its original location that a provider uses elsewhere as opposed to a graft that remains attached by a flap that the provider rotates and uses to cover nearby tissue. short_description: Repair or advancement of profundus tendon, with intact superficialis tendon; secondary with free graft (includes obtaining graft), each tendon
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs secondary repair of the profundus tendon in the finger using a free graft while keeping the superficialis tendon intact. Secondary repair is repair done at least a few days after the initial injury or after the previous surgical repair. Explanation The provider uses this procedure to treat flexor profundus tendon avulsion injury by secondary tendon advancement and repair using a free graft. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the injured tendon. He dissects through subcutaneous tissue and gains adequate exposure of the profundus tendon. He then repairs or reattaches the tendon to a different site to restore the lost function caused by injury of the tendon. He also obtains a graft from the palmaris longus or plantaris tendon and attaches it to the profundus tendon to ensure that length of the tendon is sufficient for reattachment. The provider ensures that the superficialis tendon is intact. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Use one unit of this code for each tendon repaired. Terminology Avulsion injury: Injury to the tendon due to forceful contraction of a muscle against resistance, resulting in chipping of bone. Free graft: A graft cut from its attachment and transplanted to another site. Tips Use 26370 when the provider performs primary repair of profundus tendon with intact superficialis tendon. Use 26373 when the provider performs secondary repair without a graft for a profundus tendon with intact superficialis tendon. Read Less

short_description: Repair, extensor tendon, hand, primary or secondary; without free graft, each tendon
lay_term: The provider carries out extensor tendon repair without a graft when one or more tendons in a patient’s hand has a laceration or rupture, leading to loss of normal hand movements. When the provider repairs extensor tendons within seven days of injury it’s a primary repair. If the provider repairs the tendons more than seven days after the injury and not immediately then it’s known as a secondary repair. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider identifies each torn tendon and makes an incision above the tear. He carries the incision deeper, avoiding injury to the digital nerve and neurovascular bundles. He then elevates the skin flap and easily sees the thin tendon ends. He takes care not to shred the tendon. Next, he retrieves the proximal tendon end and sews the thin damaged tendon with a needle and nonabsorbable suture by following a modified Kessler stitch or Bunnell stitch. He does not use a graft in the repair of the tendons. Finally, the provider irrigates the wound with antibiotics, sutures the incision close and applies a postoperative dressing and splint. Terminology Bunnel stitch: Technique of suturing a tendon where the stitches pass within the tendon and they criss cross the tear or laceration through the cut side on either side. Digital nerve: Branches of the median and ulnar nerves that supply the fingers and thumb. Extensor tendon: Tendons that connect muscles in the forearm to structures within the hand and fingers. Laceration: A deep cut or tear like wound caused by some blunt trauma. Modified Kessler stitch: A locking loop technique of suturing a tendon. Neurovascular bundles: Relating to the blood vessels and nerve structures. Rupture: A tear in a structure due to injury. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips When the provider performs primary or secondary repair of each tendon with free graft, report 26412, Repair, extensor tendon, hand, primary or secondary; with free graft, includes obtaining graft, each tendon There are eight different zones on the extensor surface of the hand, zone I to VIII, based on the location of the tendons. The zone of injury is important as it guides the provider towards the appropriate treatment and prognosis. Due to a superficial position of extensor tendons they are more prone to injuries. Read Less

short_description: Repair, extensor tendon, hand, primary or secondary; with free graft (includes obtaining graft), each tendon
lay_term: The provider carries out extensor tendon repair with a free graft, when one or more tendons in a patient’s hand has a laceration or rupture, leading to loss of normal hand movements. When the provider repairs extensor tendons within seven days of injury it’s a primary repair. If the provider repairs the tendons more than seven days after the injury and not immediately then it’s known as a secondary repair. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs the extensor tendon of a finger without using a graft. The provider may perform either a primary or secondary repair. Primary repair is repair done within a few days of injury. Secondary repair is repair done at least a few days after the initial injury or after the previous surgical repair. Explanation The provider uses this procedure to treat an injury of an extensor tendon by primary or secondary repair. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the injured tendon. He dissects through subcutaneous tissue and gains adequate exposure of the extensor tendon. He then repairs the tendon to restore the lost function caused by injury of the tendon. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Use one unit of this code for each tendon repaired. This code does not include the use of a graft for repair. Terminology Extensor tendon: Muscle tendon present on the back of the forearm that extends the fingers. Tips Use 26420 when the provider performs primary or secondary repair of an extensor tendon of the finger using a graft. Read Less

short_description: Repair, extensor tendon, finger, primary or secondary; with free graft (includes obtaining graft) each tendon

short_description: Repair of extensor tendon, central slip, secondary (eg, boutonniere deformity); using local tissue(s), including lateral band(s), each finger
lay_term: The provider repairs the central slip, i.e., the portion of the extensor tendon that slides over the proximal interphalangeal joint. He manipulates local tissue and the lateral bands back into their normal location to hold the tendon in place close to the bone. A secondary repair involves shortening of the functional scar and repair of the tendon. He performs the procedure to correct a boutonniere deformity and restore function and flexibility to the finger. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision over the distal interphalangeal, or DIP, joint, i.e., the finger joint at the end of the finger. The provider may also mobilize the DIP joint by performing a tenotomy of the distal tendon to release the hyperextension of the DIP joint. The provider then secures the central slip to the middle phalanx with sutures and restores extension to the proximal interphalangeal, or PIP, joint, i.e., the joint nearest the knuckle that bends downward or toward the palm. He splits the lateral bands, i.e., the structures that hold the tendon close to the bone, lengthwise and sutures them together in the midline, which creates a functional central slip. The provider controls any bleeding, removes all instruments, and finally closes the incision in layers Terminology Boutonniere deformity: A deformed position of the finger, in which the joint nearest the knuckle, the proximal interphalangeal joint or PIP, bends toward the palm while the furthest joint, the distal interphalangeal joint or DIP, bends in the other direction; injuries or inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis cause boutonniere deformities; also called buttonhole deformity. Central slip, or band: The part of the tendon that slides over the proximal interphalangeal, or PIP, joint of the finger. Extensor tendon: The tendon that allows the fingers to stretch or extend. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Hyperextension: Bending of a joint at an angle greater than 180 degrees. Phalanx, pl. phalanges: A finger bone; the thumb has two phalanges, the fingers three each; the great toe and usually the little toe have two phalanges, the middle toes three each. Rheumatoid arthritis: Chronic disease that causes disabling inflammation in the joints. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tendon sheath: Covering surrounding a tendon. Volar: Pertaining to the palm of the hand or sole of the foot. Additional Info A boutonniere or buttonhole deformity occurs when the extensor tendon is stretched at the proximal interphalangeal joint. The central slip of the extensor tendon becomes disrupted at its point of insertion into the base of the middle phalanx, which allows the head of the proximal phalanx to protrude though the defect, leaving the patient unable to fully extend the joint, and the lateral bands that hold the tendon in place move toward the palmar side of the joint. short_description: Repair of extensor tendon, distal insertion, primary or secondary; with free graft (includes obtaining graft) Notes: (For tenovaginotomy for trigger finger, use 26055)
lay_term: The provider uses an open approach to repair the distal insertion of the extensor tendon with sutures and a graft. He performs the procedure to prevent further deformity and complications. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin above the tendon area and carries the incision down to the tendon level. He extends the incision in an H or wine glass shape. He harvests a tendon graft from the palmaris longus tendon or from a toe extensor tendon. He makes an incision over the graft site, removes a portion of the tendon, and closes the incision in layers. He then sutures the graft in the gap in the extensor tendon. The provider controls any bleeding and closes the skin incision in layers. He then applies an extension splint to keep the joint in extension during healing. Terminology Distal interphalangeal joint, or DIP joint: The joint between the middle and third phalanges of the finger. Extensor tendon: The tendon that allows the fingers to stretch or extend straight out. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Mallet finger: A deformity of the distal interphalangeal, or DIP, joint that results from a blow to the tip of the finger, which causes the tendon to flex, or shorten, and the tip of the finger to bend downward; also called drop, hammer, or baseball finger. Phalanx, pl. phalanges: A finger bone; the thumb has two phalanges, the fingers three each; the great toe and usually the little toe have two phalanges, the middle toes three each. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tenovaginotomy: A procedure that consists of incision of the tendon and tendon sheath to treat trigger finger. Tips Use the same code when the provider performs the procedure as a primary repair, within one to seven days of injury, or secondary repair, more than seven days after the injury. Read Less

short_description: Tenolysis, flexor tendon; palm OR finger, each tendon
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs tenolysis, which releases the flexor tendon of the palm or finger from adhesions. This surgical procedure is limited to either the palm or finger. short_description: Transfer or transplant of tendon, carpometacarpal area or dorsum of hand; with free tendon graft (includes obtaining graft), each tendon
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers or transplants a tendon in the carpometacarpal area or back of the hand with the help of a tendon graft. The carpometacarpal area is the articulation of the wrist’s carpal bones with the proximal bases of the hand’s five metacarpal bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the back of the hand and dissects through the subcutaneous tissue to expose the tendon. He then isolates the tendon and separates it from its insertion. He obtains a graft from the palmaris longus or plantaris tendon and attaches it to the target muscle tendon to ensure that length of the tendon is sufficient for transfer. short_description: Opponensplasty; superficialis tendon transfer type, each tendon
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs opponensplasty, a surgical procedure in which the provider transfers a tendon to restore opposition function of the thumb. Thumb opposition is the ability of the thumb to move across the palm and oppose the other finger tips. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the ring finger and dissects through the subcutaneous tissue to expose the tendon. He then isolates the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon and separates it from its attachment. He next expands the natural split in the superficialis tendon and redirects the tendon to the thumb. He sutures the split end of the tendons to both sides of the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb at the point of attachment of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Use one unit of this code for each tendon transferred for opponensplasty. Terminology Metacarpophalangeal joint or MCP joint: One of five joints in each hand connecting the metacarpal bones in the palm to the phalangeal bones in the five fingers. Tips Use 26492 when the provider does tendon transfer with a graft for opponensplasty. Use 26494 when the provider performs the opponensplasty by hypothenar muscle transfer. Use 26496 when the provider performs the opponensplasty by any other surgical technique. Read Less

short_description: Opponensplasty; other methods Notes: (For thumb fusion in opposition, use 26820)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs opponensplasty, a surgical procedure in which the provider transfers a tendon to restore the opposition function of the thumb. Thumb opposition is the ability of the thumb to move across the palm and oppose the other finger tips. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the tendon and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue to expose the tendon. He then isolates the muscle tendon and separates it from its attachment. He next transfers the tendon to another location to restore and supplement the opposition function of the thumb. Use this code when the provider uses a tendon transfer method other than those described in codes 26490, 26492, and 26494. Tips Use 26490 when the provider does tendon transfer without a graft. Use 26492 when the provider does tendon transfer with a graft for opponensplasty. Use 26494 when the provider performs the opponensplasty by hypothenar muscle transfer. Read Less

short_description: Transfer of tendon to restore intrinsic function; ring and small finger
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers the tendon from one location to another to restore the intrinsic function of the ring and small fingers. Loss of intrinsic function of the hand results in hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints, between the palm and fingers, and flexion of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints of the fingers. Explanation Tendon transfer is a surgical procedure that involves moving the insertion of a tendon muscle from one location to another location. The aim is to correct the deformity and to restore the grasp. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin and dissects down to reach the involved tendon. Next, the provider separates the flexor tendon from its original insertion point and fixes it to the extensor mechanism of the hand. This transfer of the tendon restores the intrinsic function of the ring and small finger. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Interphalangeal joints: The hinge joints between the phalanges of the hand. Intrinsic function of hand: Simultaneous extension of proximal interphalangeal and distal interphalangeal joint and flexion of metacarpophalangeal joint. Metacarpophalangeal joint or MCP joint: One of five joints in each hand connecting the metacarpal bones in the palm to the phalangeal bones in the five fingers. Tips Read Less

short_description: Transfer of tendon to restore intrinsic function; all 4 fingers
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers the tendons from one location to another to restore the intrinsic function of all 4 fingers. Loss of intrinsic function of the hand results in hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints, between the palm and fingers, and flexion of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints of the fingers. This is also called a claw hand deformity. Explanation Tendon transfer is a surgical procedure that involves moving the insertion of a tendon muscle from one location to another location. The aim is to correct the deformity and to restore the grasp. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin and dissects down to reach the involved tendons. Next, the provider separates the affected flexor tendons from their original insertion points and fixes them to the extensor mechanism of the hand. This transfer of tendons restores the intrinsic function of the hand. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Intrinsic function of hand: Simultaneous extension of the proximal interphalangeal and distal interphalangeal joint and flexion of the metacarpophalangeal joint. Metacarpophalangeal joint or MCP joint: One of five joints in each hand connecting the metacarpal bones in the palm to the phalangeal bones in the five fingers. Read Less

short_description: Correction claw finger, other methods
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider corrects the curved finger deformity known as claw finger using a method not represented by a more specific code. In a typical example, the provider rearranges the location of a flexor tendon from the palm side to the side of the finger so that the flexor tendon functions as an extensor tendon from its new location. Explanation This code represents claw finger correction performed by any method that doesn’t have a more specific code. As an example, when the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the side of the middle finger and extends the incision to expose the flexor tendon. The provider uses a blunt hook to pull the tendon out while flexing the middle finger. With the help of a scalpel or sharp object he frees the tendon from surrounding soft tissues for free movement. Next, he makes a longitudinal incision on the palm near the wrist. The provider dissects down to the level of the extensor tendon, locates the tendon freed by incision of the middle finger, and pulls the tendon strip, detaching it from the phalanx of the middle finger. He splits the tendon strip, also known as a slip, in four sections. Leaving the loose split ends out from the palm incision, the provider creates an incision on the side of the index finger and inserts an instrument called a tunneller through the finger incision with forceps attached to the instrument. The provider advances the tunneller device through a gap between the soft tissue called the lumbrical canal, which is between the thumb and index finger area. He pulls the first slip section, which is toward the thumb side, and brings the slip section out from the index finger incision. He attaches the slip section with sutures to the thumb side of the finger at the proximal phalanx, where normally an extensor tendon attaches. This new location from the palm side to the side of the proximal phalanx causes extension of the joint between the metacarpal and proximal phalanx and corrects the deformity. The provider can perform the same procedure with the other three fingers, which helps in correction of the deformity. The provider may also attach the slips to tendon pulleys, which are ligament rings around the tendons, to release the tension of the tendon. At the end of the surgery, the provider closes the operative sites in layers and immobilizes the wrist with a splint. Terminology Extensor tendon: A tendon that serves to extend or straighten a part of the body. Flexor tendon: A tendon that when contracted acts to bend a joint or limb in the body. Lumbrical canal: A potential space surrounding the tendon of each lumbrical muscle; normally filled with connective tissue. Lumbrical muscle: The lumbricals are intrinsic muscles of the hand that help in reducing the angle between the metacarpal and proximal phalanx and increase the angle between two phalanges. Proximal phalanx: First bone of the finger from the side where the finger is attached to the palm. Tendon pulley: A ring–like structure around the tendon sheath that helps the tendon to keep in place and in shape during the movement of the finger. Read Less

short_description: Reconstruction of tendon pulley, each tendon; with local tissues (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider repairs the damaged tendon pulley, which is a ring–like structure around the tendon sheath that helps the tendon to keep its shape during the movement of the finger. The provider reconstructs the pulley with the help of nearby soft tissues. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision over the joint of the metacarpal and proximal phalanx, which is the finger bone nearest the palm. Or the provider may make the incision over a joint between two phalanges. He exposes the tendon pulley that requires reconstruction. Next, he removes the damaged part of the pulley with a sharp instrument and sutures the trimmed end of the pulley. He may also use any nearby soft tissue, muscle, or tendon to patch the area for a durable repair. At the end of the surgery, he irrigates and sutures the operative wound and places a splint for immobilization. Terminology Metacarpals of the hand: Long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Proximal phalanx: First phalanx from the side where the finger is attached to the palm. Tendon pulley: A ring–like structure of ligament around the tendon sheath that helps the tendon to keep in place and in shape during the movement of the finger. Tips Report 26500 for each tendon reconstructed; if the provider repairs more than one tendon, report 26500 more than once. Do not report 26500 if the provider performs a more extensive, related procedure on the same site in the same session. The code’s definition identifies this code as a separate procedure. Read Less

short_description: Release of thenar muscle(s) (eg, thumb contracture)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider makes an incision into the thenar muscle or muscles to mobilize the scarred muscle tissue causing contracture of the thumb or palm. short_description: Cross intrinsic transfer, each tendon
lay_term: In this procedure the provider transfers a tendon from one side of a finger to the other side to correct the deviation of the fingers and hand toward the small–finger side, known as ulnar drift. Most commonly rheumatoid conditions cause ulnar drift. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal curved incision on the back of the hand over the joint between the proximal phalanx and metacarpal bone, where the finger joins the hand. He dissects down to the level of the tendons, exposes the tendon that is on the thumb side, technically called the radial side, and detaches the tendon from the proximal phalanx. He then uses sutures to attach the tendon toward the little finger side of the target finger, called the ulnar side. The provider may repeat the procedure on all the affected tendons of the fingers. Use one unit of this code for each tendon treated. This procedure balances the tension on the fingers and corrects the ulnar drift deviation. After confirmation of complete correction, the provider closes the skin with sutures. Terminology Metacarpals of the hand: Long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Proximal phalanx: First phalanx, or finger bone, from the side where the finger is attached to the palm. Ulnar drift: A hand deformity in which the swelling of the joints between the proximal phalanges and metacarpal bones causes the fingers to become displaced, tending toward the little finger. Tips Report 26510 once for each distinct tendon transferred. Read Less

short_description: Capsulodesis, metacarpophalangeal joint; single digit
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider treats instability of the joint between a metacarpal bone and the proximal phalanx by incising the joint capsule and attaching it with increased tension to the metacarpal and phalanx. This code applies to work on a single digit. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an S shape incision on the palmar side of the hand over the joint between the metacarpal and proximal phalanx, where the hand meets the finger. Next, he takes the incision down to the level of the joint capsule, frees the capsule from the bones, and roughens the surface of the metacarpal head and end of the proximal phalanx. After creation of this surface, he sutures the capsule on the bony tissue or affixes it with wires with appropriate tension. After confirmation of stability, the provider closes the operative site with sutures. Terminology Capsulodesis: The correction of joint instability or dislocation of joints caused by injury or disease of the joint capsule. Metacarpals of the hand: Long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Proximal phalanx: First phalanx, or finger bone, from the side where the finger is attached to the palm. Tips Report 26516 if the provider performs the procedure on a single digit. short_description: Capsulodesis, metacarpophalangeal joint; 2 digits
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider treats instability of joints in two digits between the metacarpals and proximal phalanges by incising the joint capsule and attaching it with increased tension to the metarcarpal and phalanx. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an S shape incision on the palmar side of the hand over the joint between the metacarpal and proximal phalanx, where the hand meets the finger. Next, he takes the incision down to the level of the joint capsule, frees the capsule from the bones, and roughens the surface of the metacarpal head and end of the proximal phalanx. After creation of this surface, he sutures the capsule on the bony tissue or affixes it with wires with appropriate tension. The provider performs the same procedure on one more digit. After confirmation of stability, the provider closes the operative site with sutures. Metacarpals of the hand: Long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Proximal phalanx: First phalanx, or finger bone, from the side where the finger is attached to the palm. Tips Report 26517 if the provider performs the procedure on 2 digits. For treatment of a single digit report 26516; and for 3 or 4 digits, report 26518. Read Less

short_description: Capsulectomy or capsulotomy; metacarpophalangeal joint, each joint
lay_term: In this procedure the provider releases joint contracture by either making an incision into or excising the joint capsule between the metacarpal and proximal phalanx of a hand. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the back of the hand over the joint between the metacarpal and proximal phalanx, where the hand meets the finger. He takes the incision down to the level of the joint capsule; he uses retractors to preserve the nerves passing over it. With the combination of sharp and blunt dissection, he separates the attached tendon from the capsule. Next the provider either makes a full thickness incision into the joint capsule to release the contracture or he may cut off the capsule in cases where scarring on the joint is dense. After the procedure, he checks the movement of the joint. Once satisfactory joint movement is achieved, he sutures back the tendon and closes the surgical wound. Terminology Contracture: Refers to the permanent tightening of nonbony tissues, such as muscles, tendons, ligaments, or skin. Metacarpals of the hand: Long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Proximal phalanx: First phalanx, or finger bone, from the side where the finger is attached to the palm. Scar tissue: Dense fibrous connective tissue that forms due to a wound or cut. Tips Report 26520 separately for each joint capsule the provider treats. Read Less

short_description: Arthroplasty, metacarpophalangeal joint; each joint Notes: (To report carpometacarpal joint arthroplasty, use 25447)
lay_term: The provider excises part or all of one or more of the metacarpal bones where they articulate, or connect, with the phalanges at the metacarpophalangeal joints. He places a soft tissue spacer in place of the excised bone. He performs the procedure to correct deformity, reduce inflammation, and improve function. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the metacarpophalangeal joint, or MCPJ. He performs tendon and capsule releases as necessary to expose the neck and heads of the metacarpal bones. He then excises part or all of one or more of the metacarpal heads. He inserts soft tissue, such as a piece of fascia or an anchovy of tendon, i.e., a piece of tendon rolled up like an anchovy, between the bones. The tissue maintains the space between the bones and reduces their mobility. He closes the capsule over the metacarpals and realigns the extensor tendons. He controls any bleeding, removes all instruments and closes the incision in layers. Inflammation: The response of tissues to injury, such as pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Metacarpophalangeal joint, or MCPJ: Union of the bones of the hand, the carpal bones, and the finger bones, or phalanges. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider reconstructs or replaces one or more interphalangeal joints using adjoining tissues. He performs the procedure to correct deformity, reduce inflammation, and improve function, typically in a patient with arthritis or prior injuries. He then inserts soft tissue, such as an anchovy of tendon, i.e., a piece of tendon rolled up like an anchovy, or a piece of fascia, between them. The interposition tissue acts as a spacer to maintain the space between the bones and create a fibrous ankylosis between them. He closes the capsule over the joint. He controls any bleeding, removes all instruments and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Ankylosis: A condition following an injury, surgery, or infection, which leads to stiffness or fusion, or permanent fixation, of a joint. Arthritis: An inflammatory condition affecting one or more of the body’s joints that results in pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. short_description: Reconstruction, collateral ligament, metacarpophalangeal joint, single; with tendon or fascial graft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs the collateral ligament, the ligament that holds the joint between the hand's metacarpal and the finger's proximal phalanx together from the sides. The provider uses a tendon or fascial graft to replace the damaged part. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision on the side of the affected joint between the metacarpal of the hand and proximal phalanx of the finger. He incises down to the level of the collateral ligament. The provider uses a retractor to expose the ligament and to preserve blood and nerve supply. The provider harvests a tendon or fascia graft from the forearm, which is not separately reportable. Next, he drills holes in the lower end of the metacarpal and upper end of the proximal phalanx and affixes the graft on both the bones in the holes with the help of sutures. After confirmation of desired movement and stability of the joint, the provider irrigates both the graft donor site and operative site wounds with antibiotics and closes the wounds with sutures. Terminology Collateral ligaments: A pair of ligaments which covers the joints from the side and decide the radius of the movement of the joint, found on hinge joints commonly. Graft: A piece of living tissue that is transplanted surgically. Metacarpals of the hand: Long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Proximal phalanx: First phalanx, or finger bone, from the end where the finger is attached to the palm. Tips Report 26541 more than once only if the provider performs the procedure on more than one joint. Do not report a separate code for harvesting of the graft. Read Less

short_description: Repair non-union, metacarpal or phalanx (includes obtaining bone graft with or without external or internal fixation)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider treats a nonunion deformity in any of the phalanx bones of the fingers or metacarpal bones of the hand. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the dorsal surface, meaning back, of the hand and wrist where the metacarpal or phalanx bones are located, bringing the incision down to the level of the bone. He retracts the nerves and blood vessels to prevent any damage. The provider exposes the area of nonunion and rasps it with a burr or other sharp object to make it smooth. Next the provider measures and harvests a graft of appropriate size to fill the empty space of nonunion. The provider may use internal fixation devices like screws and pins to fix the graft. After confirmation of proper fixation, the provider irrigates the operative site and closes the operative site in layers. Terminology Nonunion: Lack of union of a bone after a fracture. short_description: Pollicization of a digit
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider creates a thumb by rearranging bony and soft tissues from a finger, typically the index finger. Providers perform this procedure in patients with an absence of the thumb by birth or due to injury. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes incisions on both the palmar and back sides of the hand over the finger to be removed, typically the index finger. She brings the incisions down to the level of the bones while preserving the nerves and ligating the blood vessels. The provider reduces the size of the finger to match the size of the thumb by removing the proximal phalanx shaft so that only the head of the proximal phalanx remains. She attaches the remaining portion of the head of the proximal phalanx to the same metacarpal but with an increased angle toward the outside. To make it function like a thumb, the provider rotates the finger toward the inside on its axis. The provider rearranges the muscles and tendons to give movements similar to the thumb. After establishing adequate stability and movement, the provider closes the operative area in layers and with flaps, if required. Terminology Metacarpals of the hand: Long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Proximal phalanx: First phalanx, or finger bone, from the end where the finger is attached to the palm. Read Less

short_description: Transfer, finger to another position without microvascular anastomosis
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes an extra finger and positions the duplicate finger or thumb in a more suitable anatomic position. This procedure treats a patient with polydactyly, or the presence of one or more extra fingers. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the duplicate digit and dissects it along with the metacarpal bone, nerve, tendon, and muscles. He next makes an incision over the digit he is preserving and adjusts its position to a better anatomical and functional location. He transfers the tendon and muscles as necessary to align and obtain as much correction as possible. He fixes the bone at the new location using implants like k wires. He ensures that the digit has an unobstructed blood and nerve supply. He closes the wound by suturing the tissue and covers it with a bulky dressing. short_description: Repair of syndactyly (web finger) each web space; with skin flaps
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider separates congenitally joined fingers by incising between them. He repairs the incision with the help of skin flaps created when the web was divided. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider applies a tourniquet to restrict blood flow to the operative field and makes a zigzag incision on the webbed skin between the joined fingers. He extends the incision to the end of the webbing to release the fingers completely from each other. Next, he uses the flaps of the skin left from the webbing to repair the operative site. Close attention is paid to maintaining vascularization (blood flow) to the flaps created when the web was divided. The provider then performs a layered closure using absorbable sutures. He also applies antibiotic ointment and a nonabsorbent bulky sterile dressing over the hand with cotton fluffs between the fingers. He may apply an above–elbow splint or cast to help immobilize and protect the hand. Terminology Congenital: A condition present from birth. Syndactyly: Fusion of two or more digits of a hand or foot by a web of tissue; the tissue web may be partial or extend to the tips of the digits; bone fusion is less common but may be present; also called conjoined or webbed digits. Web space: Soft tissue between two fingers or toes at the base. Tips This code represents the separation of a single web between two digits. Each web space is a unit. Multiple procedures to separate additional web(s) may be performed, usually at separate settings. If webbing is present on both sides of a digit, only one side will generally be treated at a time to avoid compromising blood supply. However, if multiple webs are divided at the same setting, you may report the code for each web separation; use appropriate modifiers to identify the additional procedures as separate procedures. If the same procedure is performed bilaterally during the same operative session, append modifier 50. Payers may require the provider to report two units of service when billing a claim for a procedure code with modifier 50. However, some payers do not recognize modifier 50 and require the provider to submit a claim showing the procedure code twice, once with modifier LT, for the left side, and once with modifier RT, for the right side, with one unit of service for each. Check with the payer to ascertain how they prefer the procedures to be reported. Report 26561 if both skin flaps and grafts are used in the syndactyly repair, and 26t62 if the repair involves bone and/or nails. Some carriers require preauthorization and proof that the condition causes functional impairment and the surgery being performed is medically necessary. If the condition is merely cosmetic, it likely will not be covered. Check with the patient’s carrier to determine whether the procedure is covered. If a splint or cast is applied, see CPT® guidelines to determine whether the application and/or supply can be reported separately. Read Less

short_description: Repair of syndactyly (web finger) each web space; with skin flaps and grafts

short_description: Repair of syndactyly (web finger) each web space; complex (eg, involving bone, nails)

short_description: Osteotomy; metacarpal, each
lay_term: In this procedure the provider excises part of the metacarpal bone to correct conditions such as a rotational deformity or abnormal bone growth. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the palmar surface of the hand over the affected metacarpal area. He brings the incision down through the muscles to expose the bone. The provider excises a part of the metacarpal and fixes it in place with the help of screws or wire if required. Next the provider irrigates the site and repairs the area in layers with the help of sutures. Terminology Metacarpals of the hand: Long bones in miniature that are connected to the carpal bones of the wrist and the bones of the fingers. Tips Report 26565 more than once if the provider works on more than one metacarpal. Each metacarpal is a unit. Read Less

short_description: Osteoplasty, lengthening, metacarpal or phalanx
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a surgery to lengthen a metacarpal or phalanx bone, usually by a technique known as osteodistraction. In this technique, the provider moves the two segments of a bone slowly apart in such a way that new bone fills in the gap. Explanation The provider most commonly performs this procedure to lengthen the bone in a patient with congenital shortening of a metacarpal of the hand or phalanx of the finger. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the metacarpal or phalanx to be lengthened. He then dissects through the subcutaneous tissue and incises the periosteum parallel to the skin incision, protecting the vascular and nervous tissue. Next, he cuts the bone into proximal and distal segments. He may use plates and screws to keep the bones in position. Finally, he repairs the periosteum and soft tissue and closes the wound by suturing the skin. Later, the provider may apply gradual traction across the finger to lengthen the metacarpal or phalanx bone using external fixation. After 2–3 months, new bone develops in the gap and the provider removes the external fixator device applied preoperatively. This process of lengthening bone is also known as distraction osteogenesis. Terminology Metacarpal: Five small bones of the hand that lie between the wrist’s carpals and fingers’ phalanges. Periosteum: Outer covering of the bone. Phalanx or phalanges: Bones present in the fingers of the hand; there are fourteen in each hand, three in each finger and two in the thumb. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of carpometacarpal fracture dislocation, thumb (Bennett fracture), includes internal fixation, when performed
lay_term: The provider repairs a fracture of the bone at the base of the thumb and dislocation of the articulation (joint) between the thumb bone (metacarpal bone) and the wrist (carpal) bone through an open incision; he may use small nails or wires to secure the bones. Intramedullary: Within the deep part of a structure, such as in the bone marrow. short_description: Open treatment of metacarpophalangeal dislocation, single, includes internal fixation, when performed
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of a single metacarpophalangeal dislocation, which is an abnormal separation of a joint in the hand at the base of a finger. He may use internal fixation implants like pins, wires, or screws to fix the dislocation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the dislocated joint. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the metacarpophalangeal joint. He adjusts the bone to realign the dislocated joint. He may fix the dislocated bone in place using implants like screws, nails, or wires. He closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. He places the metacarpophalangeal joint in a brace or splint for a period of four weeks. He may perform separately reportable X–ray examinations of the metacarpophalangeal joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: The provider inserts hardware, such as a screw, pin, or wire, through the skin and into the bone across a fracture to stabilize it, often with the aid of fluoroscopic imaging guidance. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips When the provider performs a closed treatment of a single metacarpophalangeal dislocation with manipulation to realign the bones, but without anesthesia, use code 26700, Closed treatment of metacarpophalangeal dislocation, single, with manipulation to realign the bones; without anesthesia. When the provider performs a closed treatment of a single metacarpophalangeal dislocation with manipulation to realign the bones, and with anesthesia, use code 26705, Closed treatment of metacarpophalangeal dislocation, single, with manipulation; requiring anesthesia. When the provider performs a percutaneous skeletal fixation of a single metacarpophalangeal dislocation with manipulation to realign the bones, use code 26706, Percutaneous skeletal fixation of metacarpophalangeal dislocation, single, with manipulation. short_description: Closed treatment of phalangeal shaft fracture, proximal or middle phalanx, finger or thumb; with manipulation, with or without skin or skeletal traction, each
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a phalangeal shaft fracture in a proximal, or middle, phalanx of a finger or thumb. Treatment includes manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone. He may also use skin or skeletal traction to reduce the fracture as part of this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the fractured fragment by exerting a pushing or pulling force on the phalanx to reduce the fracture, or to bring the dislocated bones back to their normal alignment. He may also apply skin or skeletal traction force via a pin, wire, screw, or clamp that penetrates the bone to reduce and stabilize the fracture. Next, he places the patient’s finger in a brace or splint for a period of about four weeks. He may perform a separately reportable X–ray examination of the finger or thumb bone to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Use one unit of this code for each phalangeal shaft fractures of a proximal or middle phalanx of a finger or thumb that the provider reduces. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: The provider inserts hardware, such as a screw, pin, or wire, through the skin and into the bone across a fracture to stabilize it, often with the aid of fluoroscopic imaging guidance. Phalanges: The bones present in the fingers of the hand; there are fourteen in each hand, three in each finger and two in the thumb; fingers each have three phalanges, proximal, middle, and distal. The thumb has two proximal and distal. Phalanx shaft: Central portion of a phalanx bone, a bone of the finger or thumb. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. Skeletal traction: Application of a pulling force on bones to treat skeletal disorders and fractures, keeping the bones aligned and immobilized, while relieving pressure on the muscles and nerves, allowing normal healing of a defect or fracture. Traction: Pulling force. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips When the provider performs a closed treatment of a phalangeal shaft fracture in a proximal, or middle, phalanx of a finger or thumb without performing manipulation to realign the bones, use code 26720, Closed treatment of phalangeal shaft fracture, proximal or middle phalanx, finger or thumb; without manipulation, each. When the provider performs a percutaneous skeletal fixation of an unstable phalangeal shaft fracture in a proximal, or middle, phalanx of a finger or thumb with manipulation to realign the bones, use code 26727, Percutaneous skeletal fixation of unstable phalangeal shaft fracture, proximal or middle phalanx, finger or thumb, with manipulation, each. When the provider performs an open treatment of a phalangeal shaft fracture in a proximal, or middle, phalanx of a finger or thumb and with or without using internal fixation implants, use code 26735, Open treatment of phalangeal shaft fracture, proximal or middle phalanx, finger or thumb, includes internal fixation, when performed, each. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Open treatment of phalangeal shaft fracture, proximal or middle phalanx, finger or thumb, includes internal fixation, when performed, each

He may use internal fixation implants like pins, wires, or screws to fix the fracture. Explanation The provider confirms the fracture with X–rays. Then, when the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the fractured bone. short_description: Open treatment of articular fracture, involving metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint, includes internal fixation, when performed, each
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of an articular fracture involving a metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint. The provider confirms the fracture with X–rays. He may use internal fixation implants such as pins, wires, or screws to fix the fracture. Explanation An articular fracture is a crack in the joint forming surface of a bone. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the fractured bone. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the fracture. Next, he adjusts the bone to reduce, or realign, the fractured fragments. He then fixes the fracture using implants like screws, nail, or wires. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. Next, he places the patient’s joint in a brace or splint for a period of about four weeks. He may perform a separately reportable X–ray examination of the joint to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Terminology Articular: Referring to a joint, the union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Interphalangeal joint, or IPJ: Referring to the union of the phalanges, the bones of the fingers or toes. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Metacarpal: Five small bones of the hand that lie between the carpal and phalanges. Metacarpophalangeal joint, or MCPJ: Union of the bones of the hand, the metacarpal bones, and the finger bones, or phalanges. Phalanges: They are the bone present in the fingers of hand; there are fourteen in each hand, three in each finger and two in the thumb; fingers each have three phalanges, proximal, middle, and distal, the thumb has two proximal and distal. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper allignment. Retract: Hold back incisions or edges of a wound with instruments designed to do so without injuring tissue. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips Use one unit of this code this code for each metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint articular fracture that the provider treats. When the provider performs a closed treatment of an articular fracture involving a metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint without performing manipulation, use code 26740, Closed treatment of articular fracture, involving metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint; without manipulation, each. When the provider performs a closed treatment of an articular fracture involving a metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint with manipulation to align the bones, use code 26742, Closed treatment of articular fracture, involving metacarpophalangeal or interphalangeal joint; with manipulation, each. short_description: Open treatment of distal phalangeal fracture, finger or thumb, includes internal fixation, when performed, each
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of a distal phalangeal fracture in a finger or thumb. He may use internal fixation implants like pins or screws to fix the fracture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the fractured bone. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the phalanx fracture. He then adjusts the bone to reduce the distal fractured fragments, or to bring the dislocated bones back to their normal alignment. He may fix the fracture using implants like a plate, screw, nail, or wire. He closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. He places the patient’s digit in a brace or splint for a period of about four weeks. He may perform an X–ray examination of the finger or thumb bone to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: The provider inserts hardware, such as a screw, pin, or wire, through the skin and into the bone across a fracture to stabilize it, often with the aid of fluoroscopic imaging guidance. Phalanges: The bones present in the fingers of the hand; there are fourteen in each hand, three in each finger and two in the thumb; fingers each have three phalanges, proximal, middle, and distal. The thumb has two proximal and distal. Phalanx shaft: Central portion of a phalanx bone, a bone of the finger or thumb. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips Use one unit of this code for each distal phalangeal fracture of a finger or thumb that a provider reduces. When the provider performs a closed treatment of a distal phalangeal fracture in a finger or thumb without performing manipulation to realign the bones, use code 26750, Closed treatment of distal phalangeal fracture, finger or thumb; without manipulation, each. When the provider performs a closed treatment of a distal phalangeal fracture in a finger or thumb with manipulation to realign the bones, use code 26755, Closed treatment of distal phalangeal fracture, finger or thumb; with manipulation, each. When the provider performs percutaneous skeletal fixation of a distal phalangeal fracture in a finger or thumb, use code 26756, Percutaneous skeletal fixation of distal phalangeal fracture, finger or thumb, each. short_description: Fusion in opposition, thumb, with autogenous graft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb in opposition position using an autograft. A metacarpophalangeal joint is a joint where the metacarpal bone of the hand attaches to the phalanx bone of the digit. Thumb opposition is the ability of the thumb to move across the palm and oppose the other finger tips. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to immobilize the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb to reduce the pain caused by arthritis. The fusion is done in a functional position of opposition so the outcome doesn’t hinder the thumb’s ability to oppose the tip of the fingers. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the thumb just over the metacarpophalangeal joint. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then dissects the joint capsule covering the joint to see the joint surfaces. He removes the articular cartilage from the joint surface to leave it as raw bone. He uses internal fixation devices like pins, wire, or a nail to fuse the metacarpophalangeal joint in functional position. The provider also obtains a cancellous bone graft, typically from the iliac crest, and uses it to pack the joints being fused. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider then places the thumb in a splint for a period of four weeks. short_description: Arthrodesis, carpometacarpal joint, thumb, with or without internal fixation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb with or without the help of internal fixation devices. The carpometacarpal joint is a joint where the metacarpal bone of the thumb attaches to the trapezium bone of the wrist. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to immobilize the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb to reduce the pain caused by arthritis. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin on the side of the thumb just over the carpometacarpal joint. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then dissects the joint capsule covering the joint to see the joint surfaces. He removes the articular cartilage from the joint surface to leave it as raw bone. Next, he uses a special tool to hollow the end of the thumb metacarpal to form a socket, and he shapes the surface of the trapezium like a rounded cone that can be fixed into the hollow metacarpal. He might also use some internal fixation devices like pins, wire, or a nail to provide extra stability to the fusion of the carpometacarpal joint. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider then places the thumb in a splint for a period of four weeks. short_description: Arthrodesis, carpometacarpal joint, digit, other than thumb, each; with autograft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes the carpometacarpal joint of a digit other than a thumb. He may or may not use an internal fixation device to fuse the joint. He induces artificial bone generation in the joint area with the help of a graft he obtains from another part of the patient’s body. A carpometacarpal joint is a joint where the metacarpal bone of the digit attaches to the carpal bone of the wrist. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to immobilize the carpometacarpal joint of a digit to reduce the pain caused by arthritis. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the digit just over the carpometacarpal joint. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then dissects the joint capsule covering the joint to see the joint surfaces. He removes the articular cartilage from the joint surface to leave it as raw bone. Next, he uses a special tool to hollow the end of the digit's metacarpal to form a socket, and he shapes the surface of the carpal bone like a rounded cone that can be fixed into the hollow metacarpal. He might also use internal fixation devices like pins, wire, or a nail to provide extra stability to the fusion of the carpometacarpal joint. The provider also obtains a cancellous bone graft, typically from the iliac crest, and uses it to pack the joints being fused. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider then places the digit in a splint for a period of four weeks. short_description: Arthrodesis, interphalangeal joint, with or without internal fixation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes an interphalangeal joint with or without the help of fixation devices. The goal of this procedure is often to treat pain in patients with end stage osteoarthritis of an interphalangeal joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the affected joint in the finger. He dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then retracts the muscle to gain access to the joint for fusion. He next incises the joint capsule and enters the joint. He first removes any dead or inflamed tissue from the joint cavity. He then brings the bones of the joint in close proximity, or near to each other, and fuses the joint with or without using implants like K wire, screws, or plates. Finally, he stops all bleeding at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Next, he places the patient’s finger in a brace for a period of four weeks. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone or dislocated joint in correct position. Interphalangeal joint, or IPJ: Referring to the union of the phalanges, the bones of the fingers or toes. K wire, Kirshner wire: Surgical wire that the provider uses to hold the bone together. Osteoarthritis: Inflammation of joints. Phalanx, or phalanges: Phalanges are the bone present in the fingers of hand; there are fourteen in each hand, three in each finger and two in the thumb. short_description: Arthrodesis, interphalangeal joint, with or without internal fixation; each additional interphalangeal joint (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 26861 in conjunction with 26860)

short_description: Arthrodesis, interphalangeal joint, with or without internal fixation; with autograft (includes obtaining graft), each additional joint (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 26863 in conjunction with 26862)
lay_term: In this add–on procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes an additional interphalangeal joint of the finger following arthrodesis of an initial interphalangeal joint at the same session. He may or may not use an internal fixation device to fuse the joint. He induces artificial bone generation in the joint area with the help of a graft he obtains from another part of the patient’s body. An interphalangeal joint is a joint between phalanges of the hand. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to immobilize the interphalangeal joint of a digit to reduce the pain caused by arthritis. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the digit just over the interphalangeal joint. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then dissects the joint capsule covering the joint to see the joint surfaces. He removes the articular cartilage from the joint surface to leave it as raw bone. Next, he may use internal fixation devices like pins, wire, or a nail to fuse the interphalangeal joint. The provider also obtains a cancellous bone graft, typically from the iliac crest, and uses it to pack the joints being fused. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider then places the digit in a splint for a period of four weeks. Use one unit of this code for each additional interphalangeal joint fused with autograft following initial interphalangeal joint arthrodesis at the same session. Terminology Arthrodesis: The surgical immobilization of a joint by fusion of the bones. Arthritis: Inflammation of joint. Autograft: A tissue transferred from one part of the body to another.
