short_description: Amputation, metacarpal, with finger or thumb (ray amputation), single, with or without interosseous transfer Notes: (For repositioning, see 26550, 26555)
lay_term: In this hand surgery procedure, the provider amputates the metacarpal bone along with a finger or thumb. He may or may not transfer the interosseous muscle. Explanation The provider typically performs this procedure when the patient already has a partially amputated finger or thumb following traumatic injury. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the metacarpal bone and extending to the finger or thumb. He dissects through the subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and blood vessels. He then detaches the muscle attachment from the metacarpal bone. He allows some muscle to retract while he sutures the other segment to a surrounding tendon. He then has adequate exposure of the metacarpal bone, and he makes a cut in the bone to amputate the metacarpal along with a finger or thumb. He might also transfer the interosseous muscle to a surrounding metacarpal to retain the function of the muscle. He next advances the flap of skin or soft tissue in a position to cover the cut bone and sutures the skin flap to the adjacent skin. He might leave a drain in place to clear any infection present. Terminology Amputation: Surgical removal of a complete or partial appendage of the body. Interosseous muscles: Hand muscles having their attachment on metacarpal bones; help to control the fingers. Metacarpals: Five small bones of the hand that lie between the wrist’s carpals and fingers’ phalanges. Read Less

short_description: Amputation, finger or thumb, primary or secondary, any joint or phalanx, single, including neurectomies; with direct closure
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs primary or secondary amputation of a finger or thumb at any joint or phalanx level along with the removal of nerve tissue. He performs direct closure of the wound. Primary amputation is when the provider amputates the finger or thumb at any joint or phalanx immediately after the acute injury or infection. Secondary amputation is when the provider amputates the finger or thumb at any joint or phalanx after a previous amputation that has failed to heal properly. Explanation The provider may perform this procedure when the patient already has a partially amputated finger or thumb following traumatic injury. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the site of interest. He dissects through the subcutaneous tissue and detaches the muscles from the bone. He then ligates the blood vessels. Next, he removes the digital nerves. The purpose of removal of the nerves is to minimize the chances of neuroma formation after amputation. He then makes a cut in the bone at the level of a joint or phalanx and amputates the bone. Finally, he performs direct closure of the wound by suturing the skin layers together. Terminology Amputation: Surgical removal of a complete or partial appendage of the body. Neuroma: A painful condition characterized by a benign growth in the nerve tissue. Phalanx or phalanges: Bones present in the fingers of the hand; there are fourteen in each hand, three in each finger and two in the thumb. Tips Use 26952 when the provider performs the primary or secondary amputation at any joint or phalanx of a finger including neurectomies with local advancement flaps, such as V–Y or hood. Read Less

short_description: Incision and drainage, pelvis or hip joint area; deep abscess or hematoma
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises and drains a deep abscess or hematoma in the pelvis or hip joint area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin and carries it down through the deep subcutaneous tissues to expose the hematoma or abscess. Depending upon the size of the lesion, he may carry the incision down further into the fascia or muscle or extend the incision to fully expose the abscess or hematoma. He then incises the lesion and uses a syringe or catheter to drain the pus from the abscess, or he may squeeze out the pus. If the provider performs drainage for a hematoma, he also removes the blood clots. He then flushes the area thoroughly with a saline solution. Finally, he closes the site by suturing the layers of tissue together or he may leave the site open for further drainage. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled off sac or pocket, the result of infection. Bursa: A fluid filled sac present at the gliding surfaces to reduce friction between the tissues of the body. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Hematoma: A collection of blood or blood clot in the tissues, usually caused by damage to blood vessels. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Tips When the provider performs an incision and drainage of an infected bursa in the pelvis or hip joint area, use code 26991, Incision and drainage, pelvis or hip joint area; infected bursa. short_description: Tenotomy, adductor, subcutaneous, open, with obturator neurectomy Notes: (To report bilateral procedure, report 27003 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open tenotomy, which is surgical division of a tendon, of the adductor muscle of the hip. He also performs obturator nerve removal. Explanation Tenotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider divides a muscle tendon to correct a deformity caused by congenital or acquired shortening of a muscle. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin extending from the pubis along the inner thigh over the adductor muscle. He dissects through the subcutaneous tissue and gains adequate exposure of the adductor muscle to be divided. He first identifies the anterior and posterior branches of the obturator nerve in between the muscles. Next, he removes the nerve and incises the tendon to lengthen it. This allows the muscle to return to its normal length, allowing the joint to straighten, thereby correcting the deformity. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider applies a cast to keep the hip in abduction for three to four weeks. The provider performs this procedure most commonly in cerebral palsy patients with a hypertonic adductor muscle that restricts the abduction motion. Terminology Adductor: Muscle that draws the body part toward the medial line of the body. Abduction: Movement of the body part away from the medial line of the body. Cerebral palsy: Group of nonprogressive disorders of movement and posture caused by damage to the brain. Hypertonic muscle: Tight muscle. Tips Use 27000 when the provider performs percutaneous tenotomy of the hip adductor. Use 27001 when the provider performs open tenotomy of the hip adductor without obturator neurectomy. Read Less

short_description: Tenotomy, hip flexor(s), open (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open tenotomy, which is surgical division of a tendon, of one or more flexor muscles of the hip. Explanation Tenotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider divides a muscle tendon to correct a deformity caused by congenital or acquired shortening of a muscle. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin extending from the ilium along the anterior thigh. The iliopsoas is the major hip flexor muscle that providers most commonly target. The provider dissects through the subcutaneous tissue and gains adequate exposure of the iliopsoas muscle to be divided. He separates the iliacus and psoas muscles. Next, he incises the tendons to lengthen them. In cases of severe muscle contracture, he might completely resect the psoas muscle and preserve the iliacus muscle to maintain the hip flexion. This allows the muscle or muscles to return to their normal length, allowing the joint to straighten, thereby correcting the deformity. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider applies a cast to the hip for three to four weeks. If the provider performs the 27005 procedure with an unrelated procedure, you may need to append modifier 59 to 27005. Read Less

short_description: Arthrotomy, hip, including exploration or removal of loose or foreign body
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an incision to open the hip joint. He then explores the joint and drains out or pulls out any foreign or loose body present. Explanation Arthrotomy is an incision procedure to create an opening in the joint. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin just above the hip joint, dissecting down through the subcutaneous tissue to the joint capsule. He incises and opens the joint capsule. The provider explores the joint space to detect any abnormality. He then removes any foreign body like a bullet, nail, etc., or loose body like fragments of bone or cartilage if present. Finally, he irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution and closes the wound in layers. He may leave a drain in place if required. Terminology Arthrotomy: Cutting into a joint to expose its interior. Tips Use 27030 when the provider performs the hip arthrotomy with drainage of infection. Read Less

short_description: Radical resection of tumor (eg, sarcoma), soft tissue of pelvis and hip area; less than 5 cm
lay_term: The provider performs an extensive excision of a tumor, or mass, in the soft tissues in the pelvis and hip area, suspected to be malignant, such as a sarcoma. He excises the surrounding tissues along with the mass, with the diameter of the tumor and its margins measuring less than 5 cm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision and raises subcutaneous flaps. He exposes the muscles around the tumor and cuts into the fascia. He excises and removes the tumor en bloc, or as a single specimen, with a margin of tissue around the tumor included with the mass to ensure that no pathology, or diseased tissue, remains. Lymphatics and blood vessels are ligated as needed. The area is inspected, and frozen sections are taken from tissue around the area. Based on the pathology, the provider may perform additional excision at the area. He submits the specimen for pathologic analysis. The provider then irrigates the area and inserts a drain, if necessary. He checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Frozen section: Refers to a tissue sample obtained during surgery which is submitted to the pathology laboratory for rapid processing by freezing and immediate analysis, with results relayed while surgery is taking place to aid the provider in determining the extent of tissue removal, generally when cancer is suspected. Lymph system: Maintains fluid balance by returning fluid from the spaces between tissues back to the blood stream and supports the immune system. Malignant: Cancerous, capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Radical resection: Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Sarcoma: A malignant, or cancerous, tumor of connective tissue origin, that occurs in the bone or soft tissues anywhere in the body. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips Check the documentation carefully for the size and the skin layer depth to which the surgery took place before choosing the code. Compare with 27059, Radical resection of tumor, e.g., sarcoma, soft tissue of pelvis and hip area, 5 cm or greater. When selecting a code for this type of procedure, the defining measurement is the size of the excision, not the size of the lesion. For instance, the provider might have to excise 7 cm to remove a 4.5 cm tumor. If the doctor documents only the size of the lesion and not the resection size, you could end up with a lower code. Measure before pathology, i.e., the provider should measure and document the resection size during surgery. Excised tissue shrinks dramatically during processing, so you'll undersize the excision if you base the measurement on the pathology report. Read Less

short_description: Arthrotomy with synovectomy, hip joint
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an incision to open the hip joint. He then explores the joint and removes the inflamed synovial membrane lining the joint. Explanation Arthrotomy is an incision procedure to create an opening in the joint. The goal of this procedure is to remove the inflamed synovium causing pain in the joint. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin just above the hip joint, dissecting down through the subcutaneous tissue to the joint capsule. He incises and opens the joint capsule to expose the synovium, a membrane lining the joint cavity. He then removes the inflamed synovium from the joint. Finally, he irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution and closes the wound in layers. He may leave a drain in place if required. Terminology Arthrotomy: Cutting into a joint to expose its interior. Tips Use 27030 when the provider performs the hip arthrotomy with drainage of infection. Use 27033 when the provider performs the hip arthrotomy with exploration or removal of a loose or foreign body. Read Less

short_description: Decompression fasciotomy(ies), pelvic (buttock) compartment(s) (eg, gluteus medius-minimus, gluteus maximus, iliopsoas, and/or tensor fascia lata muscle) with debridement of nonviable muscle, unilateral Notes: (To report bilateral procedure, report 27057 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises into the fascia surrounding the pelvic, or buttock compartment, in the hip to relieve pressure and increase blood flow. He performs this procedure on only one side of the buttock. He also removes the dead or damaged tissue. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin overlying the affected area to access the fascia above the affected muscle compartment. He incises the fascia and debrides all the damaged, nonviable muscle and or nerve tissue, thereby reducing the pressure on the neurovascular structures underneath the fascia. This restores the restricted blood supply and relieves the patient from symptoms. He may leave the incision open for a period of time to drain. Debridement: Removal of dead or damaged tissue. Gluteal muscle: Group of four muscles located over the hip joint. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically excises the trochanteric bursa, a bursa situated at the outer side of the hip at the level of the bony prominence called the greater trochanter. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to remove the trochanteric bursa in a patient with trochanteric bursitis, a condition resulting in a painful buttock due to inflammation of the bursa. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the lateral side of the hip. He then dissects through the subcutaneous tissue to reach the trochanteric bursa. He dissects out the inflamed bursa from the trochanteric tuberosity. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the tissues in layers. Terminology Bursa: Fluid filled sac situated between tissue like muscle, tendon, and bone that reduces the friction between the tissues. Tips Use 27060 for excision of ischial bursa. Read Less

short_description: Partial excision, wing of ilium, symphysis pubis, or greater trochanter of femur, (craterization, saucerization) (eg, osteomyelitis or bone abscess); deep (subfascial or intramuscular)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a deep partial excision of a portion of the wing of the ilium, symphysis pubis, or greater trochanter of the femur using a variety of techniques like craterization or saucerization. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to remove a portion of the wing of the ilium, symphysis pubis, or greater trochanter of the femur that might be infected. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the targeted area. He dissects down deeply through soft tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He incises the periosteum, the outer layer of bone, and reflects it. He then removes the infected area of bone using methods like craterization or saucerization. In craterization, he excises a portion of bone tissue to create a crater–like depression. In saucerization, he excavates the infected bone tissue to form a shallow saucer–like depression to facilitate the drainage of infection. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Use this code when the provider performs a deep partial excision of the infected bone. Terminology Greater trochanter: A bony prominence on the outer side of the hip. Symphysis pubis: A cartilaginous joint formed in the midline between the two pubis bones. Wing of ilium: Upper expanded portion of the ilium, the uppermost and largest part of the hip bone. Tips Use 27070 when the provider performs a superficial partial excision of a portion of the wing of the ilium, symphysis pubis, or greater trochanter of the femur. Read Less

short_description: Radical resection of tumor; wing of ilium, 1 pubic or ischial ramus or symphysis pubis
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs the radical resection of a tumor of a wing of the ilium, one pubic or ischial ramus, or symphysis pubis. Next, he detaches and divides the muscles inserting into the bone. He next removes the bone tumor, involving the wing of the ilium, one pubic or ischial ramus, or symphysis pubis, using a surgical instrument. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. short_description: Radical resection of tumor; innominate bone, total
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs radical resection of a tumor of the innominate bone. Radical resection is a procedure in which the provider excises the tumor along with a few inches of healthy tissue on either side of the tumor. An innominate bone is either of the two bones that form the sides of the pelvis, consisting of three fused components: the ilium, ischium, and pubis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin starting from the anterosuperior iliac spine extending downward toward the interior aspect of the thigh. He then dissects deeply through the subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and blood vessels. He then has adequate exposure of the innominate bone. Next, he detaches and divides the muscles inserting into the innominate bone. He next removes the innominate bone tumor, involving the entire innominate bone, cutting it from the pelvic girdle using a surgical instrument. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Anterosuperior iliac spine: Front projection of the iliac crest in the hip. short_description: Removal of hip prosthesis; complicated, including total hip prosthesis, methylmethacrylate with or without insertion of spacer
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes the total hip prosthesis by breaking the methylmethacrylate, a type of bone cement. He may or may not insert a spacer in the vacant space. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to remove a loose or damaged prosthesis before irreversible harm is done to the joint. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the hip joint and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue to reach the hip joint capsule. He identifies and protects the sciatic nerve and releases the soft tissue. He then breaks the methylmethacrylate cement to dislocate the femur prosthesis fixed in the acetabulum of the pelvis. He uses a surgical instrument to remove the cement from the border of the implant. He next removes the acetabular component of the prosthesis and removes any extra cement in the socket using a curette. He then may place a spacer in between the femur and acetabular socket. This spacer prevents the shortening of the extremity, and the spacer stays in place until the patient has a new prosthesis implanted at a later date. Finally, the provider irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution and closes the wound in layers. He may leave a drain in place if required. Terminology Acetabulum: Cup shaped socket of hip bone. Prosthesis: Artificial substitute of a missing part of the body. Revision arthroplasty: A procedure in which the surgeon removes a previously implanted artificial hip joint, or prosthesis, and replaces it with a new prosthesis. Tips Usually, the provider performs 27091 as a part of a larger procedure, revision of total arthroplasty of hip. In those cases, you should report only the larger procedure, not 27091. See 27134 for revision of total hip arthroplasty. Read Less

short_description: Injection procedure for hip arthrography; without anesthesia Notes: (For radiological supervision and interpretation, use 73525. Do not report 77002 in conjunction with 73525)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider injects contrast material into a hip joint for hip arthrography, an X–ray examination of the hip joint. He performs this procedure without administration of anesthesia to the patient. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider, using fluoroscopic guidance, inserts a needle into the joint cavity of the hip joint. Once the provider confirms the position of the needle, he may withdraw a sample of the synovial fluid for testing. He injects a contrast material into the cavity. He then performs an X–ray examination of the hip joint, which includes various positioning of the hips and additional sets of X–rays after movement of the hips. He performs this procedure without administration of anesthesia to the patient. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Injection: Use of a syringe to forcibly instill a liquid substance into tissues, vessels, or tumors; the instilling of a medicinal substance using various routes that include subcutaneous, below the skin, intravenous, within a vein, or intramuscular, into a muscle, among others; also, excessive accumulation of blood in an area causing redness. Synovial fluid: Thick fluid found in synovial joints; synovial joints are characterized by their fluid filled capsules. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips When the provider injects a contrast material into the hip joint for hip arthrography with administration of anesthesia to the patient, use code 27095, Injection procedure for hip arthrography; with anesthesia. short_description: Injection procedure for hip arthrography; with anesthesia Notes: (For radiological supervision and interpretation, use 73525. Do not report 77002 in conjunction with 73525)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider injects contrast material into a hip joint for hip arthrography, an X–ray examination of the hip joint that he performs after the injection of contrast. He performs this procedure with administration of anesthesia to the patient. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a needle into the joint cavity of the hip, using fluoroscopic guidance. He confirms the position of the needle and may withdraw a sample of the synovial fluid for testing. He injects contrast material into the cavity. He then performs an X–ray examination of the hip joint, which includes various positioning of the hips and additional sets of X–rays after movement of the hips. Terminology Contrast: A special dye used in radiology imaging to improve the visibility of internal structures or organs of the body, which providers administer to patients through various routes, including oral and intravenously; also called contrast material, contrast medium, contrast media, contrast agent, or contrast dye. Fluoroscopic guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Injection: Use of a syringe to forcibly instill a liquid substance into tissues, vessels, or tumors; the instilling of a medicinal substance using various routes that include subcutaneous, below the skin, intravenous, within a vein, or intramuscular, into a muscle, among others; also, excessive accumulation of blood in an area causing redness. Synovial fluid: Thick fluid found in synovial joints; synovial joints are characterized by their fluid filled capsules. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips When the provider injects a contrast material into a hip joint for hip arthrography without administering anesthesia to the patient, use code 27093, Injection procedure for hip arthrography; without anesthesia. short_description: Transfer, adductor to ischium
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers the adductor tendons from their origin on the pubic bones to the ischium, the lowest part of the rear hip bone. There are three main adductor muscles in a hip joint: adductor longus, brevis, and gracilis. Explanation The provider performs this procedure in spastic and other neurological conditions like cerebral palsy. The aim is to allow greater hip abduction by decreasing the strength of the hip adductors. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the pubic area at the origin of the adductor muscles. He extends this incision backward to the ischial tuberosity. Then, the provider releases the adductor muscle tendons from their origin and carries them backward to the ischial tuberosity. He next sutures the tendon to the ischial tuberosity. In this way, there is a change in the mechanics of the muscle, allowing hip abduction. Finally, the provider closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the hip in a cast for a period of four to six weeks. short_description: Transfer external oblique muscle to greater trochanter including fascial or tendon extension (graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers the external oblique muscle to the greater trochanter to compensate for paralyzed hip abductor muscles. The external oblique is the largest and most superficial of the muscles of the front abdominal wall. Explanation The aim of this procedure is to transfer the external oblique muscle to the greater trochanter of the thigh’s femur bone. The transfer helps to compensate for lost hip abductor function and to strengthen the hip abduction. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the pubic area at the insertion of the external oblique over the pubic tubercle and front half of the iliac crest. He then frees the muscle’s attachment and folds the edges to form a hood. He next makes an incision over the greater trochanter of the femur and drills holes in the trochanter. He then creates a subcutaneous tunnel along the ilium. He carries the external oblique muscle hood through this tunnel backward and sutures it to the greater trochanter of the femur. He may also use a strip of fascia lata or other tendon graft extension to allow for adequate length of the muscle to be transferred. Finally, the provider closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the hip in a cast for a period of four to six weeks. Terminology Abduction: Movement of the body part away from the medial line of the body. Hip abductor: Muscle that moves the hip joint away from the midline. Fascia lata: A layer of fibrous tissue continuous with the iliotibial band, a ligament that runs on the outer side of the thigh from hip to shin bone. Greater trochanter: A bony prominence on the outer side of the hip. Iliac crest: Upper border of the ilium, which is the uppermost and largest bone in the pelvis. Ilium: Uppermost and largest bone of the pelvis. Pubic tubercle: Rounded eminence on the upper border of the pubis. Pubis: One of the bones that makes up the pelvis. Read Less

short_description: Transfer paraspinal muscle to hip (includes fascial or tendon extension graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers a paraspinal muscle to the hip joint using a fascial or tendon graft. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to transfer the paraspinal muscle to the hip joint to compensate for the lost function of another muscle. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the paraspinal muscle to be transferred. He next detaches the muscle from its attachment and passes it to the desired location on the hip joint. He also obtains a graft from muscles like the peroneus, fascia lata, etc. Peroneus is a muscle present in the outer side of the lower leg. Fascia lata is deep fascia of the thigh. He attaches this graft to the muscle being transferred to ensure that there is enough length of muscle. He then fixes the paraspinal muscle to the desired location over the hip joint. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Fascia: A layer of fibrous tissue. Paraspinal muscle: Group of muscles present parallel to the spine. Read Less

short_description: Transfer iliopsoas; to greater trochanter of femur
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers the iliopsoas muscle from the lesser trochanter of the femur to the greater trochanter to compensate for weak hip abductor muscles. The lesser trochanter is a bony prominence on the inner side of the neck of the femur bone. The greater trochanter is a bony projection on the outer and upper side of the femur. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to improve the lateral stability of the hip joint by transferring the iliopsoas muscle to the greater trochanter of the femur. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin extending from the iliac region to the middle of the thigh. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the femoral nerve and vessels. He exposes the lateral trochanter at the insertion of the iliopsoas muscle. He then resects or isolates the insertion along with the lesser trochanter. He then transfers the iliopsoas tendon through a large window in the ilium near the sacroiliac joint. He next passes the tendon through a tunnel in the greater trochanter and secures the tendon by multiple sutures on the greater trochanter. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the hip in a cast for a period of four to six weeks. Terminology Hip abductors: Group of muscles that moves the thigh away from the midline of the body. Iliopsoas: A muscle consisting of the iliacus and psoas major muscles. Iliac region: Relating to or near ilium bone. Ilium: Uppermost and largest bone of pelvis. Sacroiliac joint: A joint between the iliac bone and the lowest part of the spine. Tips Use 27111 when the provider transfers the iliopsoas muscle to the femoral neck. Read Less

short_description: Transfer iliopsoas; to femoral neck
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers the iliopsoas muscle to the neck of the femur to compensate for a weak hip abductor muscles. The goal of this procedure is to improve the lateral stability of the hip joint by transferring the iliopsoas muscle to the neck of the femur. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin extending from the iliac region to the middle of the thigh. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the femoral nerve and vessels. He exposes the lateral trochanter at the insertion of the iliopsoas muscle. He then resects or isolates the insertion along with the lesser trochanter. He then transfers the iliopsoas tendon to the femur while keeping the thigh straight. He next creates a small window on the femur at the site of transfer of iliopsoas tendon and joins the lesser trochanter to it. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the hip in a cast for a period of about four to six weeks. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Trochanter of femur: Top part of the femur, featuring two bony prominences called the greater and lesser trochanter. short_description: Acetabuloplasty; resection, femoral head (eg, Girdlestone procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs acetabuloplasty in which she surgically modifies the shape of the acetabulum, a cup–shaped socket of the hip joint. She also resects, or cuts out the femoral head. The aim is to alleviate pain in a patient with a severe hip infection or in a patient whose bones cannot tolerate reconstruction of the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin extending from the front of the iliac area to the outer side of the thigh. She then dissects down through soft tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. She then retracts the muscles to expose the joint capsule. She next incises the capsule to enter the joint. She dislocates the femur head from the acetabulum and removes the acetabulum rim. She then resects or cuts the femur head from the femur bone using a saw. She then may remove an arthritic or degenerated portion of the acetabulum. She does not replace the femoral component, and she closes the hip joint creating a pseudo hip joint supported by muscles and fibrous tissue. Finally, she obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. She then places the patient in a hip cast for a period of four to six weeks. Terminology Acetabulum: A cup–shaped socket of the hip joint. Femur head: Rounded upper end of the femur bone. Iliac area: Relating to or located near the ilium bone of the pelvis. Pseudo joint: A false joint between two bone fragments held together by fibrous tissue. Tips Use 27120 when the provider performs acetabuloplasty only. Read Less

short_description: Conversion of previous hip surgery to total hip arthroplasty, with or without autograft or allograft
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider exposes a hip joint that has undergone a previous hip surgery other than total hip arthroplasty and replaces the hip joint by prosthesis, or artificial hip joint. He replaces both the femoral and acetabular components with or without using an autograft or allograft. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to relieve pain in a patient with hip arthritis who does not respond to more conservative treatment. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider enters the hip joint such as by opening the previous hip surgery incision. He dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue to reach the hip joint capsule. He identifies and protects the sciatic nerve and releases the soft tissue. He removes any implant that was affixed in a previous hip surgery. He then manually dislocates the hip joint and separates the femoral component from the acetabulum. He then removes the femoral head from the end of the femur using a saw. Next, he uses a reamer, a type of surgical cutting tool, in the acetabulum to create a perfect hemispherical bone socket that matches the shape of the acetabular prosthesis. He then places the acetabular prosthetic component in the socket and secures it using bone cement and, possibly, a graft. He then prepares the femoral shaft canal using a reamer or rasp for inserting the femoral prosthetic component. He inserts the femoral prosthetic stem into the femoral shaft and affixes it using bone cement. Lastly, he reunites the two components using a graft, if appropriate, and cement and reduces the hip joint, restoring the normal alignment of the hip joint. Finally, the provider irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution and closes the wound in layers. He may leave a drain in place if required. Terminology Acetabulum: Cup–shaped socket of hip bone. Allograft: A tissue transferred from one individual of the same species to another. Autograft: A tissue transferred from one part of the body to another. Prosthesis: Artificial substitute of a missing part of the body. Tips Use 27130 when the provider performs total hip arthroplasty by replacing both femoral and acetabular components in a procedure that is not a conversion of a previous hip surgery. Use 27134 when the provider performs revision arthroplasty of the hip by replacing both femoral and acetabular components. Use 27137 when the provider performs revision arthroplasty of the hip by replacing only the acetabular component with or without an autograft or allograft. Use 27138 when the provider performs revision arthroplasty of the hip by replacing only the femoral component with or without autograft or allograft. Read Less

short_description: Revision of total hip arthroplasty; both components, with or without autograft or allograft
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a previously implanted artificial hip joint or prosthesis and replaces it with a new prosthesis. He replaces both the femoral and acetabular components. He may or may not use a graft for the revision surgery. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to remove a loose or damaged prosthesis before it does irreversible harm to the joint. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the hip joint and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue to reach the hip joint capsule. He identifies and protects the sciatic nerve and releases the soft tissue. He then breaks the methylmethacrylate cement to dislocate the femur prosthesis fixed in the acetabulum of the pelvis. He uses a surgical instrument to remove the cement from the border of the implant. He next removes the femoral stem from the femoral shaft. He then removes the acetabular component of the prosthesis and removes any extra cement in the socket using a curette. short_description: Osteotomy and transfer of greater trochanter of femur (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an osteotomy, cutting the greater trochanter of the thigh’s femur bone and transferring the trochanter downward and outward on the femur bone. The greater trochanter is a bony prominence on the outer side of the hip. Explanation Osteotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider cuts a portion of a bone, typically in a wedge shape, to correct the alignment. Congenital dislocation of the hip, Perthes’ disease, and some other conditions result in prominence and elongation of the greater trochanter. This weakens the abductor muscles of the hip and may also produce painful impingement between the trochanter and the ilium of the pelvis. The effectiveness of abductor muscle function depends on the distance of the greater trochanter from the center of the femoral head. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a straight incision in the skin on the outer side of the hip over the tip of the greater trochanter and extending downward to the targeted new location of the greater trochanter on the femur bone. He dissects through soft tissue and elevates the abductor muscles through their front edge. He uses a retractor to retract the abductor muscles and another retractor to protect the tissues in front. He uses an osteotome surgical instrument to cut the greater trochanter from its base and then moves the greater trochanter downward with the help of bone forceps. He fixes the greater trochanter on its new location over the femur bone by drilling holes and by securing the bony prominence with the help of K–wire. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Abductor muscle of hip: A group of muscles in the buttock that lifts the thigh out to the side. Congenital dislocation of hip: A birth defect in which the head of the femur moves out of the socket of the pelvic bone. Femoral head: The ball at the upper end of the femur bone. Impingement: To strike or collide. Perthes’ disease: A condition characterized by the temporary loss of blood supply to the head of the femur. Tips Code 27140’s descriptor indicates it is a separate procedure, meaning that you cannot report this code separately with a related procedure when performed in an anatomically related region through the same skin incision. short_description: Osteotomy, iliac, acetabular or innominate bone
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an osteotomy, cutting a portion of the iliac, acetabular, or innominate bone of the pelvis. The iliac is the upper portion of the pelvic girdle. The acetabulum is the cup–shaped socket of the hip joint. The innominate bone is either of the two bones that form the sides of the pelvis, consisting of three fused components: the ilium, ischium, and pubis. Explanation Osteotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider cuts a portion of a bone, typically in a wedge shape, to correct the deformity or alignment. The provider most commonly performs osteotomy of the innominate bone. This procedure is known as Salter’s osteotomy. In this procedure, the provider divides the pelvis from above the anterior inferior iliac spine to the sciatic foramen. The provider performs this procedure as a means of stabilizing the hip in a child with an excessively steep acetabulum. The aim is to prevent early osteoarthritis that may result because of abnormal pressure along the edge of the steep acetabulum. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a straight incision extending from the iliac spine to the inguinal area. He dissects down through soft tissue and releases the adductor and iliopsoas muscles. He next osteomizes, or cuts, the innominate bone such as with a Gigli saw, a flexible wire saw used for cutting bone. He cuts the bone from the sciatic notch to the anterior inferior iliac spine. He next rotates the entire acetabulum forward and outward together with the pubis and ischium as a unit with the symphysis acting as a hinge. As a result, the acetabulum shifts forward and outward. This procedure flattens the excessively steep acetabular roof. He creates a separate incision and obtains a graft from the iliac bone to fix the osteotomy site. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the patient in a hip brace for a period of six weeks. Iliopsoas: A muscle consisting of iliacus and psoas major muscles. Inguinal: Relating to or situated in the region of the groin. Osteoarthritis: Degenerative inflammation of joint. Osteomizes: Cuts a portion of bone. Sciatic foramen: Either of the two openings on each side of the pelvis through which many vessels and nerves, including the sciatic nerve, exit the pelvis. Symphysis: A midline joint between the two pubic bones. Tips Use 27147 when the provider performs this osteotomy with open reduction of the hip. short_description: Osteotomy, iliac, acetabular or innominate bone; with femoral osteotomy and with open reduction of hip
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an osteotomy, cutting a portion of the iliac, acetabular, or innominate bone of the pelvis. He then reduces the dislocated hip. He also performs femoral osteotomy in which he cuts the thigh bone to correct its alignment. The iliac is the upper portion of the pelvic girdle. The acetabulum is the cup–shaped socket of the hip joint. The innominate bone is either of the two bones that form the sides of the pelvis, consisting of three fused components: the ilium, ischium, and pubis. Explanation Osteotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider cuts a portion of a bone, typically in a wedge shape, to correct the deformity or alignment. The provider most commonly performs osteotomy of the innominate bone. This procedure is known as Salter’s osteotomy. In this procedure, the provider divides the pelvis from above the anterior inferior spine to the sciatic foramen. The provider performs this procedure as a means of stabilizing the hip in a child with an excessively steep acetabulum. The aim is to prevent early osteoarthritis that may result because of abnormal pressure along the edge of the steep acetabulum. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a straight incision extending from the iliac spine to the inguinal area. He dissects down through soft tissue and releases the adductor and iliopsoas muscles. He next osteotomizes or cuts the innominate bone such as with a Gigli saw, a flexible wire saw used for cutting bone. He cuts the bone from the sciatic notch to the anterior inferior iliac spine. He next rotates the entire acetabulum forward and outward together with the pubis and ischium as a unit with the symphysis acting as a hinge. As a result, the acetabulum shifts forward and outward. This procedure flattens the excessively steep acetabular roof. He creates a separate incision and obtains a graft from the iliac bone to fix the osteotomy site. He also performs femoral osteotomy in which he cuts a wedge–shaped portion of the femur through a separate incision in the thigh bone. He secures the osteotomy site with the help of screws and plates. The aim is to correct the alignment of the femur. In addition to osteotomy, he also performs reduction of the dislocated hip ensuring that the femur head is secured correctly within the acetabulum. He then uses some extra sutures to improve the stability of the joint capsule. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the patient in a hip brace for a period of six weeks. Terminology Adductors of hip: Group of muscles that moves the thigh toward the midline of the body. Anterior inferior iliac spine: Bony projection in the front border of the hip bone. Iliopsoas: A muscle consisting of the iliacus and psoas major muscles. Inguinal: Relating to or situated in the region of groin. Osteoarthritis: Degenerative inflammation of joint. Osteotomizes: Incises a portion of bone. Sciatic foramen: Either of the two openings on each side of the pelvis through which many vessels and nerves, including the sciatic nerve, exit the pelvis. Symphysis: A midline joint between two pubic bones. Tips Use 27146 when the provider performs this osteotomy alone without open hip reduction or femoral osteotomy. Use 27147 when the provider performs this osteotomy with open reduction of the hip. Use 27151 when the provider performs this osteotomy with femoral osteotomy. Read Less

short_description: Osteotomy, pelvis, bilateral (eg, congenital malformation)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a pelvic osteotomy, by incising a portion of the pelvic bones or repairing the pelvic side of the socket. There are different types of pelvic osteotomy such as dega osteotomy or salter osteotomy. When the child suffers an alignment problem of the pelvis from birth, the provider corrects the deformity in both pelvises by any of the pelvic osteotomy methods. He excises the bone from the sciatic notch to the anterior inferior iliac spine. short_description: Osteotomy, femoral neck (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs femoral neck osteotomy, cutting a wedge–shaped portion of the femur neck to correct the femoral alignment. The femoral neck is a flat portion of the thigh’s femur bone that connects the femoral head with the femoral shaft. Explanation Osteotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider cuts a portion of a bone, typically in a wedge shape, to correct the deformity or alignment. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision extending from the iliac spine to the greater trochanter, a bony prominence on the outer side of the hip. He then dissects down through soft tissue and retracts the muscles to expose the hip joint capsule. He next incises the capsule to enter the joint. He osteotomizes two predetermined locations on the femur neck by removing wedge–shaped pieces. He uses pins and screws to secure the osteotomy site on the femur neck. He ensures he aligned the femur as required to correct the deformity. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. short_description: Osteotomy, intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric including internal or external fixation and/or cast
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an osteotomy, or a division of a portion of the bone from an area of the femur between the greater and lesser trochanter or just below the lesser trochanter to correct the alignment or deformity. He may also use an internal or external fixation device or cast to stabilize the area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision over the apex, or upper part, of the greater trochanter and moves it downwards. He dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue and retracts nerves and muscles to expose the upper end of the femur. He incises the periosteum, the outer covering of the bone. Next, he elevates the periosteum and removes a wedge–shaped piece of bone from the intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric area of femur to correct the alignment of the bone. He reattaches the periosteum and places hardware, such as a plate and screws, to stabilize the area. Alternatively, he may place external fixation to hold the correct alignment of the bones. He then closes the wound. He may apply a spica cast to immobilize the hip and maintain the correct position. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Intertrochanteric area: The portion of the femur between the greater trochanter and the lesser trochanter in the upper end of the femur. Lesser trochanter: A bony prominence on the inner side of neck of femur bone. Longitudinal: In a lengthwise direction. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Retract: Hold back incisions or edges of a wound with instruments designed to do so without injuring tissue. short_description: Bone graft, femoral head, neck, intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric area (includes obtaining bone graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider treats the defect in the femoral head, neck, intertrochanteric, or subtrochanteric area using a bone graft obtained from another area of the body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the area to be repaired. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He then has adequate exposure of the defect in the femur head, neck, intertrochanteric, or subtrochanteric area. He makes a separate incision in the iliac bone region and obtains a cancellous bone graft. He then closes the graft donor site by suturing the skin. He uses this bone graft to fill in the defect in the femur. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Bone graft: A bone tissue obtained from one bone to fix the defect in another bone. Cancellous: A spongy bone tissue that forms the bone. Femoral neck: A flat portion of the femur bone that connects the femoral head with the femoral shaft. Femur head: Rounded upper end of the thigh's femur bone. Intertrochanteric area: Area of the femur between the greater trochanter and lesser trochanter, bony prominences located on the upper part of the femur. Subtrochanteric area: Area of the femur from the lesser trochanter to the upper portion of the femur shaft. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of slipped femoral epiphysis; single or multiple pinning or bone graft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs open treatment of a slipped femoral epiphysis using single or multiple pins or by using a graft obtained from another part of the body. Slipped femoral epiphysis is a condition encountered in growing children and characterized by the femoral head, or epiphysis, slipping off the femoral neck due to fracture of the growth plate, called the physis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin extending from the iliac region to the upper end of the thigh. He then dissects down through soft tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He retracts the muscles to reach the joint capsule. He incises the joint capsule and opens the joint to expose the upper end of the femur. He then has adequate exposure of the slipped femoral epiphysis. He makes a separate incision over the ilium bone and obtains the cancellous bone graft from it. He next closes the graft donor site by suturing the skin. He uses this bone graft to repair the defect or fracture in the physis, or growth plate. He may also repair the slipped femoral epiphysis by single or multiple pinning. For that method, he makes an incision over the intertrochanteric area and inserts multiple pins through the femur head and femur neck under separately reportable imaging guidance. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Bone graft: A bone tissue obtained from one bone to fix the defect in another bone. Femoral neck: A flat portion of the femur bone that connects the femoral head with the femoral shaft. Femur head: Rounded upper end of femur bone. Intertrochanteric area: Area of the femur between the greater trochanter and lesser trochanter, bony prominences located on the upper part of the femur. Tips Use 27178 when the provider performs open treatment of the slipped femoral epiphysis by closed manipulation with single or multiple pinning. Use 27179 when the provider performs open treatment of the slipped femoral epiphysis with osteoplasty of the femoral neck. Use 27181 when the provider performs open treatment of the slipped femoral epiphysis by osteotomy and internal fixation. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of slipped femoral epiphysis; closed manipulation with single or multiple pinning

He then creates an incision and uses single or multiple pins to secure the reduced fracture in the growth plate. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Manipulation: Various manual adjustment techniques used to realign bone fragments. short_description: Open treatment of slipped femoral epiphysis; osteoplasty of femoral neck (Heyman type procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs open treatment of a slipped femoral epiphysis by removing a wedge–shaped portion of bone from the neck of the femur to reduce the fracture in the growth plate, restoring the normal alignment of the epiphysis. Slipped femoral epiphysis is a condition encountered in growing children and characterized by the femoral head, or epiphysis, slipping off the femoral neck due to fracture of the growth plate, called the physis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin extending from the iliac region to the upper end of the thigh. He then dissects down through soft tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He retracts the muscles to reach the joint capsule. He incises the joint capsule and opens the joint to expose the upper end of the femur. He then has adequate exposure of the femur neck. He removes a wedge–shaped portion of the femur neck on the inner side. He next uses a pin to rotate the epiphysis to reduce the growth plate fracture. He rejoins the ends of the femur neck at the osteotomy site using a wire or screw. short_description: Open treatment of slipped femoral epiphysis; osteotomy and internal fixation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of a slipped femoral epiphysis by removing a wedge shaped portion of bone from the neck of the femur to reduce a fracture in the growth plate. He also uses internal fixation implants to stabilize the correction in the bone. A slipped femoral epiphysis is a condition encountered in growing children characterized by slippage of the overlying end of the femur, or epiphysis, due to a fracture of the growth plate, or physis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the hip. He dissects down to the epiphysis and femoral neck. He excises a wedge of bone from the anterolateral proximal femur, near the lesser trochanter. He closes the space and internally rotates the distal fragment. He brings the head into a more normal relationship with the acetabulum and femoral shaft. He inserts pins for proper fixation of bone. He uses image intensification for guidance. He irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes all instruments, and closes the wound. He may apply a body cast. Epiphyseal plate: Cartilaginous layer at the end of a long bone responsible for bone growth; also called the growth plate or physis. Epiphysis: End portion of a long bone. Femoral neck: A flat portion of the femur bone that connects the femoral head with femoral shaft. Femur: Thigh bone. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Osteoplasty: Surgical alteration in the bone. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Physis: Another term for epiphyseal plate. Retract: Hold back incisions or edges of a wound with instruments designed to do so without injuring tissue. When the provider performs an open treatment of a slipped femoral epiphysis by closed manipulation with one or more pins, use code, 27178, Open treatment of slipped femoral epiphysis; closed manipulation with single or multiple pinning. When the provider performs an open treatment of a slipped femoral epiphysis by a surgical alteration of the femoral neck, use code 27179, Open treatment of slipped femoral epiphysis; osteoplasty of femoral neck, Heyman type procedure. short_description: Epiphyseal arrest by epiphysiodesis or stapling, greater trochanter of femur
lay_term: The provider implants screws or specialized staples into the epiphyseal area of the greater trochanter of the femur. This causes a temporary pause in the growth of that bone. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, and with tourniquet control applied, the provider incises over the epiphyseal area of the greater trochanter of the femur. The provider may identify the epiphysis by fluoroscopy. The provider deepens the incision to the bone after reflecting the appropriate layers of subcutaneous and fascial tissue and splitting the periosteum. The provider accomplishes the procedure through epiphysiodesis, in which the provider applies screw implants through the trochanter, to the epiphyseal growth plate at approximately 90 degrees and into the femur bone. Alternatively, the provider may insert specialized stapling devices into the growth plate in a similar fashion to halt the growth of the plate. The wound is closed in layers in an aseptic manner after checking for clear implantation of devices. The provider may perform fluoroscopy for confirmation of the implantation. Terminology Aseptic: Free from infection. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Epiphyseal plate: Cartilaginous layer at the end of a long bone responsible for bone growth; also called the growth plate or physis. Epiphysis: Part of a long bone that converts into bone separately from the shaft, such as the end of a long bone. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Femur: Thigh bone. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Periosteum: Membrane covering the surface of a bone. Radius: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the lateral, or outside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the thumb. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Trochanter of femur: Top part of the femur, featuring two bony prominences called the greater and lesser trochanter. Ulna: One of the two bones in the forearm, located on the medial, or inside, aspect of the arm, extending from the elbow to the fifth finger. short_description: Prophylactic treatment (nailing, pinning, plating or wiring) with or without methylmethacrylate, femoral neck and proximal femur
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider treats a defect in the femoral neck and proximal femur using fixation implants like nails, plates, or screws to prevent future issues. He may or may not use methylmethacrylate, a type of bone cement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin just above the defect in the femur bone, dissecting down through the subcutaneous tissue to the bone. He retracts the nerve and muscle tissue in the area. He then uses implants like nails, pins, plates, or wires to fix the defect in the bone and to stabilize the bone. He may or may not use methylmethacrylate, a type of bone cement, to fill the defect to provide extra stability. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Femoral neck: A flat portion of the femur bone that connects the femoral head with the femoral shaft. short_description: Closed treatment of posterior pelvic ring fracture(s), dislocation(s), diastasis or subluxation of the ilium, sacroiliac joint, and/or sacrum, with or without anterior pelvic ring fracture(s) and/or dislocation(s) of the pubic symphysis and/or superior/inferior rami, unilateral or bilateral; without manipulation
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture and/or a complete or partial separation of one or both sides of the posterior (back) side of the pelvic bones, with or without an anterior component, without manipulation. Explanation The provider treats a patient with a fracture (break) of the back (posterior) part of the pelvic ring, which may involve one or both sides (unilateral or bilateral) and include complete or partial separation (dislocation, diastasis, or subluxation) of the upper part of the pelvic bone (ilium), the large triangular bone at the end of the vertebral column (sacrum), or the joint between the two (sacroiliac joint). The injury may or may not include a break in the front (anterior) part of the pelvic ring, separation of the cartilaginous attachment at the bottom of the pelvic ring (pubic symphysis) and/or the upper (superior) and lower (inferior) parts of the flat bar of bone (ramus) that forms the lower part of the pelvic bone (ischium). Treatment does not include manipulation of the fracture, likely because it is not displaced. Treatment may include bed rest; compression, strapping, or casting; or traction. Terminology Diastasis: A separation of two bones that are normally attached to each other without a true joint, such as the pubic symphysis. Ilium: Upper part of the pelvic bone; do not confuse with ileum, part of the small intestine. Inferior pubic ramus: A short flat bar of bone that extends between the pubic bone and the ramus of the ischium. Pelvic ring: A ring of bones that connects the trunk to the legs, also known as the pelvic girdle. Pubic symphysis: A thick cartilaginous "joint" where the two large pelvic bones join in the middle at their lower ends. Sacroiliac joint, or SI joint: Bony union in the pelvis between the sacrum, the bone at the spine's base, and the ilium, the uppermost part of the hip bone. Subluxation: Partial dislocation of a bone. Superior pubic ramus: A flat bar of bone extending from the pubic bone to the wing of the ilium that forms part of the acetabulum. Report percutaneous treatment with 27216. Report open treatment with 27217 and 27218. For a similar procedure but with general anesthesia, sedation or regional anesthesia and manipulation of the fracture, report 27198. This procedure has 0 global day period. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of iliac spine(s), tuberosity avulsion, or iliac wing fracture(s), unilateral, for pelvic bone fracture patterns that do not disrupt the pelvic ring, includes internal fixation, when performed Notes: (To report bilateral procedure, report 27215 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of the iliac spine, tuberosity avulsion, or iliac wing fractures on one side of the pelvis bone. He may use internal fixation like plates or screws to fix the fracture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the site of the pelvic injury. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the pelvis. He then adjusts the bone to reduce, or realign, the fracture. He fixes the reduced fracture bone in place using hardware such as screws, nails, and plates. If there is a fracture of the iliac wing, he places a plate with screws across the fracture to secure the bone fragments. He may also place drains as necessary. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. He may perform an X–ray examination of the pelvis to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Terminology Avulsion: Forcible tearing away of the body part. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Iliac spine: Bony projection of the iliac bone. Iliac wing: Large expanded portion of the ilium bone. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Pelvic ring: A ring of bones that connects the trunk to the legs, also known as the pelvic girdle. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. Retract: Hold back incisions or edges of a wound with instruments designed to do so without injuring tissue. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Unilateral: On a single side; opposite of bilateral, on two sides. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of posterior pelvic bone fracture and/or dislocation, for fracture patterns that disrupt the pelvic ring, unilateral, includes internal fixation, when performed (includes ipsilateral ilium, sacroiliac joint and/or sacrum) Notes: (To report bilateral procedure, report 27218 with modifier 50) (For percutaneous/minimally invasive arthrodesis of the sacroiliac joint without fracture and/or dislocation, use 27279)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of a posterior pelvic bone fracture and or dislocation with fracture patterns that disrupt the pelvic ring on one side of the pelvis. He may use internal fixation like plates and screws to fix the fracture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the site of the pelvic injury. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue just under the skin, protecting the nerves and vessels. He next retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the pelvis. He then manually adjusts the bone to reduce, or realign, the fracture or dislocation, as necessary. He fixes the reduced fracture or dislocated bone in place using implants like a plate and screws to stabilize the fracture. Finally, he places drains and closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. He may perform an X–ray examination of the pelvis to confirm the reduction of the fracture. short_description: Closed treatment of acetabulum (hip socket) fracture(s); with manipulation, with or without skeletal traction
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a fracture of the acetabulum, or hip socket. Treatment includes manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone with or without skin or skeletal traction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the fractured fragment by exerting a pushing or pulling force on the pelvic bone to reduce the fracture or realign the bones. He may apply a skin traction technique such as Buck’s traction which brings together the fractured bone using light weights and counterweights that attach to the skin by way of adhesive tape or bandages to the limb or to a traction boot. He may use skeletal traction such as a tibial pin to stabilize and reinforce the fracture fragments. He uses skeletal traction force to stabilize and reinforce the fracture fragments. Application of traction causes the muscles to act as internal splints that maintain proper alignment of the bones. Skeletal traction uses force via a pin, wire, screw, or clamp that penetrates the bone, and ropes and heavier weights that attach to the implant. This type of traction may last for up to twelve weeks. He may place the patient’s leg in a brace for a period of about four to six weeks. Terminology Acetabulum: The cup shaped socket of the hip joint. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Closed treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, without making a surgical incision, with or without manipulation, and with or without the use of a traction device that applies a force. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper allignment. Skeletal traction: Application of a pulling force on bones to treat skeletal disorders and fractures, keeping the bones aligned and immobilized, while relieving pressure on the muscles and nerves, allowing normal healing of a defect or fracture. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips When the provider performs a closed treatment of an acetabulum fracture without performing manipulation, use code 27220, Closed treatment of acetabulum, or hip socket fracture or fractures; without manipulation. short_description: Open treatment of posterior or anterior acetabular wall fracture, with internal fixation

short_description: Closed treatment of femoral fracture, proximal end, neck; with manipulation, with or without skeletal traction
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a femur neck fracture, or a fracture in the upper end of the femur. Treatment includes manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone. The provider may also use skeletal traction as part of this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the fractured fragment by flexing the patient’s hip and exerting a pushing or pulling force on the hip and upper end of the femur to reduce or realign the fracture. He may also use skeletal traction force to stabilize and reinforce the fracture fragments. Application of skeletal traction causes the muscles to act as internal splints that maintain proper alignment of the bones. For skeletal traction, the provider applies force via a pin, wire, screw, or clamp that penetrates the bone, and ropes and heavier weights that attach to the implant. short_description: Open treatment of femoral fracture, proximal end, neck, internal fixation or prosthetic replacement
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of a femur neck fracture, or a fracture in the upper end of the femur. He uses internal fixation implants such as pins, wires, or screws to fix the fracture. He may also replace the damaged portion of bone with an artificial implant, if necessary. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the fractured bone. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He separates tissue and retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the neck of the femur. He adjusts the bone to reduce the fractured fragments. He fixes the fracture using implants like screws, nail, or wires. If the bone is too severely damaged or broken, the provider removes the fracture fragments and places an artificial implant as a replacement of the bone. short_description: Closed treatment of intertrochanteric, peritrochanteric, or subtrochanteric femoral fracture; with manipulation, with or without skin or skeletal traction
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a femoral fracture between, around, or below the trochanters. Treatment includes manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone with or without skin or skeletal traction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the fractured fragment by exerting a pushing or pulling force on the upper end of the femur to reduce the fracture. He may use skin or skeletal traction such as a tibial pin to stabilize and reinforce the fracture fragments. Application of traction causes the muscles to act as internal splints that maintain proper alignment of the bones. Skeletal traction uses force via a pin, wire, screw, or clamp that penetrates the bone. He places the patient’s leg in a brace for a period of about four to six weeks. He may perform an X–ray examination of the upper end of the femur bone to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Lesser trochanter: A bony prominence on the inner side of neck of femur bone. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Peritrochanteric: Around the trochanters. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper allignment. Subtrochanteric: Below the trochanters. Skeletal traction: Application of a pulling force on bones to treat skeletal disorders and fractures, keeping the bones aligned and immobilized, while relieving pressure on the muscles and nerves, allowing normal healing of a defect or fracture. short_description: Closed treatment of greater trochanteric fracture, without manipulation

Treatment does not include manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone. Explanation The provider examines the patient and confirms the fracture with x–rays. He stabilizes the fracture and advises the patient on ways to manage the pain. The treatment of a nondisplaced, stable fracture is often a period of bed rest, with the possible use of skin traction, and or a spica cast, and the use of crutches for walking, with limitations on weight bearing when the patient is finally mobile. He may perform X–ray examinations of the upper end of the femur bone to confirm the reduction of the fracture.
