short_description: Closed treatment of hip dislocation, traumatic; requiring anesthesia
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a traumatic hip joint dislocation, an abnormal separation of a joint. He performs this procedure using general anesthesia. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reduces the hip joint dislocation. He first performs an X–ray to examine the dislocated joint. He uses one of several techniques to manually adjust the bones by pushing or pulling to bring them to their normal alignment. He stabilizes the pelvis, then gently flexes or extends the hip and knee. He may apply traction to the lower extremity, and gently rotate the thigh internally or externally, to carefully move the femoral head back into its original location within the acetabulum. He may also apply gentle skin traction upon completion of the reduction procedure and or place the hip joint in a brace for a period of four to six weeks. He may perform an X–ray examination of the joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation. Terminology Acetabulum: The cup shaped socket of the hip joint. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Femoral head: Topmost part of the thigh bone. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. Traction: Pulling force. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips According to coding guidelines, codes that specify no anesthesia, i.e., without anesthesia, exclude general anesthesia but can include locals, blocks, and topicals in the surgical package. If a code indicates that anesthesia is required, i.e., requiring anesthesia, the service provided must be over and above a local, meaning a general. short_description: Open treatment of hip dislocation, traumatic, without internal fixation
lay_term: The provider performs an open treatment of a hip joint dislocation, an abnormal separation of a joint, often due to a physical injury or violence. He does not use internal fixation implants like pins, wires, or screws to fix the dislocation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the dislocated hip joint. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the hip joint. He then adjusts the bone to reduce the dislocation without disturbing the cartilage that covers the articular surfaces of the bones that form the joint. He does not fix the dislocation using implants like screws, nails, or wires. He closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. He places the patient’s leg in a brace for a period of four to six weeks. He may perform an X–ray examination of the hip joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation. Terminology Acetabulum: The cup shaped socket of the hip joint. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Femoral head: Topmost part of the thigh bone. Fracture: To break; also as in a broken bone. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper allignment. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. short_description: Treatment of spontaneous hip dislocation (developmental, including congenital or pathological), by abduction, splint or traction; without anesthesia, without manipulation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a developmental, congenital, or pathological hip joint dislocation, or an abnormal separation of a joint. He performs this procedure by performing abduction, or applying a splint or traction without administering general anesthesia to the patient and without performing manual manipulation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider reduces the hip joint dislocation. He first performs an X–ray to examine the dislocated hip joint. He stabilizes the fracture and advises the patient on ways to manage the pain. He places the patient’s hip and leg in a spica cast in a position of abduction to immobilize the hip and maintain the correct position. Alternatively, he may place the patient’s leg in a specially designed splint that exerts a continuous force of traction over the leg for a period of time to reduce the dislocation. For an infant, he may use a device such as a Pavlik harness, an external support apparatus to stabilize the hip, that uses straps that hold an infant’s hips in flexion and abduction. The provider may also use skin traction to treat the dislocation. He applies the traction to the extremity, using longitudinal force on the leg with felt, foam, or a strapping apparatus and a series of weights and pulleys to gently realign the hip. He may use this technique alone or with one of the other methods. The aim of the provider in using these techniques is to apply skin traction to bring the dislocated bone back to their normal alignment. He does not use general anesthesia or manipulation during this procedure. He may perform an X–ray examination of the joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation. Terminology Abduction: Movement of the body part away from the midline of the body. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Flexion: The act of bending a joint or limb in the body. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Pathological: Caused by physical or mental disorders. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper allignment. Splint: A device that supports and immobilizes an injured part of the body. Traction: Pulling force. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. short_description: Open treatment of spontaneous hip dislocation (developmental, including congenital or pathological), replacement of femoral head in acetabulum (including tenotomy, etc)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open treatment of a spontaneous developmental hip dislocation including a congenital or pathological hip joint dislocation, which is an abnormal separation of a joint. He performs this procedure by reducing the femoral head into the acetabulum. He also performs an adductor muscle tenotomy as part of this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider first performs an adductor tenotomy by making an incision over the upper end of the adductor muscle. He then makes an incision in the hip joint capsule. Next, he makes multiple incisions over the labrum surrounding the margin of the acetabulum thereby increasing the size of cavity, which in turn causes the reduction, or the realignment of the femur head into the acetabulum. Once he reduces the hip joint, the provider sutures the joint capsule tightly to provide extra stability to the joint. The provider then reapproximates tendons and sutures them and reattaches the iliac epiphysis to the ilium. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Epiphysis: End portion of a long bone. Femoral head: Topmost part of the thigh bone. Femur shaft: Central cavity or portion of the femur, or the thigh bone. Labrum of the hip: A rim of tissue lining the hip socket, or acetabulum. Margin: Border or outside edge. Pathological: Caused by physical or mental disorders. Reapproximate: Bring together again. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper allignment. short_description: Open treatment of spontaneous hip dislocation (developmental, including congenital or pathological), replacement of femoral head in acetabulum (including tenotomy, etc); with femoral shaft shortening
lay_term: The provider treats a spontaneous dislocation of the hip, a condition present from birth or the result of disease. Through an incision in the hip, he repositions the head of the thigh bone and shortens its shaft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision along the iliac crest, at the top of the pelvic bone, to open the anterior hip joint and expose the hip joint capsule. He separates the abductor muscles from the ilium and the rectus femoris and sartorius muscles from the pelvis. He then makes a second incision in the joint capsule and widens the acetabulum by clearing away the ligamentum teres and the fat. The provider then reduces the hip joint to align it into correct anatomical position. He shortens the shaft of femur. The provider then inserts a plate and screws in the femoral neck to secure the reduction. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Acetabulum: Depression in the hip bone that receives the head of the femur. Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body or a structure. Congenital: Present at birth. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Femoral head: Topmost part of the thigh bone. Femur: Thigh bone. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligamentum teres: Fibrous band at the head of femur responsible for producing movement and maintaining stability at the hip. Pathological: A condition resulting from disease. Rectus femoris muscle: Leg muscles located on the front and sides of the thigh that help to extend or raise the knee. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Sartorius: A long, thin muscle that crosses the front of the thigh and is responsible for cross leg rotation; also called tailor’s muscle. Tenotomy: Surgical incision of a tendon to lengthen it. Tips This code represents a unilateral service, meaning performed on one side of the hip joint. lay_term: The provider uses a minimally invasive percutaneous approach to place one or more stabilization implants into the sacroiliac joint for joint fusion. The procedure takes place under imaging guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider uses a minimally invasive approach to place one or more implants, such as bone allografts or synthetic devices, into the sacroiliac joint for joint fusion. The provider inserts a chisel into the cannula and uses the chisel to remove excess material from the target site. The provider prepares the implant on a special tool and then inserts it in the cannula. The provider deploys the implant in the prepared space. The provider ensures proper positioning. This unilateral procedure includes insertion of one or more implants in the joint. Finally, the provider removes all instruments, stops all bleeding at the surgical site, and closes the wound. short_description: Arthrodesis, sacroiliac joint, percutaneous or minimally invasive (indirect visualization), with image guidance, includes obtaining bone graft when performed, and placement of transfixation device Notes: (For percutaneous arthrodesis of the sacroiliac joint by intra-articular implant[s], use 27278) (For bilateral procedure, report 27279 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes the sacroiliac joint with the help of fixation devices, after gaining access to the joint through the skin. He may also induce artificial bone generation into the joint area with the help of a graft he obtains from the patient. The procedure takes place under image guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the ilioinguinal area, which is the lower outer area of the abdomen. He dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then detaches the abdominal muscles from the ilium to access the sacroiliac joint capsule. Next, he incises the capsule to enter the joint. He then does a thorough debridement of the sacroiliac joint cartilage using a burr. Next, he fuses the painful sacroiliac joint using K wire, staples, plates, or headless screws to restrict the movement causing pain. The provider may also obtain a bone graft from nearby bone and use it to pack the joint being fused. He performs this procedure under image guidance. Finally, he stops all bleeding at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. The provider then places the joint in a pelvic cast for a period of about four to six weeks. Terminology Arthrodesis: Fusion, or permanent joining, of a joint, or point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Burr drill: Surgical drill; also called a high speed burr. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Ilium: Upper part of the pelvic bone; do not confuse with ileum, part of the small intestine. Image guided, imaging guidance: Use of fluoroscopy, ultrasound, or other forms of imaging during surgical procedures. K wire, Kirschner wire: A thin, flexible wire or pin type structure a provider uses to join and stabilize bone fragments. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Sacroiliac, or SI, joint: Bony union in the pelvis between the sacrum, the bone at the spine's base, and the ilium, the uppermost part of the hip bone. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Read Less

short_description: Arthrodesis, symphysis pubis (including obtaining graft)

short_description: Arthrodesis, hip joint (including obtaining graft); with subtrochanteric osteotomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes the hip joint with the help of fixation devices. He induces artificial bone generation in the joint area with the help of a graft he obtains from another part of the patient’s body. He also performs subtrochanteric osteotomy, a surgical procedure that divides the shaft of the femur below the lesser trochanter, which is just below the femur’s neck. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin near the top of the femur over the tip of the greater trochanter. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue to deep fascia, preserving the nerves and veins. He then retracts the muscles to gain access to the hip joint capsule. He then cuts the capsule to enter the joint. He dislocates the femur from the acetabulum and uses a surgical instrument to remove the cartilage from the femoral head and acetabulum. He next brings the femoral head and acetabulum in close proximity and fuses the joint using K wire, powered staples, plates, or headless screws to restrict the movement causing pain. The provider also obtains a cancellous bone graft from nearby bone, usually the iliac crest, and uses the graft material to pack the joint being fused. The provider also divides the shaft of the femur just above the lesser trochanter to correct and align the leg position. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the joint in a cast for a period of four to six weeks. Terminology Acetabulum: A shallow cup shaped depression in the hip bone. Arthrodesis: The surgical immobilization of a joint by fusion of the bones. Autograft: A tissue transferred from one part of the body to another. Cancellous bone graft: A graft consisting of spongy bone that can trigger new bone formation quickly. Femur: Thigh bone. Greater trochanter: A bony protrusion on the outside of the femur, above the lesser trochanter. Lesser trochanter: A bony prominence on the inner side of the neck of the femur bone. short_description: Interpelviabdominal amputation (hindquarter amputation)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider amputates an entire leg along with one outer half of the pelvis on the same side. The provider performs this surgery very rarely, typically for severe trauma, infection, or tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates separate incisions in the front and back of the pelvis and between the thighs. She first ligates the iliac vessels and retracts the nerves. She then divides the iliac wing from the back and disarticulates the symphysis pubis in front. She then removes all major muscles to the leg and pulls the gluteal muscle flap in front for final closure. Finally, after irrigation of the wound with antibiotics, she closes the wound by suturing the flaps and packs the wound with antiseptic gauze. She may leave a temporary drain in place after the surgery to remove the excess fluid. Terminology Amputation: Surgical removal of a complete or partial appendage of the body. Disarticulation: Separation of two bones at their joint. Illiac vessels: Illiac artery and vein. Symphysis pubis: A cartilaginous joint formed in the midline between the two pubis bones of the pelvis. Wing of ilium: Upper expanded portion of the ilium, the uppermost and largest part of the hip bone. Read Less

lay_term: Use 27299 to report a pelvis or hip joint procedure that does not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs a pelvis or hip joint procedure that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises and drains an abscess, bursa, or hematoma that is in the deep structures of the thigh or knee region. He performs the procedure to treat an infection and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the abscess, bursa, or hematoma area around knee region and thigh. The provider carries the incision down through the deep subcutaneous tissues to expose the hematoma or abscess and may, depending upon the size of the lesion, extend the incision, or go down to the level of the bone, if the abscess or hematoma is that deep to fully expose the lesion. He incises the lesion and may use a syringe or catheter to help drain the pus from the abscess, or he may drain the abscess by squeezing the area. If the provider performs drainage for a hematoma, he also removes clotted blood with the help of a sharp object. He then cleans the wound and irrigates it with saline. After cleansing the wound thoroughly, he may place a drain for additional pus drainage, or he simply covers the site with gauze after irrigation with antibiotic. He removes the tube after several days and closes the remainder of the wound if necessary. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled off sac or pocket, caused by infection. Bursa: Fluid filled sac that prevents joints, muscles, and tendons from rubbing together. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Hematoma: A collection of blood or blood clot in the tissues, usually caused by damage to blood vessels. Incision and drainage, or I and D: A surgical procedure in which cysts, abscesses, or other lesions containing infective material are incised, or cut into, and the infective material drained; the procedure typically includes irrigation, or washing out, of the affected part. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Irrigation: A flushing or washout procedure. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Purulent material: Pus. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Tips When the provider incises and drains an abscess or hematoma from the forearm and wrist area, use code 25028, Incision and drainage, forearm and/or wrist; deep abscess or hematoma. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline (For incision and drainage of abscess or hematoma, superficial, see 10040-10160) Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic. Including tibial plateaus.

short_description: Incision, deep, with opening of bone cortex, femur or knee (eg, osteomyelitis or bone abscess)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the bone cortex to relieve pain, pressure, or infection due to such conditions as osteomyelitis or a bone abscess in a localized site on the upper leg or knee area. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the affected site along the femur or knee. He divides the soft tissues and muscles underneath to reach the bone. He then divides the periosteum covering the part of the bone with the infection or abscess and opens the medullary cavity using either a series of drill holes or creating a window in the bone cortex. He then drains the abscess. He may also scrape off the infected bone to reveal healthy bone. He irrigates the wound and rejoins the periosteum. The provider may close the incision in layers or keep it open for subsequent discharge and may perform a secondary closure later. Finally, he may apply a splint to help with healing. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled off sac or pocket, caused by infection. Bone cortex: The outer shell, or cortex, of a bone; also called compact bone. Bursa: Fluid filled sac that prevents joints, muscles, and tendons from rubbing together. Femur: Thigh bone Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Irrigate: Wash out. Localized: Confined to a single or small area. Medullary cavity: The inner chamber of a bone that contains the marrow, the substance that produces new blood cells. Osteomyelitis: Infection in the bone. Periosteum: A dense fibrous connective tissue that wraps the outer surface of the bone except the surface of the bone that goes in to forming joints with other bones. Splint: A device that supports and immobilizes an injured part of the body. Tips When the provider drains a deep abscess, bursa, or hematoma of the thigh or knee region, use 27301, Incision and drainage, deep abscess, bursa, or hematoma, thigh or knee region. Read Less

short_description: Fasciotomy, iliotibial (tenotomy), open Notes: (For combined Ober-Yount fasciotomy, use 27025)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open tenotomy involving surgical division or cutting of the iliotibial band, a thick band of fibers that runs the length of the outside of the hip and thigh. Explanation Tenotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider divides a muscle tendon to correct a deformity caused by congenital or acquired shortening of a muscle. Iliotibial tenotomy treats iliotibial band tightness that causes pain around the knee joint. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the outer part of the knee. He dissects through the subcutaneous tissue and gains adequate exposure of the iliotibial band to be divided. Next, he incises the iliotibial band to lengthen it. This allows the band to return to its normal length, allowing the joint to straighten, thereby correcting the deformity. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Fasciotomy: A surgical cut on the fascia to relieve the pressure. Read Less

short_description: Tenotomy, percutaneous, adductor or hamstring; single tendon (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs percutaneous tenotomy, dividing a single tendon of the adductor or hamstring through a small incision in the skin. Explanation Tenotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider divides a muscle tendon to correct a deformity caused by congenital or acquired shortening of a muscle. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin over the tendon to be released. He then locates the adductor or hamstring muscle tendon and divides a single tendon using a small surgical blade or uses another minimally invasive tool to make incisions in the tendon. This allows the muscle to return to its normal length, allowing the joint to straighten, thereby correcting the deformity. Finally, he closes the incision by suturing the skin together or using adhesive strips. Terminology Adductors: A group of muscles of the thigh that moves the thigh toward the midline of the body. Hamstrings: A group of three muscles which are responsible for bending the knee joint and for backward movement of the thigh. Tips Code 27306’s descriptor indicates it is a separate procedure, meaning that you cannot report this code separately with a related procedure when performed in an anatomically related region through the same skin incision. If the provider performs the 27306 procedure with an unrelated procedure, you may need to append modifier 59 to 27306. Use 27307 when the provider performs percutaneous tenotomy of multiple adductor or hamstring tendons. Read Less

short_description: Tenotomy, percutaneous, adductor or hamstring; multiple tendons
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs percutaneous tenotomy, dividing multiple tendons of the adductor or hamstrings through a small incision in the skin. Explanation Tenotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider divides a muscle tendon to correct a deformity caused by congenital or acquired shortening of a muscle. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin over the tendons to be released. He then locates the adductor or hamstring muscle tendons and divides multiple tendons using a small surgical blade or uses another minimally invasive tool to make incisions in the tendon. This allows the muscle to return to its normal length, allowing the joint to straighten, thereby correcting the deformity. Finally, he closes the incision by suturing skin together or using adhesive strips. Terminology Adductors: A group of muscles of the thigh that moves the thigh toward the midline of the body. Hamstrings: A group of three muscles which are responsible for bending the knee joint and for backward movement of the thigh. Tips Use 27306 when the provider performs percutaneous tenotomy of a single adductor or hamstring tendon. Read Less

Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. short_description: Radical resection of tumor (eg, sarcoma), soft tissue of thigh or knee area; less than 5 cm
lay_term: The provider performs an extensive excision of a tumor, or mass, in the soft tissues in the thigh or knee area, suspected to be malignant, such as a sarcoma. He excises the surrounding tissues along with the mass, with the diameter of the tumor and its margins measuring less than 5 cm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the area of the tumor, raises skin slaps on either side, and isolates the tumor. He identifies any neurovascular structures that may require ligation and or incision, attempting to preserve as many as possible. He excises and removes the tumor en bloc, or as a single specimen, with a margin of tissue around the tumor included with the mass to ensure that no pathology, or diseased tissue, remains. He submits the specimen for pathologic analysis. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Malignant: Cancerous, capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Radical resection: Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Sarcoma: A malignant, or cancerous, tumor of connective tissue origin, that occurs in the bone or soft tissues anywhere in the body. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips Check the documentation carefully for the size and the skin layer depth to which the surgery took place before choosing the code. Compare with 27364, Radical resection of tumor, e.g., sarcoma, soft tissue of thigh or knee area, 5 cm or greater. If two providers work together to perform the surgery, append modifier 62, Two surgeons. For your modifier 62 claim to succeed, both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must use modifier 62. You should work closely with the other provider's staff to ensure that each practice gets its fair share of the reimbursement. Medicare and most other payers reimburse procedures coded with modifier 62 at 125 percent of the regular fee schedule amount. The payer divides this between the two providers reporting the procedure, so each provider receives 62.5 percent of the standard fee. When appending modifier 62, each provider must provide his own documentation describing what portion of the procedure he performed, how much work was involved, and how long the procedure took. Make sure that both providers involved in the surgery identify the other as a co–provider. Be sure to confirm with your payer if they accept modifier 62. The Medicare Provider Fee Schedule indicates for each procedure whether you can use modifier 62. It may also indicate whether additional documentation is necessary to show why a second provider’s participation was needed in the procedure. Read Less

short_description: Arthrotomy, with excision of semilunar cartilage (meniscectomy) knee; medial AND lateral
lay_term: The provider incises the knee joint to remove damaged crescent moon shaped cartilages, or menisci, from both the medial and lateral joint compartments that separate the femur, or thigh bone, from the tibia bone in the lower leg. A torn or frayed meniscus results from a twisting injury to the knee. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the affected knee joint. He dissects down through soft tissue to expose the knee joint capsule. He then incises the capsule to open the joint. He removes torn cartilage from the medial and lateral compartments of the knee. He then smooths the rough surface of the articular, or joint, bone and debrides any torn piece of cartilage left. The provider then irrigates the area and inserts a drain. He checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Arthrotomy: Surgical incision of a joint, the point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Lateral compartment: One of three joint compartments in the knee, formed by the outer knuckle of the femur, or thigh bone, where it attaches to the tibia bone in the lower leg. Medial compartment: One of three joint compartments in the knee, formed by the inner knuckle of the femur, or thigh bone, where it attaches to the tibia bone in the lower leg. Meniscectomy: Surgical excision of a meniscus, one of the cartilages in the knee. Semilunar cartilage: Another name for the medial or lateral meniscus, the crescent moon shaped cartilages in the knee joint. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Tips When the provider performs knee arthrotomy to remove cartilage from either the medial or the lateral compartment, and not both, report 27332. Read Less

short_description: Radical resection of tumor (eg, sarcoma), soft tissue of thigh or knee area; 5 cm or greater Notes: (For radical resection of tumor[s] of cutaneous origin [eg, melanoma], see 11600-11606)
lay_term: You'll use this code for extensive surgical removal of a soft tissue tumor and surrounding tissues of the thigh or knee area, measuring 5cm or more. Explanation The physician makes an incision over the skin above the tumor and dissects the tumor away from the surrounding structures. He then identifies any neurovascular structures that may require ligation and/or incision, attempting to preserve as many as possible. The surgeon excises the tumor along with surrounding tissue and prepares the tumor and surrounding tissue for pathology. He irrigates the patient's wound and closes the incision. Terminology Radical Resection of soft tissue tumor: Surgical removal of the tumor as well as wide margins of healthy tissue. Tips Compare with 27329. Check the documentation carefully for the size and the skin layer depth to which the surgery took place before choosing the code. Your physician may use a surgical assistant during this procedure, and you should check whether your insurers will pay for that. For instance, if you review the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, you'll see that Medicare assigns the "2" indicator to this code in the "ASST SURG" column, which means that "Payment restriction for assistants at surgery does not apply to this procedure. Assistant at surgery may be paid," Medicare says. Therefore, you should bill for a surgical assistant during these procedures if the documentation demonstrates medical necessity for the assist. If the payer accepts the assistant surgeon's charge, you'll append modifier 80 for the assistant's services. Caveat: If a nonphysician practitioner (NPP) serves as an assistant surgeon, you must use modifier AS (Physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist services for assistant at surgery) to Medicare payers to represent the assistant's work. Additional Info This code is revised to replace 'neoplasm' with 'sarcoma.' Sarcomas are malignant tumors originating from tissues such as muscle, fat, blood vessels, nerves, tendons, and synovial (joint lining) tissue whereas neoplasms are simply abnormal masses or other tissue growth that can be benign or cancerous. short_description: Suture of infrapatellar tendon; secondary reconstruction, including fascial or tendon graft
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs secondary repair of the infrapatellar tendon, a tendon of the quadriceps muscle that extends from the patella to the tibia. Secondary repair is a repair performed at least a few days after initial injury or when the primary repair has failed. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision just above the patella, the kneecap, to a few centimeters below the tibial tubercle. He dissects down through soft tissue to expose the patellar tendon. He assesses the pattern of injury and quality of the patellar tendon tissue. He debrides the torn and scarred tissue present around the tendon. He then sutures the torn part of the patellar tendon using nonabsorbable sutures. He might drill holes in the lower end of the patella and pass the sutures through the holes to further strengthen the tendon repair. He may also use a fascial graft from the fascia lata, or he may reinforce the tendon of any surrounding muscle with the patellar tendon to further strengthen the repair. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Fascia lata: A layer of fibrous tissue continuous with the iliotibial band. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs secondary repair of a quadriceps or hamstring muscle tear using a graft he takes from a tendon or the fascia of the patient’s body. He also obtains a tendon or fascial graft from a surrounding muscle and uses the graft to reinforce the repair of the ruptured muscle. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. short_description: Lengthening of hamstring tendon; multiple tendons, 1 leg
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider lengthens multiple tendons of the hamstring muscles from knee to hip in one leg by incising them. Hamstring muscles are a group of three muscles, the biceps femoris, the semitendinosus, and the semimembranosus, which are responsible for bending the knee joint and for backward movement of the thigh. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the back of the thigh just above the popliteal fossa over the target tendons. He dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue and gains adequate exposure of the tendons to be divided. Next, he incises the tendons to lengthen them. Depending on the individual case, the provider may make multiple incisions in the tendon, allowing him to reattach the cut portions in a way that lengthens the tendon. This allows the muscles to return to their normal length, allowing the joint to straighten, thereby correcting the deformity. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Use this code when the provider lengthens multiple hamstring tendons in one leg. Terminology Popliteal fossa: Shallow depression located at the back of the knee joint. Tips Use 27393 when the provider lengthens a single tendon of the hamstring muscle. Use 27395 when the provider lengthens multiple tendons of the hamstring muscles in both legs. See 27390–27392 when the provider performs tenotomy of the hamstring muscle tendon. Code range 27390–27392 represents hamstring tendon tenotomy in which the provider cuts the tendon entirely or partway through allowing the muscle to be stretched while code range 27393–27395 represents hamstring tendon lengthening in which the provider cuts the tendon in two or more places. short_description: Transplant or transfer (with muscle redirection or rerouting), thigh (eg, extensor to flexor); single tendon
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers or transplants a single muscle tendon in the thigh. For example, he may transfer an extensor tendon to the flexor side allowing it to function as a flexor. Explanation Tendon transfer or transplant is a surgical procedure in which the provider moves a tendon from its normal point of attachment to another point of attachment. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the thigh over the tendon to be transferred. He then retracts the incision to the attachment of the tendon and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue. Next, he detaches the muscle tendon from its point of attachment. He then frees the muscle body, protecting the nerve and blood supply. He transfers the tendon to a new point of attachment, changing the line of action of the muscle and allowing the transplanted tendon to perform the opposite function, restoring the lost function. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Use this code when the provider transfers only a single tendon in the thigh. Terminology Extensors: Muscles that increase the angle between two bones. Flexors: Muscles that decrease the angle between two bones. Tips Use 27397 when the provider transplants or transfers multiple tendons in the thigh. Read Less

short_description: Transplant or transfer (with muscle redirection or rerouting), thigh (eg, extensor to flexor); multiple tendons
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers or transplants multiple muscle tendons in the thigh. For example, he may transfer an extensor tendon to the flexor side allowing it to function as a flexor. Explanation Tendon transfer or transplant is a surgical procedure in which the provider moves a tendon from its normal point of attachment to another point of attachment. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the thigh over the tendon to be transferred. He then retracts the incision to the attachment of the tendon and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue. Next, he detaches the muscle tendon from its point of attachment. He then frees the muscle body protecting the nerve and blood supply. He transfers the tendon to a new point of attachment, changing the line of action of the muscle and allowing the transplanted tendon to perform the opposite function, restoring the lost function. He repeats the procedure with other tendons. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Use this code when the provider transfers multiple tendons in the thigh. Terminology Flexors: Muscles that decrease the angle between two bones. Extensors: Muscles that increase the angle between two bones. Tips Use 27396 when the provider transplants or transfers a single tendon in the thigh. Read Less

short_description: Repair, primary, torn ligament and/or capsule, knee; collateral and cruciate ligaments Notes: (For ligament reconstruction, see 27427-27429)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs primary repair of the torn collateral and cruciate ligaments and/or capsule of the knee. Primary repair is one when the provider repairs the torn ligament or capsule immediately after the injury. Collateral ligaments are the ligaments on the inner or outer side of the knee joint. Cruciate ligaments are a pair of ligaments on the underside of the knee arranged like a letter X. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin on the inner or outer side of the knee, depending on the location of the torn capsule or ligament. He dissects down through soft tissue to get access to the torn ligament and/or capsule. He then repairs the torn ligament and/or capsule by suturing the torn part, or he may also fix the torn portion of the ligament or capsule back in place using a screw or K–wire. He repairs both the collateral and cruciate ligaments. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He may place a drain in place if required. Tips Use 27405 when the provider performs primary repair of the torn collateral ligament and/or capsule. Use 27407 when the provider performs primary repair of the torn cruciate ligament and/or capsule. Read Less

short_description: Autologous chondrocyte implantation, knee Notes: (Do not report 27412 in conjunction with 15769, 15771, 15772, 15773, 15774, 27331, 27570) (For harvesting of chondrocytes, use 29870)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transplants cartilage from the patient’s own body into the knee to repair an abnormality or defect that occurs due to damage of the hyaline cartilage. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider takes some of the patient’s own cartilage and stores it in an ex vivo culture to harvest more articular cartilage cells. She inserts an arthroscope to perform a biopsy of the normal cartilage and sends it to pathology for further culture to increase the number of viable cells. The provider performs a knee arthrotomy and excises the injured articular cartilage, debriding the surgical fields. She then places a gel like medium containing cultured chondrocytes into the area of defect and creates a periosteal patch graft, which the provider places around the boundary covering the chondrocytes. Terminology Arthroscopy: Use of an instrument called an arthroscope to view and treat defects in the joint. Autologous chondrocyte implantation or ACI: Implantation of healthy cartilage cells harvested from the patient and grown in the laboratory for transplantation in a subsequent procedure. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of the joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Chondrocyte: Matrix secreting cells that lodge into the cartilage. Debride: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Ex vivo culture: Harvesting and conducting tests on living cells or tissues. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Hyaline cartilage: Semi opaque bluish white cartilage in joints. Periosteum: Membrane covering the surface of a bone. Tips This code represents a unilateral service, meaning it is performed on one knee. Append modifier 50 or the RT and LT modifiers, depending on payer preference, if the provider performs the procedure on both knees. Use 29870, Arthroscopy, knee, diagnostic, with or without synovial biopsy, separate procedure, if the provider harvests chondrocytes. Read Less

lay_term: The provider uses an open approach to directly access the knee joint. She places an allograft to repair an osteochondral defect. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider applies a tourniquet to the leg she will operate on. The provider makes an incision into the knee joint to visualize the osteochondral defect, an area of joint damage affecting the cartilage and the bone under that cartilage. She debrides, measures, and marks the lesion. To prepare the site for graft implant, she may use a dowel or use more manual methods based on the shape of the lesion. She then carefully prepares the allograft so it is in the appropriate shape. She places the allograft and fixes it in place. She bends the knee and tests range of motion to confirm proper placement. She then closes the operative wound. Terminology Allograft: Graft taken from a person other than the recipient patient, such as from a tissue bank. Osteochondral: Relating to or made of bone and cartilage. Tips Code 27415 is specific to surgery requiring an open incision. If the provider performs an arthroscopic procedure, see 29867. Code 27415 has an MUE of 1 so any payer that follows Medicare guidelines will reimburse the code only once, regardless of how many separate lesions are addressed. Under those circumstances, append modifier 22 to reflect the increased complexity associated with repairing more than one lesion. If the payer does not follow Medicare guidelines, or if you are uncertain, contact the payer to determine its guidelines for the code. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. short_description: Osteochondral autograft(s), knee, open (eg, mosaicplasty) (includes harvesting of autograft[s]) Notes: (Do not report 27416 in conjunction with 27415, 29870, 29871, 29875, 29884 when performed at the same session and/or 29874, 29877, 29879, 29885-29887 when performed in the same compartment) (For arthroscopic osteochondral autograft of knee, use 29866) (For osteochondral xenograft scaffold, use 0737T)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider harvests, or obtains, small circular bone grafts from a non–weight bearing area of the joint that has a cartilage covering. He then transfers them to another area in the body to repair the damaged articular cartilage. This procedure is also known as mosaicplasty. The provider most commonly obtains grafts from non–weight bearing areas of femoral condyles. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision just parallel to the patellar tendon. He then dissects down through soft tissue and opens the joint capsule to reach the femoral condyles. He next incises the cartilage in the non–weight bearing area of the condyles and cuts bone grafts with overlying cartilage, which are circular in shape and are 4–8 mm in diameter. He then makes an incision over the area to be repaired using these grafts. He exposes the damaged cartilage surface and fixes it using multiple grafts obtained from the donor site. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Autograft: A tissue transferred from one part of the body to another. Bone graft: Bone tissue taken from one bone of the body to repair the defect in another bone. Cartilage: Smooth tissue that covers the end of the bone in a joint. Femoral condyles: Two projections on the lower end of the femur, which is the thigh bone. Patellar tendon: Central portion of tendon of the quadriceps muscle connecting the patella, which is the knee cap, to the tibia, which is the shin bone. Read Less

short_description: Anterior tibial tubercleplasty (eg, Maquet type procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider moves the tibial tubercle up from the bone and brings the tubercle forward to bring the knee cap, or patella, forward. The tibial tuberosity is a bony prominence in the shin bone below the knee cap where the patellar tendon inserts. The provider performs this procedure to reduce load on the patellofemoral joint to treat knee cap pain that occurs without arthritis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin extending from the outer side of the patella to 5–6 cm below the tibial tuberosity. He then dissects through soft tissue to expose the patellar tendon. He next elevates the periosteum, the outer covering of the bone, on the inner and outer sides of the shin bone to expose the tibial tuberosity. He cuts the bone by drilling multiple holes and using a saw. He elevates a bone block, which consists of the tibial tuberosity bone fragment along with the patellar tendon insertion, with the upper end projecting forward while the lower end remains attached to the shin bone. He ensures that the tibial tubercle is intact. He may use screws or nails to secure the bone block. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Patellofemoral joint: A joint between the patella, which is the knee cap, and the thigh's femur bone. Tibial tubercle: A bony prominence in the shin bone below the knee cap where the patellar tendon inserts. Read Less

short_description: Reconstruction of dislocating patella; (eg, Hauser type procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers the entire patellar tendon insertion as a bone block to treat a dislocating patella, a condition in which the patella, the knee cap, slips out of its normal position and causes pain and swelling. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to change the placement of the patellar tendon, which holds the knee cap in place. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the knee joint just above the patella on the inner side, extending the incision downward to the tibial tuberosity, a bony prominence in the shin bone below the knee cap. He then dissects down through soft tissue to gain access to the patellar tendon. The provider then cuts the tibial tuberosity along with the attached patellar tendon, which comprises the bone block, and moves the block toward the inner aspect of the tibia. He sutures it with the help of staples or a screw. This tightens the patellar tendon and improves the stability of the knee. He also changes the point of attachment of the vastus medialis muscle that originally inserted on the tibial tuberosity. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He may place a drain if required. This procedure is also known as a tibial tuberosity transfer or Hauser type procedure. Terminology Bone block: Tibial tuberosity along with the attached patellar tendon. Tips Use 27422 when the provider performs reconstruction of a dislocating patella with extensor realignment and/or muscle advancement or release. Use 27424 when the provider performs reconstruction of a dislocating patella with patellectomy. Read Less
