short_description: Reconstruction of dislocating patella; with extensor realignment and/or muscle advancement or release (eg, Campbell, Goldwaite type procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider transfers the entire patellar tendon insertion as a bone block to treat a dislocating patella, a condition in which the patella, the knee cap, slips out of its normal position and causes pain and swelling. He also performs realignment of the extensor muscles along with muscle transfer or release to improve the knee joint stability. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to change the placement of the patellar tendon, which holds the knee cap in place. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the knee joint just above the patella on the inner side, extending the incision downward to the tibial tuberosity, a bony prominence in the shin bone below the knee cap. He then dissects down through soft tissue to gain access to the patellar tendon. The provider then cuts the tibial tuberosity along with the attached patellar tendon, which comprises the bone block, and moves the block toward the inner aspect of the tibia. He sutures it with the help of staples or a screw. This tightens the patellar tendon and improves the stability of the knee. He then realigns and incises the extensor muscles. He pulls the vastus medialis muscle on the outer side of the knee and repositions it to cross the patella to provide stability. He may release the vastus lateralis muscle, creating a pull on the patella, which he divides or cuts to release the tightness. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He may place a drain if required. Terminology Bone block: Tibial tuberosity along with the attached patellar tendon. Campbell procedure: The provider frees the strip of fascia on the inner side of the knee from the lower end; which he then pulls to the outer side of the knee through the quadriceps tendon and back on itself to act as a sling; he then attaches it on the inner side to provide stability to the patella. Goldwaite procedure: The provider splits the patellar tendon upside down; he then pulls the outer half under the inner half and attaches it to the tibia, pulling the patella over to the medial side. Knee Extensors: Muscles in the front of the thigh that extend the knee joint. Tips Use 27420 when the provider performs reconstruction of a dislocating patella. short_description: Reconstruction of dislocating patella; with patellectomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes the patella to treat a dislocating patella, a condition in which the patella, the knee cap, slips out of its normal position and causes pain and swelling. short_description: Lateral retinacular release, open Notes: (For arthroscopic lateral release, use 29873)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises or divides the tight lateral retinaculum, a band of fibrous tissue on the outer side of the knee that supports the patella in its position against the thigh's femur bone beneath it. The provider most commonly performs this procedure to treat patellar subluxation or partial dislocation. Explanation The lateral retinaculum is a band of fibrous tissue on the outer side of the knee that may become tight, causing the patella, or knee cap, to tilt on one side. This position triggers pain in the front of the knee. The goal of this procedure is to cut the lateral retinaculum along its length to reduce the tightness and to relieve the pain. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin on the outer side of the knee cap. He dissects down through soft tissue to expose the fibrous bands that cover the patella on the outer side. He next cuts the fibrous tissue along its length, thereby reducing the excessive outward pull on the patella. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Subluxation: Partial dislocation of the bone. Read Less

short_description: Quadricepsplasty (eg, Bennett or Thompson type)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a surgical procedure on the quadriceps femoris muscle to release adhesions and improve mobility. The aim is to improve the range of the bending motion at the knee joint. Quadriceps femoris is a large muscle group on the front of the thigh and includes four muscles: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a vertical midline incision in the mid thigh extending to the level of the knee joint. He may extend the incision upward if there is extensive scarring of the vastus intermedius. He dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue layer just under the skin and retracts the tissue flaps. He dissects through the junction of the vastus lateralis and the vastus medialis to identify the rectus femoris. He next incises the tight, scarred rectus femoris to divide and lengthen it. He next checks for any fibrotic binding of the vastus intermedius to the deep surface of the rectus femoris and removes such bindings. He expands the incision to the sides of the patella, the knee cap, and breaks the adhesions attaching the undersurface of the patella to the femur. He manipulates the joint to ensure that a full range of bending motion is possible. He then achieves hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Adhesions or scarring: Bands of fibrous tissue that bind two organs or tissues together. Bennett quadricepsplasty: A procedure aimed at lengthening the entire quadriceps muscle with the drawback of loss of active knee extension, or straightening. Fibrotic: Formation of excessive fibrous connective tissue in an organ or tissue. Thompson quadricepsplasty: A procedure based principally on isolating the rectus femoris completely from the vasti and releasing the muscle in such a manner that it takes over the action of knee extension, or straightening. short_description: Arthroplasty, knee, tibial plateau; with debridement and partial synovectomy

short_description: Arthroplasty, knee, condyle and plateau; medial OR lateral compartment
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider reconstructs the diseased or damaged medial or lateral compartment of the knee along with the femoral condyles and tibial plateaus to relieve pain and improve the patient’s gait. He might also excise the femoral condyles and tibial plateaus. The provider then drills holes to insert the prosthesis, fixing it with screws or gum. The prosthesis can either be cemented or noncemented. He flushes the site with sterile saline, assures hemostasis, and closes the incision with sutures. Medial: On the inner side. Meniscus: Semi circular structure in the knee joint that provides smooth knee movement. Patella: Knee cap. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part. Tibia: Longer of the two bones of the lower leg; the fibula is the outermost, the tibia is the innermost. Tips See codes 27437, Arthroplasty of patella without prosthesis, to 27447, Arthroplasty of knee condyles and plateau, medial and lateral compartments, with or without patella resurfacing, to review the full range of codes that apply when the provider performs knee arthroplasty. This code represents a unilateral service, meaning it is performed on one knee. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a portion of the tibia bone near the knee and a portion of the fibula bone to assist with function and correcting deformities of the leg. The procedure takes place before the patient’s bones stop growing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the soft tissues to gain access to the upper tibia, below the growth plate. He then cuts a portion of bone from the upper tibia, which is the shinbone. The procedure also includes excision or osteotomy of the fibula, the lower leg bone running alongside the tibia. This allows the tibia and femur, which is the thigh bone, to bend away from damaged cartilage. The provider also commonly carries out this procedure for the correction of deformities. In a typical procedure, he may insert guide pins through the bone to assist with removing a wedge of bone by bone saw. The provider brings the bone ends together in a more anatomically correct line. Again, the procedure includes excision or osteotomy of the fibula. The provider may use either a plate or staples to make sure the bone ends remain in place for healing. He closes the incisions and places the leg in a cast. Terminology Epiphyseal closure: End of growth of bones indicates epiphyseal closure. Epiphyseal plates: Growth plates. Epiphysis: Part of a long bone that converts into bone separately from the shaft, such as the end of a long bone. Osteotomy: Cutting a bone surgically to shorten, lengthen, or change its alignment. short_description: Osteotomy, proximal tibia, including fibular excision or osteotomy (includes correction of genu varus [bowleg] or genu valgus [knock-knee]); after epiphyseal closure Notes: (To report bilateral procedure, report 27457 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes a portion of the tibia bone near the knee and a portion of the fibula bone to assist with function and correcting deformities of the leg. Typically, the provider’s aim is to shift the patient’s body weight from a damaged side of the knee to the other side of the knee, where the cartilage is still healthy. The procedure takes place after the patient’s bones stop growing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the soft tissues to gain access to the upper tibia. He then cuts a portion of bone from the upper tibia, which is the shinbone. The procedure also includes excision or osteotomy of the fibula, the lower leg bone running alongside the tibia. The procedure helps to remove any load from damaged cartilage and bone. The provider brings the cut edges of bone together and secures them such as with a staple to make sure the bone ends remain in place for healing. The provider then repairs the incision with sutures or staples. He places the leg in a cast. Terminology Epiphyseal closure: End of growth of bones indicates epiphyseal closure. Epiphyseal plates: Growth plates. Epiphysis: Part of a long bone that converts into bone separately from the shaft, such as the end of a long bone. Osteotomy: Cutting a bone surgically to shorten, lengthen, or change its alignment. Read Less

short_description: Osteoplasty, femur; shortening (excluding 64876)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically performs shortening of the femur, which is the thigh bone,to treat discrepancy of leg length in a patient or to treat a patient whose thigh bone has not healed in its proper alignment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider assesses the location for the osteotomy. The provider then makes an incision over the greater trochanter, splits the gluteus medius muscle, and identifies the pyriformis fascia, which is a sheath covering the pyriformis muscle present over the pelvis. The provider introduces a wire into the proximal femur, which is the part of the thigh bone near the hip. The provider passes a long ball–tip wire down the femur and then performs the osteotomy using a blade. After the osteotomy is complete, the provider splits the middle segment of the bone with an intramedullary cutting tool. After splitting the femur from front to back, the provider then shortens it, passing an appropriate sized intramedullary nail over the wire to secure fixation. Then the provider places a screw through the nail to make sure the bone ends remain approximated for healing. The provider closes the wounds in layers. Terminology Femur: Thigh bone. Gluteus medius muscle: Thick muscle present on the periphery of the pelvis. Greater trochanter: Large and irregular eminence of the femur bone at the hip area. Intramedullary: Present with medulla or cavity of a bone. Intramedullary nail: Metal rod which the provider passes through a long bone during a procedure; used to treat fractures. Osteoplasty: Surgical bone repair. Tips Code +64876 is an add–on code for shortening of an extremity bone performed with nerve suture; that’s why the definition of 27465 excludes +64876. Read Less

short_description: Osteoplasty, femur; lengthening
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a surgery to lengthen the femur bone, usually by a technique known as osteodistraction. In this technique, the provider moves the two segments of a bone slowly apart in such a way that new bone fills in the gap. Explanation The provider most commonly performs this procedure to lengthen the bone in cases of congenital shortening of the femur. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes drill holes above and below the site of the planned femur incision. The provider inserts screws that will be used as part of a device to gradually move the bone ends farther apart over time. The provider then makes an incision in the skin over the femur bone to be lengthened. The provider dissects through the subcutaneous tissue just below the skin and farther down, incising the periosteum parallel to the skin incision, protecting the vascular and nerve tissue. Next, the provider cuts the bone into proximal and distal segments. The provider applied additional components of the osteodistraction device. Finally, the provider repairs the soft tissue and closes the wound by suturing the skin. Later on at a different encounter, the provider may apply gradual traction across the femur to lengthen the bone using the screws. After 2–3 months, new bone develops in the gap and the provider removes the external fixator device. This process of lengthening bone is also known as distraction osteogenesis. Terminology Femur: The thigh bone. Osteogenesis: The process of laying down new bone material by cells called osteoblasts. Osteoplasty: Surgical repair of a bone. Periosteum: Outer covering of the bone. Traction: Act of drawing or pulling. Tips Use 27465 when the provider performs osteoplasty for femur shortening. Read Less

short_description: Repair, nonunion or malunion, femur, distal to head and neck; without graft (eg, compression technique)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs the nonunion or malunion of a femur fracture below the femur head and neck. She does not use a graft for this procedure. She next removes any previous implant that may be present at the fracture site. She assesses the site of malunion or nonunion and uses a surgical instrument to restore the correct alignment of the bone segments. She then uses a nongraft method, such as use of a compression plate, to fix the bone segments in place before tightening them in place with screws. short_description: Arrest, epiphyseal, any method (eg, epiphysiodesis); distal femur
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider partially or totally destroys a part of the epiphysis, known as the growth plate, at the lower end of the femur. The aim is to slow the growth of a normal leg to allow a shorter leg to grow to a matching length. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates an incision at the lower end of the femur around the knee joint. She then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, just under the skin. She then retracts the muscles and exposes the growth plate at the lower end of the femur. She first elevates the periosteum, the outer covering of the bone. Next, she uses an osteotome, a serrated surgical instrument to partially or totally excise the growth plate. Then she obtains a bone graft from the femur or iliac bones, which is a separately reportable procedure. She uses this bone graft to fill the defect she creates by the removal of the growth plate. She then sutures back the periosteum and obtains hemostasis at the surgical site. Finally, she closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. short_description: Arrest, epiphyseal, any method (eg, epiphysiodesis); tibia and fibula, proximal
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider partially or totally destroys the part of the epiphysis, known as the growth plate, at the upper end of the tibia and fibula. The aim is to slow the growth of a normal leg to allow a shorter leg to grow to a matching length. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the upper end of the tibia and fibula around the knee joint. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, just under the skin. He then retracts the muscles and exposes the growth plate at the upper end of the tibia and fibula. He first elevates the periosteum, the outer covering of the bone. Next, he uses an osteotome, a serrated surgical instrument, to partially or totally excise the growth plate from both the bones. He then obtains a bone graft from the femur or iliac bones, in a separately reportable procedure. He uses this bone graft to fill the defect he creates by the removal of the growth plate. He then sutures back the periosteum and obtains hemostasis at the surgical site. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Fibula: The outer, usually smaller bone, of the two bones of the lower leg between the knee and the ankle. Graft: A tissue transferred from one part of the body to other. Hemostasis: Stoppage of bleeding. Iliac: The upper largest part of the pelvis bone. Tibia: The inner, usually larger bone, of the two bones of the lower leg between the knee and the ankle; also known as the shin bone. short_description: Arrest, epiphyseal, any method (eg, epiphysiodesis); combined distal femur, proximal tibia and fibula
lay_term: To stop growth of the leg bones, the provider uses a technique such as implanting screws into the epiphyseal area near the knee. Explanation With the patient under anesthesia, prepped, and positioned, the provider makes an incision over the epiphyseal area of the femur, tibia, and fibula near the knee area. The provider may use fluoroscopy, or live X–ray, to identify the epiphysis. The provider deepens the incision to the bone after reflecting (bending back) the appropriate layers of subcutaneous and fascial tissue and reaching the periosteum (membrane covering the bone). The provider may accomplish epiphyseal arrest through epiphysiodesis, in which screws are implanted onto the epiphyseal growth plate. Alternatively, the provider may insert specialized stapling devices into the growth plate in a similar fashion. He performs this service for the femur, tibia, and fibula. The wound is closed in layers in an aseptic manner after the provider checks for successful implantation of devices. short_description: Arrest, hemiepiphyseal, distal femur or proximal tibia or fibula (eg, genu varus or valgus)
lay_term: To stop growth of a leg bone, the provider uses a technique such as stapling or placing a plate in the epiphyseal area near the knee. The procedure may help conditions such as genu varus, in which legs curve outward at the knee, or genu valgus, in which legs curve inward at the knee. Explanation With the patient under general anesthesia and with tourniquet control applied, the provider locates the growth plate, such as by image intensifier. The provider makes an incision in the knee area and performs dissection to reach the target bone. He takes care to avoid injury to nerves. When he reaches the target bone area, the provider places screws or screw–fixated plates across half of the growth plate to stop growth in that part of the bone. The provider ensures no soft tissue is stuck under the plates/screws. He uses imaging to confirm placement. The provider stops use of the tourniquet, achieves hemostasis, and may inject pain medication into the wound. He closes the wound in layers and applies a dressing. short_description: Revision of total knee arthroplasty, with or without allograft; 1 component
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs revision arthroplasty of any one component of the knee joint. He may or may not use an allograft to perform this procedure. Revision arthroplasty is a procedure in which the provider removes a previously implanted artificial knee joint component, or prosthesis, and replaces it with a new prosthesis. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to remove a loose or damaged prosthesis before it does irreversible harm to the joint and replace the old prosthesis with a new one. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider exposes the knee joint through the previous skin incision. He first moves the patella, or kneecap, outward and removes the synovium to expose and visualize the joint. He then removes any one of the tibial or femoral components. He first removes the granulation tissue that might have accumulated over the components. He then, using a surgical instrument, removes the cement covering the tibial or femoral component and dislodges the tibial or femoral component. He then removes excess cement that might be present over the site. He next incises the bone to prepare it for the new prosthesis. He may also use an allograft to fix the new prosthesis in place. He then uses cement to secure the new component properly. He obtains hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the tissue in layers. He may also leave a drain in place. Terminology Allograft: Transfer of tissue from one part of the body to another part. Femur: The thigh bone. short_description: Removal of prosthesis, including total knee prosthesis, methylmethacrylate with or without insertion of spacer, knee
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes the total knee prosthesis by breaking the methylmethacrylate, a type of bone cement. He may or may not insert a spacer in the vacant space. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to remove a loose or damaged prosthesis before it does irreversible harm to the joint. Providers often perform this procedure for patients with an infection or who are otherwise not appropriate candidates for current placement of a new prosthesis. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin on the previous incision line. He first moves the patella outward and removes the synovium to expose and visualize the joint. He then exposes the prosthesis to be removed. He breaks the methylmethacrylate cement to dislodge or remove the prosthesis from the tibia or femur. He uses a surgical instrument to remove the cement from the border of the implant. He then may place a spacer between the tibia and femur. This spacer prevents the shortening of the extremity, and the spacer stays in place until the patient has a new prosthesis implanted at a later date. A typical procedure involves shaping bone cement to fit in the space between the tibia and femur. Finally, the provider irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution and closes the wound in layers. He may leave a drain in place if required. Terminology Femur: The thigh bone. Patella: Knee cap. Prosthesis: Artificial substitute for a missing part of the body. Synovium: A thin membrane that lines the joint. Tibia: The shin bone. Read Less

short_description: Decompression fasciotomy, thigh and/or knee, 1 compartment (flexor or extensor or adductor)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts into the fascia of any one compartment in the thigh and/or knee to relieve pressure and increase blood flow. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to treat pressure such as that caused by compartment syndrome of the thigh, a painful condition that involves increased pressure in a muscle compartment leading to muscle and nerve damage with reduction of blood flow. The syndrome is characterized by symptoms like decreased sensation, numbness, weakness, and severe pain. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin overlying the affected area and gets access to the fascia lying above the targeted muscle compartment affected by compartment syndrome. There are three compartments in the thigh: flexor, adductor, and extensor. The flexor compartment of the thigh lies in the front of the thigh. The extensor compartment lies at the back of the thigh, and the adductor compartment lies on the inner side of the thigh. She cuts through the fascia, thereby reducing the pressure on the neurovascular structures underneath the fascia. This restores the restricted blood supply and relieves the patient from symptoms. Finally, the provider may leave the wound open at the end of the session or close the wound by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Terminology Compartment: An anatomical segment that involves muscles, nerves, and vessels confined by a fascia membrane. Debridement: Removal of dead or damaged tissue. Fascia: A fibrous tissue sheet surrounding the body under the skin and enclosing muscles. Fasciotomy: Incision through fascia. Use 27498 when the provider performs decompression fasciotomy of multiple compartments in the thigh and/or knee without debridement. short_description: Decompression fasciotomy, thigh and/or knee, multiple compartments; with debridement of nonviable muscle and/or nerve
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts into the fascia of multiple compartments in the thigh and/or knee to relieve pressure and increase blood flow. He also removes the dead or damaged tissue. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to treat pressure such as that caused by compartment syndrome of the thigh, a painful condition that involves increased pressure in a muscle compartment leading to muscle and nerve damage with reduction of blood flow. The syndrome is characterized by symptoms like decreased sensation, numbness, weakness, and severe pain. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin overlying the affected area of each compartment and gets access to the fascia lying above each muscle compartment affected by compartment syndrome. There are three compartments in the thigh: flexor, adductor, and extensor. The flexor compartment of the thigh lies in the front of the thigh. The extensor compartment lies at the back of the thigh, and the adductor compartment lies on the inner side of the thigh. He cuts through the fascia and debrides all the damaged, nonviable muscle and/or nerve tissue, thereby reducing the pressure on the neurovascular structures underneath the fascia. This restores the restricted blood supply and relieves the patient from symptoms. Finally, the provider may leave the wounds open at the end of the session or close the wounds by suturing the soft tissues in layers. Terminology Compartment: An anatomical segment that involves muscles, nerves, and vessels confined by a fascia membrane. Debridement: Removal of dead or damaged tissue. Fascia: A fibrous tissue sheet surrounding the body under the skin and enclosing muscles. Fasciotomy: Incision through fascia. Nonviable: Not able to live or develop independently. Tips Use 27496 when the provider performs decompression fasciotomy in one compartment of the thigh and/or knee without debridement. Use 27497 when the provider performs decompression fasciotomy in one compartment of the thigh with debridement of nonviable muscle and/or nerve tissue. Use 27498 when the provider performs decompression fasciotomy of multiple compartments in the thigh and/or knee without debridement. Read Less

short_description: Closed treatment of supracondylar or transcondylar femoral fracture with or without intercondylar extension, with manipulation, with or without skin or skeletal traction
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed reduction of a supracondylar fracture of the femur with manipulation to repair the broken bone and set it for healing. The major goal for applying traction is to achieve stability and correct alignment of the bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider initiates the procedure by using radiographic images to confirm the exact site of the fracture in the supracondylar region. He manipulates the fracture site using either skeletal traction or skin traction. For skeletal traction, the provider places a pin closer to the head of the tibia. For skin traction, the provider places straps around the thigh up to the foot. In both types of traction, the provider applies weight, which he gradually reduces. After removing the traction, the provider applies a cast to stabilize the fracture. Terminology Condyle: Rounded projection on the lower end of a bone, usually associated with a joint connecting with another bone. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Intercondylar extension: A fracture that extends into the joint, between the condyles. Manipulation: Type of treatment in which the provider moves the bones or muscles using his hands. Cast: A stiff or hard bandage to hold the broken bone into position. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Supracondylar fracture: Break in the bone just above the condyle. Traction device: Instrumentation that applies a force. Transcondylar: In between the condyles. short_description: Open treatment of femoral shaft fracture, with or without external fixation, with insertion of intramedullary implant, with or without cerclage and/or locking screws
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open reduction of the femoral shaft fracture with insertion of intramedullary fixation, with or without external fixation. The main goal of the procedure is to return the bones to normal alignment to ensure healthy, complete healing. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision at the site of fracture. He manually moves the bones to align the fragments in the correct anatomical position. The provider then drills hole through the center of the intramedullary canal. Then, using fluoroscopy guidance, he inserts nails into the canal to stabilize the fracture area. Along with the nails, the provider threads cerclage wires around the shaft to achieve a better reduction. Sometimes, if the fracture is complex, the provider might fix the nails with screws at the end of the bone for further improving the stability. Following this, he applies traction to hold the bone in correct anatomical alignment. Terminology Cerclage wires: Surgical wires which the providers use to hold the fractured fragments close to each other. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Epiphysis: End portion of a long bone. External fixation or ex fix: Type of skeletal traction, also called an external fixator or ex fix that enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for invasive procedures. Femur: Thigh bone. Femoral shaft: Body of femur. Fluoroscopy: Fluoroscopy is a live X–ray where the X–ray image appears on a fluorescent screen television monitor; providers often use fluoroscopy to view body structures while performing procedures. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Intramedullary: Center hollow part of the bone. Intercondylar extension: A fracture that extends into the joint, between the condyles. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Open reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy through a surgical incision; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Supracondylar fracture: Fracture at the lower end of the humerus. Traction: Pulling force. Tips If the provider performs an open reduction of the femoral shaft fracture achieving fixation with plates and screws, use 27507, Open treatment of femoral shaft fracture with plate/ screws, with or without cerclage. If the provider performs an open reduction of a supracondylar fracture with or without intercondylar extension, use 27511, Open treatment of femoral supracondylar or transcondylar fracture without intercondylar extension, includes internal fixation, when performed. If the provider performs an open reduction of a supracondylar fracture with intercondylar extension and internal fixation, use 27513, Open treatment of femoral supracondylar or transcondylar fracture with intercondylar extension, includes internal fixation, when performed. If the provider performs an open reduction of the distal end of a femoral fracture along with internal fixation, use 27514, Open treatment of femoral fracture, distal end, medial or lateral condyle, includes internal fixation, when performed. If the provider performs an open reduction of a distal epiphyseal separation along with internal fixation, use 27519, Open treatment of distal femoral epiphyseal separation, includes internal fixation, when performed. If the provider performs closed treatment of a femoral shaft fracture, see codes 27500, Closed treatment of femoral shaft fracture without manipulation to 27503, Closed treatment of supracondylar femoral shaft fracture with or without intercondylar extension or traction. You should report an appropriate code for debridement, if the provider performs debridement in the case of an open complex fracture. Read Less

guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline (For arthroscopic treatment of intercondylar spine[s] and tuberosity fracture[s] of the knee, see 29850, 29851) (For arthroscopic treatment of tibial fracture, see 29855, 29856) Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic. Including tibial plateaus.

short_description: Closed treatment of femoral fracture, distal end, medial or lateral condyle, with manipulation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider manipulates fracture fragments and performs closed reduction of a fracture at the distal end of the femur (thigh bone) that involves the medial or lateral condyles. The goal of the procedure is to ensure a correct alignment of the medial and lateral condyles of the femur along with stability. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider obtains X–rays to locate the exact site of the fracture. He then manually reduces the fracture to align the bone fragments in the normal anatomical position. The provider then applies skeletal traction, in which the provider attaches weight at the distal end of tibia, gradually reducing it to maintain stability. Terminology Closed treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, without making a surgical incision, with or without manipulation, and with or without the use of a traction device that applies a force. Condyle: A rounded, knoblike projection at the end of a bone, typically where it meets or articulates with another bone at a joint. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure's point of attachment. Lateral: Furthest to the side from the middle of the body; on or toward the side of a structure or body. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body; toward the middle or inner aspect of a structure or body. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically refers to the manipulation of fractures, dislocations, or hernias; can be open (through a surgical incision) or closed (without an incision). Skeletal traction: Application of a pulling force on bones to treat skeletal disorders and fractures, keeping the bones aligned and immobilized, while relieving pressure on the muscles and nerves, allowing normal healing of a defect or fracture. Tips If the provider performs a closed treatment of a femoral shaft fracture, see codes 27500, Closed treatment of femoral shaft fracture without manipulation to 27503, Closed treatment of supracondylar femoral shaft fracture with or without intercondylar extension or traction. If the provider performs a closed reduction of the distal end of the femur fracture that includes the condyles, use 27510, Closed treatment of femoral fracture, distal end, medial or lateral condyle, with manipulation. When reporting the global method of fracture care, an EM service may also be reported. Documentation must support a decision for surgery, modifier 57, and or a separate identifiable service, modifier 25, Significant, separately identifiable E/M service by the same physician on the same day of the procedure or other service. With either method, do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. CMS has approximately 50 Q HCPCS codes that address supply issues with casting, splinting applications. The HCPCS level–II manual offers A codes. CPT® contains CPT® code 99070, Supplies and materials, except spectacles, provided by the physician over and above those usually included with the office visit or other services rendered, list drugs, trays, supplies, or materials provided. short_description: Open treatment of femoral supracondylar or transcondylar fracture with intercondylar extension, includes internal fixation, when performed
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open reduction of a fracture of the femur (thigh bone) that extends above or across the condyle and into the space between the condyles, which may require the use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and/or wires to stabilize the fracture. The goal of the procedure is to ensure correct alignment of the bones to promote early healing of the fracture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the medial and lateral condyles of the femur. He manually reduces the fracture to its correct anatomical position. The provider may insert internal fixation devices, such as screws and plates, into the condylar fragments to immobilize the fracture, thereby achieving stabilization. Following this, he applies traction at the site to maintain the reduction. The provider ensures hemostasis and closes the incision in layers with sutures. Terminology Cerclage wires: Surgical wires which the providers use to encircle fracture fragments and hold them together. Condyle: A rounded, knoblike projection at the end of a bone, typically where it meets or articulates with another bone at a joint. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. External fixation, external fixator, or ex fix: A type of skeletal traction that enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for invasive procedures. Hemostasis: Control of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Intramedullary implant: Insertion of a medical device in the narrow cavity of the bone. Intercondylar: Situated between the condyles. Internal fixation: The use of a variety of different types of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires to stabilize a fracture; internal fixation is a fracture reduction procedure that results in fracture stabilization; when internal fixation is performed the fracture site is opened. Lateral: Furthest to the side from the middle of the body; on or toward the side of a structure or body. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body; toward the middle or inner aspect of a structure or body. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically refers to the manipulation of fractures, dislocations, or hernias; can be open (through a surgical incision) or closed (without an incision). Stabilization: Balance. Supracondylar: Situated above a condyle, a rounded projection at the end of a bone. Traction: To pull on a bone or limb, manually or through the use of a device, to realign a body part or relieve pressure during healing, such as for a fracture. Transcondylar: Smooth surface at the end of the bones between the condyles. Tips If the provider performs an open reduction of the femoral shaft fracture with insertion of an intramedullary implant, use 27506, Open treatment of femoral shaft fracture, with or without external fixation, with insertion of intramedullary implant, with or without cerclage and/or locking screws. If the provider performs an open reduction of the femoral shaft fracture achieving fixation through plates and screws, use 27507, Open treatment of femoral shaft fracture with plate/ screws, with or without cerclage. If the provider performs an open reduction of a supracondylar fracture without intercondylar extension and internal fixation, use 27511, Open treatment of femoral supracondylar or transcondylar fracture without intercondylar extension, includes internal fixation, when performed. If the provider performs an open reduction of the distal end of a femoral fracture along with internal fixation, use 27514, Open treatment of femoral fracture, distal end, medial or lateral condyle, includes internal fixation, when performed. If the provider performs an open reduction of a distal epiphyseal separation along with internal fixation, use 27519, Open treatment of distal femoral epiphyseal separation, includes internal fixation, when performed. If the provider performs a closed treatment of a femoral shaft fracture, see codes 27500, Closed treatment of femoral shaft fracture without manipulation to 27503, Closed treatment of supracondylar femoral shaft fracture with or without intercondylar extension or traction. You should report appropriate a code for debridement, if the provider performs debridement in the case of an open complex fracture. Read Less

short_description: Closed treatment of distal femoral epiphyseal separation; with manipulation, with or without skin or skeletal traction
lay_term: The provider performs a closed reduction of the distal femoral epiphyseal separation with manipulation; skin or skeletal traction may be employed. The goal of the procedure is to stabilize and reduce the separation between the epiphysis, the lower end part of the femur (thigh bone). Separation or fracture of the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) is a common, often missed injury in young children. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider manually manipulates the femoral epiphyseal separation and ensures correct anatomical alignment. The provider applies a cast that extends above and below the knee and may extend up to the hip in a young child, to prevent excessive motion. In addition, the provider sometimes applies skeletal or skin traction to maintain the reduction and for further stabilization. She removes the cast and, if applied, the traction device in three or four weeks after ensuring the fixation at the epiphysis. Terminology Cast: Plaster of Paris cover that forms a hard cover around the broken bone and maintains stability. Closed treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, without making a surgical incision, with or without manipulation, and with or without the use of a traction device that applies a force. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure's point of attachment. Epiphysis: End portion of a long bone; in children, a cartilaginous layer at the end of a long bone responsible for bone growth; also known as the epiphyseal plate, growth plate, or physis. Fixation: A stabilizing process; in reference to fractures, fixation refers to the use of a variety of different types of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires to stabilize a fracture, which can be done percutaneously (through a small incision in the skin) or through an open incision or wound. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones or manipulating a dislocated bone back into its socket. Reduction: Restoration of normal anatomy; typically refers to the manipulation of fractures, dislocations, or hernias; can be open (through a surgical incision) or closed (without an incision). Skeletal traction: Application of a pulling force on bones to treat skeletal disorders and fractures, keeping the bones aligned and immobilized, while relieving pressure on the muscles and nerves, allowing normal healing of a defect or fracture. Tips If the provider performs a closed reduction of the distal femoral epiphysis separation without manipulation, use 27516. If the provider performs an open reduction and internal fixation of the distal femoral epiphyseal separation, use 27519. When reporting the global method of fracture care, an EM service may also be reported. Documentation must support a decision for surgery, modifier 57, and or a separate identifiable service, modifier 25, Significant, separately identifiable E/M service by the same physician on the same day of the procedure or other service. With either method, do not forget to report additional supplies of casting materials. CMS has approximately 50 Q HCPCS codes that address supply issues with casting, splinting applications. The HCPCS level–II manual offers A codes. CPT® contains CPT® code 99070, Supplies and materials, except spectacles, provided by the physician over and above those usually included with the office visit or other services rendered, list drugs, trays, supplies, or materials provided. short_description: Open treatment of knee dislocation, includes internal fixation, when performed; with primary ligamentous repair, with augmentation/reconstruction
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an open reduction and internal fixation to repair a dislocated knee. He also repairs the primary ligament and performs enhancement or reconstruction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an anterior midline incision. He debrides the loose fragments and manipulates the knee to return it to the correct anatomical position. The provider then applies internal fixation devices, such as pins or screws, to achieve stability and prevent future dislocation. He also performs ligament repair and may enhance or reconstruct the ligament. The most common ligaments, which the provider reconstructs or enhances, are the anterior cruciate and the posterior cruciate ligaments. He repairs them by making a passage in the tibia and femur and inserts a graft through the passage. The provider then ensures hemostasis and closes the incision with sutures in layers. Terminology Anterior: Closer to the front part of the body or a structure. Augmentation: To increase. Cruciate ligament: Combination of ligaments in the knee that lie in a cross manner and join the tibia to femur. Dislocation: Body structure out of its normal place, especially parts of a broken bone or two structures that normally connect to form a joint. Enhancement: Improvement. Femur: Thigh bone. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Hemostasis: Control of bleeding from incisions and suture lines. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. The goal of this procedure is to control the infection in a severely infected limb. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin in a circular manner just below the area of the resection. He takes a cutting device, typically an electric saw, to remove the limb by running the device around the femur bone. short_description: Amputation, thigh, through femur, any level; secondary closure or scar revision
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs removes the leg at the thigh through the femur at any level and performs a secondary closure or revision of the scar. The provider performs amputation in case if the patient suffers a severe injury has tumor or has a severe infection that would spread to the distant parts. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs a secondary closure following the granulation of stump. He resects the scar and granulation tissue from the end of the stump and constitutes skin flaps close to the wound. The provider clears away the extra scar tissue and muscles from the end of the bone. He then approximates the skin flaps, connects them with nonabsorbable sutures, and applies temporary drains. The provider does not excise any additional bone. Terminology Amputation: Elimination of limb from the body because of any trauma, disease, or surgery complication. Femur: Thigh bone. Flap: Tissue for grafting typically removed from one place on the body and positioned in another; however, it may remain anchored and rotated from one side of an area to another. Granulation: Formation of small connective tissue around the surface of wound. Scar: Mark on the body after healing of wound. Stump: Leftover part of the extremity following an amputation. Tips When the provider performs amputation through the thigh, see codes 27590, Amputation, thigh, through femur, any level to 27596, Amputation, thigh, through femur, any level; re amputation. short_description: Decompression fasciotomy, leg; anterior and/or lateral, and posterior compartment(s) Notes: (For incision and drainage procedures, superficial, see 10040-10160) (For decompression fasciotomy with debridement, see 27892-27894)
lay_term: The provider incises the fascia to relieve pressure on the leg. He performs this procedure on anterior and or lateral compartments and the posterior compartment of the leg. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin overlying the affected area and gains access to the fascia lying above the targeted muscle compartment affected by compartment syndrome. He then cuts through the fascia and debrides any damaged nonviable tissue, thereby reducing the pressure on the neurovascular structures underneath the fascia. short_description: Arthrotomy, ankle, including exploration, drainage, or removal of foreign body
lay_term: The provider incises and opens the ankle joint, which he then explores and drains any collected fluid or removes any foreign body. He performs the procedure to diagnose problems in the ankle. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the ankle area. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue to the joint capsule. He then incises and opens the joint capsule. He explores the joint space. He removes a foreign body, such as a bullet, nail, or gravel, if present. In the absence of a foreign body, the provider simply explores the wound and drains any abnormal fluid from the area. He irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution. He may leave the wound packed open with daily dressing changes to allow for further drainage or secondary healing by granulation. If the provider repairs the incision, he may place drainage tubes and close the incision in layers with sutures, staples, and or sterile adhesive strips. Terminology Arthrotomy: Surgical incision of a joint, the point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body, such as shards of metal or a bone fragment; foreign bodies in the upper gastrointestinal, or GI, tract are typically swallowed; a swallowed object may travel to the lower GI tract or be inserted through the anus and rectum; traumatic injury can also introduce foreign bodies into the GI tract. Granulation: Formation of tissue during healing. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Secondary healing: Healing process in which wound is left open to heal by itself. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Read Less

short_description: Radical resection of tumor (eg, sarcoma), soft tissue of leg or ankle area; less than 5 cm
lay_term: The provider performs an extensive excision of a tumor, or mass, in the soft tissues in the leg or ankle area, suspected to be malignant, such as a sarcoma. He excises the surrounding tissues along with the mass, with the diameter of the tumor and its margins measuring less than 5 cm. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the area of the tumor, raises skin slaps on either side, and isolates the tumor. He identifies any neurovascular structures that may require ligation and or incision, attempting to preserve as many as possible. He excises and removes the tumor en bloc, or as a single specimen, with a margin of tissue around the tumor included with the mass to ensure that no pathology, or diseased tissue, remains. He submits the specimen for pathologic analysis. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Malignant: Cancerous, capable of spreading and causing death if untreated. Radical resection: Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Sarcoma: A malignant, or cancerous, tumor of connective tissue origin, that occurs in the bone or soft tissues anywhere in the body. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips Check the documentation carefully for the size and the skin layer depth to which the surgery took place before choosing the code. Compare with 27616, Radical resection of tumor, e.g., sarcoma, soft tissue of leg or ankle area, 5 cm or greater. If two providers work together to perform the surgery, append modifier 62, Two surgeons. For your modifier 62 claim to succeed, both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must use modifier 62. You should work closely with the other provider's staff to ensure that each practice gets its fair share of the reimbursement. Medicare and most other payers reimburse procedures coded with modifier 62 at 125 percent of the regular fee schedule amount. The payer divides this between the two providers reporting the procedure, so each provider receives 62.5 percent of the standard fee. When appending modifier 62, each provider must provide his own documentation describing what portion of the procedure he performed, how much work was involved, and how long the procedure took. Make sure that both providers involved in the surgery identify the other as a co–provider. Be sure to confirm with your payer if they accept modifier 62. The Medicare Provider Fee Schedule indicates for each procedure whether you can use modifier 62. It may also indicate whether additional documentation is necessary to show why a second provider’s participation was needed in the procedure. Read Less

short_description: Arthrotomy, ankle, with joint exploration, with or without biopsy, with or without removal of loose or foreign body

short_description: Arthrotomy, with synovectomy, ankle; including tenosynovectomy
lay_term: The provider makes an incision in the ankle and removes the diseased tendon sheath along with synovial membrane. He performs this procedure to diagnose and treat ankle problems. Now, the provider identifies the diseased tendon outside the joint, retracts it out of the wound, and removes the tendon sheath, thus relieving the inflammation, pressure, and pain. He places the tendon back into its anatomical position. He closes the soft tissues in layers with sutures, staples, and or sterile adhesive strips. Synovectomy: Surgical removal of synovial membrane. Synovial fluid: Thick fluid found in synovial joints; synovial joints are characterized by their fluid filled capsules. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Tendon sheath: Covering surrounding a tendon. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. short_description: Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor, tibia or fibula
lay_term: The provider removes a bone cyst or benign tumor from the tibia or fibula. He performs this procedure to prevent infection and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the tibia or fibula over the cyst or tumor. He carries it down through the subcutaneous tissues. He also dissects the muscle. He retracts all soft tissue layers and incises and reflects the periosteum, the outer membrane of the bone. He then excises the cyst with a burr and smooths the surfaces of the bone. He washes the area with warm saline or an antibiotic solution. Finally, the provider places the periosteum back in its original position over the bone and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He closes the incision in layers with sutures. Burr: Surgical instrument to create an opening in bone. Curettage: Use of a curet, a spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping, to remove tissue by scraping or scooping. Cyst: Sac usually containing fluid; the term cyst can also refer to an abnormal growth or to any saclike structure, such as the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Retract: Hold back incisions or edges of a wound with instruments designed to do so without injuring tissue. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Make sure that both of the doctors involved in the procedure identify the other as a cosurgeon. Also check which procedures accept cosurgeon modifiers.
