Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the tibia or fibula over the cyst or tumor. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue and muscle. He retracts all soft tissue layers and incises and reflects the periosteum, the outer membrane of the bone. He then excises the cyst with a burr and smooths the surfaces of the bone. He washes the area with warm saline or an antibiotic solution. He applies an allograft in the space created from excision of bone cyst. He may fix the graft with plate and screws. Finally, the provider controls any bleeding and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then closes the incision in layers with sutures. Terminology Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called allogeneic graft and homograft. Autograft: A tissue graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Antibiotic: A substance that inhibits infection. Benign: Not malignant, generally treatable or not needing treatment. Burr: Surgical instrument to create an opening in bone. Curettage: Use of a curet, a spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping, to remove tissue by scraping or scooping. Cyst: Sac usually containing fluid; the term cyst can refer to an abnormal growth or to any saclike structure, such as the urinary bladder or gallbladder. Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. Fibula: The outermost and smallest of the two bones of the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Retract: Hold back incisions or edges of a wound with instruments designed to do so without injuring tissue. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Tibia: The innermost and largest of the two bones in the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass; can be benign or cancerous. Tips Do not report harvesting of graft separately. When the provider removes a bone cyst or benign tumor of the tibia or fibula, use 27635, Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor, tibia or fibula. For the same service involving autograft, use 27637, Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor, tibia or fibula; with autograft includes obtaining graft. If the procedure was performed by a surgeon and a cosurgeon, append modifier 62, Two surgeons; both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must append modifier 62. When reporting surgeries involving two (or more) surgeons, you should work closely with the other operating surgeon's staff to ensure that each practice gets its fair share of the reimbursement. Medicare and most other payers reimburse procedures coded with modifier 62 at 125 percent of the regular fee schedule amount. The payer divides this between the two surgeons reporting the procedure, so each surgeon receives 62.5 percent of the standard fee. When acting as cosurgeons, two providers cannot share the same documentation. Have each provider provide a note describing what portion of the procedure he performed, how much work was involved, and how long the procedure took. Make sure that both of the doctors involved in the procedure identify the other as a cosurgeon. Also check which procedures accept cosurgeon modifiers. The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule indicates for each procedure whether you can report the same code for both surgeons. It may also indicate that Medicare allows billing the code for both surgeons with documentation only. This means that the claim will not get approved just with a CMS 1500 claim but needs the documentation to show why the cosurgeon was needed. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Repair, primary, open or percutaneous, ruptured Achilles tendon
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs primary open or percutaneous repair of an Achilles tendon tear. Primary repair is one when the provider repairs the torn tendon within a few days of the tear. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the torn Achilles tendon to be repaired. In the case of open surgery, the provider makes a single large incision on the back of the lower leg, and in the case of percutaneous surgery, he makes several small incisions rather than one large incision. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue to gain access to the torn tendon. He then brings the two ends of the tendon closer to each other and sutures them together. Methods may vary. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Achilles tendon: A tendon that connects the calf muscle to the heel bone. Tips Use 27652 when the provider performs primary open or percutaneous repair of the Achilles tendon with a graft. short_description: Repair, primary, open or percutaneous, ruptured Achilles tendon; with graft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: The provider performs repair of an Achilles tendon rupture with use the placement of a graft. He performs the procedure to restore function and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision on the medial side of Achilles tendon and identifies the site of rupture. Because the rupture is extensive and there is insufficient length of the tendon for repair, the provider harvests a graft. He makes an incision in another area and carries it down through subcutaneous tissues. He harvests a ribbon of fascia or a piece of the plantar tendon to use for the graft. He then closes the graft site with sutures. Next, he mobilizes the Achilles tendon. He trims ragged edges and brings the torn ends of the tendon together as much as possible. He then weaves the graft from distal to proximal and across the rupture site of the tendon and secures it with sutures. He then controls any bleeding and closes the soft tissue with sutures after which he closes the incision in layers. He immobilizes the patient's leg in a short leg cast for at least two weeks to allow for healing. Terminology Achilles tendon: Tendon that attaches the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, muscles on the back of the lower leg, to the ankle bone. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Percutaneous: Through the skin; percutaneous procedures employ small skin incisions through which tubes and instruments can be inserted. Plantar: Sole of the foot. Primary: Most important or the first occurrence of something. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Rupture: A tear in a structure due to injury. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips You should not code harvesting of the tendon graft separately because harvesting the graft is included. For open or percutaneous repair of a ruptured Achilles tendon, see 27650, Repair, primary, open or percutaneous, ruptured Achilles tendon. For secondary repair of a ruptured Achilles tendon, see 27654, Repair, secondary, Achilles tendon, with or without graft. For other procedures on the Achilles tendon, see 27605 to 27606, Tenotomy, percutaneous, Achilles tendon, etc. If the procedure was performed by a surgeon and a cosurgeon, append modifier 62, Two surgeons; both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must append modifier 62. When reporting surgeries involving two (or more) surgeons, you should work closely with the other operating surgeon's staff to ensure that each practice gets its fair share of the reimbursement. Medicare and most other payers reimburse procedures coded with modifier 62 at 125 percent of the regular fee schedule amount. The payer divides this between the two surgeons reporting the procedure, so each surgeon receives 62.5 percent of the standard fee. When acting as cosurgeons, two providers cannot share the same documentation. Have each provider provide a note describing what portion of the procedure he performed, how much work was involved, and how long the procedure took. Make sure that both of the doctors involved in the procedure identify the other as a cosurgeon. Also check which procedures accept cosurgeon modifiers. The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule indicates for each procedure whether you can report the same code for both surgeons. It may also indicate that Medicare allows billing the code for both surgeons with documentation only. This means that the claim will not get approved just with a CMS 1500 claim but needs the documentation to show why the cosurgeon was needed. Read Less

short_description: Repair, secondary, Achilles tendon, with or without graft
lay_term: The provider performs repair of Achilles tendon for the second time with or without use of graft because the previous one was unsuccessful or the patient reinjured the tendon. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider opens the old incision and identifies the site of previous repair. short_description: Repair, dislocating peroneal tendons; with fibular osteotomy
lay_term: The provider repairs dislocated peroneal tendons by inserting them into a groove that he makes in the fibula, the outermost and smallest of the two bones of the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. He performs the procedure to restore function and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal lateral ankle incision and dissects subcutaneous tissue to expose the fibula. He cuts a groove in the posterior aspect of the lateral malleolus, the rounded process at the bottom of the fibula. He inserts the ends of the peroneal tendons into the groove. To hold the tendons in place, he brings the bone flaps that he created when he cut the groove together to cover the tendons. Alternatively, he may cover the tendons with a wedge of bone that he cut from the lateral malleolus. He thoroughly irrigates the wound. He controls any bleeding and sutures the soft tissues in layers. He then closes the skin incision with sutures. He typically places a short leg cast. short_description: Tenolysis, flexor or extensor tendon, leg and/or ankle; single, each tendon
lay_term: The provider performs release of a single flexor or extensor tendon in the leg and or ankle. The tendon may be tight and unable to move freely due to scarring or adhesions. He performs the procedure to restore function and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the area of the affected tendon. He incises the tendon sheath and brings the tendon out of the tendon sheath. He removes adhesions or scar tissue from the tendon and places the tendon back in the tendon sheath so that it will slide and glide freely again. He then repairs the tendon sheath with sutures. He asks the patient to move his leg to make sure that tendon is gliding properly and working well. He closes the wound with sutures. He then applies a short leg cast for at least two weeks. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery, that form between tissues and organs; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Extensor tendon: Tendon that attaches an extensor muscle to bone; extensor muscles bend a joint. Flexor tendon: Tendon that attaches a flexor muscle to bone; flexor muscles unbend or straighten a joint. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Tendon sheath: Covering surrounding a tendon. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tenolysis: Breaking down adhesions to free up a tendon. Tips You should report 27680 once for tenolysis of either a flexor tendon or extensor tendon. When the provider performs tenolysis of multiple tendon through separate incisions, use 27681, Tenolysis, flexor or extensor tendon, leg and or ankle; multiple tendons through separate incisions. Append modifier 62, Two surgeons, if the provider is acting as a cosurgeon with another provider, both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must append modifier 62. When reporting surgeries involving two (or more) surgeons, you should work closely with the other operating surgeon's staff to ensure that each practice gets its fair share of the reimbursement. Medicare and most other payers reimburse procedures coded with modifier 62 at 125 percent of the regular fee schedule amount. The payer divides this between the two surgeons reporting the procedure, so each surgeon receives 62.5 percent of the standard fee. When acting as cosurgeons, two providers cannot share the same documentation. Have each provider provide a note describing what portion of the procedure he performed, how much work was involved, and how long the procedure took. Make sure that both of the doctors involved in the procedure identify the other as a cosurgeon. Also check which procedures accept cosurgeon modifiers. The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule indicates for each procedure whether you can report the same code for both surgeons. It may also indicate that Medicare allows billing the code for both surgeons with documentation only. short_description: Arthroplasty, ankle; with implant (total ankle)
lay_term: The provider reconstructs the total ankle joint with an implant to treat severe pain, which arthritis or a fracture causes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the front portion of ankle to expose the ankle joint. He dissects the tissues, moving the tendons, nerves, and blood vessels aside. He removes the damaged bone. He then reshapes and smooths the three bones of joint: the lower end of the tibia, the lower end of fibula, and the top of the talus. He then places the artificial joint prosthesis inside the joint. He applies bone cement to hold the prosthesis in place. He then places screws through tibia and fibula. He then repairs the soft tissues, controls any bleeding, and closes the wound. Terminology Arthritis: An inflammatory condition affecting one or more of the body’s joints, resulting in pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Arthroplasty: Reconstruction or replacement of a joint, the point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Implant: Any medical device inserted into the body; may also refer to an organ, graft, or tissue used to replace diseased or absent body part. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Prosthesis: An artificial device that functions like the structure it replaces. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips For the same service without implant, use 27700, Arthroplasty, ankle. Append modifier 62, Two surgeons, if the provider is acting as a cosurgeon with another provider, both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must append modifier 62. Medicare and most other payers reimburse procedures coded with modifier 62 at 125 percent of the regular fee schedule amount. The payer divides this between the two surgeons reporting the procedure, so each surgeon receives 62.5 percent of the standard fee. Have each provider provide a note describing what portion of the procedure he performed, how much work was involved, and how long the procedure took. Make sure that both of the doctors involved in the procedure identify the other as a cosurgeon. Also check which procedures accept cosurgeon modifiers. The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule indicates for each procedure whether you can report the same code for both surgeons. It may also indicate that Medicare allows billing the code for both surgeons with documentation only. This means that the claim will not get approved just with a CMS 1500 claim but needs the documentation to show why the cosurgeon was needed. Read Less

short_description: Osteotomy; fibula
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts a wedge–shaped portion of bone from the fibula, the outer and thinner of the two long bones of the lower leg. Explanation Osteotomy is a surgical procedure to cut a portion of bone to correct misalignment or deformity. The goal of fibular osteotomy is to treat deformities like malunion of a fracture, unequal leg length, etc. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the fibula on the outer side of the leg. He then cuts through soft tissue and exposes the bone. He then incises the periosteum, the outer covering of the bone, and elevates the periosteum. He removes a wedge–shaped piece of bone from the fibula. He may use implants like screws or plates to keep the bone in the corrected position after the osteotomy. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Tips Use 27705 when the provider performs osteotomy of the tibia. Use 27709 when the provider performs osteotomy of both the tibia and fibula. Read Less

lay_term: The provider incises multiple segments of tibia and fibula and places an intramedullary rod to correct alignment and to treat deformities like malunion of fracture, unequal leg length, outward bending of knee, or knock knee, inward bending of the knees toward the midline of the body. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes longitudinal incisions on the leg. He exposes the deformed bone at the convexity of the bone. He incises the curved part of bone with a bone cutter or a saw into several fragments to achieve correction. He then keeps all the parts straight and places an intramedullary rod through the medullary cavity of the bone. He uses K wires or pins to fix the rod in alignment with the bone fragments. He controls any bleeding, and closes the incision in layers. He then applies a full leg cast. Terminology Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Intramedullary: Innermost part of bone. K wires: Surgical pins mainly sued in orthopedic surgery for stabilization. Malunion: Incomplete healing or healing of a fracture in an abnormal position. Medullary cavity: The inner chamber of a bone that contains the marrow, the substance that produces new blood cells. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Tips Append modifier 62, Two surgeons, if the provider is acting as a cosurgeon with another provider, both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must append modifier 62. When reporting surgeries involving two (or more) surgeons, you should work closely with the other operating surgeon's staff to ensure that each practice gets its fair share of the reimbursement. Medicare and most other payers reimburse procedures coded with modifier 62 at 125 percent of the regular fee schedule amount. The payer divides this between the two surgeons reporting the procedure, so each surgeon receives 62.5 percent of the standard fee. When acting as cosurgeons, two providers cannot share the same documentation. Have each provider provide a note describing what portion of the procedure he performed, how much work was involved, and how long the procedure took. Make sure that both of the doctors involved in the procedure identify the other as a cosurgeon. Also check which procedures accept cosurgeon modifiers. The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule indicates for each procedure whether you can report the same code for both surgeons. It may also indicate that Medicare allows billing the code for both surgeons with documentation only. This means that the claim will not get approved just with a CMS 1500 claim but needs the documentation to show why the cosurgeon was needed. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. short_description: Repair of nonunion or malunion, tibia; by synostosis, with fibula, any method
lay_term: The provider repairs a tibial fracture that has failed to heal or has healed with poor alignment by fusing it with fibula. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision and carries it down through subcutaneous tissues to expose the old tibial nonunion or malunion. He debrides the fibrous tissue. If the fragments have failed to join, he decorticates the ends of both tibial fragments to create a bleeding bone, which promotes healing of the fracture. If the bones have healed in malalignment, he refractures the bones and again freshens the ends. He places the tibial fragments into anatomic alignment and then secures the tibia to the fibula with a plate, wires, or screws to maintain the fixation. He thoroughly irrigates the wound with an antibiotic solution to prevent infection, controls any bleeding, and closes the incision in layers. Debride: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Decorticate: Surgical excision of cortex, outer membrane of the bone. Fibula: The outermost and smallest of the two bones of the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Malunion: Incomplete healing or healing of a fracture in an abnormal position. Nonunion: Failure of a fractured bone fragments to unite properly. Subcutaneous: Below the skin. Synostosis: Fusion between adjacent bones that are normally separate; the fusion may occur by itself or with surgical intervention. Tibia: The innermost and largest of the two bones in the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. Tips Append modifier 62, Two surgeons, if the provider is acting as a cosurgeon with another provider, both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must append modifier 62. short_description: Arrest, epiphyseal (epiphysiodesis), open; distal tibia
lay_term: The provider fuses the end plates of the lower tibia to interrupt its growth. This surgical procedure stops the growth of the tibial bone to prevent it from growing longer than the fibula of the same leg or the tibia of the other leg during the growth phase. The provider performs the procedure to equalize the length of both legs as the patient grows. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the epiphysis of the distal tibia. He carries the incision down through tissues to bone. The provider makes two through and through osteotomy type incisions and removes a circular block of tibial bone. He then scrapes this block on one side to roughen the surface. He rotates the block upside down and places it back in its original position. He then fixes the block with pins. He thoroughly irrigates the wound with an antibiotic solution to prevent infection, controls any bleeding, and closes the incision in layers. Epiphysis: The end portion of a long bone. Femur: The thigh bone. Fibula: The outermost and smallest of the two bones of the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Tibia: The innermost and largest of the two bones in the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. lay_term: The provider fuses the end plates of upper and lower ends of the tibia and fibula to interrupt their growth. This surgical procedure stops the growth of the tibia and fibula to keep them from growing longer than the other leg during the growth phase. The provider performs the procedure to equalize the length of both legs as the patient grows. Explanation Although the provider can choose among various methods to perform this procedure, this describes one of them. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes incision over the epiphyses of the distal tibia and distal fibula. He carries the incision down through tissues to bone. The provider makes two through and through osteotomy type incisions and removes a circular block from each bone. He then scrapes these blocks on one side to roughen the surface. He then rotates the blocks upside down and places them back in their original position. He fixes the blocks in place with pins. The provider performs the same procedure on the proximal tibia and fibula. short_description: Prophylactic treatment (nailing, pinning, plating or wiring) with or without methylmethacrylate, tibia
lay_term: The provider strengthens a weak area in the tibia with nails, pins, plate, and or wires to a potential fracture. The provider may also apply a bone cement, such as methylmethacrylate. He performs the procedure on a patient with a bone disease, such as osteoporosis, or benign or malignant neoplasm of the bone. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the area of the tibia believed to be susceptible to fracture. He carries the incision down through subcutaneous tissues to expose the bone. He assesses the condition of the tibia and determines which fixation technique he will use. If a neoplasm is present, he excises it from the bone. He places nails, pins, wires, and or a plate to strengthen the shaft of the tibia. short_description: Closed treatment of tibial shaft fracture (with or without fibular fracture); with manipulation, with or without skeletal traction
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the tibial shaft, which requires manipulation. A fibular fracture may or may not be present; if present, the provider does not treat it separately. The provider may or may not use skeletal traction. He performs the procedure to keep the fracture in alignment and prevent displacement while the fracture heals and to relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider manipulates the fracture to reduce it and bring the two fragments into correct anatomical position. If necessary, he also applies traction to bring the fragments into proper alignment. He applies a long leg cast or splint. The casting also treats any fibular fracture that might be present. The cast or splint extends from the foot to above the knee. He may take X–rays post treatment to ensure correct alignment. Terminology Closed treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, without making a surgical incision, with or without manipulation, and with or without the use of a traction device that applies a force. External fixation, or ex fix: A type of skeletal traction, also called an external fixator or ex fix, that enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for invasive procedures. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Hairline fracture: Fracture of the cortex, or outer covering, of bone that does not go through the entire substance of the bone; repetitive strain and twisting injuries can cause hairline fractures. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Shaft: Cylindrical middle portion of a long bone. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips You should not code treatment of the fibular fracture separately. The provider does not perform reduction of the fracture in this procedure. If imaging is used, report that separately. For the same service without manipulation, use 27750, Closed treatment of tibial shaft fracture with or without fibular fracture; without manipulation. For percutaneous pin or screw fixation of a tibial shaft fracture, use 27756, Percutaneous skeletal fixation of tibial shaft fracture with or without fibular fracture for example, pins or screws. For open treatment of a tibial shaft fracture with plate and screws, use 27758, Open treatment of tibial shaft fracture with or without fibular fracture, with plate or screws, with or without cerclage. For open treatment of a tibial shaft fracture with intramedullary nail or rod, use 27759, Treatment of tibial shaft fracture with or without fibular fracture by intramedullary implant, with or without interlocking screws and or cerclage. Global reporting will include the initial cast application and all professional services for a 90–day period. The provider should not report further reassessment separately. You may report items separately such as further castings, splinting, radiographs, and supplies. These items are not included in the global period. Documentation should reflect the type of care and treatment. Neurologic and vascular status should be clinically assessed and documented as the key items in the initial assessment. Documentation should also note assessment of the extent of the fracture. Casting or splinting provide symptomatic relief for the patient and prevent further injury. Additional Info Closed fracture treatment does not involve a surgical incision. Closed treatments can be performed with or without manipulation and or traction. Manipulation means the provider must move or adjust the involved bones to improve their position or alignment. Read Less

short_description: Treatment of tibial shaft fracture (with or without fibular fracture) by intramedullary implant, with or without interlocking screws and/or cerclage
lay_term: The provider treats a tibial shaft fracture with by placing a nail or rod in the intramedullary canal. He may or may apply interlocking screws and or cerclage. This procedure may or may not involve fibular fracture. He does not treat a fibular fracture separately, if present. He performs the procedure to keep the fracture in alignment and prevent displacement while the fracture heals and to relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the tibia shaft fracture. He uses radiographic imaging to manipulate the fracture into the correct position. The provider approaches the area proximal or distal to the fracture site and threads a nail down into the intramedullary canal of the bone and across the fracture site. He may place interlocking screws at angles to the nail to further stabilize the fracture. He may also wrap the fracture site with wire. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. short_description: Open treatment of medial malleolus fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed
lay_term: The provider treats a fracture of the medial malleolus through an open incision, with placement of screws and plates. He performs the procedure to keep the fracture in alignment and prevent displacement while the fracture heals and to relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over medial malleolus fracture. He carries the incision carefully down through tissues to bone. He identifies and explores the fracture site. He places the fracture fragments together in correct anatomical position. If necessary, he fixes the fragments in place with plate and screws. He thoroughly irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution, controls any bleeding, and closes the incision in layers. He then applies a splint. He may take X–rays post treatment to ensure correct alignment. Terminology External fixation, or ex fix: Type of skeletal traction, also called an external fixator or ex fix that enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for invasive procedures. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body. Medial malleolus: Projection on the inner surface of ankle joint or lower medial portion of tibia. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Splint: Medical device to immobilize an injured joint. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips To code the open treatment, a surgical incision needs to be made. If imaging is used, report that separately. To report a closed repair of a medial malleolus fracture, see codes 27760 and 27762, Closed treatment of medial malleolus fracture, etc. Global reporting will include the initial cast or splint application and all professional services for a 90–day period. The provider should not report further reassessment separately. You may report items separately such as further castings, splinting, radiographs, and supplies. These items are not included in the global period. Documentation should reflect the type of care and treatment. Neurologic and vascular status should be clinically assessed and documented as the key items in the initial assessment. Documentation should also note assessment of the extent of the fracture. Casting or splinting provide symptomatic relief for the patient and prevent further injury. When choosing a surgical fracture code, you need to consider external and internal fixation. The CPT® code includes reimbursement for fracture fixation, whether internal or external. Use codes for external fixation when the official description does not list external fixation as part of the basic procedure. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of posterior malleolus fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed Notes: (Do not report 27767-27769 in conjunction with 27808-27823)
lay_term: The provider repairs a posterior malleolus fracture through an open incision with placement of screws and plates if necessary. He performs the procedure to keep the fracture in alignment and prevent displacement while the fracture heals and to relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the fracture site of the posterior malleolus. He carries the incision down through tissues to bone. He identifies and explores the fracture site. He places the fracture fragments together in correct anatomical position and fixes them in place with plate and screws or pins if necessary. He thoroughly irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution, controls any bleeding, and closes the incision in layers. He applies a splint. He may take X–rays post treatment to ensure correct alignment. Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Incision: A cut in the skin, tissue, vessel, or other structure, made with surgical knife called a blade or scalpel. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Posterior malleolus: Posterior portion of the inferior articulating surface of the tibia. Splint: Medical device to immobilize an injured joint. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. short_description: Open treatment of proximal fibula or shaft fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically fixes a break in the shaft or end of the fibula bone and may secure it with plates, and screws, wires, or pins, when necessary. short_description: Open treatment of trimalleolar ankle fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed, medial and/or lateral malleolus; without fixation of posterior lip
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically fixes all three fractured malleoli of the ankle, the medial, lateral, and posterior malleoli. He secures the malleoli with plates, screws, wires, or pins at two malleoli, the medial and lateral malleoli, but he applies no fixation to the posterior malleolus. The provider generally performs this procedure on unstable fractures that require fixation for additional support. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision at the ankle joint. He then identifies and explores the fracture site. He places the fracture fragments together in correct anatomical position and fixes the medial and lateral malleoli with plates and screws, wires, or pins. After achieving hemostasis, the stoppage of all bleeding, he irrigates and closes the wound. Next, he applies a brace or cast. He may take post treatment X–rays to ensure correct alignment. Terminology Fracture: To break; also a broken bone. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Lateral malleoli: Bony prominence on the outer aspect of the ankle, furthest from the middle of the body. Medial malleoli: Bony prominence on the inner aspect of the ankle, nearest to the middle of the body. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Posterior lip: Refers to the posterior malleolus. Posterior malleoli: Bony prominence on the rear aspect of the ankle. Trimalleolar: Referring to three malleoli, bony projections on the sides of the ankle joint. Tips If your provider is acting as a cosurgeon with another provider, you should report the procedure code and append modifier 62, Two surgeons. For your modifier 62 claim to succeed, both providers must submit claims for the same procedure, using the same procedure code, and both providers must use modifier 62. When reporting surgeries involving two (or more) surgeons, you should work closely with the other operating provider's staff to ensure that each practice gets its fair share of the reimbursement. Medicare and most other payers reimburse procedures with a modifier 62 at 125 percent of the regular fee schedule amount. The payer divides this between the two providers reporting the procedure, so each provider receives 62.5 percent of the standard fee. When acting as cosurgeons, two providers cannot share the same documentation. Have each provider provide a note describing what portion of the procedure he performed, how much work was involved, and how long the procedure took. Make sure that both of the doctors involved in the procedure identify the other as a cosurgeon. Also check which procedures accept cosurgeon modifiers. The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule indicates for each procedure whether you can report the same code for both surgeons. It may also indicate that Medicare allows billing the code for both surgeons with documentation only. This means that the claim will not get approved just with a CMS 1500 claim but needs the documentation to show why the cosurgeon was needed. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of trimalleolar ankle fracture, includes internal fixation, when performed, medial and/or lateral malleolus; with fixation of posterior lip
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically fixes all three fractured malleoli of the ankle, the medial, lateral, and posterior malleoli. He secures the malleoli with plates, screws, wires, or pins at two malleoli, the medial and lateral malleoli. He applies fixation to the posterior malleolus. The provider generally performs this procedure on unstable fractures which require fixation for additional support. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision at the ankle joint. He identifies and explores the fracture site. He then places the fracture fragments together in correct anatomical position and fixes all three malleoli with plates and screws, wires, or pins. After achieving hemostasis, the stoppage of bleeding, he closes the wound and applies a cast. He may take post treatment X–rays to ensure correct alignment. Medial malleoli: Bony prominence on the inner aspect of the ankle, nearest to the middle of the body. Open treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, through a surgical incision, with or without internal fixation; also called open reduction. Posterior lip: Refers to the posterior malleolus. Posterior malleoli: Bony prominence on the rear aspect of the ankle. Trimalleolar: Referring to three malleoli which are bony projections on the sides of the ankle joint. lay_term: In this procedure, the provider fixes a fracture of the weight bearing articular portion of the distal tibia by adjusting the alignment nonsurgically using skeletal traction and manipulation. The provider generally performs this procedure on unstable fractures which require manipulation to align the bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized as necessary, the provider treats a fracture of the weight bearing articular portion of the distal tibia, or the bottom of the tibia, the shinbone, at the ankle joint. The provider may first adjust the fractured fragment by exerting a pushing or pulling force to manipulate the bones to reduce the fracture or he may use traction to reduce and stabilize the fracture. He then applies a cast or brace to help stabilize the fracture. He may take post treatment X–rays to ensure the correct alignment. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Fracture: To break; also as in a broken bone. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Tibia: Larger of the two bones of the lower leg; the fibula is the outermost bone, the tibia the innermost. Tibial plafond: The lower most end of the tibia bone. Tips Use 27824, Closed treatment of fracture of weight bearing articular portion of distal tibia, eg, pilon or tibial plafond, with or without anesthesia; without manipulation if the provider does not use manipulation. short_description: Closed treatment of proximal tibiofibular joint dislocation; without anesthesia
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider treats a dislocated proximal tibiofibular joint near the patient’s knee by adjusting the alignment nonsurgically and without the need for anesthesia. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider gently manipulates and aligns the dislocated bones to their correct anatomical position. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. short_description: Open treatment of proximal tibiofibular joint dislocation, includes internal fixation, when performed, or with excision of proximal fibula
lay_term: The provider treats a proximal tibiofibular joint dislocation. He surgically opens the site of dislocation. He realigns the joint and fixes it with wires. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision and carries it down deep to the tibiofibular joint. He dissects the surrounding muscles. He identifies the target site and reduces the joint back together in correct anatomical position using bone reduction clamps. He then provisionally fixes them with K wires to maintain the reduction. To prevent knee instability, he repairs and stabilizes the attached the ligaments. If required, he may excise the proximal fibula completely or partly. Lastly, he closes the wound and applies a cast to secure the repair. He uses X–rays to ensure the correct alignment of the joint. Fibula: The outermost and smallest of the two bones of the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Kirschner wire, or K wire: Wire used to stabilize structures, such as a broken bone. Ligament: Fibrous band that connects bones and joints as well as holds organs in place. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Reduce: To restore normal anatomy; typically relates to fractures, dislocations, or hernias. Tibiofibular joint: The union of the tibia and fibula, the bones of the lower leg. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of ankle dislocation, with or without percutaneous skeletal fixation; with repair or internal or external fixation Notes: (For surgical or diagnostic arthroscopic procedures, see 29894-29898)
lay_term: The provider treats an ankle joint dislocation. He surgically opens the site of dislocation. He reduces the joint and repairs any damaged tissues. He applies hardware from within or from the outside through the skin as necessary. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a longitudinal incision and carries it down deep to the ankle joint. He dissects the surrounding muscles. He identifies the target site and reduces the joint back together in correct anatomical position using bone reduction clamps. He then internally fixes them with K wires or may use external fixators percutaneously to maintain the reduction. To prevent knee instability, he repairs and stabilizes the attached the ligaments. short_description: Arthrodesis, ankle, open Notes: (For arthroscopic ankle arthrodesis, use 29899)
lay_term: The provider permanently fuses an ankle joint to relieve pain and disability from severe arthritis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes incisions on the outside and front of the ankle. He removes the articular cartilage surfaces of the ankle joint. He prepares the underlying bone with a combination of instruments to create fresh bony surfaces. He positions the joint in neutral dorsiflexion and in slight hind foot valgus. This allows the most motion through the surrounding joints. He may excise a portion of the fibula and reposition that so that it is included in the fusion mass. He may augment the ankle fusion with bone graft taken from just below the knee or the pelvis. He applies plates and screws to fix the joint internally. He may apply an external fixation device. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Arthritis: An inflammatory condition affecting one or more of the body’s joints, resulting in pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Articular cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue covering the bony surfaces of a joint. Dorsiflexion: Extension of the toes or foot upward; opposite of plantarflexion; can refer to the hand or fingers. External fixation, or ex fix: Type of skeletal traction, also called an external fixator or ex fix, that enables the provider to make adjustments to the fixation externally and eliminates the need for invasive procedures. Fibula: The outermost and smallest of the two bones of the lower leg, joining the knee and the ankle. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis, i.e., to surgically connect two structures together. Hind foot valgus: The heel angled slightly to the outside. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Tips If the provider applies a bone graft, check with your payer to determine if it is separately reportable. Read Less

lay_term: The provider permanently fuses the union of the tibia and fibula at the ankle to relieve pain and disability. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision through the skin to open the tibiofibular joint. He excises the articular cartilage surfaces from the joint. He prepares the underlying bone with a combination of instruments to create microfractures that can knit together to create a good bleeding bone for arthrodesis. He aligns the joint in a correct anatomical position and applies internal fixation with screws or plates. He may augment the tibiofibular joint fusion with bone graft taken from just below the knee or from the pelvis. He may apply an external fixation device for further stabilization of the joint. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. short_description: Amputation, leg, through tibia and fibula
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider amputates the leg below the knee, through the bones in the lower leg, to relieve pain and or remove nonhealing tissue in the presence of poor vascular supply. short_description: Amputation, leg, through tibia and fibula; open, circular (guillotine)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider amputates the patient's leg below the knee without leaving a skin flap. He performs the procedure when rapid amputation aids in stopping rapidly ascending necrosis, or tissue death, or hemodynamic compromise. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider applies a sterile tourniquet to arrest blood flow to the leg and elevates it. He uses an oscillating, or circular, saw to amputate the leg below the knee through the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and bone in one sweep. He controls blood loss by ligating, or tying off, bleeding vessels. He applies a moist bulky dressing. He begins antibiotic treatment in the presence of infection. The patient will later undergo revision amputation when the patient has stabilized. Terminology Amputation: The intentional surgical removal of a limb or body part. It is performed to remove diseased tissue or relieve pain. Guillotine amputation: Rapid amputation, or severing of a limb, in one stroke with a circular saw; also known as a flapless amputation. Hemodynamic: Relating to the flow of blood through the heart. Prosthesis: An artificial or manmade replacement for a body part. Tourniquet: compressing device to control venous and arterial circulation to an extremity for a particular session of time. Tips For different versions of this procedure, see codes in the section 27880 to 27889, Amputation procedures on the leg, tibia and fibula, and ankle joint. Read Less

short_description: Amputation, ankle, through malleoli of tibia and fibula (eg, Syme, Pirogoff type procedures), with plastic closure and resection of nerves
lay_term: The provider amputates the foot across the bone knobs on either side of the ankle to treat nonhealing wounds of the foot due to infection or poor circulation. He excises the nerves and reconstructs the skin and tissues around the amputation site to enable walking on the stump. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision at the distal, or lower, tips of the lateral malleolus and medial malleolus, which he deepens through the subcutaneous tissue. To expose the area of amputation, he dissects the ligaments and muscles. He ligates, or ties off, major blood vessels at the site. He removes the talus, or ankle bone. He transects the calcaneus, or heel bone, with a power saw, avoiding damage to the muscle or fat in the heel, to create a heel flap for walking. He then brings forward the heel flap to cover the bony areas. The provider then irrigates the area with antibiotic solution, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Amputation: The intentional surgical removal of a limb or body part. It is performed to remove diseased tissue or relieve pain. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Lateral malleolus: Bony knob on the outside of the ankle, at the bottom of the fibula, a bone in the lower leg. Ligament: Fibrous band that connects bones and joints as well as holds organs in place. Malleolus: Bony knob on either side of the ankle on the lower leg bones, the tibia and fibula. Medial malleolus: Bony knob on the inside of the ankle, at the bottom of the tibia, a bone in the lower leg. Pirogoff: Amputation of the foot at the ankle through the joint surface of the tibia and fibula, the bones in the lower leg. Plastic closure: Surgical reconstruction in a manner that improves appearance. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Syme: Amputation of the foot at the ankle with removal of the malleoli, the bony knobs on either side of the ankle. Tips For variations on this procedure, see codes in the section 27888 to 27889, Amputation procedures on the leg, tibia and fibula, and ankle joint. Use modifier 50, Bilateral procedure, if the provider performs amputation on both ankles. Read Less
