short_description: Decompression fasciotomy, leg; anterior and/or lateral compartments only, with debridement of nonviable muscle and/or nerve Notes: (For decompression fasciotomy of the leg without debridement, use 27600)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts into the fascia surrounding the anterior and/or lateral compartments in the lower leg to relieve pressure and increase blood flow. He also removes the dead or damaged tissue. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to treat pressure such as that caused by compartment syndrome of the lower leg, a painful condition that involves increased pressure in a muscle compartment leading to muscle and nerve damage with reduction of blood flow. The syndrome is characterized by symptoms like decreased sensation, numbness, weakness, and severe pain. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin overlying the affected area and gets access to the fascia lying above the muscle compartment affected by compartment syndrome. The anterior compartment lies in front of the lower leg and the lateral compartment lies on the outer side of the lower leg. The provider may target either or both compartments. He then cuts through the fascia and debrides all the damaged nonviable muscle and/or nerve tissue, thereby reducing the pressure on the neurovascular structures underneath the fascia. This restores the restricted blood supply and relieves the patient from symptoms. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the soft tissues in layers. short_description: Incision and drainage below fascia, with or without tendon sheath involvement, foot; multiple areas
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider drains fluid from multiple infected bursal spaces underneath the fascia of the foot. The infection may or may not spread to the tendon sheath. A bursa is a fluid filled sac that lies between the muscle, tendon, and bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin and the fascia, a layer of fibrous tissue, to expose the infection. He removes the infected tissue and drains the fluid. He may remove the bursal sac if required. The tendon sheath may also be involved. If the wound is large, the provider leaves the incision open after irrigating the area, treating it with antibiotic, and packing it with gauze. Use this code when the provider performs incision and drainage below the fascia of the foot involving multiple areas. Terminology Bursa: A fluid filled sac that lies between the muscle, tendon, and bones. Tips Use 28002 when the provider performs the incision and drainage below the fascia of the foot involving a single bursal space. Read Less

short_description: Tenotomy, percutaneous, toe; single tendon
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a percutaneous tenotomy in which he incises or divides a single tendon in a toe through a small incision in the skin to correct a deformity like hammer toe. Explanation Tenotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider divides a muscle tendon to correct a deformity caused by congenital or acquired shortening of a muscle. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the skin of the toe over the tendon to be divided. He inserts a small cutting tool through the incision. Next, he incises the tendon to lengthen it. This allows the muscle to return to its normal length, allowing the joint to straighten, thereby correcting the deformity. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Terminology Hammer toe: A deformity that causes the toe to bend or curl. Tips Use 28011 when the provider performs percutaneous tenotomy of multiple tendons in a toe. Read Less

short_description: Release, tarsal tunnel (posterior tibial nerve decompression) Notes: (For other nerve entrapments, see 64704, 64722)
lay_term: The provider incises a fibrous band trapping the posterior tibial nerve in the lower leg to relieve the symptoms of tarsal tunnel syndrome, primarily pain, numbness, and tingling. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a skin incision midway between the Achilles tendon and the back of the medial malleolus, the bony knob on the outside of the ankle. She incises the retinaculum, the fibrous band protecting the surrounding nerve branches. The provider identifies the posterior tibial nerve and separates it from the artery and vein in the tarsal tunnel. She places vessel loops around the vessels and gently retract them, further releasing the nerve. If there is any scarring in the posterior tibial nerve or its branches, she opens the outer layer of the nerve wrapping and removes the scar tissue from within the nerve. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Achilles: Tendon at the heel, or calcaneal tendon. Tarsal tunnel: A narrow channel on the side of the ankle that encloses the posterior tibial nerve. Lateral malleolus: Bony knob on the outside of the ankle, at the bottom of the fibula, a bone in the lower leg. Malleolus: Bony knob on either side of the ankle on the lower leg bones, the tibia and fibula. Medial malleolus: Bony knob on the inside of the ankle, at the bottom of the tibia, a bone in the lower leg. Posterior tibial nerve decompression: Surgical incision of a fibrous brand entrapping the posterior nerve, the lower leg, as it runs through the tarsal tunnel, a narrow channel at the ankle. Tarsal tunnel syndrome: Tingling, numbness, and pain affecting the ankle and foot, the result of compression, or pressure, on the posterior tibial nerve in the lower within the tarsal tunnel. Vessel loop: A piece of suture, wire or other material that can be placed around a vessel to close off circulation while a procedure is performed. Tips If your provider may use a surgical assistant during this procedure, you should check whether your insurers will pay for that. For instance, if you review the Medicare Provider Fee Schedule, you'll see that Medicare assigns the 2 indicator to this code in the Asst. Surg. column, which means that payment restrictions for assistants at surgery do not apply to this particular procedure and that an assistant at surgery may be paid, according to Medicare, although without a guarantee. Therefore, you should bill for a surgical assistant during these procedures if the documentation demonstrates medical necessity for the assist. If the payer accepts the assistant surgeon's charge, you'll append modifier 80, Assistant surgeon, for the services of the assisting provider. Read Less

short_description: Synovectomy; intertarsal or tarsometatarsal joint, each
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a synovectomy, removing the inflamed or diseased synovium from the intertarsal or tarsometatarsal joint. Synovium is a thin membrane that lines the joint cavity. Intertarsal joints are the joints between the tarsal bones near the rear area of the foot. Tarsometatarsal joints are the joints between the tarsal and metatarsal bones of the foot. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the joint to be targeted in front of the ankle. He then dissects through soft tissue and reflects the tendon to expose the joint. He incises and opens the joint capsule to expose the synovium, a membrane lining the joint cavity. He then removes the inflamed synovium from the joint. Finally, he irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution and closes the wound in layers. Use one unit of this code for each intertarsal or tarsometatarsal joint synovectomy the provider performs. short_description: Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor, talus or calcaneus; with iliac or other autograft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a bone cyst or benign tumor of the talus or calcaneus, then harvests and implants an autograft to repair the site. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the cyst or tumor in the ankle or heel. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He identifies the tumor or cyst of the talus or calcaneus bone. The provider uses a curette to scrape or excise the lesion from the bone. He harvests the bone graft from the iliac bone and secures it to the site where the tumor or bone cyst was removed. Finally, he irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution and closes the wound in layers. Autograft: Tissue harvested from the patient’s own body used to replace diseased, damaged, or missing tissue. Benign tumor: Mass of cells, which does not spread to other parts of the body. Bone cyst: Abnormal sac usually containing fluid inside the bone. Calcaneus: Large tarsal bone of the heel. Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Iliac bone: Uppermost and widest bone of the pelvis, mainly used for bone grafts. Talus: Bone in the ankle that joins with the leg bones to form the ankle joint. short_description: Excision or curettage of bone cyst or benign tumor, tarsal or metatarsal, except talus or calcaneus; with allograft
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a bone cyst or benign tumor of the tarsal or metatarsal region, and then implants an allograft. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the skin over the cyst or tumor in the ankle or heel. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He identifies the tumor or cyst of the tarsal or metatarsal region, and then removes the lesion from the bone with a sharp cutting instrument. He harvests the allograft and secures it to the site where the tumor or bone cyst was removed. Finally, he irrigates the wound with antibiotic solution and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Anastomosis: Connection between two structures, anatomical or surgically created, such as between two blood vessels or the colon after resection of a part; types of anastomoses include end to side and side to side. Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called allogeneic graft and homograft. Benign tumor: Mass of cells which does not spread to other parts of the body. Bone cyst: Abnormal sac usually containing fluid inside the bone. Calcaneus: Large tarsal bone of the heel. Curette: Spoon shaped surgical instrument used for scraping. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Metatarsals: The five long bones located between the tarsal bones of the foot and phalanges of the toes. Phalanges: The bones present in the toes of the foot. Talus: Bone in the ankle that joins with the leg bones to form the ankle joint. Tarsal: The bones located in the midfoot and rearfoot area and are seven in number: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and lateral cuneiform. short_description: Ostectomy, complete excision; all metatarsal heads, with partial proximal phalangectomy, excluding first metatarsal (eg, Clayton type procedure)
lay_term: The provider surgically removes the bones of the second to fifth metatarsal heads completely along with their corresponding proximal phalanges to treat necrosis or infection. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes incisions over the metatarsophalangeal joints from the second to the fifth. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. The provider retracts the extensor tendons and exposes the metatarsal heads. He completely removes the metatarsal heads from the second to the fifth digit. The provider then extends the incision and partially removes the proximal phalanx of the second to fifth digits. The provider inserts pins or wires between the metatarsals and the remaining proximal phalanges of the second to fifth digits to maintain the correct position. He may apply a cast for stability. Finally, he closes the wound in layers. Terminology Cast: An external device that is used to hold a bone in the correct position. Clayton procedure: A procedure in which the provider excises the lesser metatarsal heads from the second to the fifth digit. Extensor tendon: Connects the extensor muscles, which are muscles in the hand or foot, to their bony attachments. Metatarsals: The five long bones located between the tarsal bones of the foot and phalanges of the toes. Metatarsophalangeal joints: Joints between the metatarsal head and proximal phalanges of the toes. Ostectomy: Surgical removal of a bone. Phalanges: The bones present in the fingers and toes; there are fourteen in each hand, three in each finger, and two in the thumb; in the toes, the great toe and usually the little toe have two phalanges, the middle toes three each; the singular form is phalanx. Proximal phalangectomy: Resection of the proximal phalanx. Tarsal bones: The bones located in the midfoot and rearfoot area and are seven in number: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and lateral cuneiform. Tips Use 28111, Ostectomy, complete excision of the first metatarsal head, when the provider completely removes the first metatarsal head. Read Less

short_description: Partial excision (craterization, saucerization, sequestrectomy, or diaphysectomy) bone (eg, osteomyelitis or bossing); talus or calcaneus
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes the infected portion of the talus or calcaneus bone using craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision on the posterior aspect of the foot. He dissects the soft tissues, bursa, and tendons from the insertion point of the Achilles tendon. The provider separates the Achilles tendon from its attachments and identifies the infected bone. He partially excises the infected portion of the bone. The provider excises the bone in a crater like piece, leaving a small saucer like depression in the bone, or he may instead excise the portion of the shaft of the long bone. The provider may fill the cavity left in the bone using a bone graft. Alternately, he may use sutures to reattach the Achilles tendon to the remaining calcaneus. Finally, he closes the wound in layers. Terminology Achilles tendon: A band of tissue that connects the muscle to the bone in the back of the foot. Bossing: Painful prominence. Bursa: Fluid filled sac that prevents joints, muscles, and tendons from rubbing together. Calcaneus: Large tarsal bone of the heel. Cavity: A hollow space within the body. Craterization: Surgical excision of the bone to create a crater like depression. Diaphysectomy: Surgical excision of the diaphysis. Diaphysis: Middle portion of a long bone. Exostosis: An abnormal bone growth on the surface of the bone. Necrosis: Cellular death. Ostectomy: Surgical removal of a bone. Osteomyelitis: Infection in the bone. Posterior: Closer to the back part of the body. Saucerization: Surgical removal of the bone to form a shallow depression that allows for drainage from the infected area of the wound. Sequestrectomy: Surgical removal of a sequestrum, a piece of necrotic bone. Talus: Bone in the ankle that joins with the leg bones to form the ankle joint. Tarsal bones: The bones located in the midfoot and rearfoot area and are seven in number: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and lateral cuneiform. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips Use 28122, Partial excision, craterization, saucerization, sequestrectomy, or diaphysectomy bone eg, osteomyelitis or bossing; tarsal or metatarsal bone, except talus or calcaneus, when the provider performs a partial excision of the infected portion of the tarsal or metatarsal bone using craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy. Use 28124, Partial excision, craterization, saucerization, sequestrectomy, or diaphysectomy bone eg, osteomyelitis or bossing; phalanx of toe, when the provider performs a partial excision of the infected portion of the phalanx of the toe using craterization, saucerization, or diaphysectomy. short_description: Repair, tendon, flexor, foot; secondary with free graft, each tendon (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: The provider performs a delayed repair of a rupture or tear of the tendon that enables the foot and toes to flex (bend) using a free graft that he has obtained from another part of the body. This code may be reported for each tendon repaired and includes obtaining the graft used for repair. Explanation The procedure involves using a graft to perform an open secondary repair of a tear or rupture of a "bending" tendon of foot or toe to restore joints to normal motion. Under local, regional, or general anesthesia, the orthopedist makes an incision over the secondary torn or ruptured flexor tendon of the foot. Surgery could involve the flexor hallucis longus, which bends down the big toe, or the flexor digitorum longus or its branches that bend down the second, third, fourth and fifth toes (flexion of phalanges 2 through 5). The orthopedist acquires a piece of tendon from the foot, toe, or another part of the body and grafts it to the ruptured tendon to restore function. The physician may also reattach the tendon to surrounding tissue and examine the area for other injury to nerves and blood vessels before closing the surgical field and applying sterile dressing and a cast, splint, or strap to immobilize the affected tendon(s). The orthopedist is responsible for preoperative surgical evaluation and postsurgical management. Report this code for each tendon repaired; obtaining the graft material is included in the repair, so do not report that separately. Terminology Secondary repair: Repair of an injury that usually occurs a few weeks or more after the injury. Free graft: An excised piece of tissue, unattached to its vascular supply, suitable for grafting (transplanting) to another location. Tips This code is for a secondary tendon repair that requires a graft. For coding purposes, secondary repair may also include delayed primary repair, which is performed after the first 24–hour period but within two weeks of the injury. You may list multiple units of the code if the orthopedist repairs multiple foot flexor tendons using grafts. Follow payer instructions to document multiple units using modifiers such as 59 (Distinct procedural service) or TA to T9 modifiers that identify left or right foot, and great toe through fifth digit, if appropriate. Distinguish this code from 28200, which is for primary or secondary foot flexor tendon repair that does not involve a graft. Do not assign a separate code for acquiring the graft. Read Less

short_description: Repair, tendon, extensor, foot; secondary with free graft, each tendon (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: The provider performs a delayed repair of a rupture or tear of the tendon that enables the foot and toes to straighten or unbend using a free graft that he has obtained from another part of the body. This code may be reported for each tendon repaired and includes obtaining the graft used for repair. Explanation The procedure involves open secondary repair of a torn or ruptured "straightening" tendon of the foot or toe to restore joints to normal motion. Under local, regional, or general anesthesia, the orthopedist makes a dorsal incision over the torn or ruptured extensor tendon of the foot. Surgery could involve the extensor digitorum longus, which passes across the top of the foot and attaches into the second, third, fourth and fifth toes, allowing lifting the toes upward, or surgery may involve the extensor hallucis longus and/or extensor hallucis brevis on top of the foot, which attach to the great toe and allow lifting the toe upward. The orthopedist acquires a piece of tendon from the foot, toe, or another part of the body and grafts it to the ruptured tendon to restore function. The physician may also reattach the tendon to surrounding tissue and examine the area for other injury to nerves and blood vessels before closing the surgical field and applying sterile dressing and a cast, splint, or strap to immobilize the affected tendon(s). The orthopedist is responsible for preoperative surgical evaluation and postsurgical management. Report this code for each tendon repaired; obtaining the graft material is included in the repair, so do not report that separately. Terminology Secondary repair: Repair of an injury that usually occurs a few weeks or more after the injury. Free graft: An excised piece of tissue, unattached to its vascular supply, suitable for grafting (transplanting) to another location. Tips This code is for a secondary tendon repair that requires a graft. You may list multiple units of the code if the orthopedist repairs multiple foot flexor tendons using grafts. Follow payer instructions to document multiple units using modifiers such as 59 (Distinct procedural service) or TA to T9 modifiers that identify left or right foot, and great toe through fifth digit, if appropriate. Distinguish this code from 28208, which is for primary or secondary foot extensor tendon repair that does not involve a graft. Do not assign a separate code for acquiring the graft. Read Less

short_description: Reconstruction (advancement), posterior tibial tendon with excision of accessory tarsal navicular bone (eg, Kidner type procedure) Notes: (For subcutaneous tenotomy, see 28010, 28011) (For transfer or transplant of tendon with muscle redirection or rerouting, see 27690-27692) (For extensor hallucis longus transfer with great toe IP fusion (Jones procedure), use 28760)
lay_term: The provider repositions the posterior tibial tendon in the ankle and excises an accessory tarsal navicular bone, an extra bone on the inner side of the foot, to relieve pain and discomfort. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the navicular bone upward along the course of the posterior tibial tendon. He dissects subcutaneous tissue to expose and remove the accessory navicular. To determine the need for tendon reconstruction, he checks for laxity of the posterior tibial tendon with the foot held in a neutral position. He then detaches the distal, or far, end of the posterior tibial tendon and advances it by drilling a hole through the navicular bone, passing the tendon through the hole, and suturing it back on itself to shorten the effective tendon length. He uses an alternate two–hole attachment or a surgical anchor to achieve tenodesis. The provider performs a layered closure and applies a sterile dressing and a cast with the foot in neutral position. Terminology Accessory navicular bone: An extra bone on the inner side of the foot that can cause irritation and require removal. Kidner type procedure: Surgical procedure to excise an accessory, or extra, tarsal navicular bone and reposition the posterior tibial tendon to relieve foot pain. Navicular bone: One of the tarsal bones, the seven bones of the ankle that connect to the tibia and fibula bones of the leg and to the metatarsal bones in the foot. Posterior tibial tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects the calf muscle to the bones in the ankle and foot. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue below the surface of the skin. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tenodesis: Surgical anchoring of a tendon that attaches a muscle to a joint to stabilize a tendon that slips out of place. Tips Code 28232 can be used to report a procedure that includes both a partial excision, or ostectomy, of the navicular and excision of the os navicularis, or accessory navicular, if the provider reconstructs the posterior tibial tendon in addition to the two excisions. Additional Info The most common of the extra bones in the foot, the accessory navicular bone occurs in a small percentage of the population, either as a distinct, separate bone, or fused completely or incompletely to, and thus enlarging, the navicular bone. In either case, the accessory navicular bone can interfere with the posterior tibial tendon's pull, which normally heightens the arch. When the accessory bone accompanies significant posterior tibial tendon dysfunction and flatfoot deformity, the orthopedist may perform a Kidner type procedure to excise the accessory navicular bone and advance, or shorten, the posterior tibial tendon. short_description: Capsulotomy, midfoot; extensive, including posterior talotibial capsulotomy and tendon(s) lengthening (eg, resistant clubfoot deformity)
lay_term: The provider performs an extensive repair on a clubfoot, a congenital defect, that did not respond to previous surgical correction. He incises the capsule that encloses the talotibial joint in the ankle and divides one or more tendons to lengthen them and relieve tension on the foot. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a medial ankle incision. He incises the subcutaneous tissue and fascia, releases adhesions and reflects the tendons. He identifies the talotibial capsule and incises it posteriorly to release tension on the foot. He then performs multiple tenotomies, incising and lengthening the tendons in a Z fashion. He may stabilize the bony structures with wire fixation. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. He applies an above knee cast with the foot in slight equinus position, with the toes pointing down. Terminology Capsulotomy: Surgical incision of a capsule, a protective membrane encasing a structure like a joint, lens, or kidney. Clubfoot: Also known as talipes equinovarus, a congenital or acquired condition in which the foot is severely abnormally twisted. Congenital: Present at birth. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Medial: Nearest to the middle of the body. Posterior: Closer to the back of the body or a structure. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Talotibial joint: Union of the tibia and the talus bone in the ankle. Tenotomy: Surgical incision of a tendon to lengthen it. Read Less

short_description: Syndactylization, toes (eg, webbing or Kelikian type procedure)
lay_term: The provider creates an artificial web (syndactylization) between two existing toes to correct a flail (floppy) toe caused by a congenital deformity. Explanation Syndactylization is the process of joining together digits. For congenital foot deformities that involve missing digit(s) with a large gap between existing toes, the surgeon may fuse the gap by creating an artificial syndactylization (webbing) between the toes. Under local, regional, or general anesthesia, the orthopedist makes a dorsal incision along the space between the foot cleft and extending to the ends of the two separated toes. After retracting skin and soft tissue, the orthopedist aligns the foot bones by performing osteotomies at the base of each proximal phalanx. The surgeon then closes the incisions, pulling the toes together by "webbing" the skin to eliminate the gap between the toes. The physician controls bleeding before closing the surgical field and applying sterile dressing. The orthopedist is responsible for preoperative surgical evaluation and post–surgical management. short_description: Correction, hammertoe (eg, interphalangeal fusion, partial or total phalangectomy)
lay_term: The provider repairs a hammertoe deformity, a painful condition in which the toe remains permanently bent in a downward position. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the proximal interphalangeal joint. He uses a small blade to section, or cut, the ligaments from both sides. He exposes the proximal interphalangeal joint. He exposes the head and neck of the proximal phalanx, the toe bone closest to the body, and removes it with a rongeur. He completely removes the proximal phalanx. He then inserts a wire into the middle and proximal phalanges and fuses the proximal interphalangeal joint. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. He applies a cast. Terminology Compartment syndrome: Critical build up of pressure due to fluid accumulation within a membrane covered compartment that contains vessels, nerves, and other structures; without prompt attention and release of pressure, permanent damage to these delicate structures ensues. Diabetes mellitus: Disease in which the body's production or utilization of insulin, the primary hormone involved in glucose metabolism, is insufficient, leading to high levels of blood glucose and subsequent complications, including significant damage to nerves, vessels, and multiple organs. Hammertoe: Painful deformity of a toe that is bent downward, often the result of ill fitting footwear. Interphalangeal fusion: Permanent joining of the joint between phalanges, or toe bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connects bones and joints as well as holds organs in place. Phalangectomy: Surgical excision of a phalanx, a bone in the finger or toe. Phalanx: Finger or toe bone. Proximal interphalangeal joint, or PIPJ: Joint between the bones of the toes that is closest to the body. Rongeur: Surgical instrument similar to forceps, or tongs, that can cut through bone. Use the specific T modifiers, such as T3, Left foot, fourth digit, for multiple hammertoe corrections and to specify the toe. Remember that T modifiers are anatomic modifiers, and you can only report one anatomic modifier per line item. They are traditionally used for ambulatory surgery center, or ASC, or other outpatient facilities and have only been approved for physician billing in recent years. Therefore, you may still have difficulty with some carriers accepting T modifiers from provider offices. Check your carrier guidelines and be ready with supporting documentation if needed. The most common causes of hammering are a constricted toe box in shoes that compress the toes. short_description: Correction, cock-up fifth toe, with plastic skin closure (eg, Ruiz-Mora type procedure)
lay_term: The provider corrects a hammer toe deformity in which the fifth toe curls upward by performing resection of the proximal phalanx with a volar plastic closure. Explanation Cock–up fifth toe is a hammer toe of the fifth digit. Because hammer toe procedures leave the fifth digit too straight, causing difficulty in shoes, orthopedists often perform this plastic skin closure procedure instead. The procedure involves removing a portion of the tip of the toe bone, releasing associated tendons, and pulling the toe into alignment by tight suturing of the skin. Under local, regional, or general anesthesia, the orthopedist removes an ellipse of skin from the plantar approach to the proximal phalanx of the fifth toe. The surgeon dissects and retracts the flexor tendons to expose the proximal interphalangeal joint and perform a transverse capsulotomy. After releasing the collateral ligaments, the surgeon performs a subtotal phalangectomy, removing the head of the proximal phalanx. The orthopedist checks the redundancy or laxity of the flexor and extensor tendons with the shortened phalanx and sutures the tendons, as needed. The surgeon then closes the skin in such a way that it pulls the toe into the corrected plantar–medial position. The physician controls bleeding before closing the surgical field and applying sterile dressing and splinting or taping the toe in the corrected position. The orthopedist is responsible for pre–operative surgical evaluation and post–surgical management. Terminology Hammer toe: A deformity that causes the toe to bend or curl. Tips If the patient has an angular deformity of the lessor toe that simply requires realignment of supple soft tissues, report 28313. short_description: Hallux rigidus correction with cheilectomy, debridement and capsular release of the first metatarsophalangeal joint; without implant
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically corrects a hallux rigidus deformity without the need for an implant. Hallux rigidus is pain and stiffness due to arthritis, or inflammation in the metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe, or the joint where the head of the metatarsal bone attaches to the first bone of the greater toe. The condition causes pain, stiffness, and restriction of movement. The provider also performs a cheilectomy, or the removal of bone spurs from the joint, along with debridement and capsular release of the metatarsophalangeal joint to free tightened connective tissue and loosen the ball and socket joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the metatarsophalangeal joint. The provider explores the joint for loose bodies and joint abnormalities. The provider debrides any excessive synovial tissue. The provider then uses a saw to cut the bony spurs present on the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. The provider next excises the eroded joint surface of the metatarsal head. Finally, the provider obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound, such as by suturing the soft tissue in layers. short_description: Correction, hallux valgus with bunionectomy, with sesamoidectomy when performed; with resection of proximal phalanx base, when performed, any method
lay_term: The provider removes bone from a bunion, a foot deformity that causes a bump near where the big toe joins the foot. The provider also may remove the sesamoid bones (pea–shaped bones under the big toe joint). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the foot over the target area to reach the first metatarsophalangeal joint, where the foot’s metatarsal bone meets the proximal phalanx (bone of the big toe). The provider may use various methods to remove the prominent or hypertrophied (increased) bone of the bunion (hallux valgus) from the side and possibly other areas of the metatarsal head. The provider also may remove excess bone from the base of the proximal phalanx. The provider also may perform a sesamoidectomy, or removal of one or both sesamoid bones, two pea–shaped bones under the big toe joint. The provider may correct, resect (cut out), or release soft tissues. The provider checks for bleeding and closes incisions. Terminology Bunion: A deformity that develops on the first metatarsal bone and causes the big toe to bend toward the second toe. Metatarsals: The five long bones located between the tarsal bones of the foot and phalanges of the toes. Metatarsophalangeal joint: The joint between a metatarsal bone in the foot with the first phalanx bone of a digit (toe). Phalanges: The bones present in the fingers and toes; there are fourteen in each hand, three in each finger, and two in the thumb; in the toes, the great toe and usually the little toe have two phalanges, the middle toes three each; the singular form is phalanx. Proximal: Located close to the center of the body or close to a structure’s point of attachment. Resect: To excise (cut out) tissues, organs, or other structures, in whole or in part. Sesamoid bones: Small bones within a tendon where it passes over a joint; a sesamoid bone lies under the metatarsal head of each toe and, when inflamed, causes pain. Tips There are multiple codes for bunionectomies. Be sure to select the code based on the procedure performed. Read Less

These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). short_description: Osteotomy; calcaneus (eg, Dwyer or Chambers type procedure), with or without internal fixation
lay_term: The provider chooses among various approaches to perform an osteotomy of the calcaneus, or heel bone. He surgically incises the bone to create a controlled break and then realigns the bone. He performs this procedure to treat conditions such as abnormally high or low arches or other conditions affecting foot alignment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider chooses among various techniques, depending on the deformity. In a typical procedure, she incises the skin and dissects down through tissues to bone; she makes sure that she protects the sural nerve, the nerve on the side of the heel and foot. After exposing the calcaneus, the provider uses an osteotome to make incisions to form a wedge shape in the bone. Once she removes the wedge, she aligns the bones into a new position. She may fix the bones in place with screws and wire. The provider controls any bleeding, removes all instruments, and finally closes the incision in the skin in layers. Terminology Dissection: Separation of tissue by layers; blunt dissection separates tissue layers using the fingers; sharp dissection separates tissue layers with a blade. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Osteotome: A surgical instrument used to cut bone. Tips Techniques you may see for calcaneal osteotomy include Evans, performed toward the front of the heel bone; Dwyer, with incisions starting on the outside of the heel and joining on the inside with bone taken from the side of the heel; medial shift, which frees a bone fragment and moves it to the inside of the foot; or lateral shift, which frees a bone fragment and moves it to the outside of the foot. short_description: Osteotomy; talus
lay_term: The provider chooses among various approaches and performs an osteotomy of the talus, or ankle bone, i.e., he surgically incises or transects the bone and then realigns it. He performs this procedure to treat an irreducible dislocation of the ankle or fractures of the body and neck of the talus and reduce chronic ankle instability. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider chooses among various approaches, such as anterolateral, posterolateral, anteromedial, or transmalleolar, depending on the deformity. He incises the skin and dissects down through tissues to bone; he makes sure that he protects the sural nerve, the nerve on the side of the heel and foot. The provider uses osteotomes to make a wedge–shaped cut into the bone, cracks the medial malleolar bone, and then uses a curette and rongeurs to remove bone to the opposite cortex, the outer covering of the bone. Once the wedge is removed, he aligns the bones into a new position. He fixes the bones in place with screws and wire. The provider controls any bleeding, removes all instruments, and finally closes the incision in the skin in layers. Terminology Dissection: Separation of tissue by layers; blunt dissection separates tissue layers using the fingers; sharp dissection separates tissue layers with a blade. Image intensifier: Component that converts X–ray images to visible images the provider views on a screen, often used in orthopedic surgery. Osteotome: A surgical instrument used to cut bone. Transmalleolar: Through the malleolus, the rounded bony process on either side of the ankle. Tips During or after the procedure, the provider may use image intensifiers, separately reportable, to check the proper placement of bones. If your provider uses a surgical assistant during this procedure, you should check whether your insurers will pay for that. The Medicare Provider Fee Schedule assigns the number 2 indicator to this code in the assistant surgeon column, which means that payment restriction for surgical assistants does not apply to this procedure. Therefore, you should bill for a surgical assistant for these procedures if the documentation demonstrates medical necessity for the assist. When an assistant surgeon assists an operating or principal surgeon during an entire procedure, the code requires modifier 80, Assistant surgeon. When your provider needs surgical assistance for only part of a procedure, you’ll use modifier 81, Minimum assistant surgeon. When a physician or a physician assistant assists for the entire surgical procedure because a medical resident was unavailable to assist, attach modifier 82, Assistant surgeon, when qualified resident surgeon not available. If a nonphysician practitioner, NPP, i.e., physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist serves as an assistant provider, you must use modifier AS, in addition to modifier 80 or 82, to represent the assistant's work to Medicare payers. short_description: Osteotomy, tarsal bones, other than calcaneus or talus; with autograft (includes obtaining graft) (eg, Fowler type)
lay_term: The provider performs an osteotomy of the tarsal bones, i.e., he surgically incises or transects the foot bones adjacent to the articulation, or joint, between the foot and the leg, and then realigns the bones. He also places a bone graft to fill in gaps in the tarsal bones and straighten the deformity. This procedure excludes the two tarsal bones closest to the articulation, i.e., the calcaneus, or heel bone, and the talus, or ankle bone. The provider performs this procedure to fixate a talus fracture or repair a deformity such as a tarsal coalition and maximize the movement of the ankle joint. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision transversely, or crosswise, over the involved tarsal bones, which can include the cuneiform, navicular, or cuboid bones. The provider retracts associated nerves and tendons and incises the abnormal bony, cartilaginous, or fibrous connections between the tarsal bones. He then realigns the bones. The provider determines that a graft is needed to fill the gaps in the tarsal bones and straighten the deformity. He can use bone harvested from various sites, such as the iliac crest or the bone taken from the wedge osteotomy of the lateral cuboid. If he chooses to harvest the bone graft from the iliac crest, he makes an incision over the iliac crest, dissects down through the layers of tissue until he reaches bone, and then removes a portion of bone to use as an autograft. He closes the incision over the iliac crest in layers. He then places the graft in the space between the tarsal bones. Finally, the provider controls any bleeding, removes all instruments, and closes the incision in the skin in layers. He applies a sterile dressing and a cast or splint. Terminology Autograft: A graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Cartilaginous: Pertaining to the connective tissue that holds bones in position. Fibrous: Pertaining to a type of connective tissue, most commonly collagen, a type of protein. Fowler type osteotomy: A surgical procedure performed to correct metatarsus adductus, or a deviation of the forefoot toward the midline. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Iliac crest: Upper edge of the ilium, the upper part of the pelvic bone; also called the crest of the ilium. Tarsal coalition: An abnormal connection between tarsal bones. Although the condition may be congenital, symptoms may not arise until much later. Tips You should check the documentation to confirm that the provider used an autograft. The provider should document where he harvested the graft from to help you determine that he did use an autograft. If you do not see this documentation, check with the provider to be sure you choose the proper code because obtaining the graft, called harvesting, is included in this code; do not report the bone harvesting separately. If the provider did not perform an autograft, use 28304, Osteotomy, tarsal bones, other than calcaneus or talus. If your provider uses a surgical assistant during this procedure, you should check whether your insurers will pay for that. The Medicare Provider Fee Schedule assigns the number 2 indicator to this code in the assistant surgeon column, which means that payment restriction for surgical assistants does not apply to this procedure. Therefore, you should bill for a surgical assistant for these procedures if the documentation demonstrates medical necessity for the assist. When an assistant surgeon assists an operating or principal surgeon during an entire procedure, the code requires modifier 80, Assistant surgeon. When your provider needs surgical assistance for only part of a procedure, you’ll use modifier 81, Minimum assistant surgeon. When a physician or a physician assistant assists for the entire surgical procedure because a medical resident was unavailable to assist, attach modifier 82, Assistant surgeon, when qualified resident surgeon not available. If a nonphysician practitioner, NPP, i.e., physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist serves as an assistant provider, you must use modifier AS, in addition to modifier 80 or 82, to represent the assistant's work to Medicare payers. short_description: Osteotomy, with or without lengthening, shortening or angular correction, metatarsal; first metatarsal
lay_term: The provider performs an osteotomy of the first metatarsal bone to remove a bunion and realign the metatarsal bone and the toe. He may or may not lengthen, shorten, or correct an angular deformity of the first metatarsal. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the metatarsophalangeal joint. He deepens the incision through skin and soft tissue and takes care to identify and retract all vital neurovascular structures. He excises the medial eminence, or the bony bump or prominence, from the metatarsal bone. If he needs to lengthen the bone, he may transect it and pull the two pieces apart a little bit, allowing osseous, or bony, regrowth to fill in the gap. If he needs to shorten the metatarsal bone, he removes a portion of the bone and rejoins the two ends. To correct an angular deformity, he realigns the metatarsal bone with the toe and fixes it into place with metal screws to ensure that the bone heals in correct alignment. The provider then checks for and controls any bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in layers. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Metatarsal bones: Five bones that make up the foot; they connect to the tarsal bones of the ankle and to the phalanges, or bones of digits, or toes. Metatarsophalangeal joint: The joint between the head of the metatarsal bone and the first bone of the toe. Neurovascular: Pertaining to nerves and blood vessels. Osteotomy: Surgical incision, excision of a portion, or transection of a bone to shorten, lengthen, or change its alignment. Transection: Cutting through or across a structure. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. short_description: Osteotomy, with or without lengthening, shortening or angular correction, metatarsal; first metatarsal with autograft (other than first toe)
lay_term: The provider performs an osteotomy of the first metatarsal bone, other than the one that articulates, or connects, with the first toe. He may or may not lengthen, shorten, or correct an angular deformity of the first metatarsal. He performs a bone graft using bone harvested from the patient to correct shortening of the first metatarsal. He performs the procedure to correct a deformity and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the metatarsophalangeal joint. He deepens the incision through skin and soft tissue and takes care to identify and retract all vital neurovascular structures. He excises the medial eminence, or bony bump or prominence, from the metatarsal bone. To correct an angular deformity, he realigns the metatarsal bone with the toe and fixes it into place with metal screws or wire to ensure that the bone heals in correct alignment. The provider determines that a bone graft is needed. He can harvest bone from various sites, the iliac crest being the most common site. If he chooses to harvest the bone graft from the iliac crest, he makes an incision over the iliac crest, dissects down through the layers of tissue until he reaches bone, and then removes a portion of bone to use as an autograft. He closes the incision over the iliac crest in layers. He then places the graft in the space between the cut ends of the metatarsal bone. The provider then checks for and controls any bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in layers. Terminology Autograft: A graft harvested from another location in the patient’s own body. Harvest: Remove skin, a portion of a vessel, bone, or other tissue from a patient or donor, generally to be used for grafting or anastomosis. Metatarsal bones: Five bones that make up the foot; they connect to the tarsal bones of the ankle and to the phalanges, i.e., the bones of the digits, or toes. Metatarsophalangeal joint: The joint between the head of the metatarsal bone and the first bone of the toe. Neurovascular: Pertaining to the nerves and the blood vessels. Osteotomy: Surgical incision, excision of a portion, or transection of a bone to shorten, lengthen, or change its alignment. Tips You should check the documentation for confirmation that the provider used an autograft. The provider should document where he harvested the graft from to help you determine that he did use an autograft. If you do not see this documentation, check with the provider to be sure you choose the proper code because obtaining the graft, called harvesting, is included in this code; do not report the bone harvesting separately. If the provider performed the same procedure but without an autograft, use 28306, Osteotomy, with or without lengthening, shortening or angular correction, metatarsal; first metatarsal. If your provider uses a surgical assistant during this procedure, you should check whether your insurers will pay for that. The Medicare Provider Fee Schedule assigns the number 2 indicator to this code in the assistant surgeon column, which means that payment restriction for surgical assistants does not apply to this procedure. Therefore, you should bill for a surgical assistant for these procedures if the documentation demonstrates medical necessity for the assist. When an assistant surgeon assists an operating or principal surgeon during an entire procedure, the code requires modifier 80, Assistant surgeon. When your provider needs surgical assistance for only part of a procedure, you’ll use modifier 81, Minimum assistant surgeon. When a physician or a physician assistant assists for the entire surgical procedure because a medical resident was unavailable to assist, attach modifier 82, Assistant surgeon, when qualified resident surgeon not available. If a nonphysician practitioner, NPP, i.e., physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist serves as an assistant provider, you must use modifier AS, in addition to modifier 80 or 82, to represent the assistant's work to Medicare payers. short_description: Osteotomy, with or without lengthening, shortening or angular correction, metatarsal; other than first metatarsal, each
lay_term: The provider performs an osteotomy of any metatarsal bone other than the first. He may or may not lengthen, shorten, or correct an angular deformity of the metatarsal. He performs the procedure to repair a foot deformity and realign the metatarsal bone and the toe. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over a metatarsophalangeal joint, except for the first metatarsal. He deepens the incision through skin and soft tissue and takes care to identify and retract all vital neurovascular structures. He excises the medial eminence, or bony bump or prominence, from the metatarsal bone. If he needs to lengthen the bone, he may transect it and pull the two pieces apart a little bit, allowing osseous, or bony, regrowth to fill in the gap. If he needs to shorten the metatarsal bone, he removes a portion of the bone and rejoins the two ends with a screw or wire. To correct an angular deformity, he realigns the metatarsal bone with the toe and fixes it into place with metal screws to ensure that the bone heals in correct alignment. The provider then checks for and controls any bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in layers. Terminology Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. Metatarsal bones: Five bones that make up the foot; they connect to the tarsal bones of the ankle and to the phalanges, or bones of digits, or toes. Metatarsophalangeal joint: The joint between the head of the metatarsal bone and the first bone of the toe. Neurovascular: Pertaining to nerves and blood vessels. Osteotomy: Surgical incision, excision of a portion, or transection of a bone to shorten, lengthen, or change its alignment. Transection: Cutting through or across a structure. short_description: Osteotomy, with or without lengthening, shortening or angular correction, metatarsal; multiple (eg, Swanson type cavus foot procedure)
lay_term: The provider performs an osteotomy of multiple metatarsal bones to treat a foot deformity called pes cavus and realign the bones in their proper position. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over metatarsal bones of the foot, except for the first metatarsal. He deepens the incision through skin and soft tissue and takes care to identify and retract all vital neurovascular structures. He moves the lateral tendons, i.e., the fibrous tissue that connects muscle to bone, medially. He addresses any deformities noted in multiple metatarsals. If he needs to lengthen the bone, he may transect it and pull the two pieces apart a little bit, allowing osseous, or bony, regrowth to fill in the gap. If he needs to shorten the metatarsal bone, he removes a portion of the bone and rejoins the two ends with a screw or wire. To correct an angular deformity, he realigns the metatarsal bone and fixes it into place with metal screws to ensure that the bone heals in correct alignment. The provider then checks for and controls any bleeding, removes any instruments, and finally closes the incision in layers. Terminology Excision: Removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also resection. Metatarsal bones: Five bones that make up the foot; they connect to the tarsal bones of the ankle and to the phalanges, or bones of digits, or toes. short_description: Osteotomy, shortening, angular or rotational correction; proximal phalanx, first toe (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs an osteotomy, cutting a portion of the bone of the proximal phalanx in the first toe to correct alignment and deformity. Explanation Osteotomy is a surgical procedure in which the provider cuts a portion of a bone, typically wedge–shaped, to correct a deformity. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the proximal phalanx of the greater toe. He then cuts through soft tissue and incises the periosteum, the outer covering of the bone. He then elevates the periosteum and removes a wedge–shaped piece of bone from the proximal phalanx to correct the alignment of the bone. He may also use implants like nails, screws, or wire to fix the bone in correct alignment. He then attaches back the periosteum and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissues together. Terminology Phalanx or phalanges: Bones present in the toes; each toe has three phalanges except the greater toe which has only two phalanges. If the provider performs the 28310 procedure with an unrelated procedure, you may need to append modifier 59 to 28310. Read Less

short_description: Reconstruction, angular deformity of toe, soft tissue procedures only (eg, overlapping second toe, fifth toe, curly toes)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically corrects an angular deformity of the toe, like curly toes, by releasing the tight soft tissues and by transferring the muscle tendons. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the toe. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, just under the skin. Next, he retracts nerves and blood vessels to identify the tight muscle tendons and other soft tissues and adhesions. He then releases the tight soft tissue, which may include opening the joint capsule. He may transfer the muscle tendons from their original attachments to new locations so that the muscle no longer pulls on the joint in a way that causes a toe deformity. Finally, he stops bleeding at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He places the foot in a soft dressing or cast for a few weeks to maintain the corrected alignment of the toe. The entire surgical procedure involves work on soft tissues without any cutting of the bone. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery, that form between tissues and organs; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Curly toes: A deformity in which the toes are bent downward or sideways toward the sole of the foot. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Read Less

short_description: Repair, nonunion or malunion; tarsal bones
lay_term: The provider performs surgical repair of fractured tarsal bones that have either healed in the wrong position, i.e., malunion, or have not rejoined, i.e., nonunion. These complications occur when the fractured site has a poor blood supply or gets infected. He performs the procedure to restore function and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the tarsal bones and exposes the old fracture. He removes all scar tissue from between the fractured fragments. The exact procedure will vary based on the fracture location and the type of nonunion or malunion. If a nonunion is present, the provider realigns the bones and fixes them in place. He may need to remove some of the devitalized bone from the fracture surfaces so that the ends will rejoin and heal. If a malunion is present, the provider realigns the bones; again, he may need to incise, excise, or completely remove some of the tarsal bones to achieve an adequate alignment. In both instances, he typically stabilizes the fractured metatarsal bones with metal plates, rods and pins. After he surgically corrects the malunion or nonunion, the provider controls any bleeding, closes the incision, and applies a sterile dressing and splints, casts, or straps. Terminology Devitalized bone: Dead bone; bone that cannot produce living cells due to trauma or loss of blood supply. Tarsal bones: Seven bones of the ankle; they connect to the tibia and fibula bones of the leg and to the metatarsal bones in the foot. Read Less

short_description: Repair, nonunion or malunion; metatarsal, with or without bone graft (includes obtaining graft)
lay_term: The provider performs surgical repair, which includes placement of a bone graft, of fractured metatarsal bones that have either healed in the wrong position, i.e., malunion, or have not rejoined, i.e., nonunion. These complications occur when the fractured site has a poor blood supply or gets infected. He performs the procedure to restore function and relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the metatarsal bones and exposes the old fracture. He removes all scar tissue from between the fractured fragments. The exact procedure will vary based on the fracture location and the type of nonunion or malunion. If a nonunion is present, the provider realigns the bones and fixes them in place. He may need to remove some of the devitalized bone from the fracture surfaces so that the ends will rejoin and heal. If a malunion is present, the provider realigns the bones; again, he may need to incise, excise, or completely remove some of the tarsal bones to achieve an adequate alignment. If the provider determines that a graft is needed to fill the gap between two bone fragments, he can harvest bone from various sites, the iliac crest being the most common site. If he chooses to harvest the bone graft from the iliac crest, he makes an incision over the iliac crest, dissects down through the layers of tissue until he reaches bone, and then removes a portion of bone to use as a graft. He closes the incision over the iliac crest in layers. He then places the graft in the space between the bone fragments. He stabilizes the fractured metatarsal bones with metal plates, rods and pins. After he surgically corrects the malunion or nonunion, the provider controls any bleeding, closes the incision, and applies a sterile dressing and splints, casts, or straps to stabilize the bone in proper alignment. Iliac crest: Upper edge of the ilium, the upper part of the pelvic bone; also called the crest of the ilium. Tarsal bones: Seven bones of the ankle; they connect to the tibia and fibula bones of the leg and to the metatarsal bones in the foot.
