guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. For radical resection of tumor(s) of cutaneous origin (eg, melanoma), see 11600-11646. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty and complex bone repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. It may require removal of the entire bone if tumor growth is extensive (eg, clavicle). Radical resection of bone tumors is usually performed for malignant tumors or very aggressive benign tumors. If surrounding soft tissue is removed during these procedures, the radical resection of soft tissue tumor codes should not be reported separately. Code selection is based solely on the location of the tumor, not on the size of the tumor or whether the tumor is benign or malignant, primary or metastatic.

short_description: Reconstruction, toe(s); syndactyly, with or without skin graft(s), each web
lay_term: The provider incises connective tissue (web) between fused digits, one web at a time, to treat syndactyly (digits fused together by a web of tissue). Skin graft, if performed, is included with this procedure. Explanation After the patient is prepped and anesthetized, the provider applies a tourniquet to restrict blood flow to the operative field and makes a zigzag incision between the joined toes and removes excess tissue. He debrides the area before applying skin grafts, if any. Close attention is paid to maintaining vascularization (blood flow) to the flaps created when the web was divided. The provider then performs a layered closure using absorbable sutures. He also applies antibiotic ointment over any skin grafts and a nonabsorbent bulky sterile dressing over the foot with cotton fluffs between the toes. He may apply an splint or cast to help immobilize and protect the foot. Terminology Syndactyly: Fusion of two or more digits of a hand or foot by a web of tissue; the tissue web may be partial or extend to the tips of the digits; bone fusion is less common but may be present; also called conjoined or webbed digits. Tips This code represents the separation of a single web between two digits. Each web space is a unit. Multiple procedures to separate additional web(s) may be performed, usually at separate settings. If webbing is present on both sides of a digit, only one side will generally be treated at a time to avoid compromising blood supply. However, if multiple webs are divided at the same setting, you may report the code for each web separation; use appropriate modifiers to identify the additional procedures as separate procedures. As noted in the descriptor for this code, if skin grafts are employed, they are included in the procedure and should not be reported separately. If the same procedure is performed bilaterally during the same operative session, append modifier 50. Payers may require the provider to report two units of service when billing a claim for a procedure code with modifier 50. However, some payers do not recognize modifier 50 and require the provider to submit a claim showing the procedure code twice, once with modifier LT, for the left side, and once with modifier RT, for the right side, with one unit of service for each. Check with the payer to ascertain how they prefer the procedures to be reported. If a splint or cast is applied, see CPT® guidelines to determine whether the application and/or supply can be reported separately. Read Less

short_description: Closed treatment of calcaneal fracture; without manipulation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a closed treatment of a calcaneal fracture, a crack or break in the calcaneus, or the heel bone. Treatment does not include manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone nor does it require open surgery. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider performs a closed treatment of a calcaneal bone fracture. If the break appears clean and well aligned as evident from a separately reportable X–ray, he performs no manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone to regain alignment. The provider stabilizes the fracture and advises the patient on ways to manage the pain. He places the patient in a cast, brace, or splint for a period of about four to six weeks to help with healing. He may perform a separately reportable X–ray examination of the heel bone to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Closed treatment: Treatment of a fracture, or broken bone, without making a surgical incision, with or without manipulation, and with or without the use of a traction device that applies a force. Fracture: To break; as in a broken bone. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips When the provider performs a closed treatment of a calcaneal fracture with manipulation to regain alignment of the broken bones, use 28405, Closed treatment of calcaneal fracture; with manipulation. short_description: Closed treatment of talus fracture; without manipulation
lay_term: The provider stabilizes a nondisplaced fracture of the talus, a small bone that sits between the calcaneus (heel bone) and the two long bones of the lower leg, typically by applying a cast. Explanation A talus fracture is a crack or break in the talus, a small bone between the heel and the two bones of the lower leg, which forms the part of the ankle closest to and above the heel bone (calcaneus). This code describes closed fracture care when the bone fragment(s) are appropriately aligned without manipulation by the physician. The orthopedist treats an anterior or posterior talus bone fracture that does not involve aligning displaced bone fragments by stabilizing the ankle while it heals. The orthopedist is responsible for presurgical evaluation and postsurgical management. Terminology Closed reduction: Treatment of a fracture (broken bone) without making a surgical incision, with or without manipulation, and with or without the use of a traction device that applies a force. Tips This code describes talus fracture treatment that does not involve open or percutaneous surgery or manipulation. For closed talus fracture treatment requiring manipulation, see 28435; for percutaneous talus fracture treatment with manipulation and skeletal fixation, see 28436. For open talus fracture treatment with or without internal fixation, see 28445. The surgical package for this code includes patient exam, initial cast/strap application, cast removal and follow–up exam, so don't bill those separately. You can separately report the X–ray using the appropriate code such as 73600 to 73630 for ankle or foot radiological exam. Do not use the generic tarsal bone code 28450 for this service, even though the talus is a tarsal bone; use the more specific talus code 28430 instead. Read Less

short_description: Percutaneous skeletal fixation of talus fracture, with manipulation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs treatment of a talus fracture using screws and pins through the skin. He also performs manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone. Explanation A talus fracture is a crack in the talus bone, a small bone that sits between the heel bone and two bones of the lower leg. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the fractured fragment by exerting pushing or pulling force on the foot and leg to reduce the fracture. He next creates a small incision in the skin over the fractured site. He then inserts pins and screws through this incision to hold the reduced fracture fragment in place. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the skin. He next places the ankle in a cast or brace for a period of four to six weeks. He may perform a separately reported X–ray examination of the talus to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. short_description: Open osteochondral autograft, talus (includes obtaining graft[s]) Notes: (Do not report 28446 in conjunction with 27705, 27707) (For arthroscopic osteochondral talus graft, use 29892) (For open osteochondral allograft or repairs with industrial grafts, use 28899)
lay_term: The provider performs osteochondral autograft on a patient's talus to treat a symptomatic osteochondritis dissecans lesion, abbreviated as OCD. The procedure involves moving healthy tissue from one area of the patient’s body to a defective area of the ankle bone through an open incision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision down to the area of the talus defect. He then scrapes and excises the area of defect until he reaches the healthy part of the bone. The provider then uses a coring reamer system to crop an osteochondral graft from the patient’s articular cartilage. He inserts the graft into the damaged part of the talus possibly using pins and screws. Finally, he ensures hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, at the site and closes the excised area in layers. Terminology Articular cartilage: Tissue covering the ends of the bone, where the two bones join to each other. Coring reamer system: System to collect cylindrical bone, thereby creating a tunnel in the bone. Osteochondral autograft: Transferring healthy cartilage from one part of the body to an area of defect in another part of the same person. Osteochondritis dissecans: Separation of joint cartilage from underlying bone. Talus: Ankle bone. Tibia: Bone present in the lower front area of the leg; also called a shinbone. Tips Report 28446 only once for osteochondral repair irrespective of the number of harvests and grafts the provider uses in the procedure. Read Less

short_description: Percutaneous skeletal fixation of metatarsal fracture, with manipulation, each
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs treatment of a metatarsal bone fracture using screws and pins through the skin. Treatment includes manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone. Metatarsals are the five long bones located between the tarsal bones of the foot and phalanges of the toes. Explanation A metatarsal fracture is a crack in the metatarsal bone. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the fractured fragment by exerting pushing or pulling forces on the foot to reduce the fracture. He next creates a small incision in the skin over the fractured site. He then inserts pins and screws through this incision to hold the reduced fracture fragment in place. He next places the foot in a cast or brace for a period of four to six weeks. He may perform a separately reported X–ray examination of the metatarsal bone to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Use one unit of this code for each metatarsal bone fracture the provider treats. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. Tips Use 28470–28475 when the provider performs closed treatment of a metatarsal fracture. Use 28485 when the provider performs open treatment of a metatarsal fracture with or without internal fixation. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs open treatment of a metatarsal fracture. She may or may not use internal fixation implants like pins or screws to fix the fracture. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the fractured bone. She then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. She next retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the metatarsal fracture. She then adjusts the bone to reduce the fractured fragments. short_description: Closed treatment of fracture great toe, phalanx or phalanges; without manipulation
lay_term: The provider repairs a great toe or phalanx fracture without surgery and without manipulation. Explanation Closed treatment means that the provider does not break the skin to treat the patient’s fracture. The provider also does not manipulate the fracture to repair it, meaning that he does not realign the ends of the fractured bone to its original position. Once the provider confirms the great toe or phalanx fracture by X–ray, he typically tapes the broken toe to an adjacent toe to hold it into place to promote healing. He also places gauze between the toes for moisture absorption. The provider instructs the patient to replace the tape and gauze as needed and to elevate and limit weight bearing on the affected foot. For patients with diabetes or toe numbness, the provider will not tape the toes together but instead will fit the patient with a rigid flat soled shoe to wear for up to three weeks. In other cases, the provider may fit the patient with a fracture brace or walking cast with a toe plate. The patient may also need to use crutches for walking. short_description: Percutaneous skeletal fixation of fracture great toe, phalanx or phalanges, with manipulation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs treatment of a phalanx or phalanges fracture in a great toe using screws and pins through the skin. Treatment includes manipulation, or adjustment, of the fractured bone. Phalanges are bones of the toe. There are three in each toe except the greater toe, which has two phalanges. Explanation Fracture is a break, or crack, in the continuity of a bone. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider adjusts the fractured fragment by exerting pushing or pulling force on the toe to reduce the fracture. He next creates a small incision in the skin over the fractured site. He then inserts pins and screws through this incision to hold the reduced fracture fragments in place. He next places the toe in a splint or brace for a period of four weeks. He may perform a separately reported X–ray examination of the toe to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. Tips Use 28490 when the provider performs closed treatment of a fracture in a great toe phalanx without manipulation. Use 28495 when the provider performs closed treatment of a fracture in a great toe phalanx with manipulation. Use 28505 when the provider performs open treatment of a fracture in a great toe phalanx with or without internal fixation. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of sesamoid fracture, with or without internal fixation
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs open treatment of a sesamoid bone fracture in the foot. He may or may not use internal fixation implants like pins or screws to fix the fracture. Sesamoid bones are small irregular bones present within a muscle tendon or capsule. In the foot, the most common location of a sesamoid bone is the underside of the ball of the foot under the great toe. Explanation Fracture is a break, or crack, in the continuity of a bone. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the fractured bone. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. He next retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the sesamoid fracture. He then adjusts the bone to reduce the fractured fragments. He may fix the fracture using implants like screws, nails, wires, etc. Finally, he closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. He next places the toe or foot in a splint or brace for a period of four weeks. He may perform a separately reported X–ray examination of the sesamoid bone to confirm the reduction of the fracture. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone in correct position. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. Tips Use 28530 when the provider performs closed treatment of a sesamoid fracture. Read Less

short_description: Closed treatment of tarsal bone dislocation, other than talotarsal; without anesthesia
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs closed treatment of a tarsal bone dislocation, which is abnormal separation of a joint. This code excludes talotarsal joints. She performs this procedure without using anesthesia on the patient. Tarsal bones are located in the midfoot and rearfoot area and are seven in number: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and lateral cuneiform. A talotarsal joint is a joint of the talus with another tarsal bone. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, the provider reduces the tarsal bone dislocation, other than one involving a talotarsal joint. She first performs a separately reportable X–ray to examine the dislocated joint. She then manually adjusts the bones by pushing or pulling to bring them to their normal alignment. She does not use anesthesia during the reduction procedure. She next places the foot in a splint or brace for a period of four weeks. She may perform a separately reported X–ray examination of the joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone or dislocated joint in correct position. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone to its proper alignment. Tips Use 28545 when the provider reduces a tarsal bone dislocation other than a talotarsal joint and the service requires anesthesia. Use 28570–28575 when the provider reduces a talotarsal joint dislocation. Read Less

short_description: Closed treatment of talotarsal joint dislocation; requiring anesthesia
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs closed treatment of a talotarsal joint dislocation, which is abnormal separation of a joint. She performs this procedure using anesthesia. She may or may not use internal fixation implants like pins or screws to fix the dislocation. Tarsal bones are located in the midfoot and rearfoot area and are seven in number: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and lateral cuneiform. Metatarsals are the five long bones in the foot that connect the ankle area to the toes. A tarsometatarsal joint is a joint between the tarsal and metatarsal bones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the dislocated joint. She then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, protecting the nerves and vessels. She next retracts the muscles to have adequate exposure of the dislocated bones. She then adjusts the bones to reduce the dislocation. She may fix the reduced joint using implants like screws, nails, wires, etc., for extra stability. Finally, she closes the wound by suturing the skin layers together. She next places the foot in a splint or brace for a period of four weeks. She may perform a separately reported X–ray examination of the joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone or dislocated joint in correct position. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone or dislocated joint to its proper alignment. Tips Use 28600 when the provider reduces a tarsometatarsal joint dislocation without using anesthesia. Use 28605 when the provider reduces a tarsometatarsal joint dislocation and the service requires anesthesia. Use 28606 when the provider performs percutaneous skeletal fixation of the tarsometatarsal joint, with manipulation. Read Less
guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Radical resection of bone tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. short_description: Closed treatment of metatarsophalangeal joint dislocation; without anesthesia
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs closed treatment of a metatarsophalangeal joint dislocation, which is abnormal separation of a joint. He performs this procedure without using anesthesia for the patient. Metatarsals are the five long bones in the foot that connect the ankle area to the toes. Phalanges are bones of the toe. There are three in each toe except the greater toe, which has two phalanges. The metatarsophalangeal joint is a joint where the metatarsal bone of the foot attaches to the phalanx bone of the toe. He then manually adjusts the bones by pushing or pulling to bring them to their normal alignment. He does not use anesthesia during the reduction procedure. He next places the foot or toe in a splint or brace for a period of four weeks. He may perform a separately reported X–ray examination of the joint to confirm the reduction of the dislocation. Terminology Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone or dislocated joint in correct position. Reduction: A medical procedure to return a broken bone or dislocated joint to its proper alignment. Tips Use 28635 when the provider reduces a metatarsophalangeal joint dislocation and the service requires anesthesia. Use 28636 when the provider performs percutaneous skeletal fixation of the metatarsophalangeal joint, with manipulation. Use 28645 when the provider performs open treatment of the metatarsophalangeal joint dislocation with or without internal fixation. Read Less

short_description: Open treatment of metatarsophalangeal joint dislocation, includes internal fixation, when performed

short_description: Percutaneous skeletal fixation of interphalangeal joint dislocation, with manipulation

He also performs manipulation, or adjustment, of the separated bones to reduce the dislocation. Phalanges are bones of the toe. There are three in each toe except the greater toe, which has two phalanges. An interphalangeal joint is a joint between two phalanges of a toe. He next creates a small incision in the skin over the dislocated joint. He then inserts pins and screws through this incision to hold the reduced dislocation in place. short_description: Arthrodesis; triple
lay_term: A triple arthrodesis is performed in patients with degenerative arthritis or trauma. During this procedure, the provider fuses three joints of the ankle (subtalar, talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints) together to completely mobilize the ankle joint. Explanation While the patient is prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a curved dorsolateral incision on the foot from the talonavicular joint to the inferior aspect of the lateral malleolus. He incises the site farther, careful to protect the dorsolateral branch of the superficial peroneal nerve. He incises the inferior retinaculum and detaches the extensor digitorum brevis. The provider opens the lateral aspect of talonavicular joint, the calcaneocuboid joint, and the posterior facet of the subtalar joint. He removes the anterior projection of calculus and exposes the calcaneocuboid joint and sinus tarsi. He removes articular cartilage of the calcaneocuboid and subtalar joint. The provider then exposes the talonavicular joint by making a medial incision; he exposes the saphenous vein. He also exposes the talonavicular joint dorsally, medially, and inferiorly. He then removes the articular cartilage. The provider uses various internal fixation devices like K wires and screws to hold the joints together. Read Less

short_description: Arthrodesis, midtarsal or tarsometatarsal, multiple or transverse
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes multiple or transverse midtarsal or tarsometatarsal joints with the help of fixation devices. Midtarsal joints are combined joints of either the talus with the navicular bone or the calcaneum with the cuboid bone. Tarsometatarsal joints are also known as Lisfranc joints. They are the joints of the first, second, and third cuneiforms, and the cuboid with the bases of the metatarsal bones. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to treat pain in patients with end stage osteoarthritis of midtarsal or tarsometatarsal joints. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the affected joints in front of the ankle. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then retracts the muscle to gain access to the joints to be fused. He next cuts the joint capsule and enters the joint. He first removes all dead or inflamed tissue from the joint cavity. He then brings the bones of the joints in close proximity, or nearness, and fuses the joints using implants like K–wire, screws, or plates. He may also use a cancellous bone graft to fuse the joints to provide extra stability. Finally, he obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the ankle in a cast or brace for a period of four to six weeks. Use this code when the provider fuses multiple joints. Cancellous bone graft: A graft consisting of spongy bone that can trigger new bone formation quickly. Tarsal: These bones are located in the midfoot and rearfoot area and are seven in number: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and lateral cuneiform. short_description: Arthrodesis, midtarsal or tarsometatarsal, multiple or transverse; with osteotomy (eg, flatfoot correction)
lay_term: The provider surgically immobilizes multiple or transverse midtarsal or tarsometatarsal joints with the help of fixation devices. He also performs an osteotomy, the surgical removal of a portion of the shaft of the metatarsal bone to correct a flat foot deformity. The goal of this procedure is to treat pain in patients with end stage osteoarthritis of the midtarsal or tarsometatarsal joints. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin over the affected joints in the front of the ankle. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then retracts the muscle to gain access to the joints to be fused. He next incises the joint capsule and enters the joint. He removes all dead or inflamed tissue from the joint cavity. Next, he removes a portion of the shaft bone of the metatarsal bone to correct the flat foot deformity. He then brings the bones of the joints in close proximity, or nearness, and fuses the joints using implants such as K wire, screws, pins, or plates. He may also use a cancellous bone graft to fuse the joints to provide extra stability. He performs this procedure on multiple joints and metatarsals. Finally, he stops all bleeding at the surgical site, irrigates the wound, and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the ankle in a cast or brace for a period of about four to six weeks. Use this code when the provider fuses multiple joints. Brace, cast, or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone or dislocated joint in correct position. Calcaneum or calcaneus: The heel bone situated on the back of foot. Cancellous bone graft: A graft consisting of spongy bone that can trigger new bone formation quickly. Cuboid bone: One of the seven tarsal bones present on outer side of the foot. Cuneiforms: Three tarsal bones present on the back portion of the foot. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Kirschner wire (K wire): A thin, flexible wire or pin type structure a provider uses to join and stabilize bone fragments. Navicular bone: One of the seven tarsal bones present on top of the foot Osteoarthritis: Inflammation of joints. Osteotomy: Cutting into bone; bone incision. Subcutaneous: Below the surface of the skin. Talus: One of the bones in the foot that forms the ankle joint and is situated between the foot and the lower leg bones. Tarsal: Seven bones in the midfoot and rear foot area: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and lateral cuneiform. short_description: Arthrodesis, midtarsal or tarsometatarsal, single joint Notes: (For first metatarsal-cuneiform joint fusion without concomitant removal of the distal medial prominence of the first metatarsal for hallux valgus correction, use 28740)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes a single midtarsal or tarsometatarsal joint with the help of fixation devices. Midtarsal joints are combined joints of either the talus with the navicular bone or the calcaneum with the cuboid bone. Tarsometatarsal joints are also known as Lisfranc joints. They are the joints of the first, second, and third cuneiforms, and the cuboid with the bases of the metatarsal bones. Explanation The goal of this procedure is to treat pain in patients with end stage osteoarthritis of midtarsal or tarsometatarsal joints. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the affected joint in front of the ankle. She dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. She then retracts the muscle to gain access to the joint to be fused. She next cuts the joint capsule and enters the joint. She first removes all dead or inflamed tissue from the joint cavity. She then brings the bones of the joint in close proximity, or nearness, and fuses the joint using implants like K–wire, screws, or plates. She may also use a cancellous bone graft to fuse the joint to provide extra stability. Finally, she obtains hemostasis at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. She then places the ankle in a cast or brace for a period of four to six weeks. Use this code when the provider fuses a single joint. Cancellous bone graft: A graft consisting of spongy bone that can trigger new bone formation quickly. Metatarsals: These are the five long bones located between the tarsal bones of the foot and phalanges of the toes. Osteoarthritis: Inflammation of joints. Tarsal: These bones are located in the midfoot and rearfoot area and are seven in number: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, and lateral cuneiform. short_description: Arthrodesis, with extensor hallucis longus transfer to first metatarsal neck, great toe, interphalangeal joint (eg, Jones type procedure) Notes: (For hammertoe operation or interphalangeal fusion, use 28285)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically immobilizes the interphalangeal joint of the great toe. He also transfers the extensor hallucis longus tendon from its insertion on the toe’s phalanx bone to the metatarsal bone of the foot. An interphalangeal joint is a joint between the two phalanges of the great toe. The goal of this procedure is typically to treat pain in patients with end stage osteoarthritis of an interphalangeal joint of the great toe. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the interphalangeal joint of the great toe. He dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, preserving the nerves and veins. He then retracts the muscle tendon to gain access to the joint to be fused. He next cuts the joint capsule and enters the joint. He first removes all dead or inflamed tissue from the joint cavity. He then brings the bones of the joint in close proximity, or nearness, and fuses the joint using implants like K wire, screws, or plates. He then identifies the extensor hallucis longus tendon, which the provider attaches to the first metatarsal bone from its original insertion on the phalanx bone. Finally, he stops bleeding at the surgical site and closes the wound by suturing the soft tissue in layers. He then places the toe in a splint or brace for a period of weeks. This surgical procedure is also known as a Jones type procedure. Terminology Arthrodesis: The surgical immobilization of a joint by fusion of the bones. Brace or splint: An external device that is used to hold a broken bone or dislocated joint in correct position. Extensor hallucis longus: A muscle situated in front of the leg that extends the foot’s big toe. Interphalangeal joint, or IPJ: Referring to the union of the phalanges, the bones of the fingers or toes. K wire: A surgical metal wire that provider uses for bone stabilization. Metatarsal bones: Five bones that make up the foot; they connect to the tarsal bones of the ankle and to the phalanges, or bones of digits, or toes. Osteoarthritis: Inflammation of joints. Phalanx or phalanges: Phalanges are bones of the fingers or toes; there are three in each toe and finger except the big toes and thumbs, which have two phalanges each. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Read Less

short_description: Amputation, foot; midtarsal (eg, Chopart type procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider amputates the foot just in front of the heel and ankle. The amputation is at the midtarsal joints through the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints. Midtarsal joints are also known as transverse tarsal joints. They are combined joints of either the talus with the navicular bone or the calcaneum with the cuboid bone. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin just distal to the talonavicular joint in front of the ankle. He then creates the skin flaps that he will require to cover the stump later on. He ligates the dorsalis pedis artery and retracts the nerves. He next divides the capsule of the talonavicular joint and releases the posterior tibial tendon. He then lengthens the Achilles tendon and attaches it to the neck of the talus bone to support the function of the tibialis anterior and posterior tendons. He then may divide, lengthen, or transfer some other tendons as required to prevent contracture post amputation. He then incises the ligaments covering the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints and separates the foot through these joints. This procedure of foot amputation is also known as Chopart’s amputation. Finally, after irrigation of the wound with antibiotics, he closes the wound by suturing the flaps and packs the wound with antiseptic gauze. Terminology Amputation: Surgical removal of a complete or partial appendage of the body. Achilles tendon: Largest and strongest tendon at the back of the leg that connects the calf muscle to the back of the heel. Dorsalis pedis artery: A blood vessel in the leg that supplies oxygenated blood to the dorsal, or upper, surface of the foot. Stump: Distal end of the limb left after amputation. Talus: A small bone that sits between the calcaneum, which is the heel bone, and the two long bones of the lower leg. Talus neck: Cylindrical area between the head and body of the talus bone; directed forward and inward. Tibial anterior: Largest muscle located in the anterior, or front, compartment of the lower leg. Tibial posterior: A muscle located in the posterior, or back, compartment of the lower leg. Tips Use 28805 when the provider performs amputation of the foot at the transmetatarsal level. Read Less

short_description: Amputation, foot; transmetatarsal
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider amputates the foot by cutting it across the metatarsal bones. Metatarsals are the five long bones located between the tarsal bones of the foot/ankle and phalanges of the toes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision around the base of the toes in a circumferential manner extending over to the metatarsal. He then creates the long skin flap that he will require to cover the stump later on. He ligates the dorsalis pedis artery and retracts the nerves. He then transects and divides the muscles’ tendons. He may also lengthen and transfer some muscles as required. He finally cuts the foot through the metatarsal bones transversally and removes the front portion of the foot. Next, he closes the wound by suturing the flaps and packs the wound with antiseptic gauze. Terminology Amputation: Surgical removal of a complete or partial appendage of the body. Dorsalis pedis artery: A blood vessel in the leg that supplies oxygenated blood to the dorsal, or upper, surface of the foot. Stump: Distal end of the limb left after amputation. short_description: Amputation, metatarsal, with toe, single

lay_term: The provider administers high energy sound waves, to the sole of the foot to stimulate healing of the plantar fascia, the thick band of connective tissue that holds up the arch of the foot. She uses ultrasound guidance as a directional aid. She performs the procedure with the patient under regional or general anesthesia due to the painful nature of the treatment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider directs high energy sound waves directly to the skin of the foot over the plantar fascia using an extracorporeal shock wave therapy device. She uses ultrasound guidance to aid in directing the high energy sound waves to their target. Extracorporeal shock wave therapy, or ESWT: High energy sounds waves administered under regional or general anesthesia to promote healing of tissues in plantar fasciitis, a condition in which the connective tissue supporting the arch of the foot becomes inflamed and painful, and lateral epicondylitis, or tennis elbow, in which the tendons of the elbow become inflamed and painful from repetitive use. Integumentary: Referring to the skin. Musculoskeletal: Involving muscles and bones. Plantar: Refers to the sole, or underside, of the foot. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. short_description: Unlisted procedure, foot or toes
lay_term: Use 28899 to report procedures in the foot or toe that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs a procedure on the foot or toe that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis, and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

short_description: Removal or bivalving; gauntlet, boot or body cast
lay_term: The provider removes or modifies an existing cast covering the body, foot, or hand when no longer required, needs replacement, or has become too tight due to excessive swelling. Explanation The provider uses a cast saw to cut through the cast on both sides of the body or extremity, creating front and back halves of the cast. She inserts a cast spreader, an instrument that separates the cast along the cutting line to break the two halves apart. She uses blunt edge bandage scissors to cut through the padding material close to the skin. She removes the two cast halves if healing is complete or if she will replace the cast. If healing is not complete and bivalving is necessary to reduce swelling, she secures the front and back halves of the cast in place with bandage material. She assesses the fit and makes adjustments as necessary. Terminology Bivalving: Cutting a cast into two parallel sides to relieve swelling or pressure. Cast saw: A cutting instrument with a circular blade that vibrates instead of spinning, cutting through cast material but not a patient’s skin. Gauntlet cast: A cast that covers the hand and wrist, named for its similarity to a medieval armored glove. Tips This code should be employed only for casts applied by another provider. If your practice applied the cast, do not report removal or bivalving as codes in the Application of Casts and Strapping series include these services. Code 29700 describes a unilateral procedure. If the provider performs it bilaterally, then you will either report this code with two units, twice with modifier 50, Bilateral procedure, appended to the second code, or once with modifier 50 appended. Check with your payer for their preference. Use the appropriate modifier to indicate the target arm or leg, RT, Right side, and LT, Left side. Use the appropriate code for evaluation and management (E/M) if the key components of an E/M service are met, which are patient history, physical examination, and medical decision making. Apply modifier 25, Significant, separately identifiable evaluation and management service by the same provider on the same day of the procedure or other service. Read Less

short_description: Removal or bivalving; shoulder or hip spica, Minerva, or Risser jacket, etc.
lay_term: The provider removes or modifies an existing spica cast of the shoulder or hip or a body cast of the Minerva or Risser type when no longer required, needs replacement, or has become too tight due to excessive swelling. Explanation The provider uses a cast saw to cut through the cast along both its sides, creating front and back halves of the cast. She inserts a cast spreader, an instrument that separates the cast along the cutting line to break the two halves apart. She uses blunt edge bandage scissors to cut through the padding material close to the skin. She removes the two cast halves if healing is complete or if she will replace the cast. If healing is not complete and bivalving is necessary to reduce swelling, she secures the front and back halves of the cast in place with bandage material. She assesses the fit and makes adjustments as necessary. Terminology Bivalving: Cutting a cast into two parallel sides to relieve swelling or pressure. Cast saw: A cutting instrument with a circular blade that vibrates instead of spinning, cutting through cast material but not a patient’s skin. Minerva cast: A cast that covers the upper body, including the trunk and spine, neck, jaw, and head, to treat abnormal curvature of the spine and injuries and conditions that affect the neck. Risser jacket: Encases the entire trunk of the body, extending over the neck to include the head, and applies localized pressure to an abnormal curvature of the spine; also called a Risser localizer jacket. Spica cast: A body cast that covers the hips and one or more lower extremities, in a hip spica, or covers the chest and one or more shoulders, in a shoulder spica; spica casts take their name from the overlapping V pattern of the wrapping of the cast material, which resembles a stalk of wheat. short_description: Wedging of cast (except clubfoot casts)

She cuts pieces of cork into wedges of the correct size to correct the angulation of the fracture. She inserts the wedges into the cast at the appropriate positions and takes another X–ray for confirmation. short_description: Arthroscopy, temporomandibular joint, diagnostic, with or without synovial biopsy (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider inserts an arthroscope into the temporomandibular joint, or jaw joint, to inspect the joint for damage or disease that cause pain or dysfunction of the jaw, such as temporomandibular joint disorder. If necessary, she takes a biopsy, or tissue sample, of the synovial membrane that covers the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the temporomandibular joint area. She inserts the arthroscope through the incision and into the temporomandibular joint. She instills saline solution to inflate the area around the temporomandibular joint to improve her field of view. She examines the entire temporomandibular joint area. She then inserts an instrument to biopsy the synovial lining of the joint. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. short_description: Arthroscopy, shoulder, diagnostic, with or without synovial biopsy (separate procedure) Notes: (For open procedure, see 23065-23066, 23100-23101)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the shoulder joint with an arthroscope, inspecting for causes of pain and limitation of motion. short_description: Arthroscopy, shoulder, surgical; capsulorrhaphy Notes: (For open procedure, see 23450-23466) (To report thermal capsulorrhaphy, use 29999)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the shoulder joint with an arthroscope. He inserts additional instruments to repair any tears found in the joint capsule. Tearing of the joint capsule can be caused by falling on an outstretched arm, a twisting injury, or a forceful blow to the shoulder area, and lead to dislocation of the shoulder. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes three small incisions in the shoulder area. He inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the shoulder joint. He instills saline solution to expand the area around the shoulder joint. lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the shoulder joint with an arthroscope to look for and remove loose or foreign bodies. short_description: Arthroscopy, shoulder, surgical; synovectomy, complete Notes: (For open procedure, see 23105)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the shoulder joint with an arthroscope to inspect and remove damaged synovial membrane between the bony surfaces and the joint capsule. She inserts instruments and excises all of the synovial tissue in the joint. The provider performs a complete synovectomy for chronic inflammatory conditions causing pain and limitation of motion or to remove a tumor. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes three small incisions in the shoulder area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the shoulder joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the shoulder joint for better visualization. She views the entire shoulder joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments to excise the entire synovial membrane. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Chronic: A condition that is long lasting, typically to slow develop, and with symptoms of less severity than an acute condition. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Synovectomy: Excision of synovial tissue, the membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Tumor: Abnormal growth of tissue or mass; can be benign or cancerous. short_description: Arthroscopy, shoulder, surgical; debridement, limited, 1 or 2 discrete structures (eg, humeral bone, humeral articular cartilage, glenoid bone, glenoid articular cartilage, biceps tendon, biceps anchor complex, labrum, articular capsule, articular side of the rotator cuff, bursal side of the rotator cuff, subacromial bursa, foreign body[ies]) Notes: (For open procedure, see specific open shoulder procedure performed)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the shoulder joint with an arthroscope. He inserts additional instruments and excises a minimal amount of damaged tissue in the shoulder joint caused by trauma to the shoulder. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes three small incisions in the shoulder area. He inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the shoulder joint. He instills saline solution to expand the area around the shoulder joint. He views the entire shoulder joint area using the camera of the scope. He then inserts additional instruments and performs a limited debridement, which will include one or two discrete structures such as humeral bone, humeral articular cartilage, glenoid bone, glenoid articular cartilage, biceps tendon, biceps anchor complex, labrum, articular capsule, articular side of the rotator cuff, bursal side of the rotator cuff, subacromial bursa, or foreign bodies in the shoulder joint. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Humeral head and neck: The rounded head and narrow neck of the long bone in the arm that runs from the shoulder to the elbow. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Subacromial bursa: A bursa present just below the acromion process, a bony projection of the shoulder blade (scapula) at the shoulder; a bursa is a fluid–filled sac that prevents joints, muscles, and tendons from rubbing together. lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the shoulder joint with an arthroscope. She inserts additional instruments to lyse, or destroy, adhesions, and restore free movement of the shoulder. She manipulates the shoulder as necessary. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the shoulder area. She inserts the arthroscope through the incision and into the shoulder joint. She instills saline solution to inflate the area around the shoulder joint and improve her field of view. She inserts additional instruments to free up and remove adhesions. She manipulates the joint as necessary. Blunt dissection: Separation of tissue layers using the fingers; sharp dissection separates tissue layers using a blade. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Lysis of adhesions, or adhesiolysis: Freeing up adhesions by cutting and dividing, typically with a combination of sharp and blunt dissection. Manipulation: Use of the hands or instruments to move a structure into position, such as manipulation of a fracture site to realign the underlying bones. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. He inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the shoulder joint. He instills saline solution to expand the area around the shoulder joint. He views the entire shoulder joint area using the camera of the scope. He then inserts additional instruments and performs repairs to the shoulder blade to decompress, or relieve pressure, on structures that rub together abnormally. short_description: Arthroscopy, shoulder, surgical; with rotator cuff repair Notes: (For open or mini-open rotator cuff repair, use 23412) (When arthroscopic distal clavicle resection is performed at the same setting, use 29824 and append modifier 51)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the shoulder joint with an arthroscope. She inserts additional instruments to repair a torn rotator cuff, the grouping of muscles and tendons that surround and support the shoulder joint. Rotator cuff tears frequently result from sports injuries and repetitive overhead motion of the arm, causing pain and limitation of movement. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the shoulder area. She inserts the arthroscope through the incision and into the shoulder joint. She instills saline solution to inflate the area around the shoulder joint and improve her field of view. She inspects the tendons and muscles of the rotator cuff area. She inserts additional instruments to repair tears to the soft tissues, remove bone spurs, and free up adhesions. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Blunt dissection: Separation of tissue layers using the fingers; sharp dissection separates tissue layers using a blade. Bone spurs: Small bony growths that occur at the edge of a bone where it meets another bone, often the result of arthritis; also called osteophytes. Clavicle: The collarbone, a horizontal bone that connects the sternum, or breastbone, to the scapula, or shoulder blade. Distal: Located away from the center of the body or away from a structure’s point of attachment. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Resection: Surgical removal of tissue, organ, or other structure in whole or in part; also called excision.
