short_description: Arthroscopy, shoulder, surgical; biceps tenodesis Notes: (Do not report 29828 in conjunction with 29805, 29820, 29822) (For open biceps tenodesis, use 23430)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the shoulder joint with an arthroscope. She inserts additional instruments to repair an unstable biceps tendon, the fibrous band that connects the biceps muscle in the forearm to its bony attachment at the shoulder join. Biceps tenodesis corrects instability of the biceps tendon due to biceps tendonitis, inflammation of the tendon, which tends to accompany other shoulder problems, such as chronic instability, arthritis, and impingement syndrome. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the shoulder area. She inserts the arthroscope through the incision and into the shoulder joint. She instills saline solution to inflate the area around the shoulder joint and improve her field of view. She inspects the muscles and tendons in the joint. She anchors the biceps tendon in place by excising the damaged portion and reattaching healthy tendon to the humerus. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Biceps tendon: Fibrous tissue that attaches the biceps muscle, responsible for motion of the forearm, to its bony attachment at the shoulder and at the elbow. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Humerus: Bone in the upper arm. Impingement syndrome: Irritation, swelling, and pain of the tendons in the shoulder due to intermittent entrapment and compression during motion of the shoulder joint. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. short_description: Arthroscopy, elbow, diagnostic, with or without synovial biopsy (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the elbow joint with an arthroscope to assess for causes of pain and limitation of movement. If necessary, she takes a sample of the synovial tissue that lines the joint and submits it to a laboratory for analysis and diagnosis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the elbow area. She inserts the arthroscope through the incision into the elbow joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the elbow joint. She views the entire joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments to take a biopsy of the synovial tissue and submits it for analysis. She inspects the ligaments and other structures in the elbow. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the elbow joint with an arthroscope to look for and remove loose or foreign bodies. Arthroscopic removal of loose body(ies) or foreign body(ies) (ie, 29819, 29834, 29861, 29874, 29894, 29904) may be reported only when the loose body(ies) or foreign body(ies) is equal to or larger than the diameter of the arthroscopic cannula(s) used for the specific procedure, and can only be removed through a cannula larger than that used for the specific procedure or through a separate incision or through a portal that has been enlarged to allow removal of the loose or foreign body(ies). Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. short_description: Arthroscopy, elbow, surgical; debridement, limited
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the elbow joint with an arthroscope. She inserts additional instruments and excises a minimal amount of damaged tissue in the elbow joint caused by trauma to the elbow. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the elbow area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the elbow joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the elbow joint to improve her field of view. She inspects the entire elbow joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments and performs a limited debridement of the tissues in the elbow joint, cutting away damaged tissue. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the structures in the joint. Debridement: Surgical removal of damaged, diseased, or unhealthy tissue from wounds to allow healthy tissue to grow. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Tips Surgical endoscopy and arthroscopy always include a diagnostic endoscopy or arthroscopy code. Never use a diagnostic code with surgical code. If the provider performs a diagnostic arthroscopy and discovers she must perform an open repair of a previously unknown condition, you can report both the open repair and the diagnostic arthroscopy by appending the 59 modifier, Distinct procedural service, to the diagnostic arthroscopy code. short_description: Arthroscopy, elbow, surgical; debridement, extensive
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the elbow joint with an arthroscope. She inserts additional instruments and excises extensive damaged tissues in the elbow joint caused by trauma to the elbow. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the elbow joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the elbow joint. She views the entire elbow joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments and performs an extensive debridement of the tissues in the elbow joint, removing damaged tissue, scar tissue, and adhesions in the front and back of the elbow. She debrides tendons and muscle tissue as necessary. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Tendon: Fibrous tissue that connects muscles to bones. Tips Surgical endoscopy and arthroscopy always include a diagnostic endoscopy or arthroscopy code. Never use a diagnostic code with surgical code. If the provider performs a diagnostic arthroscopy and discovers she must perform an open repair of a previously unknown condition, you can report both the open repair and the diagnostic arthroscopy by appending the 59 modifier, Distinct procedural service, to the diagnostic arthroscopy code. short_description: Arthroscopy, wrist, diagnostic, with or without synovial biopsy (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the wrist joint with an arthroscope to assess for causes of pain and limitation of movement. If necessary, she takes a sample of the synovial tissue that lines the joint and submits it to a laboratory for analysis and diagnosis. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the wrist joint. She views the entire joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments to take a biopsy of the synovial tissue and submits it for analysis. She inspects the ligaments and other structures in the wrist. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. short_description: Arthroscopy, wrist, surgical; synovectomy, partial
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the wrist joint with an arthroscope to inspect and repair the membrane between the bony surfaces and the joint capsule. She inserts instruments and excises a portion of synovial tissue that has become inflamed, causing the patient pain and limitation of motion. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the wrist area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the wrist joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the wrist joint. She views the entire wrist joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments to excise the inflamed portion of synovial membrane. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Synovectomy: Excision of synovial tissue, the membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. short_description: Arthroscopy, wrist, surgical; excision and/or repair of triangular fibrocartilage and/or joint debridement
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the wrist joint with an arthroscope. She inserts additional instruments to repair or remove the triangular fibrocartilage, a supporting cartilage in the wrist that is a common source of pain when damaged. She excises a minimal amount of additional damaged tissue in the wrist joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the wrist area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the wrist joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the wrist joint to improve her field of view. She inspects the entire wrist joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments and excises the triangular fibrocartilage and performs limited debridement in the wrist joint, cutting away any additional damaged tissue. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. short_description: Endoscopy, wrist, surgical, with release of transverse carpal ligament Notes: (Do not report 29848 in conjunction with 11960) (For open procedure, use 64721)
lay_term: The provider inserts an endoscope into the wrist joint to divide the transverse carpal ligament and reduce compression on the median nerve in the carpal tunnel that results in pain and numbness. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the wrist area. She inserts an endoscope through the incision into the wrist joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the wrist joint. She views the entire joint area using the camera of the scope and identifies the transverse carpal ligament. She divides the ligament to release the pressure on the median nerve and tendons in the carpal tunnel. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS): Pain, numbness, and tingling affecting the fingers and hand, resulting from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. Carpal tunnel: Passageway formed by the concave carpus bone and the flexor retinaculum covering it on the palmar side of the wrist through which the median nerve passes; the carpal tunnel also houses ten flexor tendons of the hand. Endoscope: A stiff or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon, bladder, or stomach; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Median nerve: Responsible for muscles in the forearm and sensation in the fingers; originates from the brachial plexus and branches out to the thumb, index, and middle fingers of the hand. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Transverse carpal ligament: Fibrous band that extends across the carpal bones in the wrist, tightly enclosing the nerve and tendons within a tunnel; also called flexor retinaculum. Tips This code is an endoscopic procedure to treat carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). For an open repair you should turn instead to 64721, Neuroplasty and or transposition, median nerve at carpal tunnel. On occasion, the provider may also decompress the ulnar nerve at Guyon's canal, 64719, Neuroplasty and or transposition, ulnar nerve at wrist, to treat ulnar nerve syndrome, multiple neuritis syndrome, or injury to the ulnar nerve, during the same open session. Note that payers will apply a multiple procedure reduction to 64719 if you report it during the same session as 64721. Read Less

short_description: Arthroscopically aided treatment of tibial fracture, proximal (plateau); bicondylar, includes internal fixation, when performed (includes arthroscopy) Notes: (For bone graft, use 20900, 20902)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs treatment of a tibial plateau fracture involving both the inner and outer tibial condyles using an arthroscope. He may or may not use an internal fixation device to fix the fracture. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates two small incisions on either side of the patellar tendon over the knee joint. He then introduces the arthroscope through one of the portals and examines the knee joint for a tibial plateau fracture. He then debrides any damaged tissue present within the joint. He may manipulate the fracture fragments if displaced to reduce the fracture. He then may use internal fixation devices like a screw to fix the fracture. He removes all the instruments from the portals. Finally, he closes the incisions and covers them with bandages. Finally, he may place the knee in a brace for a period of four weeks to allow the fracture to heal. Use this code when the provider treats a bicondylar fracture, a break in continuity of both condyles of tibia. short_description: Arthroscopy, hip, diagnostic with or without synovial biopsy (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the hip joint with an arthroscope, inspecting for causes for pain and limitation of motion. If necessary, she takes a sample of the synovial tissue that lines the joint and submits it to a laboratory for analysis and diagnosis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes three small incisions in the hip area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the hip joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the hip joint. She views the entire hip joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments to take a biopsy of the synovial tissue and submits it for analysis. She inspects the ligaments and other structures in the hip. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Tips Surgical endoscopy and arthroscopy always include a diagnostic endoscopy or arthroscopy code. Never use a diagnostic code with a surgical code. If the provider performs a diagnostic arthroscopy and discovers she must perform an open repair of a previously unknown condition, you can report both the open repair and the diagnostic arthroscopy by appending the 59 modifier, Distinct procedural service, to the diagnostic arthroscopy code. short_description: Arthroscopy, hip, surgical; with removal of loose body or foreign body
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the hip joint with an arthroscope to look for and remove loose or foreign bodies. Loose and foreign bodies, which include things like small pieces of broken cartilage or suture anchors inserted at a prior surgical procedure, lead to pain, inflammation, scar tissue formation, adhesions, and restriction of motion of the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the hip area. She inserts the arthroscope through the incision and into the hip joint. She instills saline solution into the area to inflate the area around the hip joint. She inspects the joint and uses instruments to secure and remove any loose or foreign bodies. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body, such as shards of metal or a bone fragment. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. short_description: Arthroscopy, hip, surgical; with synovectomy

short_description: Arthroscopy, hip, surgical; with femoroplasty (ie, treatment of cam lesion)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs surgical arthroscopy of a hip with femoroplasty to treat a cam lesion. Femoroplasty means re–shaping the head of the thigh’s femur bone to restore its spherical shape. A cam lesion is a bump on the surface of the femoral head that causes femoroacetabular impingement, a condition of too much friction in the hip joint. It commonly occurs in athletes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider first applies traction, a pull force on the hip joint that increases the joint space to allow for adequate visualization of the hip joint during arthroscopy. She then creates two to three small incisions called portals over the hip joint. She next inserts the pen–sized tiny camera through one of the incisions, or portals, to look inside the joint. She inserts the surgical instrument through the second portal. She first incises the capsule to allow for better visualization of the femur head. She then, using the arthroscope, localizes the bump on the surface of the femur head and the femoral neck that impinges on the acetabulum during a movement of the hip joint. She then uses a burr or shaver to remove the bone growth from the femur head and femur neck. Finally, she repairs the capsule and removes all the instruments from the portals. She then closes the incisions and covers them with bandages. Terminology Acetabulum: A cup–shaped socket of the hip joint. Arthroscopy: Also known as keyhole surgery, the provider uses an arthroscope, a tiny camera, to look inside the joint and to treat joint problems. Femur head: Rounded upper end of the thigh’s femur bone. Femoral neck: A flat portion of the thigh’s femur bone that connects the femoral head with the femoral shaft. Femoroacetabular impingement: A condition of too much friction between the femoral head and the acetabulum. Impingement: To collide or strike. Tips Use 27161 when the provider performs an open femoroplasty. Read Less

short_description: Arthroscopy, hip, surgical; with acetabuloplasty (ie, treatment of pincer lesion) Notes: (Do not report 29914, 29915 in conjunction with 29862, 29863)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs surgical arthroscopy of a hip using acetabuloplasty to treat a pincer lesion. Acetabuloplasty means re–shaping the acetabulum, a cup shaped socket of the hip joint, to restore its normal shape. A pincer lesion involves an abnormally shaped socket that excessively covers the femoral head thus causing femoroacetabular impingement, a condition of too much friction in the hip joint. It reduces the range of motion in the hip joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider first applies traction, a pull force on the hip joint that increases the hip joint space to allow for adequate visualization of the joint during arthroscopy. He then creates two to three small incisions called portals over the hip joint. He next inserts the pen–sized tiny camera through one of the incisions, or portals, to look inside the joint. He inserts the surgical instrument through the second portal. He first incises the capsule to allow for better visualization and may also detach the labrum if required to access the acetabular rim. He then, using the arthroscope, localizes the acetabular deformity that collides with the femur head. He then uses a burr or shaver to remove a portion of the acetabular rim. Finally, he repairs the capsule and labrum, if detached, and removes all the instruments from the portals. He then closes the incisions and covers them with bandages. Femoroacetabular impingement: A condition of too much friction between the femoral head and the acetabulum. Femoral head: Rounded upper end of the thigh’s femur bone. Fibrocartilage: A type of cartilage having a large number of fibers. Impingement: To collide or strike. Labrum: Fibrocartilage tissue around the articular surface of the hip joint. Read Less

lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the knee joint with an arthroscope to inspect and repair the cartilage covering the bony surfaces of the knee joint. She inserts instruments to transplant healthy articular cartilage from a donor source to replace damaged tissue that causes pain and limitation of motion. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the joint. lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the knee joint with an arthroscope to inspect and repair a damaged meniscus, a cushion of cartilage in the joint, that causes pain and limitation of motion. short_description: Arthroscopy, knee, diagnostic, with or without synovial biopsy (separate procedure) Notes: (For open autologous chondrocyte implantation of the knee, use 27412)
lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the knee joint with an arthroscope to assess for causes of pain and limitation of movement. If necessary, she takes a sample of the synovial tissue that lines the joint and submits it to a laboratory for analysis and diagnosis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the knee joint. She views the entire joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments to take a biopsy of the synovial tissue and submits it for analysis. She inspects the ligaments and other structures in the knee. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Autologous chondrocyte implantation, or ACI: Implantation of healthy cartilage cells harvested from the patient and grown in the laboratory for transplantation in a subsequent procedure. Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Ligament: Fibrous band that connect bones and joints as well as hold organs in place. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Tips Surgical endoscopy and arthroscopy always include a diagnostic endoscopy or arthroscopy code. Never use a diagnostic code with a surgical code. If the provider performs a diagnostic arthroscopy and discovers she must perform an open repair of a previously unknown condition, you can report both the open repair and the diagnostic arthroscopy by appending the 59 modifier, Distinct procedural service, to the diagnostic arthroscopy code. Don't forget to identify the specific anatomical site. Use the appropriate modifier, RT, Right side, and LT, Left side. Read Less

short_description: Arthroscopy, knee, surgical; for removal of loose body or foreign body (eg, osteochondritis dissecans fragmentation, chondral fragmentation)
lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the knee joint with an arthroscope to look for and remove loose or foreign bodies. Loose and foreign bodies, which include things like small pieces of broken cartilage, lead to pain, inflammation, scar tissue formation, adhesions, and restriction of motion of the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution into the area to inflate the area around the knee joint. She inspects the joint and uses instruments to secure and remove any loose or foreign bodies. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery, that form between tissues and organs; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Chondral: Related to cartilage, strong but flexible fibrous connective tissue found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body, such as shards of metal or a bone fragment. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Osteochondritis dissecans: A joint condition in which the cartilage layer separates from the end of the bone, following an injury. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Tips Surgical endoscopy and arthroscopy always include a diagnostic endoscopy or arthroscopy code. Never use a diagnostic code with a surgical code. If the provider performs a diagnostic arthroscopy and discovers she must perform an open repair of a previously unknown condition, you can report both the open repair and the diagnostic arthroscopy by appending the 59 modifier, Distinct procedural service, to the diagnostic arthroscopy code. short_description: Arthroscopy, knee, surgical; synovectomy, limited (eg, plica or shelf resection) (separate procedure)
lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the knee joint with an arthroscope to inspect and repair the membrane between the bony surfaces and the joint capsule. She inserts instruments and excises a fold of synovial tissue that has become inflamed or damaged, causing the patient pain and limitation of motion. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the knee joint. She views the entire knee joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments to excise the inflamed or damaged fold of synovial membrane called the medial plica or medial shelf. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Plica resection: Removal of one of four small folds of tissue in the synovial membrane of the knee joint; the medial plica may become irritated or damaged due to injury, requiring removal. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Shelf resection: Also known as medial plica resection; excision of the medial plica, one of four small folds in the synovial membrane covering the knee joint. Synovectomy: Excision of synovial tissue, the membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Tips Your provider may document this procedure as a plica resection or shelf resection instead of a limited synovectomy. Read Less

short_description: Arthroscopy, knee, surgical; synovectomy, major, 2 or more compartments (eg, medial or lateral)
lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the knee joint with an arthroscope to inspect and repair the membrane between the bony surfaces and the joint capsule. She inserts instruments and excises synovial tissue that has become inflamed or damaged, causing the patient pain and limitation of motion. She removes the synovium from two or more compartments in the knee, including the medial or lateral compartments, or both, in a major synovectomy procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution to expand the area around the knee joint. She views the entire knee joint area using the camera of the scope. She then inserts additional instruments and performs a major synovectomy, excising the inflamed or damaged synovial membrane from two or more compartments, e.g. medial or lateral. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Joint capsule: Fluid filled sac that encloses a joint, or union of musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Lateral compartment: One of three joint compartments in the knee, formed by the outer knuckle of the femur, or thigh bone, where it attaches to the tibia bone in the lower leg. Medial compartment: One of three joint compartments in the knee, formed by the inner knuckle of the femur, or thigh bone, where it attaches to the tibia bone in the lower leg. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Synovectomy: Excision of synovial tissue, the membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. Synovium: Membrane separating the joint capsule from the bone surfaces. short_description: Arthroscopy, knee, surgical; abrasion arthroplasty (includes chondroplasty where necessary) or multiple drilling or microfracture
lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the knee joint with an arthroscope. She repairs the joint by reshaping the articular cartilage covering its ball and socket, grinding its surface and in some cases drilling the cartilage or excising it and puncturing the underlying bone to create small fractures, or breaks, encouraging new growth. The procedure relieves pain and improves mobility in the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution into the area to expand the area around the knee joint. She inspects the joint and uses instruments to reshape the cartilage lining of the joint surfaces, grinding the surfaces. If necessary, she drills small holes through the cartilage down to bone or excises a portion of damaged cartilage and uses an awl, a pointed instrument, to make multiple punctures in the subchondral bone. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Abrasion arthroplasty: Refinishing the surfaces of a joint through a grinding process. Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Articular cartilage: Strong, flexible fibrous tissue that lines the surfaces of a joint. Chondroplasty: Surgical repair of cartilage tissue, typically in a joint, such as the knee. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Microfracture: Surgical technique in which a provider excises a small portion of damaged cartilage covering the knee joint and punctures the underlying bone in multiple places, creating small breaks, or fractures, to encourage revascularization and the growth of healthy cartilage. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Tips Surgical endoscopy and arthroscopy always include a diagnostic endoscopy or arthroscopy code. Never use a diagnostic code with a surgical code. Don't forget to identify the specific anatomical site. Use the appropriate modifier, RT, Right side, and LT, Left side. Read Less

short_description: Arthroscopy, knee, surgical; with meniscectomy (medial AND lateral, including any meniscal shaving) including debridement/shaving of articular cartilage (chondroplasty), same or separate compartment(s), when performed
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs arthroscopic examination of the knee joint. She removes the damaged and torn meniscus from the medial and lateral compartments of the knee joint along with meniscal shaving. She may also perform shaving or debridement of the damaged articular cartilage, or chondroplasty, in the same or a separate compartment. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates two to three small incisions on either side of the patellar tendon over the knee joint. She next inserts a pen sized tiny camera through one of the incisions, or portals, or look inside the joint. She inserts the surgical instrument through the second portal. Through the third incision, she may introduce fluid in the joint to expand the joint for better visualization. She next performs arthroscopy, or examination of the knee joint using the camera, and checks the integrity of the meniscus. She then uses surgical instruments like a motorized cutter and scissors to remove the torn meniscal fragments from both the medial and lateral compartments. She next performs shaving of the remaining menisci. She then may examine the articular cartilage in the same or separate compartments and then debride damaged portions, called chondroplasty, if required. She removes all the instruments from the portals. Finally, she closes the incisions and covers them with bandages. short_description: Arthroscopy, knee, surgical; with lysis of adhesions, with or without manipulation (separate procedure)

short_description: Arthroscopy, knee, surgical; drilling for osteochondritis dissecans with bone grafting, with or without internal fixation (including debridement of base of lesion)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the knee joint with an arthroscope to identify areas of osteochondritis dissecans, where the cartilage separates from underlying bone. She excises a portion of the lesion and drills damaged cartilage to encourage growing bone to reattach. She applies bone grafts and in some cases inserts screws to hold the cartilage in place. The procedure relieves pain and improves mobility in the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution to inflate the area around the knee joint and improve her field of view. She identifies areas of osteochondritis desiccans. She inserts additional instruments to debride the base of these lesions. She drills holes in the damaged cartilage to encourage new growth. She inserts bone graft material. If necessary, she inserts screws to secure the cartilage to the bone. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Bone grafting: Surgical procedure that replaces missing bones with material from the patient's own body, or from an artificial, synthetic, or natural substitute. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Lesion: Area of damaged or diseased tissue. Osteochondritis dissecans: A joint condition in which the cartilage layer separates from the end of the bone, following an injury. short_description: Arthroscopically aided anterior cruciate ligament repair/augmentation or reconstruction
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the knee joint with an arthroscope. She identifies and repairs a tear in the anterior cruciate ligament and repairs it with tissue taken from elsewhere in the knee or, if necessary, from a donor source. The procedure relieves pain and improves mobility in the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution to inflate the area around the knee joint and improve her field of view. She identifies the tear in the anterior cruciate ligament. She inserts additional instruments and repairs the ligament by first harvesting tissue from a tendon in the knee. Alternatively, she uses donor graft. She then applies the tissue graft, augmenting the anterior cruciate ligament and completing the repair. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue that is strong but flexible; it is found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Donor graft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called homograft, allogeneic graft, and allograft. Internal fixation: The use of hardware, such as plates, screws, nails, and wires, to stabilize a fracture, in an open surgical procedure. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. short_description: Arthroscopically aided posterior cruciate ligament repair/augmentation or reconstruction
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the knee joint with an arthroscope. She identifies and repairs a tear in the posterior cruciate ligament and repairs it with tissue taken from elsewhere in the knee or, if necessary, from a donor source. The procedure relieves pain and improves mobility in the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the knee area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the knee joint. She instills saline solution to inflate the area around the knee joint and improve her field of view. She identifies the tear in the posterior cruciate ligament. She inserts additional instruments and repairs the ligament by first harvesting tissue from another tendon in the knee. Alternatively, she uses donor graft. She then applies the tissue graft, augmenting the posterior cruciate ligament and completing the repair. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. short_description: Arthroscopy, ankle, surgical, excision of osteochondral defect of talus and/or tibia, including drilling of the defect
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the ankle joint with an arthroscope. She identifies and repairs a defect in the cartilage covering the bony surfaces of the talus, or ankle bone, and or the tibia, one of the bones of the lower leg. She excises the defect and drills holes in the underlying bony tissue to encourage growth of healthy tissue. The procedure relieves pain and improves mobility in the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the ankle area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions into the ankle joint. She instills saline solution to inflate the area around the ankle joint and improve her field of view. She identifies the osteochondral defect and inserts additional instruments to excise it. She then drills multiple holes in the underlying bone. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Osteochondral: Referring to tissue composed of cartilage covered bone. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Tarsals: Seven bones of the ankle; they connect to the tibia and fibula bones of the leg and to the metatarsal bones in the foot. short_description: Arthroscopically aided repair of large osteochondritis dissecans lesion, talar dome fracture, or tibial plafond fracture, with or without internal fixation (includes arthroscopy)
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the ankle joint with an arthroscope to identify areas of osteochondritis dissecans, where the cartilage separates from underlying bone, with fracturing of the cartilages called the talar dome and tibial plafond. She identifies the area of the osteochondritis desiccans lesion with fracturing of the talar dome or tibial plafond. She repairs these defects and, if necessary, she inserts screws to secure the cartilage to the bone as internal fixation. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. short_description: Endoscopic plantar fasciotomy
lay_term: The provider examines the tissue inside the heel with an endoscope to access the fascia of the plantar surface, or bottom, of the foot. She incises the fascia to relieve pain from plantar fasciitis, a chronic inflammatory condition of the heel, when nonsurgical treatments fail. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes two small incisions on either side of the heel. She inserts an endoscope through one incision to view the structures in the heel. She inserts a small scalpel through the other incision and incises the proximal medial aspect of the plantar fascia. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. short_description: Arthroscopy, ankle (tibiotalar and fibulotalar joints), surgical; with removal of loose body or foreign body
lay_term: The provider examines the inside of the tibiotalar and fibulotalar joints of the ankle with an arthroscope to look for and remove loose or foreign bodies. Loose and foreign bodies, which include things like small pieces of broken cartilage, lead to pain, inflammation, scar tissue formation, adhesions, and restriction of motion of the joint. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes small incisions in the ankle area. She inserts the arthroscope through one of the incisions and instills saline solution to expand the viewing area. She inspects the tibiotalar and fibulotalar joints. She inserts instruments to secure and remove any loose or foreign bodies. The provider then irrigates the area, checks for bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incisions. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery, that form between tissues and organs; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Chondral: Related to cartilage, strong but flexible fibrous connective tissue found on the surface of joints and composes structures like the nose and ear. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Fibulotalar joint: The bony union, or joint, connecting the fibula, one of the bones in the lower leg, and the talus, or ankle bone. Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body, such as shards of metal or a bone fragment. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. Osteochondritis dissecans: A joint condition in which the cartilage layer separates from the end of the bone, following an injury. Saline solution: A sterile solution containing water and sodium chloride, or salt. Tibiotalar joint: The bony union, or joint, connecting the tibia, or shinbone, and the talus, or ankle bone. Arthroscope: A tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera used for viewing the inside of a joint. Articular cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue covering the bony surfaces of a joint. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Surgical endoscopy/arthroscopy always includes a diagnostic endoscopy/arthroscopy. When arthroscopy is performed in conjunction with arthrotomy, add modifier 51. Arthroscopic removal of loose body(ies) or foreign body(ies) (ie, 29819, 29834, 29861, 29874, 29894, 29904) may be reported only when the loose body(ies) or foreign body(ies) is equal to or larger than the diameter of the arthroscopic cannula(s) used for the specific procedure, and can only be removed through a cannula larger than that used for the specific procedure or through a separate incision or through a portal that has been enlarged to allow removal of the loose or foreign body(ies). Section Specific Guideline All services that appear in the Musculoskeletal System section include the application and removal of the first cast, splint, or traction device, when performed. Supplies may be reported separately. If a cast is removed by someone other than the physician or other qualified health care professional who applied the cast, report a cast removal code (29700, 29705, 29710). Subsequent replacement of cast, splint, or strapping (29000-29750) and/or traction device (eg, 20690, 20692) during or after the global period may be reported separately. A cast, splint, or strapping is not considered part of the preoperative care; therefore, the use of modifier 56 for preoperative management only is not applicable. Codes for obtaining autogenous bone grafts, cartilage, tendon, fascia lata grafts or other tissues through separate incisions are to be used only when the graft is not already listed as part of the basic procedure. Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Fracture and dislocation treatment codes appear throughout the Musculoskeletal System section. These codes are categorized by the type of treatment (closed, percutaneous, open) and type of stabilization (fixation, immobilization). There is no coding correlation between the type of fracture/dislocation (eg, open [compound], closed) and the type of treatment (eg, closed, percutaneous, open) provided. For example, a closed fracture may require open treatment. Fracture/Dislocation Treatment Definitions Manipulation: Reduction by the application of manually applied forces or traction to achieve satisfactory alignment of the fracture or dislocation. If satisfactory alignment (reduction) is not maintained and requires subsequent re-reduction of a fracture or dislocation by the same physician or same qualified health care professional, append modifier 76 to the fracture/dislocation treatment code. Traction: The application of a distracting or traction force to the spine or a limb. Skeletal traction includes a wire, pin, screw, or clamp that is attached to (penetrates) bone. Skin traction is the application of force to a limb using strapping or a device that is applied directly to the skin only. Closed treatment: The treatment site is not surgically opened (ie, not exposed to the external environment nor directly visualized). Closed treatment of a fracture/dislocation may be performed without manipulation (eg, application of cast, splint, or strapping), with manipulation, with skeletal traction, and/or with skin traction. Casting, splinting, or strapping used solely to temporarily stabilize the fracture for patient comfort is not considered closed treatment. Percutaneous skeletal fixation: Treatment that is neither open nor closed. In this procedure, the fracture fragments are not visualized, but fixation (eg, pins, screws) is placed across the fracture site, typically with imaging guidance. Open treatment: The site is opened surgically to expose the fracture/dislocation to the external environment for treatment, or the fracture/dislocation is treated through the traumatic wound or an extension thereof or is treated with an intramedullary nail or other internal fixation device placed through a surgical exposure that is remote from the fracture site with or without direct visualization of the fracture site. External fixation: The use of pins and/or wires that penetrate the bone(s) and interconnection devices (eg, clamps, bars, rings) for fracture/dislocation treatment. External fixation may be used for temporary or long-term fracture/dislocation treatment. Uniplanar external fixation places all the pins in approximately the same plane but may also include triangular fixation across a joint. Multiplanar external fixation uses transosseous wires and threaded pins placed in several planes that are held with interconnected stabilizing and/or tensioning rings and/or half rings. External fixation may be used for all types of fracture/dislocation treatment (ie, closed, percutaneous, open). Codes for external fixation are reported separately only when external fixation is not listed in the code descriptor as inherent to the procedure. Reporting Fracture and/or Dislocation Treatment Codes The physician or other qualified health care professional providing fracture/dislocation treatment should report the appropriate fracture/dislocation treatment codes for the service he or she provided. If the person providing the initial treatment will not be providing subsequent treatment, modifier 54 should be appended to the fracture/dislocation treatment codes. If treatment of a fracture as defined above is not performed, report an evaluation and management code. Excision/Resection Soft Tissue Tumors Definitions Excision of subcutaneous soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the simple or marginal resection of tumors confined to subcutaneous tissue below the skin but above the deep fascia. These tumors are usually benign and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on the location and size of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on the physician's judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. For excision of benign lesions of cutaneous origin (eg, sebaceous cyst), see 11400-11446. Excision of fascial or subfascial soft tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of tumors confined to the tissue within or below the deep fascia, but not involving the bone. These tumors are usually benign, are often intramuscular, and are resected without removing a significant amount of surrounding normal tissue. Code selection is based on size and location of the tumor. Code selection is determined by measuring the greatest diameter of the tumor plus that margin required for complete excision of the tumor. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Digital (ie, fingers and toes) subfascial tumors are defined as those tumors involving the tendons, tendon sheaths, or joints of the digit. Tumors which simply abut but do not breach the tendon, tendon sheath, or joint capsule are considered subcutaneous soft tissue tumors. Radical resection of soft connective tissue tumors (including simple or intermediate repair) involves the resection of the tumor with wide margins of normal tissue. Appreciable vessel exploration and/or neuroplasty repair or reconstruction (eg, adjacent tissue transfer[s], flap[s]) should be reported separately. Extensive undermining or other techniques to close a defect created by skin excision may require a complex repair which should be reported separately. Dissection or elevation of tissue planes to permit resection of the tumor is included in the excision. Although these tumors may be confined to a specific layer (eg, subcutaneous, subfascial), radical resection may involve removal of tissue from one or more layers. Radical resection of soft tissue tumors is most commonly used for malignant connective tissue tumors or very aggressive benign connective tissue tumors. The margins refer to the most narrow margin required to adequately excise the tumor, based on individual judgment. The measurement of the tumor plus margin is made at the time of the excision. Explanation The provider performs an arthroscopic procedure in the musculoskeletal system that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Terminology Arthroscopy: Use of tiny camera to view inside of a joint. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis, and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less
